In a tragic incident in Texas, at least nine people have died and over 100 undocumented immigrants may have been transported in a tractor-trailer, according to federal authorities. The trailer was discovered at a Walmart lot in San Antonio after an employee called the police following a request for water from someone inside. Upon investigation, eight bodies and 31 injured individuals were found. A ninth victim later died at a hospital.

This incident is being condemned as a major case of human smuggling, with authorities vowing to pursue and punish those involved. The KFC Double Down Chicken Sandwich has been released, featuring two boneless Original Recipe Filets, bacon, and cheese sandwiched together instead of a traditional bun. The International Criminal Court (ICC) has initiated a preliminary investigation into allegations of crimes against humanity committed by Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte and other officials during the government's anti-drug crackdown. The investigation will focus on events since July 1, 2016, in the context of the "war on drugs" campaign.

A man self-immolated in St. Peter's Square, Vatican City, on December 19th. The incident occurred around 8:30 local time when the 51-year-old man doused himself with gasoline and set himself on fire. Initial attempts to extinguish the flames were made by a Jesuit priest who used his jacket, followed by two police officers who employed a fire extinguisher. The man is currently in critical condition at a hospital, while the first responders are being treated for smoke inhalation and hand injuries. Orexigen Therapeutics Inc.'s stock nearly doubled after winning a U.S. panel recommendation for their prescription diet pill Contrave. The FDA advisers stated that the weight-loss benefits of Contrave outweigh the risks of elevated pulse and blood pressure, and a large study on cardiovascular risk can wait until after approval. The FDA's support for Contrave eases concerns that caused Orexigen shares to drop more than a third this year. The drug, a combination of two approved drugs that target different parts of the brain influencing appetite and cravings, helped twice as many patients lose at least 5% of their weight compared with a placebo after 56 weeks in clinical trials. An Arizona family faced a difficult situation when they encountered a flight delay while trying to reach their loved one's funeral in Tennessee. The family, who were headed to the funeral of Jay W. On Wednesday night, a shooting outside Frederick High School in Maryland occurred during a junior varsity basketball game. Two students were injured and taken to a hospital in Baltimore, though their injuries are not considered life-threatening. Police have not yet identified any suspects or motives for the attack, and the shooter(s) remain at large. The school was closed on Thursday as police searched for evidence and interviewed witnesses, while staff reported to work as usual. Other Frederick County schools remained open. The victims were teenagers but did not attend Frederick High School. Police are investigating possible gang-related motives or connections to rival teams. The school will reopen on Friday.

"Bridge of Spies" is a Cold War drama directed by Steven Spielberg and written by Matt Charman, Joel Coen, and Ethan Coen. The film stars Tom Hanks as James Donovan, a New York insurance lawyer who finds himself drawn into international intrigue when he defends a Soviet spy in court and later negotiates prisoner exchanges during the U-2 spy plane incident of the early 1960s. Mark Rylance plays Rudolf Abel, the Soviet spy at the center of the story. The film is based on a true story and has been praised for its smart writing, strong performances, and atmospheric cinematography, but some critics have found it to be long and tonally wobbly. Overall, "Bridge of Spies" is a complex and thoughtful drama that challenges the audience to trust where it's going and rewards those who stick with it.

The Gilmore Girls follow-up movies have been officially greenlit by Netflix, with six original cast members confirmed to reprise their roles. Leading the return are Alexis Bledel and Lauren Graham as Lorelai and Rory Gilmore, joined by Scott Patterson (Luke), Kelly Bishop (Emily), Sean Gunn (Kirk), and Keiko Agena (Lane). The revival, which is being treated as a farewell season, consists of four 90-minute movies written and directed by Amy Sherman-Palladino and her husband Daniel Palladino. Notable absences include Liza Weil (Paris Gellar) and Yanic Truesdale (Michel Gerard). The exact title and premiere date of the revival are yet to be announced, along with further details about the number of episodes and where it fits in the Gilmore Girls universe.

Two suspected drug-smuggling tunnels linking warehouses in Tijuana and San Diego have been discovered by U.S. and Mexican authorities. The first tunnel, found on Tuesday, was approximately 600 yards long, equipped with lighting, a crude rail system, and wooden trusses. The second tunnel, discovered on Thursday, is more sophisticated, featuring ventilation and a multi-tiered electric rail system. A 73-year-old California woman has been arrested for overseeing the logistics of one passageway. No drugs or other contraband were found in either tunnel or the warehouses on either side of the border. The passages are the sixth and seventh super tunnels found between Tijuana and San Diego since 2010, costing millions of dollars to build.

The G20 summit in Toronto resulted in an agreement among the world's largest economies to cut their annual budget deficits by half by 2013 and stabilize overall debt by 2016. President Obama emphasized the need for continued growth to support the fragile global economic recovery, while acknowledging the importance of fiscal sustainability in the medium term.

The agreement was a compromise between those advocating for immediate deficit reduction, such as Canada's Prime Minister Stephen Harper and Germany, and those favoring a more measured approach, including President Obama and the U.S. The final statement included caveats to ensure that deficit reduction would not harm growth and would be tailored to each country's specific circumstances.

The summit also discussed banking regulations, but could not agree on a proposal for a global bank tax. The leaders reaffirmed a deadline for agreeing on new capital standards for banks by their next meeting in November 2010 in Seoul, South Korea. However, some countries might not implement the standards by 2012 as initially planned.

Overall, the summit reflected a consensus theory for how the world economy needs to change, with heavily indebted Western nations steadily taming government deficits, and surplus-rich nations "rebalancing" to boost local spending and demand. Ivanka Trump used a personal email account to send hundreds of messages discussing official White House business last year, according to reports. The emails were discovered during a review into her correspondence and contained both logistical and potentially sensitive information. While the emails did not contain classified information, some may have been in violation of federal records rules. This situation has raised questions about Ivanka Trump's compliance with email usage policies, as well as comparisons to Hillary Clinton's use of a private email server during her tenure as Secretary of State. The discovery alarmed some advisers to President Trump, who feared that Ivanka Trump's practices bore similarities to Clinton's personal email use, which was a focus of Donald Trump's 2016 campaign against Clinton. Some aides were startled by the volume of Ivanka Trump's personal emails and taken aback by her response when questioned about the practice. The White House has stated that Ivanka Trump occasionally used her private account before being briefed on the rules, but none of her messages contained classified information. The discovery was made as part of a public records lawsuit and was reported by the Washington Post.

The longtime Chief Financial Officer of the Trump Organization, Allen Weisselberg, was granted immunity by federal prosecutors in New York during the course of the Michael Cohen investigation. According to reports, Weisselberg is identified as "Executive 1" in the criminal information filed by prosecutors in the Michael Cohen case. Prosecutors claim that Cohen sent an invoice to Weisselberg for a payment meant to reimburse Cohen for a payment to Stormy Daniels, and Weisselberg later directed another Trump Organization executive to pay from the Trust for this expense. Weisselberg has been working for the Trump Organization since the 1970s and was also treasurer of the Donald J. Trump Foundation. He has been mentioned by Cohen in a recorded phone conversation about a payment to suppress a story about Trump's alleged relationship with Playboy model Karen McDougal. President Trump's former personal attorney, Michael Cohen, pleaded guilty to eight criminal charges on Tuesday.

In response to the death of King Bhumibol Adulyadej in Thailand, authorities have issued warnings to traders against raising prices unfairly for black mourning attire. The Commerce Ministry has deployed teams to survey the market for black clothing and fabric, ensuring that the public is not taken advantage of during the royal mourning period. Traders have been asked to clearly label their prices and not engage in hoarding or unreasonable price increases, with violators facing severe penalties. Despite some price increases, shoppers continue to buy black shirts for the one-year mourning period, with many stating that the higher prices are acceptable given the circumstances.

In Philadelphia, a fatal stabbing occurred among three workers of a cleaning company contracted by Frontier Airlines at Philadelphia International Airport. The incident took place in a break room near Gate E6, which is a secure area. An argument over a break room light escalated into a physical altercation, resulting in one worker being stabbed in the thigh. The victim, 28-year-old Aaron Jenkins, later died at Penn Presbyterian Trauma Center.

The suspect, identified as 35-year-old Kevin Emanuel, and another man involved in the fight fled the scene but were later apprehended by police. The weapon used in the crime is believed to be a box cutter commonly used in their jobs. The incident did not disrupt airport services or endanger travelers. Both Emanuel and the other individual are charged with murder and possession of an instrument of a crime, and it's unclear if they have retained legal counsel.

The article discusses the challenges faced by Afghan army units due to a lack of equipment repair and replacement capabilities. This is causing problems for units across the country, including Hamidullah's battalion, which recently inspected their equipment and found that 75% of their armored vehicles were out of commission. The U.S. military had been responsible for repairing Afghan equipment for years, but as the Afghan army started doing more of the fighting, the Americans stopped repairing Afghan equipment. This has left Afghan commanders struggling to get the gear and parts they need, with some units waiting three years for key parts or for Humvees to be replaced due to bureaucratic inefficiency. Sen. Marco Rubio (R-FL) and Florida Lt. Gov. Carlos Lopez-Cantera had a conversation about politics following the Orlando massacre, with Lopez-Cantera urging Rubio to reconsider running for his Senate seat. Rubio has been resisting pressure from Senate leaders and donors to rethink retiring from the Senate, but Lopez-Cantera's conversation removed one of the biggest obstacles to Rubio running again: their longtime friendship. The Jefferson County judge has dismissed the capital murder charge against Gabe Watson in the death of his wife, Tina, during their honeymoon scuba diving trip in Australia in 2003. Judge Tommy Nail stated that there was no evidence to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Watson intentionally killed Tina for monetary gain. The courtroom erupted in cheers from Watson's supporters, and Watson walked out of the courthouse after the ruling. The Thomas family left without commenting. The dismissal came before the defense even presented its case, and it marked an unusual ruling in a two-week trial. Gabe Watson faced life in prison without parole if convicted.

The convention also includes a roll call to officially nominate Obama and Vice President Biden for a second term, and the arrival of President Obama himself.

The study, published in Computers in Human Behavior, investigated the influence of media (email and voicemail) and task type (romantic and utilitarian) on psychophysiological responses of senders and message content. Results showed that individuals sending romantic emails were more emotionally aroused and used stronger, more thoughtful language than those leaving voicemails. This was due to the ability for senders to modify email content during composition, which is not possible with voicemail recordings. The study also found that the medium used can shape message content, with senders of utilitarian messages sending less positive emails than voicemails, while those composing romantic messages included more positive and arousing emotional content in emails and less in voicemails. Contrary to media naturalness theory, the researchers found that email's been in popular use since the 1990s and has become less unnatural for millennials, who have grown up with it. The study was conducted by placing skin sensors on subjects' faces and feet to measure emotional responses and arousal levels.

The discovery was made through DNA tests from the genealogy website 23andMe. The women are now considering themselves new friends and plan to meet more of their extended families at a reunion later this month.

In a statement, Tesla has provided updates regarding the fatal crash of a Model X on March 23rd in Mountain View, California. The driver, Walter Huang, was an Apple engineer who reportedly complained about the car's Autopilot veering towards the same barrier multiple times before the accident.

According to Tesla, Autopilot was engaged with adaptive cruise control follow-distance set to minimum in the moments leading up to the collision at 9:27 a.m. The driver had received several visual and one audible hands-on warning earlier in the drive, but their hands were not detected on the wheel for six seconds prior to the crash.

The severity of the accident is attributed to a highway safety barrier, known as a crash attenuator, which was crushed in a previous accident without being replaced. Tesla claims they have never seen this level of damage to a Model X in any other crash.

Tesla's data shows that Tesla owners have driven this same stretch of highway with Autopilot engaged roughly 85,000 times since its introduction in 2015. The company maintains that Autopilot makes the world safer for vehicle occupants, pedestrians, and cyclists.

On March 18, 2014, a shooting incident occurred at the Excalibur Hotel and Casino in Las Vegas. A suspect, initially identified as "John Doe," was later identified as Joey Kadmiri, was arrested after a struggle with performers from an all-male dance revue called Thunder From Down Under. The suspect had entered the locker room and stolen property belonging to the dancers.

During the altercation, the suspect pulled out a .44 Magnum handgun and pointed it at a dancer's head, but was subdued by the performers before any shots were fired. One of the dancers was injured during the struggle but was treated and released. The suspect suffered injuries during the physical confrontation and was later hospitalized for treatment.

The suspect was booked into Clark County Detention Center on charges of attempted murder with a deadly weapon, attempted robbery with a deadly weapon, and burglary with a deadly weapon. The show at Excalibur remained on schedule for the following day. The incident serves as an example of the performers' quick thinking and bravery in thwarting the gunman.

Historian Fletcher Crowe, an alumnus of Florida State University (FSU), and Anita Spring, a professor emeritus of anthropology at the University of Florida, announced that Fort Caroline is not located near Jacksonville, Florida, as previously thought, but on Rhetts Island, southeast of Darien, Georgia. The fort was long believed to be located east of downtown Jacksonville, Fla., on the south bank of the St. Johns River, with the Fort Caroline National Memorial situated just east of Jacksonville’s Dames Point Bridge.

Crowe and Spring made their announcement at "La Floride Française: Florida, France, and the Francophone World," a conference hosted by FSU’s Winthrop-King Institute for Contemporary French and Francophone Studies and its Institute on Napoleon and the French Revolution. The researchers say they found evidence in 16th-century maps at the Bibliothèque Nationale de France, including some in Latin, Spanish, and English, that pinpointed the location of Fort Caroline.

Jonathan Pollard, a notorious spy for Israel who was sentenced to life in prison in 1987 for spying on behalf of Israel, has been granted parole after serving 30 years. The United States Parole Commission announced that Pollard, now 60, met the legal standards and will be released just before Thanksgiving, on November 20. His lawyers, Eliot Lauer and Jacques Semmelman, have been working pro bono for his release for the past 15 years.

Pollard's release could potentially ease tensions between the United States and Israel, particularly in relation to the Iran nuclear deal, which has been a point of contention between President Barack Obama and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. However, the White House has denied that Pollard's release is connected to the Iran deal. The Justice Department also confirmed Pollard's release date on Tuesday.

The 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi, Russia are underway with a focus on several notable athletes to watch. Mikaela Shiffrin, an 18-year-old alpine skier, is expected to be the heir apparent to Lindsey Vonn and has already won a gold medal at the world championships in slalom. Shaun White, a snowboarder known for his daring stunts and multiple Olympic medals, withdrew from the inaugural Olympic slopestyle competition due to safety concerns over the course's height and difficulty. Other athletes to watch include figure skaters, female ski jumpers, and participants in new events such as team figure skating and women's moguls. However, there have been concerns about the safety of some events, particularly slopestyle snowboarding, due to injuries sustained by several competitors during training sessions. Additionally, security measures for the games have been a topic of discussion, with Russian officials assuring that they are taking all necessary precautions to ensure safety.

A DVD containing a brutal double beheading was sent to American professional gambler RJ Cipriani and his wife Greice Santo by Owen Hanson, a California man who had previously sent them threats for not paying a $2.5m debt. Hanson, who had connections to Mexican and South American drug cartels, pleaded guilty to racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to distribute drugs and was sentenced to 21 years and three months in prison. The debt originated from money Cipriani lost on VIP blackjack tables in Sydney's The Star casino in 2011, which had been purposefully lost after realizing he was being set up to launder Hanson's cocaine profits. Hanson had smuggled hundreds of kilograms of cocaine into Australia through connections in Mexico and Peru, selling a kilogram for $230,000 in Australia compared to $20,000 in Los Angeles. RJ Cipriani, who also goes by the name Robin Hood 702, was able to avoid prosecution for laundering the money through The Star casino.

President Donald Trump called the acting director of the National Park Service on Saturday to complain about a retweet from the agency's account that compared his inaugural crowd size unfavorably with Barack Obama's in 2009. The call was confirmed by White House deputy press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who said Trump took action to fix the issue. Trump also reportedly ordered the acting director to produce additional photographs of the inauguration to prove that media reports of low attendance were false. This incident is part of a larger battle between the new administration and some career government employees over public communications, with the National Park Service becoming an unlikely protagonist in this dispute.

Archaeologists from the University of Leicester discovered two 1,000-year-old skeletons holding hands at the Chapel of St Morrell in Hallaton, England. The dig, led by archaeologist Vicky Score, has been ongoing for four years and has uncovered a total of 11 skeletons dated to the 14th century. The pair of skeletons are believed to be of similar age and have been removed for further investigation.

The chapel is an ancient site of pilgrimage and may have served as a special place of burial during that time. Other findings include fragments of stone, wall plaster, led from the windows, silver pennies dating between the 12th and 16th centuries, and remains of a previous Roman building beneath the chapel.

Among the other skeletons found was an older male who was killed by a sharp implement to the head, possibly a pole axe, and a young male buried in a pit with his legs raised to his chest, which archaeologists believe may have been the result of a disease.

The discovery of the medieval chapel and its previous Roman building suggests that the hilltop has been a special place for over 2,000 years. The site is believed to have been used as a place of pilgrimage and healing in the past.

The White House Honey Brown Ale, believed to be the first beer brewed on the White House grounds, has been released. President Barack Obama had been discussing the beer for weeks but refused to disclose details until now. The recipe includes light malt extract, amber crystal malt, honey, gypsum, yeast, and corn sugar. The beer was brewed by White House chef Sam Kass in the White House kitchen. A 4-year-old cancer patient named Jillian Massey from Coopersburg, who was previously hospitalized in Philadelphia for brain cancer, has initiated a charitable drive to collect gifts for her hospital friends she left behind. What started as a wish for 50 presents has grown exponentially, reaching over 3,000 toys intended for patients at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. Jillian's mother created an Amazon wish list to help gather the gifts, and her colleagues from a homebuilding company have been instrumental in promoting it. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a significant milestone in human rights history, proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly on December 10, 1948. Drafted by representatives from various legal and cultural backgrounds worldwide, the UDHR sets out fundamental human rights that should be universally protected. It has been translated into over 500 languages.

The Declaration emphasizes the inherent dignity and equal rights of all individuals, regardless of race, color, sex, religion, or nationality. It includes articles on life, liberty, security, freedom from slavery and torture, privacy, freedom of movement, property rights, thought, expression, assembly, association, education, and social security. The UDHR also highlights the importance of equality in marriage, work, and public service, as well as the right to rest, leisure, and a standard of living adequate for health and well-being.

Title: Feeling Younger May Lower Mortality Rates, According to New Research

Summary: A study published in JAMA Internal Medicine suggests that feeling younger than one's actual age could have health benefits, as it is associated with a lower death rate among older adults. The research found that participants who felt 3 or more years younger had a mortality rate of 14.3%, compared to 18% for those whose self-perceived age was close to their actual age and 24.6% for those who felt older than their actual age. The study also identified social experiences that can affect self-perceived age, such as role transitions, stress, and health problems. Further research is needed to validate these findings and investigate the mechanisms underlying the association between self-perceived age and mortality rates.

1. Feeling younger than one's actual age may be associated with a lower death rate among older adults.

The family, including Steve Esmond, his wife Theresa Devine, and their two teenage sons, were staying at the resort when they began having seizures on March 20. They were airlifted to hospitals on the mainland, with the sons currently in critical condition. The EPA is investigating the use of the pesticide methyl bromide at the resort, which is prohibited for residential use and has been linked to the family's illness. The Justice Department is also investigating the company responsible for applying the pesticide, Terminix. The EPA has confirmed that methyl bromide was used in the complex and is continuing to investigate the details of the family's exposure. The resort management company, Sea Glass Vacations LLC, has terminated its contract with Terminix and the unit under investigation is currently unoccupied. The EPA is working to ensure that such an incident does not happen again.

The 5th Circuit Court of Appeals has upheld key parts of Texas' strict anti-abortion law, which could leave as few as seven abortion clinics in Texas. This decision enforces hospital-like structural requirements for abortion clinics, including specific room and doorway sizes, air sterilization systems, backup generators, and blood supplies on hand. These requirements are controversial, with abortion providers arguing they are unnecessary and will force many clinics to close.

Before the law passed in 2013, there were 40 abortion clinics in Texas, but now there are only 17, with seven meeting the new building standards. The remaining clinics are primarily located in major cities like Austin, Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth, and San Antonio.

The court made an exception for one clinic, Whole Woman's Health in McAllen, which won't be required to meet all building requirements or gain admitting privileges for one doctor. However, the remaining restrictions could make it impractical for some clinics to remain open, particularly those in smaller cities like El Paso, where the closest abortion provider would require a 1,200-mile round trip to San Antonio or crossing the border into New Mexico.

The ruling was made by a three-judge panel and is the latest decision in a lawsuit challenging some of the toughest abortion restrictions in the country. The case

Russia has appointed actor Steven Seagal as a "special representative" to promote US-Russia relations in the humanitarian sphere, including collaboration in culture and youth exchanges. This unpaid role is similar to United Nations' goodwill ambassador positions. Seagal, who became a Russian citizen in 2016 and is a close friend of Russian President Vladimir Putin, has been an ardent supporter of Putin and has defended his government against allegations of election meddling in the US.

In a separate development, during a visit to Tunisia, Russia's Minister Youssef Chahed discussed plans to strengthen trade, economic, and investment cooperation with Tunisian Prime Minister Y. Shahed. The Russian Federation proposed a program for trade, economic, and scientific cooperation between the two countries for 2019-2021, which was agreed upon by the Tunisian Prime Minister to be expedited for approval at an upcoming meeting. Additionally, they discussed accelerating the ratification of previously signed agreements on nuclear energy cooperation and other projects related to visa facilitation, automotive transportation, and environmental protection. The Tunisian side expressed interest in involving Russian companies, particularly those specializing in construction of automobile and rail infrastructure, in relevant tenders.

The meeting also highlighted the development of cooperation between Tunisia and Russian regions, specifically between Tunisia and Tatarstan,

A 59-year-old man named James Zordel from Russell, Kansas, died after colliding with a black cow on his motorcycle late Friday night. The accident occurred on a paved rural road about six miles south of Interstate 70 near Russell. There were no witnesses and it's unclear if the cow suddenly appeared or if Zordel was speeding. The Kansas Highway Patrol reported that Zordel, who wasn't wearing a helmet, died at the scene. The incident is recorded in Kansas Highway Patrol crash logs.

Bill and Kris Bresnan, a couple from Toms River, New Jersey, have been married for nearly 40 years. During their marriage, Bill has written over 10,000 love letters to Kris - one each night of their marriage. Their unique love story began when they met in a classroom in 1974 and continued to grow as they commuted together on the Long Island Railroad. The couple shares their secrets to happiness, including never going to bed angry, doing things together, and expressing love daily through notes, cards, and small gestures. They have organized their collection of love letters into a "love diary" and continue to add to it every day.

Amanda Longacre, the former Miss Delaware who was stripped of her title for being too old, has filed a class action lawsuit against state pageant officials and the Miss America organization seeking to be reinstated and $3 million in damages. The lawsuit alleges that Longacre and other contestants were recruited to compete before being told they were too old, and claims that pageant officials knowingly recruit ineligible contestants to boost participation and take advantage of them for fundraising and appearances. Longacre is seeking the full year's reign in Delaware, restoration of her scholarships, an age waiver to compete for Miss America, and $500,000 in damages for herself. The Miss America Organization has said that the lawsuit has no merit and they will vigorously defend it.

The Arcade Fire's interactive music project, "The Wilderness Downtown," is a unique and immersive experience that allows users to create a personalized, interactive music video for their single "We Used to Wait." By entering the address of the home they grew up in, users can navigate through windows displaying various visual elements such as videos, vector animations, satellite shots, and even postcard writing to their younger selves. The project, directed by Chris Milk, utilizes HTML 5 and is optimized for Chrome, offering a blend of video, interactive content, and traditional web elements. This innovative approach to music videos could potentially revolutionize the industry, moving from television to the internet, taking advantage of the web's capabilities while incorporating Google Maps data for a nostalgic touch. The project has been well-received, with users expressing feelings of nostalgia upon seeing their old neighborhoods.

In this summary, eight members of the Rhoden family were killed in rural Ohio in what authorities are calling a carefully planned and "sophisticated operation." The investigation is ongoing, with more than 200 law enforcement officials involved. Autopsy results show that most victims were shot multiple times, some as many as nine, and some had bruising indicating a struggle. Marijuana-growing operations were found at three of the four crime scenes, and investigators are considering the possibility of a Mexican drug cartel being involved. No motive or suspects have been identified yet. Funeral arrangements for the victims have not been announced.

Google has launched a new service aimed at wedding planning, offering consumers the ability to create a wedding website, edit photos, and plan their wedding using templates on Google Sites, Docs, and Picnik. The company partnered with wedding planner Michelle Rago for the templates and tips, and is hosting a wedding sweepstakes with a $25,000 prize and the chance to have Rago help plan the winning couple's wedding. This latest move by Google is part of their efforts to integrate themselves into consumers' lifestyles, following the launch of Google Health in 2008. However, concerns about privacy have been raised in the past regarding Google's access to sensitive personal information. Michelle Rago, a renowned wedding planner and destination expert, provides tips for planning the perfect wedding, whether it takes place on the beaches of Bali or in one's parents' backyard.

MasterCard has announced plans to introduce biometric security checks for online payments, allowing customers to verify their identity using selfies and fingerprints instead of passwords. The new system, which will be rolled out this summer in multiple countries including the UK, US, and Netherlands, aims to make online transactions more secure and user-friendly by replacing traditional passwords with biometric authentication. MasterCard's safety and security division chief Ajay Bhalla stated that consumers dislike passwords due to their lack of security and convenience, and that biometrics offer a more modern and effective solution. The new system will require users to download an application on their PC, tablet, or smartphone, and will involve blinking into the camera during selfie verification to prevent fraudulent use of photos. MasterCard insists that its other security mechanisms will be able to detect suspicious behavior and prevent interception of biometric data. The company is not alone in experimenting with facial scans as authentication tools; China's e-commerce giant Alibaba has also demoed a pay-with-your-face system, while Microsoft's Windows 10 and Google's Android operating systems already allow users to unlock devices using facial recognition. Security researchers have raised concerns about the potential for biometric checks to be compromised, but MasterCard maintains that its other security measures will prevent or detect such behavior. The new system is expected to help reduce fraud levels and potentially lower costs for merchants

In a town hall event in Rochester, New Hampshire, Donald Trump faced criticism for failing to correct an audience member who claimed President Obama is Muslim and suggested getting rid of Muslims. The comment sparked immediate backlash from advocacy groups, members of Trump's own party, and Democratic presidential candidates. White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest condemned the remarks, while Hillary Clinton called them "just plain wrong" and "hateful." Republican candidate Chris Christie criticized Trump for not correcting the questioner and argued that leaders have a responsibility to clarify misinformation. The incident recalls Trump's 2011 quest to challenge Obama's birthplace, which ended with Obama releasing his long-form birth certificate. A recent CNN/ORC poll found that 29% of Americans believe Obama is Muslim, including 43% of Republicans. Trump has been one of the leading skeptics of Obama's birthplace and recently said he did not know where Obama was born. The incident follows a debate performance that garnered mixed reviews for Trump.

Ricky Gervais returned as host for the 73rd annual Golden Globes and did not disappoint in his bluntly sarcastic and offensive monologue. He mocked several Hollywood stars including Sean Penn, Caitlyn Jenner, Roman Polanski, Jennifer Lawrence, Jeffrey Tambor, Ben Affleck, and Mel Gibson. Gervais's jokes included mocking the Hollywood Foreign Press for deeming The Martian a comedy, joking about Jennifer Lawrence demanding equal pay in Hollywood, and making offensive comments about Mel Gibson that were bleeped by NBC. Before the ceremony, Gervais tweeted a shirtless photo of himself with a profane message warning that he would offend Hollywood on Sunday night. This was Ricky Gervais's fourth time hosting the Golden Globes, and he is known for his dark sense of humor and controversial jokes involving celebrities in the audience.

A Pembroke Pines Police Officer, Sgt. Jennifer Martin, was allegedly denied service at an Arby's restaurant due to her occupation as a police officer. The manager of the restaurant claims it was a misunderstanding and a bad attempt at humor. However, the incident has sparked controversy and a boycott of the fast-food chain by law enforcement officers and their families. The CEO of Arby's has apologized to the Pembroke Pines Police Department and offered free meals to uniformed cops in South Florida as a gesture of goodwill. The employee involved in the incident was fired, while another was suspended. The police union is calling for the employee who refused service to be terminated and for a national boycott of Arby's until corrective action is taken. The incident has also led to an outpouring of support from competitors such as McDonald's, Whole Foods, and Dunkin' Donuts.

Speaker John Boehner has reiterated his stance that President Barack Obama must accept entitlement cuts and no tax increases in order for Congress to approve a debt-ceiling increase, as negotiations between the GOP and Democratic leaders continue at the White House to prevent a U.S. debt default. Boehner's comments come after Obama praised him for exploring a "grand bargain" that would involve cuts to popular entitlement programs like Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security in exchange for up to $1 trillion in new revenue. However, Boehner pulled out of talks with Obama over the weekend due to criticism from conservative lawmakers and activists.

Boehner emphasized that the disagreements between the two parties are primarily about policy, not process or personalities. He stated that he and the president disagree on the need for more revenues through taxes on job creators and the extent of entitlement reform required to solve the problem. Boehner insists that a debt-limit increase bill cannot include tax increases and must be accompanied by spending cuts larger than the increase in the debt limit, as well as restrictions on future spending.

Boehner also called for the passage of a balanced-budget amendment, which will be considered by the House next week. He emphasized that any deal to raise the borrowing limit must involve significant tax reform and serious changes to entitlement

During a hearing at the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, Representative Mo Brooks (R-Ala.) questioned Philip Duffy, president of Woods Hole Research Center, about the reasons for rising sea levels. Duffy attributed the rise primarily to melting surface ice, with Antarctica contributing significantly. Brooks suggested other factors such as ground subsidence, erosion due to silt deposition by rivers like the Mississippi and Nile, and cliff collapses displacing water. However, Duffy stated that on human timescales, these effects are minuscule compared to the impact of climate change. Brooks also disputed the notion that global warming is causing sea levels to increase, citing his local NASA base as evidence for Antarctic ice growth. The hearing highlighted ongoing debates about climate change and its causes.

The document discusses ongoing negotiations between Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, the White House, and Democratic leaders regarding a debt ceiling deal. After significant progress in talks between McConnell and Vice President Biden on Saturday night, both sides agreed to postpone a partisan-tinged cloture vote to give time for a compromise. The biggest outstanding issues are Republican insistence on deficit reductions without new tax revenues and the enforcement mechanism for a joint House-Senate committee to achieve estimated $1.6 trillion in savings by the end of this year. Democrats are concerned that their priorities, such as more revenues and fewer Medicare savings, may be compromised in the process. The vote on the debt ceiling measure was 246-173 in the House, but it has yet to be voted on in the Senate. The negotiations could set the stage for a compromise just three days before the Treasury says it will be unable to pay all the nation's bills.

The document discusses a potential significant increase in cigarette prices in New Zealand as part of efforts to make the country smoke-free by 2025. The most extreme pricing scenario suggests a packet of cigarettes could cost up to $100 NZD (approximately £50) by 2020, achieved through an immediate shock increase followed by annual increases of 30%. However, this model is considered "probably unrealistic."

The Prime Minister, John Key, has expressed concerns that such drastic price hikes could fuel a black market for cigarettes. Associate Health Minister Tariana Turia has taken a firm stance, stating her willingness to take whatever measures are necessary to achieve the smoke-free goal.

Other proposals in the document include regulating tobacco as a highly toxic substance, banning smoking in cars with children, increasing anti-smoking media campaigns, and removing tobacco from duty-free sale. It's important to note that this briefing paper is an internal policy discussion and does not represent government policy at this time.

The PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) has taken full responsibility for the Best Picture mix-up at the 89th Academy Awards, where La La Land was initially announced as the winner instead of Moonlight. PwC partner Brian Cullinan accidentally handed presenters Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway the envelope containing the winner of Best Actress, which was intended for Emma Stone. The error was not corrected quickly enough, leading to confusion on stage and multiple speeches by La La Land's creators before the mistake was rectified. PwC has expressed remorse for those affected by the mix-up, including Beatty, Dunaway, host Jimmy Kimmel, and the casts of both films. The accounting firm is reviewing its protocols and may implement changes such as stationing two auditors at each stage entrance to prevent similar errors in the future. Cullinan's tweet about Emma Stone just before the error occurred has also come under scrutiny.

A music fan named Craig Mandell has launched a crowdfunding campaign titled "Don’t Let Nickel Back" to prevent the Canadian band from performing in London, inspired by a similar successful effort that brought Foo Fighters to Virginia. The campaign aims to discourage Nickelback through emails, with each $1 donation resulting in one email sent to the band's management. The severity of the message depends on the amount donated, ranging from polite requests to more forceful messages or even attached mp3s of Nickelback's music. Mandell states that all proceeds will go to charity or therapy for those affected by the band. Meanwhile, a separate crowdfunding campaign to bring Foo Fighters to Cornwall has already reached its £150,000 target but still needs to secure the band's agreement to play a show in the English county.

The film "True Grit," directed by Joel and Ethan Coen, is a Western drama based on Charles Portis' 1968 novel. The story follows a 14-year-old girl named Mattie Ross who hires a one-eyed marshal named Rooster Cogburn to help her find the killer of her father. Mattie and Rooster are joined by a Texas Ranger named La Boeuf, and their journey leads them into dangerous territory filled with violence and corruption. The film stars Jeff Bridges as Rooster Cogburn, Hailee Steinfeld as Mattie Ross, Matt Damon as La Boeuf, Josh Brolin as the killer Tom Chaney, and Barry Pepper as a scarred thug named Lucky Ned. The Coen brothers have adapted the film faithfully from the novel and have created a beautifully shot, entertaining Western that showcases the quirks of the genre while maintaining a tight narrative structure. Jeff Bridges delivers a nuanced performance as Rooster Cogburn, earning affection for his character despite his tough exterior. The film received positive reviews for its acting, direction, and faithfulness to the source material.

Rhonda Thill, a St. Paul woman, lost her husband Randy Thill in a motorcycle accident three weeks ago. Despite losing his wedding ring after the accident, she was determined to find it. A group of bikers from Los Valientes and Sober Soldiers motorcycle clubs helped search for the ring at the scene of the accident on U.S. 61 in St. Paul. Jay Stevens, vice president of Sober Soldiers, found the ring in the median grass behind a weed. The group returned the ring to Rhonda Thill, who was overwhelmed with gratitude for their efforts. A benefit event, "Riding with Randy -- Benefit and Poker Run," is being held on September 5th at St. Paul Saloon to raise funds for the family.

The story is about a family, the Bracamontes, who hired a live-in nanny named Diane Stretton for their three children in Upland, California. After several weeks, the family claimed that Stretton stopped working and refused to leave her room after being fired on June 6. Stretton has since agreed to move out by July 4 under certain conditions but the Bracamontes are concerned she might try to barricade herself in her room when they are out of town for a family wedding on that date. The case has raised questions about the eviction process and landlord/tenant laws, as Stretton was given a room as part of the employment agreement. It is also revealed that Stretton has a history of litigation, including multiple cases in Southern California counties dating back to 2002.

On June 8, 2018, a federal judge temporarily blocked the deportation of Pablo Villavicencio, an Ecuadorean restaurant worker who was arrested while making a delivery to a Brooklyn Army base in New York. The Legal Aid Society obtained the temporary stay for Villavicencio after a hearing in Manhattan federal court. Villavicencio, who has no criminal record, was arrested on June 1 while making a delivery to Fort Hamilton. He had been ordered to leave the United States in 2010 but stayed. The judge granted the stay until July 20, and Villavicencio will remain in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody in New Jersey until his case goes to court. Governor Andrew Cuomo of New York has called for an investigation into the case, stating that recent detentions raise significant legal questions. The attorneys plan to work with Villavicencio to help him secure valid immigration status.

The article discusses the new Showtime series "The Big C," starring Laura Linney as a high school teacher diagnosed with Stage IV melanoma. The show is framed as a comedy, but critics find that it often falls short of being funny and instead comes across as overly zany and unnatural. Linney's character, Cathy, is portrayed as a formerly reserved woman who suddenly begins to speak her mind and live each day as if it were her last. The show also features a strong cast including Oliver Platt, John Benjamin Hickey, Phyllis Somerville, Gabriel Basso, and Gabourey Sidibe. However, the critics find that some of the other characters are not as well-developed and the overall tone of the show is uneven, with heavy scenes that feel poorly timed and directed. The article concludes by noting that "The Big C" could have been a great show, but ultimately falls short due to its inconsistent tone and character development.

A shootout occurred early Wednesday morning at a mobile home in Meigs County, Tennessee, resulting in the death of Timothy Dewayne Johnson, 52, and the hospitalization of his nephew Larry Eugene Johnson Jr., 28. The incident appears to have been over a prized pet fighting rooster named "Bubba."

Timothy Johnson was found dead in the driveway with apparent gunshot wounds, while Larry Johnson was inside the trailer with a gunshot wound to his chest. According to reports, Timothy Johnson had confronted his nephew about the alleged theft of the gamecock.

Larry Johnson told a bystander that his uncle had drawn a gun and that he was trying to grab it when he was shot. Larry Johnson then fired multiple times with a semi-automatic handgun, while Timothy Johnson fired a single-action .38-caliber revolver.

The district attorney's office is awaiting the conclusion of an autopsy and toxicology results before presenting the case to the Meigs County grand jury, which next meets in November. Both families have expressed regret over the incident and maintain that the two men had a good relationship prior to this event.

The story highlights the case of Kendrick Johnson, a 17-year-old who was found dead in a rolled-up gym mat at Lowndes County High School in January. His death was initially ruled accidental by state medical examiners, who concluded that he suffocated after getting stuck while reaching for a sneaker. However, his parents never accepted this explanation and commissioned a second autopsy in June.

During the second autopsy, it was discovered that Kendrick's internal organs were missing from his body. The organs had been replaced with newspaper before burial, which added to the family's skepticism of the official findings. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation and Harrington Funeral Home, who had custody of Kendrick's body after his death, have given conflicting accounts regarding the handling of the organs.

A former FBI agent, Harold Copus, has questioned how Kendrick died based on death scene imagery obtained by CNN. The U.S. Justice Department initially declined to open a civil rights investigation into the case, but federal prosecutors in south Georgia are now considering opening their own probe. Kendrick's parents believe that he did not die accidentally and have been pushing for answers.

President Barack Obama called for daily meetings with House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to reach a budget deal and prevent a government shutdown by the end of the week. The meeting on Tuesday was unsuccessful, leading to Obama's demand for continued discussions. Both sides remain far apart in their negotiations, with Republicans pushing for deeper spending cuts and Democrats accusing them of attaching social policy agendas to the spending bill. A one-week extension plan proposed by Boehner could reassure conservative lawmakers but has not resolved the impasse over policy riders. The White House and government agencies have begun preparing for a potential shutdown.

In summary, President Donald Trump's tweet about the London subway attack drew criticism from British officials, including Prime Minister Theresa May, who found his comments unhelpful. Trump suggested that the individuals responsible for the attack were "in the sights of Scotland Yard" and should have been dealt with more proactively. This comment was met with rebukes from UK officials, as it implied that law enforcement had failed to act appropriately. The incident has strained the special relationship between the US and UK, potentially affecting intelligence sharing arrangements. Trump later called May to express his sympathies and pledged continued collaboration in the fight against terrorism.

The Great Recession significantly impacted the retirement plans of many Americans, with approximately 40% of people aged 45 and over pushing back their retirement plans. This could have wide-ranging effects on Social Security, financial markets, and future workforce demographics. A large portion of those with incomes under $25,000 reported having no retirement savings or pension, contrasting with only 10% of those earning $100,000 or more.

The survey also revealed that one-fourth of respondents are unsure about their retirement plans, which is a concerning sign as many Americans are becoming responsible for their own retirement planning. Among those aged 55 to 64 who had not yet retired, only 18% plan to follow the traditional retirement model, with many expecting to keep working as long as possible or take on part-time jobs instead.

The Federal Reserve's report also highlighted that a quarter of families are "just getting by" or struggling to make ends meet more than five years after the end of the Great Recession. Retirement, education, and jobs were identified as Americans' biggest financial concerns. The survey found that wage growth has been soft throughout the recovery, straining household budgets and dampening consumer spending.

Ariel Winter, the 19-year-old star of "Modern Family," is known for her bold and confident presence on social media, often posting scantily clad photos with a carefree attitude towards criticism. However, during an appearance on Conan, she used a baby voice that was met with criticism from fans and the media. In an interview with Elite Daily, Winter discussed her social media posts and stated that she doesn't let trolls and haters affect her self-confidence. Recently, Winter also faced backlash for wearing a revealing dress to a "Modern Family" event, but she responded by defending her choice on Instagram, stating that people should be allowed to express themselves as they please.

Japanese author Haruki Murakami, known for his surrealist novels and reclusive nature, will answer questions from readers on his own website from January 15 to 31, 2021. The responses will be published until the end of March on a special page called "Murakami's Place" on the company's website. Murakami is a bestselling author whose books have been translated into over 50 languages and feature characters bonding through pain. He is also a passionate runner, fan of cats, and devout supporter of Tokyo's Yakult Swallows baseball team. The questions can be about literature, his likes and dislikes, or any other topic that piques his interest. This is a rare opportunity for Murakami's legions of fans to communicate directly with the author who spends much of his time hiding from the media.

The initial bombing raids on Islamic State targets in Syria mark a significant offensive against the terrorists who have threatened U.S. interests and security at home, following their beheadings of two American journalists. President Obama has promised a long-term campaign to "degrade and ultimately destroy" Islamic State, with air strikes also targeting the Khorasan Group, an Al Qaeda offshoot. However, questions arise about the U.S.'s plans for a prolonged air campaign in Syria, given that the country's leadership did not invite intervention. The U.S.'s change of mind about intervention in Syria is due to the swift sequence of events involving Islamic State in Iraq and the threat they pose.

The prospect of U.S. military advisors accompanying Iraqi troops into battle is troubling, as there are concerns about the clarity of the U.S.'s strategy and achievable aims in Syria and Iraq. While Islamic State is a heinous group and a threat to U.S. interests, it remains unclear whether the threat justifies an ever-escalating role for the U.S. military in both countries.

In a death penalty case, the Supreme Court declined to intervene in the conviction and sentence of Ronald Mikos, a foot doctor who was accused of murdering a disabled nurse to prevent her from testifying against him in a Medicare fraud trial. Mikos did not testify during his trial, and prosecutors argued that his silence showed a lack of remorse. The 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the sentence, and the case is now awaiting execution in federal prison.

In a separate development, federal prosecutors announced they will seek the death penalty for Brendt Christensen, a former University of Illinois graduate student accused of kidnapping, torturing, and killing a visiting scholar from China in June 2017. Prosecutors allege that Christensen has claimed "additional victims" and expressed a desire to be known as a killer. The decision to seek the death penalty requires the approval of U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions, and it is expected to delay the trial for months.

The last person to be sentenced to death in a federal courtroom in Illinois was Dr. Ronald Mikos, who is still awaiting execution in federal prison in Terre Haute, Ind. The article discusses an ongoing investigation by the U.S. Justice Department into allegations of bribery in Wal-Mart's Mexican subsidiary, Walmart de Mexico. The investigation is focused on potential violations of the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA). The New York Times reported that Wal-Mart de Mexico paid more than $24 million in bribes to win construction permits, and when a whistleblower alerted top executives in 2005, they launched an investigation but then shut it down without reporting the information to law enforcement.

The allegations threaten Wal-Mart's cleaned-up image that it has worked hard to maintain after facing criticism for paying low wages and putting small businesses out of business. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, which includes an arm with ties to Wal-Mart, has been pushing for the FCPA to be scaled back, arguing that it is too broad and bad for business. Two Wal-Mart executives listed as board members of the Chamber's Institute for Legal Reform in 2010 were Jeff Gearhart, Wal-Mart’s general counsel, and Thomas Hyde, a former corporate secretary who stepped down in August 2010.

Wal-Mart has stated that it takes compliance with the FCPA seriously and is committed to having a strong anti-corruption

The Nevada couple Mark and Debby Constantino, known for their appearances on the reality television show "Ghost Adventures," were found dead in a barricaded apartment in Sparks, Nevada following a standoff with police. The incident began when police received a call about a man found dead at a home in northwest Reno where Debby Constantino had been living. She was missing and later found inside the Sparks apartment with her estranged husband, Mark Constantino. During the standoff, Mark Constantino shot at officers who approached the door but were not injured. The couple was known for their paranormal investigations and lectures around the country. Debby Constantino had obtained a restraining order against her estranged husband last week and they were scheduled to appear in court regarding their pending divorce. Officers heard several shots fired when they knocked on the apartment door and heard a man yelling at police to leave. The couple's daughter lived in the apartment where they were found. Police did not release a cause of death and are still investigating.

The movie "Sparkle," a remake of a 1976 film, serves as both a tribute and a farewell to the late Whitney Houston, who filmed it before her death in February. Houston delivers a powerful performance in one scene where she sings "I'm singing because I'm happy" in a church setting. However, the movie as a whole is criticized for being formulaic and unremarkable, with a plodding storyline that often feels like a flat Supremes biopic. The film revolves around three sisters trying to make it as a girl group in Detroit during the Motown era of 1968, with Houston portraying their churchgoing single mother who warns against the pitfalls of the entertainment industry. The movie also features performances by Cee Lo Green and Mike Epps. Despite its flaws, Houston's performance is praised as a lingering sense of loss and celebration, making it a poignant swan song for the iconic singer.

U.S. Supreme Court Associate Justice Antonin Scalia was found dead at a West Texas ranch on February 13, 2016. He was 79 years old. The cause of death is believed to be natural causes, but an autopsy will not be performed. Scalia was a conservative icon and the intellectual cornerstone of the court's modern conservative wing. He served on the Supreme Court since 1986 and was the first Italian American to do so. His death has far-reaching implications for the Supreme Court, as he was in the middle of a round of major cases set to be decided this summer, including Fisher v. University of Texas at Austin, which challenges the university's affirmative action policy, and a case that contests Obama's immigration policy. The replacement for Scalia would be President Barack Obama’s third Supreme Court nomination.

A Catholic priest in the Philippines has been suspended after using a hoverboard during Christmas Eve Mass, which was captured on video and went viral. The diocese of San Pablo stated that the Mass is the church's highest form of worship and it is not a personal celebration where one can introduce something to get attention. The priest acknowledged his action was wrong and promised not to repeat it, spending some time for reflection. The incident serves as a wake-up call for him. Hoverboards were among the popular Christmas gifts this year despite their potential dangers.

A 14-year-old girl from Greenwood, Delaware fell from a stopped gondola ride at Six Flags Amusement Park in Queensbury, NY on Saturday night. The incident occurred on the "Sky Ride" around 8 PM. The girl, who was riding with a child relative, fell approximately 25 feet from a stationary two-person car. She was treated by park emergency medical staff and transferred to Albany Medical Center in stable condition with no serious injuries.

An unidentified 47-year-old man from Schenectady, NY, who attempted to catch the falling girl, sustained a back injury and was treated and released from a hospital. The ride has been closed until a thorough review can be completed, and officials have stated that there does not appear to be any malfunction of the ride. No further information is available at this time.

Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney released his U.S. tax returns on Tuesday, showing he pays a lower effective tax rate than many top wage-earners due to most of his income coming from investment profits, dividends, and interest. For 2010 and estimates for 2011, Romney will pay $6.2 million in taxes on an income of $42.5 million, with an effective tax rate of 13.9 percent in 2010 and 15.4 percent expected for 2011. The lower rates are due to the U.S. tax code favoring investment income over wage income.

President Barack Obama will renew his appeal for a "Buffett rule" in his State of the Union speech on Tuesday, aiming to make the tax code fairer and ensure that the ultra-wealthy pay their "fair share" of taxes. Romney did not release returns from the years 1984-1999, when he made his fortune as a private equity financier with Bain Capital, but those lucrative years gave him a special tax advantage through "carried interest."

On May 1, 2017, SpaceX successfully launched a classified National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) mission named NROL-76 from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The launch was initially delayed due to high-altitude winds, but CEO Elon Musk confirmed the successful launch and landing of the Falcon 9 rocket via Twitter. This marked SpaceX's first dedicated mission for the NRO and their fourth rocket landing on land as they continue their efforts towards making reusable rockets routine. The mission was highly anticipated as it marks a new era of competition between SpaceX and United Launch Alliance for government contracts, with SpaceX aiming to drastically cut launch costs and potentially fulfill Musk's vision of colonizing Mars.

In this summary, Josh Duggar, a former reality star from the show 19 Kids and Counting, is being sued by Matthew McCarthy for allegedly using McCarthy's image on several dating sites, including Ashley Madison. The lawsuit claims that McCarthy has been humiliated due to his association with Duggar's porn life, as well as receiving harassing messages. The suit seeks damages, and Duggar has not yet responded to these allegations.

This profile was linked to Duggar due to its location, occupation, and the fact that it stopped appearing online around the same time as Duggar's reported credit card payments for Ashley Madison accounts. However, there is no definitive evidence linking this user to Duggar. The Internet continues to search for signs of alleged infidelity by Duggar on various dating sites.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages as they are created and archive the pages they refer to, aiming to fix broken links on the web by replacing them with archived versions of the original pages. In other news, UC Irvine has faced criticism for withdrawing over 500 admission offers due to enrollment issues, leading to an increased number of applicants than anticipated. This resulted in a stricter approach to processing admissions, causing anxiety among some students whose offers were rescinded. The university has since apologized and is expediting the review process for appeals, with 63 students already reinstated as of Friday. Some students have reported errors on their part or that of their high schools leading to the withdrawal of their admission offers.

The U.S.'s top general in Afghanistan, Gen. John Allen, is under investigation for alleged inappropriate communications with Jill Kelley, a Tampa socialite who triggered the FBI investigation that led to David Petraeus's downfall as CIA director. The investigation revealed numerous emails between Allen and Kelley dating back to 2010, but no sensitive or classified material has been found in the messages so far. Gen. Allen denies having an affair with Kelley or sharing any classified information with her. The nomination of Gen. Allen as commander of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is on hold pending the investigation's results. Jill Kelley is also an "honorary consul" of South Korea, a symbolic position that has no official responsibilities.

Tony Curtis, the legendary Hollywood actor known for films like Spartacus and Some Like it Hot, disinherited his five children, including actress Jamie Lee Curtis, in his final will and testament. The will, written five months before his death from cardiac arrest at age 85, leaves his estate to his fifth wife Jill Vandenberg Curtis. One of the children attempted to contest the will in court but was unsuccessful. Curtis's widow released a statement saying that the will and his passing wishes are private family matters. Tony Curtis had children with three of his wives – Janet Leigh, Christine Kaufmann, and Leslie Allen – and died at his home in Nevada in September 2017.

Austin Tice, an American journalist, was captured while reporting on the civil war in Syria in August 2012. Since then, his family - Marc, Debra, and others - have been without him for three Christmases and are facing a fourth. The families of four other American hostages who were killed by the Islamic State have urged President Obama to take action to find and return Tice. Tice is the last unaccounted-for American reporter in the Syrian civil war, and his parents have asked the White House to increase search efforts. State Department spokesman John Kirby stated that U.S. officials are working through the Czech government to find information on Tice's welfare and whereabouts. The families of the slain hostages, including James Foley, Steven Sotloff, Abdul-Rahman Peter Kassig, and Kayla Mueller, have written a joint letter to President Obama urging him to use all appropriate means to bring Tice home safely. The families are bonded together by tragedy and terror, and they have asked the administration not to hesitate in leveraging all appropriate means to find Tice and secure his release. Tice is believed to have been seized by loyalists of the Syrian regime, and he has not been seen since a video clip showing him in custody shortly after his disappearance in mid-August 2012.

A video game titled "Active Shooter," which allowed players to simulate school shootings, was set to be released on Steam, the PC's largest platform for buying and selling games. However, Valve Corporation, which runs Steam, has removed the game following an investigation that found the developer and publisher were a person named Ata Berdiyev, who had previously been removed from the platform due to customer abuse, copyright infringement, and user review manipulation. The game drew criticism from survivors of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School shooting in Parkland, Florida, as well as Senator Bill Nelson (D-FL), who called it "inexcusable." The developer initially planned to remove the shooter's role but later defended the game, arguing that it did not promote violence. The game's removal follows a similar controversy in 2011 over another game, "School Shooter," which portrayed the Columbine school shooting.

House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi has stated that she will not negotiate for President Trump's proposed border wall, calling it a "manhood issue" for him. Pelosi emphasized that Democrats support border security but prefer to focus on strengthening existing measures as part of comprehensive immigration reform. The upcoming December showdown over the border wall funding is expected to be a significant point of contention between Trump and Democrats. If Democrats win the House majority in November, Pelosi could have more leverage in negotiations. Pelosi also discussed her confidence in being re-elected as speaker if Democrats win the majority and outlined their legislative priorities for next year, including lowering healthcare costs, increasing paychecks, improving green infrastructure, campaign finance reform, gun control, and protecting Dreamers. Regarding oversight responsibilities, Pelosi reiterated her view that impeachment is divisive but emphasized the importance of holding Trump accountable.

In this article, Adam Wainwright, the National League starting pitcher at the 2014 All-Star Game, paid tribute to Derek Jeter by stepping aside during their first at-bat, allowing Jeter a moment of applause. However, after giving up a hit to Jeter and contributing to the American League's victory, Wainwright caused controversy by revealing that he had intended to give Jeter "pipe shots" (easy pitches) due to his respect for the retiring Yankees legend. This comment led to criticism, with some perceiving it as disrespectful or undermining the integrity of the game.

The article also discusses the issues with the current All-Star Game format, which awards home-field advantage in the World Series based on its outcome. The author argues that this system has created too many pitfalls and minefields due to the involvement of multiple constituencies, including fans, players, and managers. The author suggests that changes should be made, such as limiting team representation and ensuring that top players play all nine innings rather than making cameos.

The article concludes by suggesting that Wainwright's controversial comment may have inadvertently highlighted the need for MLB to reconsider the All-Star Game format ahead of the 2015 event in Cincinnati.

On June 14, 2016, a Chinese tourist was fined $1,000 and a $30 court processing fee for walking off the boardwalk in the Mammoth Hot Springs thermal area at Yellowstone National Park. The visitor reported that the individual walked on the terrace formations near Liberty Cap, broke through the fragile travertine crust, and collected thermal water for medicinal purposes. The tourist admitted to not reading the safety information given upon entering the park. This incident comes after another tourist death in the park a week prior, when a man fell into one of Yellowstone's hot springs. Park officials urge visitors to stay on designated trails and boardwalks for their safety and to protect the park's natural resources.

The BBC reports on Taiwan's ongoing struggle with an oral cancer epidemic linked to the widespread use of Betel Nuts. The nut, which is popular in many Asian countries, is chewed for its stimulating effects and is often combined with other ingredients like slaked lime, cardamom, cinnamon, and tobacco. This combination exacerbates the danger as all these ingredients are known carcinogens.

Taiwan has one of the highest rates of oral cancer in the world, with 80-90% of diagnosed men admitting to chewing Betel Nuts. The Taiwanese government is taking steps to combat this issue by providing free programs aimed at convincing people to quit Betel Nuts and offering incentives to farmers to cut down their Betel palm trees and grow other crops. However, the nut remains legal.

The Betel Nut habit has been linked to a range of serious health issues, including oral cancer, oral submucous fibrosis (a condition that can cause stiffness in the mouth and loss of jaw movement), gum irritation, tooth decay, and potential interactions with other drugs or herbal supplements.

Health organizations and governments around the world are working to increase awareness about the risks associated with Betel Nut use. Taiwan has declared an annual "Betel Nut Prevention Day" and city officials in Taipei have implemented fines for spitting Betel nut juice

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has ruled out running for president in both 2012 and 2016 during an interview in New Zealand. She expressed satisfaction with her current role as Secretary of State and acknowledged the United States' readiness for a female president. The midterm elections held in the U.S. on Tuesday saw Democrats losing control of the House of Representatives, while maintaining a slim majority in the Senate. The results have been interpreted as a referendum on President Barack Obama, raising questions about the Democratic Party's future candidates. During her visit to New Zealand, Clinton also addressed concerns about the Trans-Pacific Partnership and defended President Obama's actions regarding the economy.

The Treasury Department has released emails showing that senior officials may have disregarded warnings and possibly brushed aside a potential conflict of interest while pushing for government support for solar-panel maker Solyndra LLC. Solyndra received a $535 million loan guarantee from the Department of Energy in 2009, with the loan coming from a part of the Treasury Department. The emails suggest high-level advocacy for Solyndra despite concerns about its viability and legal issues, as well as potential conflicts of interest. Steven J. Spinner, a senior member of the Energy Department's loan guarantee oversight office, pushed for the loan approval even though his wife's law firm represented Solyndra, and he had promised to recuse himself from matters related to the loan application. The emails also show that some White House officials were concerned about Solyndra's health and the haste with which the loan guarantees were moving, while others were eager to hurry it along for public relations purposes. The company declared bankruptcy in August 2011 and is now being investigated by the Justice Department over potential misleading financial information provided to federal authorities.

The article discusses President Obama's speech on Afghanistan, where he outlined his plans for troop deployment and withdrawal. The speech was met with mixed reactions, with some praising its focus on national self-interest and realism, while others criticized it for lacking a clear exit strategy and glossing over issues within the Afghan government. The article also touches upon the doom loop of Western liberalism, discussing the potential negative effects of immigration on economies and cultures in Europe. Alvin Cross Jr., a man from Albany, Georgia, was arrested and sentenced to one year in prison after accidentally texting his probation officer asking for drugs. The incident occurred when Cross, who was on probation for an unknown offense, mistakenly sent a message asking "you have some weed?" to his probation officer. Upon receiving the message, the probation officer contacted police, who then raided Cross's home and discovered a bag of cocaine. Cross pleaded guilty on Monday to cocaine possession and violating his probation. This incident serves as a reminder to be careful when using cellphones, especially when communicating sensitive information.

The report by the Commission on Wartime Contracting in Iraq and Afghanistan highlights significant issues with the federal government's overreliance on contractors in Iraq and Afghanistan, particularly in military, reconstruction, and training programs. The commission criticizes the government for turning to contractors for too many purposes, including monitoring other contractors, and for not adequately controlling the process.

The report calls for major reforms to how the government awards and monitors contracts, including creating special teams of full-time federal workers to deploy and monitor projects, restricting reliance on contractors for security, and embedding government workers responsible for command and control and oversight. The commission also notes that contractors often face great risks, with over 2,200 contractor employees having died and over 49,800 injured between September 2001 and December 2010.

The report estimates that tens of billions of dollars have been wasted out of the $117 billion spent on contractors in Iraq and Afghanistan since 2002 due to waste, fraud, and abuse caused by significant errors. The commission is holding a hearing to review the report's findings and is urging the government to take action to reform its contracting programs.
