A major chemical spill in West Virginia's Elk River last week affected over 300,000 residents, highlighting the state's history of regulating its coal and chemical industries. Critics argue that West Virginia has a pattern of resisting federal oversight, putting workers and the population at risk. The spill came from a ruptured tank storing 4-methylcyclohexane methanol (MCHM), a chemical used to wash coal. No charges have been filed against Freedom Industries, the company that owns the plant, but an investigation is ongoing. The cleanup process shows signs of improvement, and officials hope to lift the water ban soon. This incident has sparked discussions about West Virginia's reliance on its coal and chemical industries, with some questioning whether this industry-heavy focus comes at the expense of environmental regulations and public safety.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the former head of the International Monetary Fund, gave his first interview since being charged with attempted rape in New York, maintaining that the encounter was consensual and a moral failing on his part. He also dismissed separate claims by a French writer that he tried to rape her during a 2003 interview as imaginary. Strauss-Kahn faced criminal charges over the New York incident, but they were dropped last month. However, he is still facing a civil suit brought by the maid, an immigrant from Guinea. He said he would take time to reflect on his future in politics, but did not rule it out entirely. The interview came off as somewhat scripted and unruffled. Strauss-Kahn faced additional allegations of sexual assault in France, which are currently under investigation by police.

Starbucks Corp. has partnered with Danone SA to sell Greek yogurt parfaits and other similar items, marking another move by the coffee shop operator to expand its presence on grocery shelves. The co-branded products, named "Evolution Fresh, Inspired by Dannon," will first be sold in Starbucks cafes next spring, then in supermarkets in 2015. Sales overseas are a possibility.

Starbucks aims to tap into the growing yogurt market, with U.S. consumers on average eating about half as much yogurt as Canadians and a third as much as Europeans. The company has been diversifying its traditional coffee business by expanding into packaged products and food, having recently acquired Evolution Fresh and Teavana, among other ventures.

The partnership with Danone will help Starbucks gain access to millions of consumers through Danone's distribution network, while also building awareness for Evolution Fresh. Danone's Oikos brand Greek yogurt was the best-selling food product launched in the U.S. last year, according to an annual poll by IRI. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed, but Starbucks expects no additional capital expenses due to Danone handling distribution.

The document "Baby Name Report Card: Beneficial and Harmful Baby Names" by Albert Mehrabian, Ph.D., discusses the impact of baby names on personal, social, and work-related activities throughout a person's lifetime. The book provides experimental findings showing that desirable or attractive names are treated more favorably than undesirable or unattractive ones.

The report categorizes names into five dimensions: ethical-caring, popular-fun, successful, masculine-feminine, and overall attractiveness. Each name is scored on these dimensions, with scores ranging from 0 to 100, with 50 being an average score. For example, "John" received a high Success score of 98, while "Knut" received a low Success score of 11.

The report also includes guidelines for selecting names that will impart positive and beneficial impressions, as well as information on common issues in name selection and how to change a name. It provides lists of girls' and boys' names along with their scores in each dimension.

The document also discusses the tension between traditional family names and modern parents' desire for unique and personalized names. Some older relatives may offer incentives, such as money or family businesses, to have their names passed down to the next generation. However, many modern parents prioritize choosing a name that suits their child and reflects their personality.

The article discusses a controversial obituary for Cornelia June Rogers Miller, who passed away in February 2017. The obituary, published by the Cherokee Scout in Murphy, North Carolina, was written in a scathing manner and accused Miller of having no hobbies, making no contributions to society, and using drugs. The obituary also stated that her presence would not be missed by many.

Miller's son, Robert, responded to the obituary, stating it was untrue and blaming his sisters for writing it. However, one of Miller's sisters denied writing the obituary. After the obituary appeared, a viewer contacted WTVC to say that some sections were plagiarized from a 2008 obituary for Dolores Aguilar that ran in the Vallejo Times Herald in California.

Robert Miller expressed his disappointment and called the obituary tragic and sad, stating it was unfortunate that his family members didn't have better things to do. He hopes that the memories his parents shared in Murphy won't be forgotten, and wants his mother to be remembered as a loving, generous woman.

In a surprising turn of events, Playboy twins Karissa and Kristina Shannon have moved back into the Playboy Mansion, less than two days after Hefner's fiancee Crystal Harris left. This comes a year and a half after the twins initially moved out. It appears that Karissa has ended her relationship with Sam Jones III to rejoin Hefner. Meanwhile, a former Democratic staffer named Jackson A. Cosko was arrested by U.S. Capitol Police for allegedly posting private information about Republican senators on Wikipedia. The arrest is tied to the investigation into the posting of personal information about these senators during the hearing as they discussed sexual assault allegations against Kavanaugh.

He was arrested on charges including making public restricted personal information, witness tampering, threats in interstate communications, unauthorized access of a government computer, identity theft, second-degree burglary, and unlawful entry.

The personal information of Republican Sens. Lindsey Graham, Mike Lee, and Orrin Hatch was posted on their respective Wikipedia pages during the hearing. The information has since been removed, but it included home addresses and phone numbers that were partially incorrect. The document contains news and media content related to the political campaign of Jon Huntsman during the 2013 presidential election. Specifically, it highlights a humorous advertisement created by Huntsman's daughters as a parody of Herman Cain's controversial "smoking man" ad. In the video, titled Jon2012Girls and posted on YouTube in October 2011, the daughters mimic Cain's ad with horn-rimmed glasses and false mustaches while promoting their father's candidacy. Instead of a cigarette, they blow soap bubbles to emphasize their support for Huntsman. This event occurred separately from the Supreme Court hearings and rulings on the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) and California's Proposition 8 in 2013.

A fatal jewelry robbery occurred at Rolling Oaks Mall on San Antonio's Northeast Side, resulting in one death and seven injuries. According to San Antonio Police Chief William McManus, two suspects attempted a jewelry store robbery and two good samaritans intervened. One of the samaritans was shot dead by one of the suspects. The second suspect fled shooting six people inside the mall. The incident is being treated as a robbery gone wrong. Police are still searching for the second suspect, while the first one is in custody. The names of those involved have not been released yet.

Audi has introduced an innovative system that allows drivers to know how long it will take for a traffic light to change from red to green. This industry-first feature wirelessly links vehicles to traffic management computers in select US cities and is expected to be available in five to seven cities by the end of this year. The countdown is displayed in the instrument cluster, with the counter stopping once four seconds are left before the light turns green. Audi's Connect Prime service, which costs $199 for six months, will offer this feature on the 2017 Q7 SUV and A4 sedan built after June 1. The system aims to make driving more enjoyable by reducing the "white-knuckle" experience associated with traffic lights. Future enhancements may include the car turning off during stops or using red light information to take alternative routes. This technology is seen as crucial for the development of self-driving cars, and Audi emphasizes its built-in nature compared to apps from companies like Apple and Google.

Miley Cyrus is releasing her new album "Can't Be Tamed" on Monday, and she is asserting her independence by doing it her way. Some critics have criticized her for being too provocative in her music videos and outfits, but Cyrus argues that she is simply expressing herself and being true to her music. She also plans to shed her Disney persona, "Hannah Montana," when the show ends this year. Meanwhile, Heather Locklear is reportedly moving from a psychiatric ward at a southern California hospital into a long-term facility for ongoing mental health and substance abuse issues. Sources close to her family have spoken with doctors who believe that Locklear needs more significant long-term care than what can be provided at the hospital.

West Virginia Democratic Governor Jim Justice announced on Thursday that he will switch to the Republican party, joining President Donald Trump at a rally in Huntington. Justice's decision reflects his state's rightward tilt and Trump's popularity in the region. The governor's move may complicate matters for Senator Joe Manchin, who is up for reelection in 2018 and is already facing challenges from Republicans. The announcement blindsided many West Virginia Democrats, with some expressing disappointment and feelings of betrayal. The switch is seen as a sign that the state is embracing Republicans on both the federal and state levels.

In a game between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Tampa Bay Rays on August 10, 2013, Juan Uribe was caught off guard at third base, resulting in an out. This happened when he failed to keep his foot on the base after dusting himself off during a play. Yasiel Puig shared a humorous reminder for Uribe not to make the same mistake again, using the phrase "El pie en la base" (Keep your foot on the base) in a tweet that included a video of the incident.

The article discusses escalating violence in Syria, particularly in the towns of Haffa and Homs, where the UN has expressed concern about potential massacres by the Syrian government. The US state department has urged access to Haffa for UN observers, who have been denied entry. The UN Secretary General Ban Ki-moon and peace envoy Kofi Annan have voiced grave concerns about the violence in these areas.

The article also mentions that the six-point plan brokered by Mr. Annan to address the Syrian conflict, which includes an end to violence, humanitarian aid, political detainees' release, freedom of movement for journalists, and peaceful demonstrations, has largely collapsed.

The Syrian government is accused of killing civilians in the regions of Houla and Qubair earlier this month. The Syrian government denies these accusations, blaming foreign-backed armed terrorist gangs for the violence.

Heavy fighting was also reported in several other Syrian cities, including Rastan, Talbisa, Idlib province, and Deir al-Zour, where a car bomb explosion killed 10 people.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau announced plans to regulate large loan servicers in the $1.2 trillion student debt market, citing issues with loan servicers tripping up borrowers, particularly when they seek to change repayment terms. A report from The Institute for College Access and Success shows that the average student debt load continues to rise, with last year's graduates holding an average of $29,400 in student loans, up from $26,600 held by 2011 graduates. Rising tuition and stagnant family incomes are contributing to the need for students to borrow. The report also shows that students from Delaware graduated with the highest average debt, while those in South Dakota were the most likely to graduate with debt. While most students take out federal loans, a fifth hold private loans, which can be more difficult for borrowers to manage and have less flexible repayment plans. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's annual student loan ombudsman report also highlighted issues with private loan servicers allocating payments to maximize late fees and pay off low-interest loans first rather than costlier high-interest loans.

A 45-year-old man named Robin Lee was arrested by British Transport Police for charging his iPhone using a socket on a London Overground train. The incident occurred on July 10th, and Lee was initially arrested for "abstracting electricity" under section 13 of the Theft Act 1968, which carries a maximum custodial sentence of five years. After becoming aggressive when objecting to his arrest, he was further arrested for unacceptable behavior.

Lee posted an image of his custody record on Twitter but later deleted it. Sockets on London Overground trains are marked as for use by cleaners only. Members on a forum dedicated to the London Underground have pointed out that these sockets are for cleaning equipment deployed when trains are in depots and not intended for public use due to the risk of power surges.

The British Transport Police stated that officers were called to Camden Road station after Lee became aggressive towards a PCSO when challenged about his use of a plug socket on an Overground train. The police will review Lee's behavior before sending details to the Crown Prosecution Service, which will decide if charges should be brought.

Additionally, it was mentioned that 19-year-old Nick Silvestri made headlines in New York last week for attempting to charge his phone on a fake socket during a Broadway play.

A missing University of Virginia student, Hannah Graham, was last seen on Friday/Saturday morning, and police are currently searching for a person of interest described as a black male in his late 20s or early 30s with a close-shaved head, goatee, and a slight "beer belly." Graham is approximately 5'11" tall with blue eyes, light brown hair, and freckles. She was last seen wearing a black crop top with mesh cutouts.

Police are asking for the public's help in finding any information about her whereabouts or the person of interest. Surveillance videos have been released showing Graham with an unidentified white male on Friday night, and police have interviewed this man. A reward totaling $50,000 is being offered for information about the cause of her disappearance.

A community search will be held this coming Saturday and Sunday, and a candlelight vigil will be held for Graham at the UVA Amphitheater on Thursday night. The Charlottesville Police Department has released the description of the person of interest, asking anyone with information to call the tip line at 434-295-3851.

A gathering of top CEOs from major tech companies such as Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Facebook, Alibaba, and others took place at Microsoft's campus in Redmond, Washington. The performances by Affleck and Pike are highly praised, with Affleck's character portrayed as likable yet potentially suspicious, and Pike delivering a career-defining role as Amy. The film is generally well-received until the final 20 minutes, where some critics feel it loses its appeal due to plot developments that deviate from the movie's initial logic and cleverness.

Scientists in East Africa are training rats to detect tuberculosis (TB) among prison inmates, using the animals' highly developed sense of smell. The rats, trained by APOPO, a Belgian non-governmental organization, have already proven effective in detecting TB and landmines. In Tanzania, where TB is most common, many cases go undiagnosed due to lack of awareness or resources for screening. APOPO plans to use the rats to screen prisons in Tanzania and Mozambique, aiming to expand the program to other high-risk areas such as shantytowns, factories, and HIV/AIDS patients. The rats are trained to recognize the presence of TB in sputum samples and are rewarded when they succeed. The rats' accuracy at detecting TB is almost 100%, but they cannot distinguish between normal and drug-resistant strains. APOPO's current programs have screened over 340,000 TB samples, preventing over 36,000 further infections. Khadija Abraham, an expert at Tanzania's National Leprosy and Tuberculosis Programme, believes the rats could be a valuable solution for detecting TB in rural areas.

The Trigana Air Service plane that was flying from Jayapura to Oksibil in Indonesia's Papua province crashed into a mountain, killing all 54 people on board. The wreckage was found at an altitude of 2,600 meters (about 8,500 feet) and the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder were recovered. Rescuers faced difficulties due to rugged terrain and bad weather in reaching the crash site. The victims included three local government officials and two members of the local parliament. This incident marks another tragedy in Indonesia's aviation history, following a string of airline disasters in recent years. The cause of the crash is still under investigation by Indonesia's transportation safety commission.

The Democratic National Convention on Tuesday was marked by a surprising level of energy and enthusiasm, as noted by various journalists. David Gergen commented that the enthusiasm in the hall was more palpable than at the Republican convention. POLITICO's Dylan Byers observed that there was more energy in one speech than during the entire three days of the Republican Convention. The family comedy, based on the popular app game, features the voices of Jason Sudeikis, Sean Penn, Maya Rudolph, Danny McBride, and Josh Gad. Despite mixed reviews from critics (42% positive on RottenTomatoes), audiences slightly embraced it more (61% liked it). The movie's success is attributed to its appeal to both the game's audience and family audiences who have been drawn to PG-rated movies this year.

Neighbors 2: Sorority Rising opened at No. 3 with $21.8 million, while Shane Black's The Nice Guys was welcomed with a better-than-expected $11.3 million in fourth place. The Jungle Book rounded out the top five with $11 million. Final box office figures are expected on Monday.

The latest iPad, announced by Apple, will go on sale on Friday. Despite some criticisms for lacking features such as extra storage options, smaller-screen models, Adobe Flash, and camera flash, the new iPad is expected to sell up to 60 million units this year. The device strongly resembles the iPad 2 but offers improvements including a spectacular display, improved camera, dictation feature, and on some models, access to faster cellular networks. Prices for the new models range from $499 to $829, while the iPad 2 is now available at a reduced price of $399. The new iPads are the first to access 4G or 4th generation data networks being deployed nationally by AT&T and Verizon Wireless, each with variations on how wireless is delivered. The new display on the iPad offers four times the number of pixels as the iPad 2, making it sharper than an HDTV. Apple has managed to maintain long battery life between charges despite the upgrades. The new iPad may not be a game-changer like the original tablet, but it is expected to continue Apple's success in the market.

Verma went on earned leave in December 1990 and did not return to work thereafter, defying orders to do so. An inquiry against him was initiated in September 1992, but it took another 22 years for his dismissal due to delays and non-cooperation from Verma. The urban development minister, M. This incident highlights the issue of absenteeism in India's bureaucracy, which is known for being work-shy. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has taken steps to improve attendance levels among civil servants, including unannounced visits to government offices and implementing fingerprint scanners for signing in at work.

He also vowed not to attack unless threatened but emphasized the need to focus on mass-producing nuclear warheads and ballistic missiles for operational deployment this year.

However, they also caution that improving relations between the two Koreas is seldom achieved and could be an attempt to drive a wedge between Seoul and Washington.

The article discusses a study commissioned by the International Bottled Water Association (IBWA) to determine the amount of water used in producing one liter of bottled water. The study found that for North American companies, it takes 1.39 liters of water to make one liter of bottled water. This is less than the water required for other packaged beverages such as soda (2.02 liters), beer (4 liters), wine (4.74 liters), and hard alcohol (34.55 liters).

However, environmental activists argue that the study does not take into account the entire water footprint, including the water used for packaging. Ertug Ercin from the Water Footprint Network suggests that companies should include all freshwater used in production, including water used for packaging, to find opportunities for conservation. He notes that three liters of water might be used to make a half-liter bottle, and that drilling for oil to make plastic and making paper also requires water.

Despite this, bottled water companies are working towards being as efficient as possible with water, according to Chris Hogan from the IBWA. However, he notes that it is difficult to know where to stop when considering all the factors involved in calculating a product's water footprint.

Jennifer Westfeldt, star of "Friends With Kids", and Greg Kinnear will begin performances of the new play "The Power of Duff" at Vassar's Powerhouse Theater in upstate New York on Wednesday. The theater has a summer camp vibe due to the presence of actors and creative types. Westfeldt joked about being kicked out of camp when she was 13 because her boyfriend took her out for pizza, but these days it's a whole new game. Jon Hamm, Westfeldt's longtime boyfriend and "Mad Men" hunk, has visited the campus.

The pop superstar is due to take her MDNA tour to Poland on 1 August, when residents traditionally observe a minute’s silence to commemorate the 1944 Warsaw Uprising against the Nazi occupation. The Associated Press reports that the first parts of a controversial U.S. missile defense system, known as THAAD (Terminal High-Altitude Area Defense), have arrived in South Korea following North Korea's test launch of four ballistic missiles into the ocean near Japan. The deployment of THAAD has angered not only North Korea but also China and Russia, who see its powerful radars as a security threat.

China has responded by saying it will take "necessary measures" to protect itself and warning that the U.S. and South Korea should be prepared to bear the consequences. The U.S. military says THAAD can intercept and destroy short and medium-range ballistic missiles during the last part of their flights, and Washington and Seoul maintain that the system is defensive and not meant to be a threat to Beijing or Moscow.

Some South Korean liberal presidential candidates have expressed concerns that the security benefits of having THAAD would be curtailed by worsened relations with neighbors China and Russia. Protests against a South Korean retail giant, Lotte, which agreed to provide one of its golf courses in southern South Korea as the site of THAAD, have been triggered by China's condemnation of the deployment.

The North's test launch of ballistic missiles is believed to be a protest against ongoing U.S.-South Korean military drills that it views as an invasion

The new study published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute suggests that drinking alcohol before a woman's first pregnancy increases her risk of developing both benign breast disease (BBD) and breast cancer later in life. This association holds regardless of whether a woman continues to drink after her first pregnancy.

The study, led by Dr. Ying Liu from Washington University School of Medicine, analyzed data from over 91,000 women who participated in the Nurses' Health Study II and had no history of cancer when they began. The researchers found that drinking alcohol during the time frame between a woman's first menstrual period and her first pregnancy increases the risk of both breast cancer and BBD (a risk factor for breast cancer).

The study indicates a dose-dependent relationship, meaning the more a woman drinks during this time, the higher her risk of developing breast cancer. The researchers also found that longer intervals between the first menstrual period and first pregnancy showed stronger associations compared with shorter intervals. Drinking after the first pregnancy was associated with breast cancer risk but not BBD.

The study provides evidence that alcohol intake before the first pregnancy may play a significant role in breast cancer etiology, potentially having important implications for breast cancer prevention. The researchers suggest that women should reduce their drinking, especially before the first pregnancy, to lower their breast cancer risk.

In a rally in North Dakota, President Trump emphasized the importance of maintaining Republican control of the Senate this fall, particularly in light of Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy's retirement. Trump argued that Republican Rep. Kevin Cramer, who is challenging Democratic Sen. Heidi Heitkamp in one of the GOP's top opportunities to pick up a Senate seat, would support his agenda and court picks, while Heitkamp will not. Kennedy's retirement gives Trump the opportunity to appoint another conservative justice to the Supreme Court, which could shift the balance of the court for decades. Trump has a list of 25 potential nominees from which he plans to choose.

The FBI is investigating an alleged hacking attempt on the Democratic National Committee's (DNC) voter database. The DNC believes this incident, which was detected on Tuesday, was the beginning of a sophisticated attack. The DNC, a cloud service provider, and a security research firm collaborated to thwart the potential attack by identifying a fake login page designed to gather usernames and passwords for access to the party's database. This incident underscores ongoing concerns about cyber threats, particularly as midterm elections approach. The DNC has emphasized that its voter file is its most sensitive information, and experts have highlighted the vulnerability of various election systems to manipulation by foreign and domestic entities. Microsoft recently reported hacking attempts on the Senate and conservative think tanks in the U.S., while Facebook identified a political influence campaign aimed at potentially disrupting the midterms.

A tourist ferry named El Almirante capsized in a reservoir near Medellin, Colombia on June 25, 2017, resulting in nine deaths and 28 people missing. The boat was carrying approximately 170 passengers for the holiday weekend. Rescue operations were carried out by local firefighters, air force pilots, and other boats. Survivors reported that the boat seemed overloaded and no one on board was wearing a life vest. The cause of the sinking is still unclear. The reservoir, located near the rocky outcrop of El Penol, is a popular weekend destination and was especially busy due to a long holiday weekend. Authorities are asking passengers or their loved ones to report to a rescue center for further information.

On November 3, 2011, a peaceful Occupy Wall Street protest in Oakland, California turned violent as protesters broke into a vacant building, shattered windows, and set fires. The protests shut down the Port of Oakland, one of the nation's busiest shipping ports, and prompted solidarity rallies across the US. At least four protesters were hospitalized with various injuries, including one who needed stitches after fighting with an officer. Several officers were also injured but did not require hospitalization. The protests gained momentum in recent weeks as part of a far-flung movement challenging the world's economic systems and distribution of wealth. Organizers in Oakland viewed the strike and port shutdown as a significant victory, although police said that about 7,000 people participated in demonstrations throughout the day that were peaceful except for a few incidents of vandalism at local banks and businesses. The larger Occupy movement has yet to coalesce into an organized association and until the port shut down had largely been limited to scattershot marches, rallies, and tent encampments since it began in September. Smaller-scale demonstrations were also held in New York, Philadelphia, Los Angeles, and elsewhere to show support for the Oakland movement. The protests have faced criticism from some media outlets and city officials who view them as being hijacked by crazies and criminals

Angel Gonzalez, a man who spent 20 years in prison for an abduction and rape conviction that was later overturned, was released on Tuesday night after being cleared of a separate property damage charge. The new DNA evidence showed the presence of bodily fluids from two other men at the crime scene, contradicting Gonzalez's confession and the victim's identification of him as one of her attackers. Gonzalez was exonerated on Monday, and his immigration status is now being considered by Citizenship and Immigration Services. During his time in prison, Gonzalez educated himself and learned various skills such as painting and mentoring other prisoners.

A Russian man identified as Colonel Anatoliy Chepiga, an intelligence officer with a history of service in Chechnya and Ukraine, is accused of being involved in the Salisbury poisoning incident. The UK government believes he travelled to the UK on a false passport under the name Ruslan Boshirov, along with another Russian national named Alexander Petrov. Chepiga was awarded the "Hero of the Russian Federation" medal in 2014 for his service, which is typically handed out by the Russian president and suggests he may have been involved in operations in Ukraine. Both men are wanted by UK authorities, but Russia does not extradite its own nationals. The claims were made following an investigation by Bellingcat, an investigative website that uses open-source computer software and social media to gather information.

The women were lured into his house by him using the names of his children, whom they knew. The article discusses a significant increase in weight among American men and women since the 1960s. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the average American woman now weighs 166.2 pounds, which is almost identical to what American men weighed in the 1960s. Men have gained nearly 30 pounds over this period, with an average weight of 195.5 pounds today. The average waist circumference for American women is 37.5 inches and 39.7 inches for men.

The study also reveals that more than one-third (35.1%) of U.S. adults over the age of 20 are considered obese, with 69% being either overweight or obese. Overweight and obesity rates are also high among children, with more than 1-in-5 U.S. children between ages 12-19 classified as obese, and 17.7% of kids ages 6-11 at obesity levels.

The article further notes that Americans are now the world's third-heaviest people, trailing only the Pacific Island countries of Tonga and Micronesia. The average U.S. adult is 33 pounds heavier than the average Frenchman and 70 pounds heavier than the average Bangladeshi

However, on Friday, a coalition of Shiite political blocs chose Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki as their candidate for Iraq's top government job, which could potentially break the impasse.

A man named Michael Whalen is facing animal abuse charges in Virginia Beach, VA, after shooting and burying his 15-year-old dog, Allie, who had Cushing's disease. Whalen claims that he shot Allie due to her uncontrollable seizures during the night, which required his full attention and were too painful to witness. He buried Allie on the Oceanfront, but was later charged with burying trash as well. Whalen is speaking out to set the record straight and hopes his case will shed light on euthanasia rights. His court date is in June. The incident sparked controversy, with some arguing that a gunshot is not considered a form of euthanasia according to current guidelines and standards.

The Japanese Yamazaki Single Malt Sherry Cask 2013 has been named the best whisky in the world by whisky expert Jim Murray, marking the first time a Japanese whisky has claimed the top spot in the World Whisky Bible's 12-year history. Scottish distilleries are reportedly in shock as this year's winner surpassed all Scottish malts, with the Yamazaki receiving 97.5 marks out of 100. The English tipple Chapter 14 Not Peated from the English Whisky Company was awarded the best European whisky of the year. Murray, who reviewed over 4,500 different whiskies, criticized Scottish distilleries for producing mediocre malts and called for a "little dose of humility" to address any shortcomings. The winning Yamazaki is rare, with only 18,000 bottles made and available in select specialist shops in the UK for approximately £100.

The Giver is a film adaptation of Lois Lowry's 1993 young adult novel, set in a dystopian future where humans live in solitary communities with restrictive rules to avoid war. In this society, "Sameness" is crucial and art, love, and animals are not allowed. The story follows Jonas (Brenton Thwaites), who is chosen to be the community's new Receiver, the person who receives all the memories of what the world was like before the antiseptic civility. He becomes the apprentice to the Giver (Jeff Bridges), the elder who possesses all the world’s collective memories. The film boasts a good cast but falls flat on the screen, as it is too similar to other young-adult works about dystopian futures and lacks originality.

One of the packages was deemed "destructive" and had to be deactivated offsite by a bomb squad. The airport was evacuated around 6 p.m., with passengers being bused to offsite hotels as transportation became available. Passengers remained calm throughout the incident. Associated Press reporters contributed to this report. In the Indian town of Sadiya, Upper Assam, an unknown species of spiders, believed to be similar to tarantulas and highly aggressive, have caused panic and two reported deaths. The spiders invaded the town on May 8 during a Hindu festival, biting several residents who were attending. One resident, Purnakanta Buragohain, died in the hospital after being bitten, and another unidentified schoolboy also died of an alleged spider bite.

Local hospitals have been overwhelmed with people seeking treatment for spider bites, and a team of scientists from Dibrugarh University and Gauhati University arrived on May 22 to investigate the incident and find an antidote. Dr L R Saikia, head of the Department of Life Sciences at Dibrugarh University, said that the spider is a new species and its venom needs to be tested before it can be definitively called a killer spider.

British naturalist Dr Vejay Singh suggested that the swarming could be attributed to an environmental crisis, such as flooding, which would cause the spiders to search for higher ground. The town of Sadiya is also home to a leading Maoist community, according to The Hindustan Times.

The Islamists have reportedly retreated from key towns like Timbuktu but have taken Diabaly in a counter-attack. France began a military intervention on Friday to halt the Islamist advance towards Bamako. The UN Security Council has convened to discuss Mali at France's request, and various African countries have pledged troops for a West African intervention force. A tiny octopus with a unique appearance resembling a cross between a Pac-Man ghost and a Pokemon creature, yet unnamed, has been discovered in the depths of Monterey Bay. The octopus belongs to the Opisthoteuthis genus, which also includes Pearl, the pink flapjack octopus from Finding Nemo. Researcher Stephanie Bush at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute is considering naming this new species Opisthoteuthis adorabilis due to its cute appearance. The naming process for a newly discovered species can take several years, involving publishing papers, collecting specimens, and distributing them to museums. The Bluefin-21 submarine, searching for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, has scanned over 90% of the designated underwater search area without finding any significant leads. An object found near Augusta, Australia, was initially considered an "object of interest," but further analysis revealed it was not related to the missing plane. The search for the aircraft continues with multiple military aircraft and ships participating in the operation. Despite no findings after 48 days of searching, authorities are planning a long-term strategy, potentially expanding the search area if necessary. Authorities are also preparing for the possibility of finding the flight data recorders, which would provide valuable information about the plane's disappearance. The search is ongoing, with no signs of ending soon as officials aim to solve the mystery surrounding Malaysia Airlines Flight 370.

The discovery of Homo floresiensis, nicknamed "hobbits" due to their small size, was made in Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores in 2003. These ancient human relatives stood about 3.5 feet tall and weighed around 75 pounds. Initially, it was believed that they lived as recently as 12,000 years ago, potentially coexisting with modern humans. However, a new analysis suggests that these hobbits actually vanished from the island much earlier, between 100,000 and 60,000 years ago, based on five independent dating methods. This new timeline casts doubt on the possibility of cross-species encounters with modern humans. The confusion about the hobbit's extinction was due to the complex geological layers in the cave site, which led to an initial misinterpretation of the sediment ages. Further excavations and research at Liang Bua and other sites on Flores could provide more insights into the development, lifestyle, and extinction of this mysterious species.

The NFL has announced that Super Bowl 50, scheduled for February 2016 at Levi's Stadium in San Francisco, will use Arabic numerals instead of Roman numerals in its logo, marking a departure from the league's tradition since Super Bowl V in 1971. The change was made due to aesthetic reasons, as the "L" was deemed less pleasing than the previously used X's, V's, and I's. After Super Bowl XLIX in Arizona in February 2015, the NFL will resume using Roman numerals for Super Bowl LI in Houston in 2017.

Former Massachusetts state senator Brian Joyce was arrested and charged with over 100 crimes, including racketeering, wire fraud, extortion, and money laundering in a federal indictment. The charges allege that Joyce used his legislative position for personal gain by accepting bribes and kickbacks from private individuals and entities in exchange for official actions. A new mother, Monica Thompson, has filed a lawsuit against Portland Adventist Medical Center for $8.6 million, alleging negligence that led to her accidentally smothering her 4-day-old son, Jacob, while heavily medicated with painkillers and sleep aids. The incident occurred on August 6, 2012, when a nurse brought the baby to Thompson's bed in the middle of the night for breastfeeding. Thompson dozed off, and when she woke up, she found that Jacob wasn't breathing. Despite emergency procedures and life support, Jacob died ten days later.

The lawsuit claims that the hospital was negligent for medicating a breastfeeding mother without proper supervision, putting the infant in her bed, and lacking clear policies on the potential dangers of such practices. The suit also seeks damages for emotional distress and counseling expenses for Thompson's depression and post-traumatic stress disorder.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has previously warned against bed-sharing due to safety concerns, particularly in maternity wards. This incident highlights the potential risks associated with parents sharing beds with their newborns. The lawsuit was filed by Lake Oswego attorney Diego Conde.

The summary of the document suggests that a new study challenges the common belief that yawning increases oxygen supply to the brain. Instead, it proposes that yawning functions to manage brain temperature for improved alertness and mental efficiency. The research was conducted by a team led by Psychologist Andrew Gallup of SUNY College at Oneonta, USA, and Jorg Massen and Kim Dusch of the University of Vienna.

The study found that contagious yawning is most frequent when the temperature is around 20°C. The researchers measured contagious yawning frequencies of pedestrians outdoors in Vienna, Austria, during both winter and summer months and compared these results to an identical study conducted in Arizona, USA. They concluded that yawning appears to be unhelpful when the air temperature is as hot as the body or freezing, as the cold air is unnecessary or could even be harmful.

The study suggests that yawning is related to regulating brain temperature and creating a state where arousal in a yawner can be achieved. The researchers believe that the spreading of this behavior via contagious yawning could function to enhance overall group vigilance. This adds to accumulating research suggesting that the underlying mechanism for yawning, both spontaneous and contagious forms, is involved in regulating brain temperature.

Actor Mark Wahlberg, now 43, has filed an application with the Massachusetts Board of Pardons to have his decades-old assault conviction erased. This ruling comes after Nestle's claim that the four-finger shape of the KitKat bar has become synonymous with the snack over its 80-year history. However, Cadbury, owned by US company Mondelez International, argued that the shape alone was not distinctive enough for consumers to associate it with the rival snack.

The case will now return to the UK High Court for a final decision. If Nestle fails to secure the trademark, it would prevent other confectionery producers from making chocolate bars of the same shape or size. This ruling is the latest development in a more than 10-year legal battle between the two companies, which started when Cadbury tried to trademark the purple color used on its Cadbury chocolate wrappers.

A Japanese woman was allegedly gang-raped by an organized group of men over a period of more than a month, starting from November 23, in India. A 15-year study suggests that women who have had their appendix or tonsils removed may be more fertile. The researchers, from the University of Dundee, analyzed medical records from over half a million British women and found that for every 100 pregnancies in women who had not undergone any procedures, there were 134 pregnancies in women who had their appendix removed, 149 pregnancies in women who had their tonsils removed, and 143 pregnancies in women who had both removed. The study challenges the previous belief that appendectomies can damage fertility by blocking the fallopian tubes. The researchers are now eager to understand why fertility appears to increase after these surgeries, with possible explanations being a biological effect due to reduced inflammation or increased promiscuity leading to more infections and subsequent surgery. It is important to note that women should not seek appendectomies or tonsillectomies specifically to improve their fertility, but if they need one, the operation will not reduce their future chances of pregnancy.

The Baltic Sea is home to thousands of shipwrecks, particularly from the two World Wars, with approximately 1,000 known objects in German waters alone. Thomas Dehling, a maritime expert, oversees the surveying and mapping of these underwater artifacts for potential dangers to shipping. Scientists led by Philippe Jeandet analyzed a sample of the preserved champagne and found differences in alcohol content, sugar levels, and chemical composition compared to modern-day Veuve Clicquot. The Boy Scouts of America (BSA) has proposed to lift the ban on gay youth members but maintain the exclusion of gays as adult leaders. This decision is set to be voted on by the BSA's National Council during a meeting in Texas, scheduled for May 20th. The change comes after surveys sent out this year showed that a majority of scouting community members support lifting the ban for youth members.

The proposal has received mixed reactions, with some gay rights groups demanding a complete lifting of the ban, while conservative and religious groups have expressed opposition to including gays as adult leaders. The Mormon Church, one of the largest supporters of the Scouts, is currently studying the proposal.

This decision by the BSA is significant in the ongoing debate over gay rights in the United States, where public opinion is shifting towards greater acceptance. The Supreme Court is expected to rule on parts of a federal law defining marriage as between a man and a woman, and the military repealed its ban on openly gay soldiers in 2011.

The BSA's proposal would allow gay youth to become scouts but require them to resign when they become adults. This could lead to a situation where a gay youth member would have to leave the Scouts upon turning 18. The policy remains unchanged for adult leaders, who must continue to meet the group's adult standards to remain in the organization.

Scientists have discovered a crow-sized, bird-like dinosaur named Caihong juji in China with colorful rainbow-like feathers that lived 161 million years ago during the Jurassic Period. The discovery suggests a more colorful Jurassic World than previously imagined. The dinosaur had iridescent feathers, particularly on its head, neck, and chest, with colors that shimmered and shifted in the light, like those of hummingbirds. The dinosaur was a two-legged predator with a Velociraptor-like skull and sharp teeth, probably hunting small mammals and lizards. It had crests above its eyes that looked like bony eyebrows. Caihong is the earliest-known creature with asymmetrical feathers, a trait used by birds to steer when flying. The dinosaur's full scientific name means "rainbow with a big crest."

Juan Salaz, a 37-year-old American citizen who escaped from a Texas prison in 1997, has been captured by Mexican authorities after nearly 16 years on the run. Salaz was serving three concurrent 35-year sentences for aggravated kidnapping with a deadly weapon and two counts of attempted capital murder of a police officer. He escaped by climbing over three 16-foot razor wire topped fences from the Garza East prison in Beeville, Texas. Salaz was suspected of being in Monterrey, Mexico as recently as three years ago, with investigators believing he had family support in Houston helping him cross the border. He now faces additional charges for his escape and will be extradited to the U.S. once the Mexican government approves it. With Salaz's capture, Jose Fernando Bustos-Diaz remains the only Texas prison fugitive, having escaped in 2010 from the Brisco Unit in Dilley, near San Antonio.

A 25-year-old German man developed seizures after solving Sudoku puzzles, which he enjoyed doing in his free time. The seizures were triggered by a three-dimensional imagination that activated when he solved Sudoku puzzles. This unusual response was due to hypoxia (oxygen deprivation) suffered during an avalanche, which resulted in the death of inhibitory fibers in the right centro-parietal region of his brain. Normally, this area is activated when 3D imagination is used. With fewer inhibitory fibers, when the man used his 3D imagination to solve Sudoku puzzles, it led to an overactivation of this brain region, causing clonic seizures in his left arm. The man has been seizure-free for more than five years by giving up Sudoku and taking anti-epileptic medication regularly.

The drug works by triggering the production of melanin in the skin, similar to how UV light does, but without causing damage. The researchers are currently testing the safety of the drug and plan to combine it with sunscreen for maximum protection from solar radiation. The drug may also potentially allow for a "ginger tan" as it could bypass the genetic mutation that causes red hair and fair skin to disrupt the normal process where UV light leads to dark melanin.

California has agreed to end its prolonged isolation of imprisoned gang leaders, moving away from a practice that kept hundreds of inmates in segregation units for over a decade. The new policy will only isolate inmates who commit new crimes behind bars and no longer lock gang members in soundproofed cells solely to prevent them from directing illegal activities.

The settlement aims to limit the duration of isolation, create restrictive custody units for inmates who refuse rehabilitation programs or break prison rules, and house those who might be in danger if they live with other inmates. The conditions in solitary confinement were previously criticized as cruel and unusual punishment, with about half of the nearly 3,000 inmates held in such units having no physical contact with visitors and limited reading materials and communications with the outside world.

The lawsuit was initially filed by two killers serving time in the security housing unit at Pelican Bay in 2009. The settlement is seen as a significant step towards ending solitary confinement in California and across the country, according to Jules Lobel, the lead attorney for the Center for Constitutional Rights. However, concerns have been expressed by prison guards' unions about potential increased danger for guards due to the policy changes.

A large crack has formed in a window on the 36th floor of San Francisco's sinking Millennium Tower, prompting officials to investigate the condition of the glass panel and adjacent curtain wall system. The study conducted by researchers from the University of York reveals that exposure to small doses of fluoxetine, the generic name for Prozac, can disrupt the courtship behavior of wild starlings. The researchers found that male starlings sang less and were more aggressive towards female starlings that had been exposed to Prozac-laced worms. Female starlings, on the other hand, did not seem to be affected in their attraction towards males that had consumed small amounts of Prozac. The study suggests that this could potentially lead to fewer baby birds being born and a decline in the number of starlings, but further research is needed to confirm this. The findings add to growing evidence that environmental concentrations of pharmaceuticals can alter important traits related to individual fitness and population dynamics.

The Pueblo Board of Water Works was not aware of the spill until reporters made inquiries. SkyMall, the in-flight shopping catalog known for its quirky and often humorous product offerings, has filed for bankruptcy protection due to increased use of electronic devices on planes and competition from online retailers like Amazon. The company's sales have been declining since 2013, with revenue dropping from $33.7 million in 2013 to $15.8 million for the nine months ended September 28, 2014. Delta and Southwest Airlines are among its creditors. The company plans to sell its online retail business and other assets through a court-supervised auction.

A group of 12 boys and their football coach who had been trapped in a flooded cave in Thailand for 10 days have been found alive by rescuers. They were discovered on Monday night, nine days after they entered the caves in Chiang Rai province following a football training session. The boys are believed to be mostly non-swimmers, complicating the rescue efforts. Rescuers are now considering various methods to bring them to safety, including teaching them to dive or waiting for the flooding to recede. The boys have received their first food and medical treatment since they were trapped, with none of them reported to be in a serious condition. The Thai authorities have appealed for donations of full-face scuba diving masks small enough to fit the boys, as well as infrastructure to be built within the cave to facilitate their evacuation. The rescue operation has gripped the nation and families of the missing group were ecstatic at news of their discovery.

The new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found no direct link between antidepressant use during pregnancy, specifically selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), and one type of birth defect, heart malformations. This contradicts previous research that suggested taking antidepressants during pregnancy could be risky. The study was conducted over a seven-year period from 2000 to 2007, using data from 46 states and Washington D.C., focusing on women on Medicaid without supplementary private insurance. The researchers looked at various factors that could interfere with the data, including maternal age, income, education, depression diagnoses, and other psychotropic medications. The study found no increased risk of heart defects in babies born to mothers who took antidepressants during the first three months of pregnancy. However, the findings contradict two previous studies that warned about the risks associated with paroxetine (Paxil) and early prenatal exposure.

Howard Stern, a long-time friend of Donald Trump, expressed concerns about Trump's mental health and wellbeing due to his presidency. Stern believes that Trump desires acceptance and admiration, which he may not receive in the role of president. The parents of a missing 3-year-old girl in Richardson have hired attorneys and are no longer cooperating with investigators. The child, Sherin Mathews, was last seen at 3 a.m. Saturday by her father, Wesley Mathews, who has been arrested on a child endangerment charge. The mother of the missing girl is reportedly distraught and has hired an attorney to avoid any potential conflict of interest. An FBI Evidence Response team processed the family's home, and the search for Sherin has expanded beyond the immediate neighborhood. The girl's father directed her to stand outside their home after she wouldn't drink her milk at 3 a.m., but he discovered that she was gone when he returned 15 minutes later. The delay in reporting the matter is concerning to police, and they are continuing to search for Sherin.

The Los Angeles City Council voted to raise the minimum wage to $15 per hour by July 2020, making it the largest city in the U.S. to do so. The decision is part of a broader national effort to alleviate poverty and spur similar increases in other parts of the country. However, business groups have expressed concerns that the mandate will force employers to lay off workers or leave the city altogether due to increased labor costs. The proposal affects 609,000 workers by 2019, with average annual earnings increasing by $4,800 in 2014 dollars. The move toward a higher minimum wage has been led by Democrats seeking to address income inequality and follows similar wage increase measures in Seattle and San Francisco.

The article discusses the Indianapolis Colts' loss to Jacksonville Jaguars, securing them the No. 1 pick in the upcoming draft. Peyton Manning, who missed the entire season due to neck surgery, spoke about his recovery and the possibility of playing with next year's top draft pick, Stanford quarterback Andrew Luck. The Colts' future is uncertain as they are in a state of transition, with questions surrounding coach Jim Caldwell's job security and the potential retirement of long-time center Jeff Saturday. Seven students and one teacher from Otawara High School in Tochigi Prefecture have died after being caught in an avalanche at Nasu Onsen Family Ski Resort, north of Tokyo. More than 40 people were injured, including two who are in critical condition. The incident occurred during a three-day mountain climbing event involving students from seven high schools and their instructors. The region had received heavy snow over the past two days and avalanche warnings were in effect. Rescue efforts were hampered by bad weather conditions, with dozens of troops involved. An investigation will be conducted to determine whether professional negligence played a role in the incident.

The deputy director of the White House's Office of National Drug Control Policy, Michael Botticelli, admitted at a House Oversight Committee hearing that marijuana is less deadly than alcohol. However, he maintained that marijuana is not a benign drug and poses a "totality of harm." Despite President Obama's recent comments supporting state-based efforts to legalize marijuana, the administration still opposes such efforts. The hearing highlighted the ongoing conflict between federal and state laws regarding marijuana, with some officials expressing concerns about disparities in enforcement policies affecting minorities. The D.C. city council recently voted to decriminalize marijuana possession, putting Congress in a position to potentially intervene due to its authority over D.C. municipal laws.

Engineers at the University of Twente in the Netherlands have developed sperm-like robots inspired by human sperm cells. The robots, named "MagnetoSperm," are controlled using magnetic fields and could potentially be used for medical applications such as targeted drug delivery and in vitro fertilization.

The MagnetoSperm consist of a flexible tail made from a strong but flexible polymer, with a metal-coated head that is steered by the magnetic field. The researchers were able to navigate the robots towards a fixed point by adjusting the magnetic field changes with a computer. Despite moving at a slower pace than human sperm, the MagnetoSperm demonstrate precise navigation and could be useful for positioning materials in nanomanufacturing.

The researchers plan to test the technique in more complicated environments and work on making their robots smaller and faster. Dr Matthew Baker, who studies molecular motors at the Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute in Sydney, called the work "very cool" but noted that the tiny contraptions are not traditional robots as they rely on an external magnetic field for power and navigation.

Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez has turned to a controversial horse placenta healer from Serbia, Marijana Kovacevic, to address the team's injury crisis. England defender Glen Johnson and Fabio Aurelio flew to Belgrade for treatment on their calf injuries, joining other Premier League stars like Robin van Persie of Arsenal who have sought her unorthodox methods. Liverpool currently have several injury concerns, including Fernando Torres' inguinal hernia, Alberto Aquilani's recovery from a long-term back injury, and lingering doubts about Riera and Martin Skrtel.

In Kolkata, India, a Jet Airways plane arriving from Patna experienced a bomb scare and subsequent smuggling investigation after two lunch boxes containing 12 gold bars each were discovered hidden in the plane's toilets during routine cleaning. The gold bars, weighing approximately 1 kg each and worth around $1.18 million, are believed to have originated from Dubai, the flight's usual route being between Dubai and Mumbai, India's largest gold market.

This incident highlights a rise in gold smuggling into India due to increased import duties and restrictions, making it difficult for authorities to keep up with the numerous smuggling groups operating. Finance Minister P. Chidambaram acknowledged that these measures have led to a slight increase in smuggling activities.

Investigations are ongoing, involving questioning of airline and airport staff, as well as checking the profiles of passengers on the flight from Dubai. Previously, a man was arrested for concealing 5 kg of gold in an Air India plane's toilet in Dubai.

Airport authorities are taking measures to prevent future incidents, such as educating staff about aircraft maps and asking crew members to report passengers spending extended periods in the toilets.

The case remained unsolved until March 2014 when an investigator revisited the cold case and sent DNA samples for testing. Seven months later, state DOJ technicians reported that the DNA in the semen found on Derryberry's body matched the genetic profiles of Patterson and Harbour, who each had their DNA collected due to past criminal activities.

Authorities are awaiting forensic results to determine if Long was drugged and whether gunpowder residue was found on her hands. The World Health Organization (WHO) has declared Cuba as the first country in the world to successfully stop the transmission of both HIV and syphilis from mothers to their babies. This achievement is considered one of the greatest public health achievements possible, marking a significant step towards an AIDS-free generation.

The prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV can be achieved through the administration of drugs to both the mother and the newborn, provided that the mother has been tested and knows she is infected, and the necessary drugs are available. In 2013, 67% of pregnant women infected with HIV in low- and middle-income countries were able to get the required drugs.

Similarly, stopping syphilis transmission can be achieved through the administration of antibiotics to treat the infection. WHO estimates that nearly 1 million pregnant women worldwide are infected with syphilis annually, leading to numerous deaths or premature births of infected babies.

Cuba's success in eliminating mother-to-child transmission is attributed to its universal access to healthcare and prenatal care, early HIV and syphilis testing, and treatment for mothers who test positive. This achievement is expected to encourage other countries to redouble their efforts in the fight against AIDS and sexually transmitted infections.

The electronic construction signs in Dallas were hacked over the Memorial Day weekend, displaying political messages targeting Donald Trump and promoting Bernie Sanders for president. A massive mudslide in Washington state on March 23, 2014, left at least eight people dead and dozens missing. The slide, which was about a mile wide, destroyed dozens of homes and buried a mile-long stretch of Highway 530 under 20 feet or more of mud. The area around the Big Four ice caves will remain closed until search and rescue teams can assess the safety of the caves and recover the deceased victim of the collapse.

The article discusses an incident where a diner named Allison Hiromi was kicked out of the Down House restaurant in Houston for making a negative comment about a bartender on Twitter. This marks one of the first instances of a customer being asked to leave a restaurant due to online behavior.

The incident occurred when Hiromi called a bartender a "twerp" on Twitter, and the manager asked her to leave over the phone. The Down House owner Chris Cusack stated that any business is allowed to set the tone of their establishment, and if a customer starts calling names, they are unlikely to stay for long.

The incident has sparked discussions on social media, with some people vowing never to go to Down House again, while others believe the restaurant owes Hiromi an apology. However, Barbara Magana-Roberston, a public relations representative, believes that all the talk, whether positive or negative, may ultimately be beneficial for the restaurant's visibility in the long run.

Restaurateurs and bar owners aim to encourage patrons to enjoy their experiences and share them on social media. A new internet prank called "Put 'em in a coffin" has caused damage to a Houston resident's BMW and his wife's car. The prank involves teenagers performing a backward dive onto the hood of cars, as seen in viral videos on YouTube and social media. James McHugh, the victim, had both hoods smashed in, with the damage estimated to cost around $4,000. The incident was captured by McHugh's home security camera showing a group of seven young men approaching his car last Friday night on Plaza del Sol Park. McHugh expressed frustration over the senseless and expensive prank.

James Joseph Dresnok, an American soldier who defected to North Korea in 1962 and was believed to be the last US defector living there, passed away last year at the age of 74. Dresnok's sons, Ted and James, confirmed his death in a video interview on the state-run Uriminzokkiri website. The brothers, who were born in North Korea and speak Korean with a heavy northern accent, pledged their loyalty to Kim Jong-un and criticized the US for raising "war hysteria madness" in the region. Tensions have been escalating between Pyongyang and Washington due to North Korea's recent testing of intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBM). Dresnok, who was known as Joe, had crossed a minefield at 21 to reach North Korea after his wife divorced him and he was reportedly about to be court-martialed. He was the subject of a British documentary in 2006 and expressed satisfaction with his life in Pyongyang, despite the country's isolation. Dresnok also stated that he would not leave North Korea even if offered a billion dollars in gold.

In a groundbreaking study, researchers have found microplastics in stool samples from eight individuals across eight countries. The study, presented at UEG Week in Vienna, revealed the presence of various types of plastic, most commonly polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate, which are commonly used in plastic bottles. On average, 20 microplastic particles were found per 10g of stool. The participants were exposed to plastics through consumption of plastic-wrapped foods or drinking from plastic bottles. The study suggests that humans may be ingesting microplastics unintentionally and highlights the need for further research on their potential health effects.

Dennis Rodman, a former NBA player known for his friendship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, returned to North Korea as a private citizen for a visit. This marks his first trip since President Donald Trump took office. Rodman's purpose is to promote sports in North Korea and potentially establish some form of dialogue between the two countries. His trip is sponsored by a digital currency company that provides services for the marijuana industry.

Rodman has been criticized for visiting North Korea during times of high tension between the US and North Korea over its weapons programs. He has received the red-carpet treatment on past trips since 2013, but his visits have also been condemned by human rights activists. Rodman has previously encouraged former US President Barack Obama to contact Kim Jong-un, a concept referred to as "basketball diplomacy" in the US press.

In 2014, Rodman arranged a basketball game with other former NBA players and North Koreans, and he also suggested that an American missionary was at fault for his own imprisonment in North Korea, remarks for which he later apologized. The visit is a political minefield due to the strained relations between the US and North Korea, as Americans are considered enemies in North Korea.

Rodman's trip is being sponsored by Potcoin, a digital currency used to buy and sell marijuana in state-regulated markets.

The U.S. President Barack Obama has stated that he will veto a bill introduced in the Senate allowing Congress to weigh in on any deal reached with Iran regarding its nuclear capabilities. The bill would require the submission of any agreement within five days of concluding a final deal with Iran and would prohibit Obama from suspending or waiving sanctions on Iran for 60 days after a deal. The negotiations between the U.S., Russia, China, France, Germany, Britain, and Iran have reached a crucial stage, with a basic framework agreement due by the end of March. Tensions have arisen between the U.S. and Israel ahead of a speech in Washington by Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu, who is expected to warn against a possible nuclear deal with Iran. The Obama administration has expressed concern that Netanyahu's visit could jeopardize ongoing negotiations with Iran and has accused him of trying to undermine the talks.

Mexico's President Enrique Pena Nieto has announced a nationwide anti-crime plan in response to public outrage over the abduction and suspected massacre of 43 college students in Iguala, Guerrero state. The plan includes proposals to put local police under the control of state governments, simplify divisions between federal, state, and local law enforcement, establish a national identity number or document, and deploy more federal police to troubled regions like Guerrero, Michoacan, Jalisco, and Tamaulipas. The reforms aim to address rampant corruption and lawlessness in Mexico, particularly within municipal police forces that are often co-opted by drug cartels. The proposals will be presented to Congress next week and include the launch of a single, nationwide emergency phone number. President Pena Nieto's announcement comes two months after the students disappeared, sparking mass protests across the country.

Former American model Christina Estrada was awarded a $68 million divorce settlement from her wealthy Saudi businessman ex-husband, Sheikh Walid Juffali, in London's High Court. The settlement includes cash and assets worth approximately £75 million ($102 million), making it the largest "needs award" ever granted by an English court. Estrada had been seeking a total of $309 million from Juffali, who is worth an estimated $10 billion, but the final settlement falls short of her initial request. The divorce was controversial as Juffali divorced Estrada under Islamic law without her knowledge while still married to another woman and welcoming two children with her. Estrada argued in court that she needed £1 million per year for clothes, including £40,000 for fur coats, £109,000 for haute couture dresses, and £21,000 for shoes. The settlement includes a Lamborghini car worth $300,000 or an additional $140,000 payment. Juffali could not attend court due to advanced lung cancer treatment in Switzerland.

The European Chess Union (ECU) has implemented a new dress code for chess tournaments, following observations that many players were not dressing appropriately during games. The ECU General Secretary, Sava Stoisavljevic, stated that this is the first European tournament where these regulations are being applied. The rules aim to ensure players wear proper clothes, similar to dress codes in other sports.

Regarding women's attire, the regulations state that shirts should be buttoned up to the second button from the top, and there are no restrictions on skirt length mentioned yet. However, Stoisavljevic expressed a desire for some limit due to comments received from spectators and coaches about players wearing very short skirts.

The ECU also prohibits caps or hats, except for religious reasons, to avoid cheating. The new dress code was introduced during the 2012 European Individual Women Chess Championship in Gaziantep, Turkey, and includes detailed guidelines for both men and women's attire during games and award ceremonies. Players who fail to adhere to the dress code may face warnings or even be denied access to the playing area.

The new regulations aim to maintain a classy image for chess tournaments, as some players were observed dressing inappropriately, potentially causing distractions during games. The ECU believes these rules will be more useful during men's events and expects minimal trouble

The Trump administration has denied a request from the House Oversight Committee for additional information on payments received by former national security adviser Michael Flynn from foreign governments, including Russia-backed television station RT and other Russian firms. The committee is investigating whether Flynn broke the law by failing to disclose these payments when applying for a security clearance in 2016.

During a private briefing on Tuesday, the Oversight Committee reviewed documents from the Pentagon that suggest Flynn may have failed to disclose foreign income from Russia and Turkey when applying for his security clearance. The Zhangjiajie Grand Canyon Glass Bridge in China, set to open next month, will be the world's longest and highest glass-bottomed bridge. It spans 430 meters between two cliffs at an altitude of 300 meters above ground. To assure safety concerns, a BBC reporter performed a safety test by hitting one of the panels with a sledgehammer, which showed cracks but remained intact. The bridge is designed by Israeli architect Haim Dotan and can hold up to 800 people at once. Plans include using it as a fashion runway and a bungee jumping point. However, concerns about safety have been raised following incidents like the Yuntaishan glass bridge in China's Henan province that cracked last September due to a tourist dropping a thermos flask on one of the panels.

On Tuesday night, a powerful magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck the Caribbean Sea off the coast of Honduras, causing shaking across much of the nation and triggering tsunami warnings that were later cancelled. The epicenter was located about 202 kilometers north-northeast of Barra Patuca, Honduras, and 303 kilometers southwest of George Town, Cayman Islands, at a depth of approximately 10 kilometers below the surface. Although there were initial concerns about potential damage and casualties, no serious incidents were reported. The northern coast of Honduras closest to the quake's epicenter is sparsely populated, with much of it covered by nature reserves. This earthquake was one of the largest to hit the Caribbean in recorded history, surpassed only by the 2010 quake that devastated Haiti.

Roman Polanski is a renowned film director, known for his works such as Rosemary's Baby and Chinatown. Born in Paris in 1933, he moved to Hollywood in 1968. Tragedy struck when his wife, actress Sharon Tate, was murdered by members of the Charles Manson cult in 1969. In 1977, Polanski was indicted on six criminal counts for having sexual relations with a minor. The alleged act involved a 13-year-old girl and took place in the home of actor Jack Nicholson. Despite fleeing the US after his discharge from psychiatric evaluation, Polanski continued to face the possibility of prison if he returned. In recent news, Polanski's lawyer is seeking to unseal secret testimony that could potentially resolve his decades-old child rape case and allow him to return to the United States.

Search teams are investigating a number of sounds detected by ships in the southern Indian Ocean as potential leads in the ongoing search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, which disappeared nearly a month ago with 239 people on board. A Chinese ship reported picking up electronic signals twice, once on Friday and again on Saturday, and an Australian naval vessel is pursuing a separate detection. The detections are being treated as "an important and encouraging lead," but have not yet been verified as related to Flight 370. Up to 10 military planes, two civil aircraft, and 13 ships will assist in Sunday's search, which will take place in three separate areas about 2,000 kilometers northwest of Perth, Australia. White objects were also spotted near the area where the sound was detected, but there is no confirmation that they are related to Flight 370. The search for the missing airliner is being led by the Australian Maritime Safety Authority and is entering its most intensive phase before batteries on the data recorders fade.
