An employee at the printing business besieged by the attackers, named as Lilian Lepere, helped police kill the terrorists after texting tactical information to them from his hiding place within the building. The brothers had taken a hostage but released him after he helped Said with a neck wound he had sustained in a firefight with police. A separate siege at a kosher supermarket in Paris also ended, resulting in four deaths and the discovery of several hostages who were later freed. The attacks were claimed by al-Qaeda as revenge for the magazine's satire of the Prophet Muhammad. Both brothers had prior convictions related to terrorism and were on the U.S. no-fly list.

The 15-year-old girl, Jahi McMath, who was declared brain dead in 2013 after a tonsillectomy, is reportedly "as healthy and beautiful as ever" according to her mother's recent Facebook update. This update comes three months after the family moved Jahi from Children's Hospital Oakland to an unidentified long-term care facility following a legal battle over her care. The family has since relocated to Franklin Township, New Jersey, where they have been living.

Jahi's family is currently suing the hospital for the allegedly botched surgery and accusing officials of pressuring them to donate Jahi's organs. Her mother, Nailah Winkfield, has also filed a federal lawsuit to void her daughter's death certificate. The family has expressed gratitude for the support they have received from the public, stating that it has helped raise awareness about Jahi's condition and potentially changed societal views on brain death. However, many medical experts argue that being brain dead essentially means being dead, and it may be just a matter of time before Jahi’s body functions shut down completely.

A federal class-action lawsuit has been filed against Spin Master, the manufacturer of Hatchimals, a popular toy that hatched from an egg during the holiday season. The lawsuit alleges that millions of families were disappointed when their Hatchimals failed to hatch as advertised, causing frustration and anger among consumers. Jodie Hejduk, the lead plaintiff, purchased a Hatchimal for her daughter's birthday but was disappointed when it did not hatch. The lawsuit seeks compensatory, statutory, and punitive damages, as well as a recall of defective Hatchimals. Spin Master has denied the allegations and stated that they provided troubleshooting support and replacement products for those few consumers whose toys did not work as anticipated.

A measles-like virus known as morbillivirus is causing a mass die-off of bottlenose dolphins along the U.S. East Coast, with over 330 carcasses found since July 1 between New York and North Carolina. The outbreak has been declared an Unusual Mortality Event by NOAA, which has tested 33 beached dolphins, finding that 32 had either confirmed or suspected cases of the virus. The die-off is reminiscent of a similar outbreak in 1987-88 and is expected to continue until spring 2014. Scientists are collecting tissue samples from deceased dolphins for further analysis, but there is no easy way to identify morbillivirus infection just by looking at a carcass. The virus suppresses the immune system of dolphins, causing lesions on their skin, lymph nodes, and brain. There is almost no chance the virus can spread to humans, as it is species-specific. However, NOAA advises swimmers with open wounds to take precautions in areas where infected dolphins have been found, as sick dolphins often contract other infections that can spread to humans. At this point, there isn't a vaccine or easy way to stop the virus from spreading among wild populations of bottlenose dolphins.

NASA is developing a concept for a nuclear-powered, one-ton robotic submarine named the Titan Submarine to explore Kraken Mare, one of the methane seas on Titan, Saturn's moon. The sub will be equipped with a seafloor camera and sampling system and could study the moon's tides, weather, shoreline, and potentially search for evidence of life forms in super-chilly, gassy environments.

The Titan Submarine is still in its preliminary stages, and it might not be deployed until around 2047. The sub will likely be transported to Titan using a space plane like Boeing's X-37, which could make a soft water landing on Kraken Mare and jettison the sub or drop it at low altitude via a parachute.

Titan is an unusual moon with an atmosphere one-and-a-half times denser than Earth's, mostly nitrogen and methane, and temperatures reaching -179 degrees Celsius (-290 degrees Fahrenheit). The article from CNN reports that the identity of John Doe No. 89, a victim found in San Francisco in 1979 with multiple gunshot wounds, has been revealed as Andy Drath. Drath's half-sister, Dr. Willia Wertheimer, submitted DNA that proved crucial in the identification process. The discovery brings closure to Drath's family and demonstrates the importance of not giving up on cold cases. The article also includes a slideshow of infamous serial killers throughout history.

The pending trial of Charlo Greene, a former reporter who quit live on air to advocate for marijuana legalization in Alaska, raises questions about the ongoing war on drugs and could have broader legal implications as more states move towards legalization. Greene is facing increased charges, potentially up to 54 years in prison, for her involvement with the Alaska Cannabis Club, which she founded after quitting her job in 2014. The club was targeted by law enforcement despite marijuana being legalized in Alaska in 2014. Greene's case has been criticized as a "modern day lynching" and raises concerns about the disproportionate targeting of people of color for marijuana offenses. Despite her viral on-air resignation, Greene struggles to gain support for her criminal case.

The incident was captured on dashcam video. Authorities found a .38-caliber pistol in Ford's car and a wad of cash covered in red ink. Ford is also suspected in bank robberies in Stow and Akron, including one at the FirstMerit branch in Streetsboro where he handed a teller a note demanding money without producing a gun. A California man captured a terrifying video of a great white shark breaking into a shark cage with a diver inside during a diving trip off Mexico's Guadalupe Island last week. The diver, Ming Chan, emerged unharmed but shaken after the incident. In the video, the shark smashed through the cage and leaped out the top, causing the diver to end up outside the bottom of the cage, looking down on two great white sharks. The videographer explained that the shark was temporarily blinded and unable to swim backwards when it lunged at a bait tied to the cage, causing it to break through. Despite the incident, both Chan and the videographer plan to return for another great white shark adventure next year. The video became one of the biggest viral videos of 2016. Following the incident, the boat crew reviewed the cage design and bait techniques to ensure safety for both sharks and divers.

However, after an independent lab examination, the results confirmed that the product was chicken and not a rat as claimed by Dixon. KFC is now asking for an apology from Dixon for making false claims. The man initially spoke with the restaurant manager who allegedly admitted to serving him a rat, but later retained an attorney and refused to communicate directly with KFC.

The document discusses a new children's book titled "The Rabbit Who Wants To Fall Asleep," written by Swedish psychologist Carl-Johan Forssen Ehrlin. The book has become Amazon's bestseller and is designed to help children fall asleep within minutes through psychological reinforcement techniques.

The story follows Roger the Rabbit, who embarks on a quest for sleep with the assistance of characters like Uncle Yawn, Sleepy Snail, and Heavy-Eyed Owl. The language pattern and sentence structure in the book are said to keep children focused on relaxation and induce sleep.

An escape tunnel has been discovered at the site of the infamous Nazi death camp in Sobibor, Poland. The tunnel, found 5 feet below the surface and spanning 32 feet, was likely dug by prisoners desperate to escape the camp. Although there's no evidence that anyone used it successfully, the tunnel provides physical evidence of prisoners trying to escape. Sobibor operated between 1942 and 1943, claiming an estimated 250,000 lives, mostly Jews. The camp was razed after a prisoner uprising in October 1943, making archaeological excavations challenging. In addition to the tunnel, researchers have found a crematorium, human skeletal remains, and personal items belonging to children.

John Forbes Nash Jr., the renowned mathematician and subject of the Oscar-winning film "A Beautiful Mind," passed away in a car accident last month along with his wife, Alicia. In remembrance, Princeton University has digitized and released Nash's academic file, which includes a recommendation letter from his undergraduate advisor Richard Duffin that played a crucial role in his acceptance into Princeton's graduate school in 1948. The letter described Nash as "a mathematical genius."

Nash went on to win the Nobel Prize for economics in 1994 and was also awarded the Abel Prize for mathematics posthumously. His dissertation, titled "Non-cooperative games," introduced the concept of the "Nash equilibrium," a significant contribution to game theory that has been cited over 7,000 times. Nash's dissertation was remarkably short, just 27 pages long, and cited only two sources: John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern, the founders of game theory, and himself.

In this case, Robert McCoy is on Louisiana's death row for a triple homicide he vehemently denies committing. His defense attorney, Larry English, admitted his guilt in the trial, despite McCoy's objections. This strategy was employed to potentially get a conviction on a lesser murder charge and avoid the death sentence.

However, McCoy's attorneys argue that English's actions violated the Sixth Amendment's promise of "assistance of counsel for his defense." They claim that English's actions were not in line with the defendant's right to make decisions about his own defense and misrepresented McCoy's innocence.

The Supreme Court is set to review McCoy's conviction, addressing the question of whether it violates the Constitution for a defense counsel to concede a client's guilt over the accused's express objection. Malaysian Airlines Flight MH17 was downed by a Russian-made Buk missile, according to a final report by the Dutch Safety Board. The missile hit the front left of the plane, causing other parts to break off and structural damage. In a landmark High Court case, a severely disabled woman in the final stages of multiple sclerosis lost her challenge to Ireland's absolute ban on assisted suicide. The court ruled that the ban is justified to protect vulnerable individuals and does not breach the woman's personal autonomy or equality rights under the Constitution and European Convention on Human Rights.

Fleming, a former university lecturer, had argued that the blanket ban on assisted suicide breached her personal rights under the Constitution and ECHR due to her specific circumstances. She feared a distressing and undignified death and wanted the lawful right to be helped to die by her partner without risking his prosecution.

The court's decision follows high-profile right-to-die cases in Britain, where similar bids for legal assistance to die have been unsuccessful. Assisted suicide is only permitted in four European countries: Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Switzerland. If Fleming chooses to appeal the decision, it will go to the Supreme Court.

This incident has caused concern among guitar builders due to the retroactive nature of the law, potentially requiring them to prove the provenance of wood they acquired decades ago. The government's enforcement of the Lacey Act aims to reduce illegal logging and promote responsible sourcing of wood.

In this summary, Jonah Hill hosted SNL for the third time, giving a solid performance despite the overwhelming cast size of 17 members. The reviewer found the "Lamborghini" sketch hilarious and appreciated Leonardo DiCaprio's appearance during the monologue. However, they expressed concerns about the large cast making it difficult to get to know individual members, including Brooks Wheelan.

Other notable sketches included a reimagined version of Spike Jonze's "Her", where Hill fell in love with his own operating system, and an interview with Kenan Thompson as the Miami police officer who arrested Justin Bieber. The reviewer also commented on the upcoming departure of Seth Meyers and the replacement by Colin Jost. Overall, the episode scored 5.73 out of 10.

Lady Gaga's latest album, 'Born This Way,' has been banned in Lebanon due to its lyrics being deemed offensive to Christianity and having poor taste. The ban follows a similar decision made regarding her single 'Judas.' Malaysia has also banned the title track of the album for promoting homosexuality. The album went platinum in its first week in the US, but its release has been met with controversy overseas due to Gaga's perceived religious insensitivity. In response to the bans, Gaga encouraged young people in affected countries to speak up and have their voices heard. She previously criticized the influence of institutionalized religion on government in a recent interview with The Guardian.

News Corp has announced the closure of its 168-year-old U.K. tabloid, News of the World, following a scandal involving controversial reporting tactics and phone hacking. The paper, known for its investigative journalism, celebrity gossip, and right-wing political stance, was accused of intercepting voice mails of everyday people, including a 13-year-old murder victim, as well as celebrities.

James Murdoch, News Corp's deputy chief operating officer, stated that the allegations were "inhuman" and had no place in the company. The closure comes after years of investigations into the use of private detectives to break into mobile phone voice mails of celebrities and political leaders.

The controversy has threatened a proposed buyout of British Sky Broadcasting Group PLC by News Corp, and may delay regulatory approval for the deal. The paper accounts for significantly less than half of News Corp's U.K. publishing operations, which are valued at about $1.3 billion.

Nine-year-old James Savage from Los Banos successfully swam from San Francisco Aquatic Park to Alcatraz Island and back on June 14, 2016. This achievement makes him the youngest swimmer on record to complete this challenging open water journey, breaking a previous record held by a 10-year-old. During his swim, James faced strong currents and cold water, but with encouragement from his coach and father, he persevered. The swim took approximately two hours and was supported by a fleet of paddlers. After completing the swim, James expressed his intention to swim the length of the Golden Gate Bridge next.

The trial of former U.S. Senator John Edwards is ongoing, with updates being provided on Twitter and Facebook by The News & Record. Andrew Young, a longtime aide to Edwards, testified about his role in covering up Edwards' affair with Rielle Hunter in 2007 while Edwards was running for president. Young revealed details about the money used to conceal the relationship, including a special "bat phone" that Edwards used to contact Hunter, and how Edwards asked him to claim paternity of Hunter's baby. Edwards has pleaded not guilty to violating campaign finance laws related to nearly $1 million in contributions from heiress Rachel “Bunny” Mellon and Texas trial lawyer Fred Baron that were used to cover up the affair. Edwards is accused of knowingly breaking the law by using illegal campaign donations to keep his mistress quiet and his '08 presidential chances alive, while the defense maintains that it was Young's idea to claim paternity and solicit money from Mellon without Edwards' knowledge.

Justin Bieber announced during an interview that he was retiring after releasing his new album "Journals," but it appears this statement was made in jest, as sources close to him have since confirmed that he is not actually retiring from the music industry. The album, which consists of 10 previously released songs and five unreleased tracks, was released on iTunes from December 16th through January 2nd, 2014. Bieber's "Believe" concert documentary will also be released in theaters on Christmas Day.

The viral video on Steven Stubenraugh's Facebook page, which has garnered over 3.8 million views, depicts a man punching a kangaroo after it had a dog in a headlock. The incident occurred during a wild pig-hunting trip organized for Kailem, who passed away from cancer last week. The man, known as "Goo," is a zookeeper at Taronga Western Plains Zoo, although this has not been officially confirmed. The dog is reportedly unharmed due to wearing a breastplate designed to protect it from boar tusks. The punch was meant as self-defense and was not intended to harm the kangaroo significantly, according to trip organizer Mathew Amor.

The New York Post is reporting that there are discussions about JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon as a potential replacement for current Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner. However, it's unclear if Dimon would be a natural fit in the Obama administration due to differences on key issues such as the establishment of a consumer-protection agency and how to handle too-big-to-fail banks. Dimon opposes the agency and has defended big banks' right to exist, which contradicts White House policy. Additionally, Dimon has no plans to leave JPMorgan for at least the next six or seven years. Geithner is still facing criticism in Congress over his handling of the government's financial-system bailout, persistently high unemployment, and the weakness of the dollar.

The U.S. speedskating team will switch back to their previously-approved Under Armour suits for the remainder of the Winter Olympic Games in Sochi, after struggling with a new suit design that was introduced only last month. The team's poor performance throughout six events, including the world's top-ranked skaters Shani Davis and Heather Richardson, led to pressure for the change. The Mach 39 suits, developed with defense contractor Lockheed Martin, were marketed as the fastest ever in the sport but became a target of criticism this week from athletes who claimed the vents on the back of the suit were letting in air and making it harder for them to skate with proper form. The team will revert to the older suits they wore during more successful World Cup events last fall, which have already been brought to Sochi by some skaters. Under Armour expressed confidence in the performance benefits of all three suit configurations provided to the team.

The federal contractor Reality Winner, a 25-year-old who was charged with leaking a classified document about Russian hacking of U.S. electoral systems to The Intercept, had a top-secret security clearance despite being young and having an active social media presence. This is common in the NSA as many frontline intelligence workers are young enlisted personnel. Winner served in the Air Force from 2010 until December 2016 and worked as a contractor at an NSA facility in Georgia. Her arrest highlights a cultural shift where a small but growing subset of spy agency employees are leaking secrets to the public, such as Chelsea Manning and Edward Snowden. Winner's Twitter account shows her disdain for Trump and follows accounts related to Anonymous and WikiLeaks. She is facing one count of "gathering, transmitting or losing defense information." Her attorney believes the government has a political agenda in going after her client.

An American financial trader named Josh Sanchez-Maldonado, aged 24 from Puerto Rico, has gone missing in London after traveling there for a job interview. He was last seen leaving his hotel on October 22 and was due to return to the US via Dublin the next day but did not catch the flight. His family is highly concerned for his well-being and have come to the UK to plead for information about his whereabouts. Sanchez-Maldonado was staying at the St. Giles Hotel in Feltham, London, and had arrived in the UK on his first solo trip outside the US. The family described him as a "very goal oriented, very organized, detailed, kind, lovable and respectful person." Police are growing increasingly concerned for his safety and well-being, and anyone with information about his whereabouts is asked to contact the police.

Anne Hathaway and her husband Adam Shulman have welcomed their first child, a baby boy named Jonathan Rosebanks Shulman, on March 24. The couple announced the news to Us Weekly and E! News. Hathaway revealed her pregnancy for the first time in January through an Instagram post, and later posted a photo of her growing baby bump ahead of the Oscars. She had expressed her desire to have a family since she was 16, and in 2012, she stated that she wanted to adopt and have as many children as she could afford. The couple had a relaxed baby shower with friends in March before the birth.

The Kenai City Council in Alaska is considering a proposal to introduce a cat leash law, similar to the existing dog leash law, due to an increase in complaints about roaming cats and a growing cat population at the Kenai Animal Shelter that has strained its resources. The ordinance would require cats to be restrained at all times by a leash, chain, fence, or building, with a maximum penalty of up to $500 per violation.

The proposal was introduced by Mayor Pat Porter and council member Tim Navarre, who cited an increase in complaints about cats roaming freely, defecating on private property, invading plant beds, and disturbing residents' peace. Kenai Animal Control Office Jessica Hendrickson has observed an increase in cat complaints but doesn't have detailed records due to the lack of a current Kenai Municipality Code regarding cat confinement.

Residents Bridgit Gillis and Sheila Holtzen have emphasized such complaints, expressing concerns about cats using their yards as litter boxes and causing health issues. The Kenai Animal Shelter currently has six live traps available for residents to borrow for 14 days.

A rally was held outside the NFL's headquarters in New York on August 23, 2017, with over 1,000 people in attendance to show support for former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick. Kaepernick, who refused to stand for the national anthem as a protest against police brutality, remains unsigned after opting out of his contract with the team in March. Critics argue that his lack of a job is due to his on-field talent, while supporters claim he is being blackballed for his advocacy. The NAACP has called for a meeting with NFL commissioner Roger Goodell to discuss Kaepernick's situation and has accused the league of blackballing him. Some other players have followed in Kaepernick's footsteps, with some kneeling during the national anthem in this year's preseason. The rally concluded after about an hour and a half of speeches, poems, and prayers.

The latest Gallup-Healthways Well-Being Index ranks Hawaii as the state with the highest resident well-being, followed by Alaska. This ranking is based on factors such as residents' sense of purpose, community, social and financial status, and physical health. Nationally, overall well-being remained statistically the same between 2014 and 2015, but there were improvements in areas like financial well-being and perceptions of life satisfaction. However, obesity continued to rise, and more part-time employees were seeking full-time work.

The West dominated the top 10 spots, while the South dominated the bottom 10. Hawaii scored highest by physical well-being, Delaware had the highest sense of purpose, South Carolinians were most socially fulfilled, Alaskans felt most financially secure, and Montanans were happiest with their sense of community.

West Virginia ranked last, followed by Kentucky. Alabama showed the most improvement, rising 18 spots from the previous year. The report also notes positive trends such as a decline in the national uninsured rate, a decline in the overall smoking rate, and an increase in reported exercise. However, food and healthcare insecurity and obesity rates continue to be concerns.

The article discusses the rise of the Joint Special Operations Command (JSOC), a secretive military unit within the United States that has grown significantly since the September 11 attacks in 2001. JSOC is made up primarily of the Army's Delta Force, Navy SEAL Team 6, Air Force's 24th Special Tactics Squadron, and Army's 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment and 75th Ranger Regiment.

The unit has been involved in numerous intelligence-gathering missions and lethal raids, mostly in Iraq and Afghanistan, but also in countries not at war with the United States such as Yemen, Pakistan, Somalia, the Philippines, Nigeria, and Syria. JSOC is known for its extreme secrecy, with troops often working undercover in civilian government agencies or U.S. embassies abroad, and has a reputation for being highly effective in counterterrorism efforts.

The president has given JSOC the authority to select individuals for its kill list and to kill them rather than capture them, a practice that has been criticized as amounting to assassination. JSOC's operations are not considered covert action, but many national security officials argue that they are similar enough to require presidential findings and congressional notification.

Two middle school girls charged with attempting to kill a classmate in Waukesha, Wisconsin, to gain favor with the fictional character Slender Man were ruled competent to stand trial on Thursday. The rulings came after a hearing where mental health experts offered differing conclusions on the defendants' competency. One of the defendants was diagnosed with schizophrenia.

Anissa Weier, 13, was found competent by Waukesha County Circuit Judge Michael Bohren after a three-hour hearing. Morgan Geyser, 12, had been set for a similar hearing but her defense team agreed to the finding of state psychiatrist Kenneth Casimir that she is now competent to proceed.

The girls are charged with attempted first-degree intentional homicide and face up to 60 years in prison if tried as adults. If their cases are moved to juvenile court, they could be held until they're 25. The preliminary hearings, which were charged in June, are now set for February.

At the hearing, mental health professionals testified that Weier was intelligent and cooperative but lacked strategic decision-making ability due to her age and immaturity, not any mental illness. Psychiatrist Robert Rawski thought she showed she could rationally participate in court proceedings and adequately aid in her defense.

Shaniece Luke, a Harlem woman, has received an $11.67 million medical bill from the state Office for People with Developmental Disabilities (OPWDD) for her mentally disabled brother Rasheen Rose's Medicaid assistance between August 2002 and his death in 2012. Luke's attorney, Aaron DePass, believes the bill is retaliation for filing a wrongful death lawsuit against OPWDD and the Queens developmental center where Rose died. The medical examiner ruled Rose's death a homicide due to injuries caused by being physically restrained. Luke alleges that three staff members, including one who sat on Rose, restrained him for up to 30 minutes, leading to his death. Assemblyman Harvey Weisenberg has called the bill an outrage and retaliation. The OPWDD declined comment citing pending litigation.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to archived pages when the original ones are changed or removed. This aims to fix broken links on the web. Meanwhile, actress Salma Hayek mourned the death of her dog Mozart, who was found shot last week on her ranch. Hayek delivered Mozart from his mother's womb nine years ago and described him as loving and loyal. She expressed hope that authorities in Washington State will bring justice for Mozart. The actress shared photos of herself with her dogs on Instagram, including one cuddling with a canine co-star on the set of 'Drunk Parents'. Last July, Hayek was among several A-listers who were outraged over the killing of Cecil the Lion.

The Supreme Court nomination hearing for Brett Kavanaugh began on Tuesday with partisan quarreling, protests, and arrests. Despite Democratic opposition due to political stakes, investigations surrounding President Trump, and potential role in moving the court to the right, there is a sense of inevitability that Kavanaugh will be confirmed, possibly before the first day of the new term on October 1st. The hearing was marked by rancorous exchanges between Democrats and Republicans, with Kavanaugh declaring that the court "must never, never be viewed as a partisan institution." Kavanaugh's confirmation would give Trump his second appointment to the Supreme Court. Barring any major surprises, the committee is expected to vote along party lines to send Kavanaugh's nomination to the full Senate, where Republicans can confirm him without Democratic votes, though they will have little margin for error.

The article discusses two significant events in British politics. Firstly, BBC's political editor Nick Robinson was criticized for violently destroying an anti-war activist's placard during a live broadcast. The incident occurred when the protester repeatedly interrupted Robinson's report. In response to public backlash, Robinson admitted his mistake and expressed regret on his blog.

Secondly, Ed Balls, the symbol of Labour's crushing electoral defeat in 2015, gave his first interview since then. He reflected on his political career, highlighting achievements such as keeping Britain out of the euro, establishing an independent Bank of England, raising education leaving age to 18, implementing Sure Start, introducing the national minimum wage, and changing the health service. Balls also expressed a sense of loss after Labour's defeat but remained optimistic about the future.

On Tuesday, U.S. stocks experienced a decline due to disappointing earnings reports from major companies like Microsoft Corp. and Caterpillar Inc., which raised concerns about the impact of a strong dollar on earnings growth. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 234 points, or 1.3%, to 17445, while the S&P 500 declined 19 points, or 0.9%, to 2038, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 60 points, or 1.3%, to 4711. Microsoft's shares fell 8.5% after the company set its financial forecast for the fiscal year below Wall Street estimates, citing the strong U.S. dollar. Caterpillar's disappointing 2015 outlook and fourth-quarter earnings that missed expectations also contributed to the decline.

The strong U.S. dollar has been a major factor in the tepid outlook for current earnings season, with low expectations driven by the drop in oil prices and weak economic activity overseas. Analysts had expected earnings to rise 1.1% from a year earlier, but the S&P 500 is on track to see earnings inch up 0.1%.

Steve Simoff, a 61-year-old janitor from Davis City, Missouri, walks more than 35 miles to his overnight job at Lakeside Casino in Osceola, Iowa. Due to financial constraints, he often walks along Interstate Highway 35, hitching rides when possible. Simoff's daily commute begins at 3:30 p.m. and can take up to four hours, but he sees it as a necessary step to support his family, including his wife Renee and grandson Steven III. His story mirrors that of James Robertson from Detroit, who made national headlines for walking 21 miles round trip to his factory job. Simoff's community often helps him on his way, with sympathetic good Samaritans offering rides. Despite the challenges, Simoff remains humble and dedicated to his work.

Michael Vaudreuil, a former custodian at Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI), has been hired as an engineer by Pratt & Whitney in Connecticut. After years of juggling full-time work and school, Vaudreuil graduated from WPI with a mechanical engineering degree on May 14. His story went viral after the graduation ceremony, attracting attention from media outlets worldwide. Following his appearance on NBC Nightly News, four employees from Pratt & Whitney contacted him independently about job opportunities. Vaudreuil will start working in July with Pratt & Whitney's Production Integrated Product Team (PIPT), focusing on jet engine combustion chambers and turbine and exhaust systems. His new position is a perfect fit, as he previously earned an associate's degree in aeronautical technology from Wentworth Institute of Technology. Vaudreuil hopes his story will change the perception of older graduates and job candidates, emphasizing the importance of life experience and never underestimating someone's potential.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the son of the late US Attorney General, announced a $100,000 challenge to prove the safety of vaccines, particularly those containing mercury-based preservative thimerosal. He claimed he has spoken with White House staff multiple times about creating a vaccine safety commission under President Trump. Kennedy's claims have been repeatedly denounced by medical organizations and physicians as incorrect and dangerous. The American Academy of Pediatrics led 350 medical organizations in expressing "unequivocal support" for the safety of vaccines last week. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has also stated that there is no link between vaccines and autism. Kennedy's claims were immediately denounced by scientists as incorrect, and his motivations with the newly announced challenge were criticized as a dangerous ploy. Actor Robert De Niro, who also participated in the event, defended Kennedy's statements and expressed concern about vaccine safety.

Aaron Schock, a Republican congressman from Illinois, is challenging Americans to get healthier this summer through the Fit for Life Summer Challenge. The challenge aims to help individuals lose weight and reduce their risk of heart disease, diabetes, stroke, and other diseases. Schock, who is known for his unconventional approach to politics, embraces fitness as a personal responsibility and has launched an initiative called Fit for Summer, Fit for Life to encourage Americans to take control of their health. He believes in leading by example and maintains a muscular physique despite the constant pressure of politics. Schock is committed to addressing major issues that will affect his own generation the most, including energy and the environment, the budget deficit, spiraling health-care costs, and a growing obesity crisis. He has already established himself as a leader in Congress and is known for his media-friendly profile and irrepressible optimism.

Three Hawaii-based Marines are facing court-martial for allegedly hazing a fellow Marine, Lance Cpl. Harry Lew, who later committed suicide in Afghanistan. The three Marines, Sgt. Benjamin E. Johns, Lance Cpl. Jacob D. Jacoby, and Lance Cpl. Carlos Orozco III, are charged with wrongfully humiliating and demeaning Lew, as well as assault and cruelty and maltreatment. They will face a general court-martial for the most serious charges. The Marines allegedly punched, kicked, made Lew do pushups, and poured sand in his face as a form of punishment for falling asleep on duty multiple times. The case has gained attention due to Lew's connection to U.S. Rep. Judy Chu of California, who stated that her nephew was "hazed and tortured" before his death. The Marines are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Joan Rivers received a star-studded funeral on Sunday, with celebrities from Hollywood, fashion, media, and business attending the service at New York's Temple Emanu-El. Notable attendees included Kathy Griffin, Kelly Osbourne, Sarah Jessica Parker, Whoopi Goldberg, Howard Stern, Bernadette Peters, Alan Cumming, Tommy Tune, Clive Davis, Carolina Herrera, Michael Kors, Barbara Walters, Geraldo Rivera, Diane Sawyer, Kathie Lee, Hoda Kotb, Andy Cohen, Barry Diller, and Donald Trump.

The service was filled with humor, as Rivers had requested in her book "I Hate Everyone ... Starting With Me." The program included an excerpt from the book where Rivers joked about wanting Meryl Streep to cry in five different accents and a wind machine to blow her hair like Beyoncé's. There were also jokes about Rivers' plastic surgery, sex life, and humor.

Rivers was a trailblazer for comedians, particularly women, and had a successful career as a TV talk show host, actress, fashion critic, and jewelry designer. She died on August 28 after undergoing a throat procedure at an Upper East Side clinic, and the cause of death is still being investigated by the New York state health department and the medical examiner.

Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg, during an interview, humorously discussed their experiences with films that didn't meet expectations. Rogen referred to a specific film where he mentioned the need to talk loudly due to the engine noise and announcements on flights. He also joked about The Green Hornet, a movie they co-wrote and starred in, calling it "the perfect storm of bad things happening." Goldberg added that they were making the film for both America and China simultaneously. Rogen humorously suggested that they should avoid making expensive movies where they can't incorporate their signature crude humor, implying that they have learned over the years to play to their strengths.

A man named Kenneth Bachman from Sewell, New Jersey took an Uber ride from a party near West Virginia University, which ended up costing him $1,635.93 as he was unintentionally taken to his home in Gloucester County, New Jersey, more than 300 miles away. Bachman had been drinking at the party and passed out during the ride. The Uber driver took the passenger to the destination he requested, and after realizing what happened, Bachman agreed to pay the fare. It is unclear who holds the record for the longest trip via a car-sharing service, but in the summer, three Chinese professionals called an Uber to take them from the Dallas-Fort Worth area to Nashville when their connecting flight was canceled. That's more than 650 miles and took over 11 hours.

In a tragic incident in Queens, New York, an 11-year-old boy named Anthony Perez McClean died after he bravely jumped into a frozen pond to save his 12-year-old friend who had fallen through the ice. The accident occurred at Forest Park around 4 p.m., and rescuers found Perez unconscious in the water. Despite CPR efforts on the scene and during transportation to Jamaica Hospital, he was pronounced dead upon arrival.

Perez's neighbors described him as a friendly, outgoing, and helpful child who loved to assist others. The pond where the incident took place used to be a baseball field but was later converted into a pond, which some neighbors believe should have remained as a safer option.

The FDNY urged parents to warn their children about the dangers of playing on frozen bodies of water in winter, emphasizing that the ice is not safe and can lead to tragic consequences. Some rescuers also fell through the ice while trying to save Perez, and two firefighters were treated for hypothermia. The incident serves as a reminder about the importance of caution when playing near frozen bodies of water during winter months.

Ozzy Osbourne has expressed his disapproval towards the Westboro Baptist Church, a notorious anti-gay group, for using his song 'Crazy Train' during protests against gays in the military at the U.S. Supreme Court. The church is appealing a $5 million lawsuit award to the family of Lance Cpl. Matthew Snyder, whose funeral they had previously protested. At this week's protests, church members distorted Ozzy's song into a hate-mongering chant, which contradicts its original message promoting tolerance and understanding.

A severe winter storm has been affecting multiple states across the US, causing numerous disruptions and hardships. Over a million homes and businesses are without power in four states, with New York declaring an emergency. Airlines have canceled over 2,700 flights, and the Northeast is experiencing heavy snowfall, ice, and freezing temperatures. In Boston, up to 2 inches of snow per hour may fall, with as much as a foot predicted in parts of Massachusetts. The storm has resulted in at least three weather-related deaths, including a 58-year-old man in Kansas. Despite the challenges, some are taking it in stride, while others are eager for the winter to end. This is just one of several recent storms affecting the country, with another potentially on the horizon this weekend.

George Lucas, the creator of Star Wars, apologized for criticizing Disney's handling of the franchise and calling them "white slavers" in a recent interview with Charlie Rose. In the interview, Lucas discussed his decision to stay out of the new installment, "The Force Awakens," as Disney took a different approach than he would have taken if he were still at the helm. Lucas sold Lucasfilm to Disney in 2012 for $4 billion and felt that Disney didn't want him involved in the new movies because he would cause trouble. Lucas also discussed other topics, such as his acting career and potential roles in films like Batman Forever and Spider-Man.

Urban Meyer, coach of Ohio State University, issued a statement to The Dispatch addressing accusations about Aaron Hernandez's treatment while he was coached by Meyer at the University of Florida. Meyer stated that there have been several inaccurate reports about Hernandez's behavior and drug tests during his time at Florida, and that Hernandez was held to the same drug testing policy as every other player. Some critics have labeled Meyer an enabler for his handling of Hernandez. In a new issue of Rolling Stone magazine, contributing editor Paul Solotaroff delivers a detailed investigation into Aaron Hernandez's life, which includes allegations that Hernandez was a regular user of the hallucinogenic drug PCP and that he had become so paranoid by heavy use that he started carrying a gun wherever he went. The article also alleges that Hernandez's college coach at the University of Florida, Urban Meyer, may have helped cover up failed drug tests and violent incidents involving Hernandez.

Sarah Palin, former Alaska Governor and vice presidential candidate, was granted a 20-day protective order against an 18-year-old Pennsylvania man named Shawn R. Christy on Monday. The protective order was issued by Alaska Magistrate Judge Colleen Ray after she found probable cause to believe that Christy had stalked Palin and made implied threats through phone and written messages.

Palin testified in the hearing that she feared for her life and the safety of her family, stating that Christy had sent her a receipt for a gun purchase and claimed he was buying a one-way ticket to Alaska. She also mentioned that Christy had contacted Palin's friend, Kristan Cole, since 2009, sending letters of up to 10 pages long expressing his intentions to come to Alaska with a shotgun.

Christy allegedly claimed to have had an affair with Palin and made statements suggesting he believes he has some kind of relationship with her daughter, Willow. Christy was ordered to have no contact with Palin's family, stay a mile away from her home, and stay away from a Wasilla area high school. A protective order was also issued for Kristan Cole.

In a court dispute over the estate of late actor Alan Thicke, his sons Robin and Brennan have filed legal documents against his widow, Tanya Callau. The sons claim that Callau is attempting to obtain a larger share of Thicke's estate than what was intended in his will, and they are taking action to uphold the will and prenuptial agreement. The sons accuse Callau of threatening to go to tabloids if her demands are not met, but no specific dollar amount has been mentioned. Thicke and Callau signed a prenup when they married in 2005, and the sons say she is now challenging its validity. The brothers are seeking a judge's enforcement of the will and prenup to protect their father's legacy. Tanya Callau's attorney has denied making any threats to take private family matters public.

Jason Rosenthal, the husband of author and filmmaker Amy Krouse Rosenthal who passed away from ovarian cancer last year, recently gave a candid TED Talk about his late wife's final days and his journey to find joy again after losing his companion of more than 26 years. In March 2017, just 10 days before her death at the age of 51, Amy published an essay titled "You May Want to Marry My Husband" in the New York Times as a kind of personal ad for Jason. Jason is now trying to honor his late wife by finding beauty and joy in simple moments, and has set up a foundation in her name to raise money for ovarian cancer research and children's literacy, causes that were near and dear to Amy's heart. Despite the instances of humor and joy, Jason is still haunted by the last moments he spent with Amy and the image of carrying her lifeless body down their stairs to be cremated.

President Trump's first budget proposal, titled "America First: A Budget Blueprint to Make America Great Again," will be unveiled on Thursday. The plan calls for a significant increase in military spending and steep cuts across much of the rest of the government. Some agencies could see reductions of more than 20% including the Agriculture, Labor, State, and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The budget proposal also includes eliminating future federal support for the National Endowment for the Arts, the National Endowment for the Humanities, and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Within EPA alone, 50 programs and 3,200 positions would be eliminated.

The proposed cuts could represent the widest swath of reductions in federal programs since the drawdown after World War II, potentially leading to a sizable cutback in the federal non-military workforce. The budget proposal is likely to face stiff resistance from lawmakers on Capitol Hill, even from Republicans, due to concerns about large cuts in foreign aid and diplomacy.

The president must still reach a separate agreement with Congress by the end of April regarding a temporary funding bill to avoid a partial government shutdown. The budget proposal will factor squarely into these negotiations. The document summarizes an unfortunate incident that occurred on the set of the upcoming movie about Fred Rogers, titled "You Are My Friend," starring Tom Hanks. A 61-year-old man named James M. Emswiller, who was involved in the sound production of the film, died after falling from a balcony during a break in filming. The incident happened around 7:30 p.m. on Thursday night in Mount Lebanon, Pennsylvania, located about 20 miles southeast of Pittsburgh.

Emswiller may have suffered a medical event prior to the fall, and no one reported seeing him fall, but people did hear him hit the ground. The police are investigating the matter, and Sony Pictures/Tri-Star Pictures expressed their condolences to Emswiller's loved ones, friends, and colleagues.

Emswiller had won an Emmy Award in 2015 for his work on the TV movie "Bessie." The film is inspired by a real-life friendship between Rogers and journalist Tom Junod. Filming was canceled for the evening and remains on hold. The movie is set to hit theaters in October 2019.

A 1-year-old Chinese boy named Hanhang was eating chow mein with his family in Chaoyang City when he tripped and fell, causing a chopstick to be lodged up his nose. His parents removed the chopstick and took him to the hospital for treatment, but doctors failed to notice that the chopstick had punctured his brain and small pieces were still lodged in his head. Hanhang's condition worsened at home, with repeated vomiting and lethargy, and he was brought back to the hospital where an X-ray revealed the chopstick piece. A British couple returned home from a Caribbean cruise with identical parasitic infections they contracted while sunbathing on a beach in Martinique. The infections caused itchy, red rashes on the couple's backsides. They sought help from medical staff on the cruise ship and later at a hospital in Cambridge, England, but their condition did not improve. Doctors diagnosed them with "cutaneous larva migrans," a skin condition caused by a hookworm infection. The most common culprit for the infection in the Caribbean is the hookworm Ancylostoma braziliense. People can pick up the parasite after encountering hookworm larvae, which are excreted in the feces of infected animals, typically dogs or cats, onto sandy beaches or moist soil. The couple may have contracted the infection by sitting bare-bottomed on the sand or by having sand get into their bathing suits. Once a hookworm larva penetrates a person's skin, it can burrow around, leaving a trail-like rash of inflamed skin known as a "creeping eruption." In some cases, the larvae can migrate to the lungs, causing symptoms such as coughing and shortness of breath. The couple was eventually treated with anti-parasitic medication and made a full recovery.

The FCC has proposed a draft to eliminate net neutrality rules, which would allow internet providers to create fast and slow lanes, prioritize their own traffic, and block apps or services. The proposal removes nearly all net neutrality rules, with the exception of public disclosure requirements. The commission argues that this change will promote broadband investment and innovation by reducing regulatory uncertainty and lowering compliance costs.

The FCC also suggests that consumer protections are unnecessary because the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) will now have oversight of ISPs. However, the FTC may not necessarily disapprove of blocking, throttling, or paid prioritization. The commission argues that large web companies like Google and Netflix are too wealthy to be unfairly advantaged by ISPs, and any deals between them would need to comply with antitrust laws.

The proposal also prevents states from passing their own net neutrality laws, stating that it could pose an obstacle to the delivery of broadband service. The order is set to be voted on at the commission's December 14th meeting and is expected to pass. Net neutrality supporters argue that this change could unfairly advantage ISPs and put consumers at risk by loosening regulatory oversight.

McDonald's has announced that it will switch to paper straws at its restaurants in the United Kingdom and Ireland, starting in September. This change follows successful trials of paper straws at select locations. The fast food chain uses 1.8 million straws daily at its 1,361 UK and Ireland restaurants, and aims to complete the transition by 2019. The move towards paper straws is part of a broader effort to reduce plastic waste, as plastic straws are the sixth most common type of litter globally and only 1% are recycled. The UK government has encouraged other companies to follow McDonald's lead, and several large UK restaurant chains have already stopped using plastic straws. However, concerns have been raised about the impact on people with disabilities who rely on plastic straws for independence. McDonald's will still provide plastic straws upon request, but they will be kept behind the counter. The company has also started testing alternatives to plastic straws in other countries and plans to offer them only when requested by customers in some markets.

The monumental chestnut tree that provided comfort to Anne Frank during her hiding from the Nazis fell due to heavy wind and rain on August 23, 2021. Parts of the tree were later offered for sale on an online auction website. The tree had been suffering from fungus and moths that caused half of its trunk to rot. The Netherlands' Trees Institute, one of the supporters of the preservation project, expressed surprise at the news of the tree's fall and said it was unclear why the support structure failed. Clones of the tree have been taken and planted in various locations, but it is not yet clear if a new tree will replace the original one on the same spot. Anne Frank made several references to the tree in her diary, which has become one of the most widely read documents to emerge from the Holocaust.

However, it was not appropriate for the couple due to religious reasons, so they sought help from a US-based team of scientists at New Hope Fertility Center in New York City. The study used data from over 21,000 people aged 65 and older, and found that the average amount of education increased significantly between 2000 and 2012, from 11.8 years to 12.7 years. Researchers believe that better education may create more connections in the brain, making it easier to keep thinking normally as one ages. The study also found that while obesity, a lack of exercise, and poor diet can increase the risk of Alzheimer's, rates went down as more people developed high blood pressure, diabetes, and other cardiovascular diseases. The decline in dementia prevalence occurred even though there was an increase in the age- and sex-adjusted prevalence of these risk factors among older adults. The study suggests that increased treatment for these conditions may have contributed to the decline in dementia risk.

This behavior is attributed to lower-status males feeling threatened by the entrance of a woman into their competitive arena and attempting to maintain their social rank through aggression. Higher-skilled players were found to be more positive towards female gamers as they have less to fear from hierarchical reorganization and may behave in this manner to support and attract them. The study suggests that video games offer a unique opportunity to examine sexist behavior and provides insights into the factors affecting male hostility towards women.

Data Privacy Day is observed this Friday to emphasize the importance of personal data protection. Facebook has announced two new features to enhance user security:

1. Secured Connection: Facebook will now allow users to experience the platform entirely over HTTPS, providing an encrypted connection to keep data more secure, especially when using public Internet access points. However, this option may slow down Facebook due to longer loading times and some unsupported features. The feature is being rolled out gradually and will be available soon in Account Settings under advanced security features.

2. Social Authentication: In case of suspicious activity on a user's account, Facebook may use social authentication to verify identity by showing pictures of friends and asking the user to name them. This method aims to make account security more social and less vulnerable to human hackers.

Facebook encourages users to visit their Security Page for information on keeping personal data safe online. The new features aim to prevent hijacking of accounts on open or poorly secured wireless networks, as highlighted by the browser extension Firesheep. However, Facebook is criticized for rolling out these security measures slowly and not making HTTPS a default option yet.

The study published in the journal Current Biology on October 5, 2015, reveals that the Chernobyl disaster zone, which was evacuated after a nuclear accident in 1986, is now teeming with wildlife such as elk, roe deer, red deer, wild boar, and wolves. The researchers found that mammal populations have bounced back and are now similar to those in four uncontaminated nature reserves in the region. The number of wolves living in and around the Chernobyl site is more than seven times greater than can be found in those nature reserves. The study demonstrates that, despite nearly three decades of chronic radiation exposure, the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone supports an abundant mammal community. The researchers conclude that the effects of human habitation, including hunting, farming, and forestry, are more damaging to wildlife than is radiation poisoning. The findings may hold important lessons for understanding the potential long-term impact of the Fukushima disaster in Japan.

The film is due out on December 18, 2015. The title for the movie has also been revealed as 'Star Wars: The Force Awakens'. The cast includes a mix of established actors and fresh faces, with some relative unknowns such as John Boyega, Domhnall Gleeson, and Daisy Ridley joining the franchise. The film will continue the story three decades after the events of 'Return of the Jedi'.

Three astronauts safely returned to Earth on September 2nd, ending a record-breaking mission for NASA's Peggy Whitson who spent an extended 288 days aboard the International Space Station (ISS). During her stay, she set a new record for the most cumulative time in space by an American with 665 days accrued. Her crewmates, Jack Fischer and Russian cosmonaut Fyodor Yurchikhin, spent 136 days on their mission. The Soyuz MS-04 spacecraft undocked from the ISS and landed on the steppes of Kazakhstan after a three-hour journey back to Earth. Whitson's return marks the longest single spaceflight by a woman of any nationality. Recovery teams are currently helping the astronauts with medical checks, and they will soon be returning home to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston and Russia's cosmonaut center in Moscow. The ISS will be occupied by three crewmembers until September 12th when the Expedition 52/53 crew arrives.

A political action committee named Trump Has Tiny Hands PAC has been launched in response to the ongoing debate about Donald Trump's hand size during the Republican presidential campaign. The debate began when Marco Rubio joked about Trump's hands, and Trump responded by defending his hand size and accusing Rubio of lying. The PAC was created by Henry Kraemer, who expressed concerns about Trump's ability to handle official matters with small hands. Yelp also joined in the joke by updating their app description to make a sly reference to the hand size controversy. The debate has been ongoing, with former Spy Magazine editor Graydon Carter also teasing Trump over his hand size in the past.

Vermont lawmakers Chris Pearson and Jean O'Sullivan have proposed a bill to reinstate alcohol prohibition in Vermont as a tactic to push for marijuana legalization. The bill, if passed, would impose penalties similar to those for marijuana possession on alcohol consumption, with fines of up to $500 and potential imprisonment for those involved in its sale and distribution.

The lawmakers argue that the bill highlights the irony of marijuana remaining illegal while alcohol, a more dangerous substance, is legal. They cite scientific studies showing that marijuana has a lower risk of mortality compared to alcohol and other commonly used drugs. The bill is part of an ongoing effort to legalize marijuana in Vermont, with H.277 proposing its legal sale and regulation, and Senate Bill 95 also introducing marijuana legalization this year.

The lawmakers argue that tax revenue from a legal marijuana market could help address Vermont's budget deficit, estimated at $113 million. A Rand Corporation study suggests that Vermonters spent between $125 to $225 million on marijuana in 2014, and potential tax revenue from a legal market could range from $20 to $70 million annually.

Despite the bill's intention to highlight the dangers of alcohol compared to marijuana, both lawmakers do not want it to pass. The bill has yet to be acted upon

A memorial for Michael Brown, a black teenager fatally shot by a white officer in Ferguson, Missouri, was destroyed overnight on December 26th. Supporters gathered and rebuilt the memorial by morning after it was intentionally crashed into by a car. Officer Timothy Zoll, the Ferguson Police Department's public relations officer, initially said no crime had been reported in connection to the memorial's destruction and referred to it as "a pile of trash in the middle of the street." However, he later admitted to misleading his superiors about his interview with The Washington Post. As a result, Officer Zoll was placed on unpaid leave, and the Ferguson Police Department expressed regret for his negative remarks about the memorial.

The article discusses two unusual animal-related experiences that are gaining attention online. Firstly, a video from Weirdnews.about.com showcases nonvenomous snakes giving massages to a man, with some snakes focusing on his belly or back while others explore his face. This may cause discomfort or fear for many viewers.

Secondly, Doseng.org reports on the Maesa Elephant Camp in Chiang Mai, Thailand, where tourists can opt for an elephant massage. However, instead of a baby elephant as advertised, they often encounter adult elephants that step on their backs to "help ease stress." This practice has raised concerns due to the potential danger posed by these large animals.

In summary, the article highlights two controversial animal-related activities: snake massages and elephant massages in Thailand, which have sparked debate over their comfort level and ethical implications.

The document summarizes President Obama's efforts to secure support for the Iran nuclear deal from Democratic lawmakers, as opponents led by pro-Israel group AIPAC are expected to lobby heavily against it. Obama will deliver a speech on Wednesday arguing that the vote on the deal is crucial and comparing it to the decision to go to war in Iraq. He plans to make himself available to answer questions or concerns from skeptical lawmakers, dispatch cabinet members to outline the provisions of the agreement, and conduct media interviews next week. The administration aims to build support to sustain a presidential veto of legislation rejecting the accord. Three Democratic senators have already declared their backing for the deal, along with several House Democrats. Obama is urging support for the Iran nuclear deal while criticizing opponents' claims that it would open a pathway for Iran to obtain a nuclear weapon. The speech will be delivered at American University in Washington, where President Kennedy gave a speech proposing a nuclear test ban treaty with the Soviet Union during the Cold War. The White House seems to be encouraging comparisons between the two speeches. The deal would relax sanctions against Iran in exchange for a promise not to develop nuclear weapons and inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency. Critics, including every major Republican presidential candidate, say Iran cannot be trusted and that the economic benefits of the deal will only strengthen Iran's ability to threaten Israel and foment extremism throughout the Middle East.

The new book, "Mockingbird Songs: My Friendship with Harper Lee," by Wayne Flynt reveals insights into the life of Harper Lee, the reclusive author of "To Kill a Mockingbird." According to the book, Lee called Truman Capote a compulsive liar in her letters. Lee and Capote were friends and writing partners for years, with Lee serving as Capote's assistant during research for his book In Cold Blood. However, Capote gave Lee no credit for her work when he published the book. The friendship between Lee and Capote ended due to jealousy over Lee's literary success.

The book also reveals that Lee was nervous before interviews and speaking engagements, often vomiting beforehand. Lee shied away from the media and fame due to a fear of obsessive fans and concerns about stalkers and assassination. She only asked Flynt not to write about her while she was living, but felt that the book allows her to speak beyond the grave without risking her privacy.

Flynt also discusses Lee's relationship with Truman Capote in the book, including her revelation about his lying habit and the reason for their falling out. The book is set to be released on May 2nd.

Missing California woman Jamie Tull, a former public elementary school teacher from Riverbank, was found alive on August 4, 2017, after being missing for nearly three weeks. She was discovered by family and friends near the site of her crashed car in Le Grand, Merced County. Tull had been struggling with emotional issues and stopped taking her prescription medicine. During her time missing, she survived by eating a few bugs and drinking from a dirty cattle trough. Authorities found her emaciated, sunburned, and lying in tall grass. She was flown to a hospital for medical treatment and will be returned to her relatives for care. Tull's father confirmed that she has bipolar disorder and had not taken her medication for about six months due to advice from a pastor and his wife.

A military veteran died at the Veterans Affairs Hospital in Albuquerque, New Mexico, after waiting for an ambulance to take him to the emergency room located 500 yards away. The man collapsed in the hospital cafeteria and staff followed policy by calling 911, but it took 20-25 minutes for the ambulance to arrive due to a local policy under review. The death comes amidst ongoing scrutiny of the Department of Veterans Affairs for long delays in treatment and medical appointments, as well as reports of veterans dying while on waiting lists. The incident has sparked calls for an outside investigation and reform at the Albuquerque VA.

Ethan Couch, the Texas teen who was sentenced to probation for a deadly drunken-driving wreck in 2013 and later fled to Mexico, is facing deportation proceedings. His attorney, Fernando Benitez, based primarily out of Tijuana, is representing him in Mexico. Benitez has filed a petition claiming that Couch's constitutional and civil rights may have been violated, arguing that his crimes in the United States should not affect Mexican officials or courts.

Couch and his mother were detained by Mexican authorities on Monday night in Puerto Vallarta after missing a probation meeting in early December. Although Tonya was deported Wednesday evening, Ethan was granted a temporary injunction by a Mexican judge due to Benitez's legal maneuvers. An evidence hearing in the case is likely to take place at the end of the month, with a judge having up to 90 days to issue a ruling after that.

Benitez denies reports that Couch had a gun at the time of his detention and insists that his client did not have a gun. He hopes to meet with Couch next week in Mexico City, where he is being held at an immigration facility. Tonya Couch is currently in a Los Angeles jail cell pending a hearing and eventual transfer back to Texas. She is facing a charge of Hindering Apprehension of a Felon and has a bail set

The Daily Caller, a right-wing news site, is offering a weekly gun giveaway until Election Day in November 2012. The gun, an FMK9C1 designed by Jim Pontillo and manufactured in California, is engraved with the Bill of Rights. To enter, individuals must sign up for email updates from The Daily Caller. The contest is open to legal residents of the United States where firearms are legally transferable, and winners must pass a background check and comply with other requirements.

Jim Pontillo, the gun's manufacturer, has expressed extreme right-wing views on his company's website and in columns for Human Events. He has criticized American progressives for promoting communism and claimed that those calling for secession are not fanatics but are acting "in the Founding tradition." He also claims that liberalism is changing America for the worse, and that firearm ownership encourages individual initiative and threatens progressive ideologies.

The Daily Caller launched their "Guns and Gear" section in December 2011, which largely reprints and repackages news releases, articles, and op-eds from National Rifle Association sources. The site has also followed the NRA in promoting attacks on Attorney General Eric Holder regarding the failed ATF Operation Fast and Furious.

Clarissa Dickson Wright, a renowned British cook, food historian, and television personality, passed away at the age of 66 in Edinburgh. Known for her eccentricity and irreverence, she rose to fame as one half of the BBC's Two Fat Ladies duo alongside Jennifer Paterson. The pair was celebrated for their indulgent recipes and unconventional approach to cooking, which attracted both praise and criticism. Dickson Wright had a tumultuous past, having battled alcoholism and growing up in an affluent family with an abusive father. Despite her controversial views on hunting and vegetarianism, she was respected for her knowledge of food history and her advocacy for countryside pursuits. In recent years, she published a well-received book on English food and served as the Rector of the University of Aberdeen. Her death was mourned by many in the worlds of food and television.

A woman with an extremely drug-resistant form of tuberculosis (XDR-TB) is being treated at the National Institutes of Health outside Washington, D.C., after traveling to multiple states in the U.S. before seeking treatment. The patient arrived in the U.S. from India through Chicago O'Hare airport and also spent time in Missouri and Tennessee. XDR-TB is a rare form of TB that is resistant to almost all known TB drugs, making it difficult to treat and potentially dangerous for those who come into close contact with the patient. Health officials are working to identify people who may have been exposed to the patient, including those who sat in the same row or near her on the flight from India. The patient is currently being treated in a special isolation room at the NIH Clinical Center and has been undergoing testing to determine what drugs may help her. Only about a third to half of XDR-TB cases can be cured, and treatment can cost upwards of $430,000. It is not yet clear who will pay for this patient's treatment. The public is generally not at risk for TB, but health officials are taking the situation seriously due to the rarity and danger of XDR-TB.

The article discusses a controversy surrounding the U.S. military's order for soldiers who re-enlisted during the height of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars to repay thousands of dollars in signing bonuses. Approximately 10,000 soldiers are affected by this issue, with nearly $100 million misspent in California alone. The Pentagon argues that the law requires them to reclaim overpayments due to improper use of military troop-level incentives. Soldiers who served their contract terms are being asked to repay key incentives, leading to financial hardship and anger among veterans. One veteran, Christopher Van Meter, refinanced his mortgage to pay back $46,000 in re-enlistment bonuses and student loan repayments. The California National Guard is helping soldiers navigate the appeals process but claims they are legally bound to recover the overpayments.

A Seattle-bound Alaska Airlines flight was forced to make an emergency landing at the Minneapolis St Paul Airport on Monday morning after a passenger attempted to open a door mid-flight. The unruly passenger, estimated to be in his 20s, reportedly tried to open a rear door of the 737, but it is impossible to do so due to air pressure differences between inside and outside the plane during flight. The crew managed to calm him down and divert the flight to Minneapolis where he was arrested upon landing. The man may face charges, but it's unclear at this time. The flight eventually arrived in Seattle around 1 p.m. PST after a delay. Passengers described the situation as being handled professionally by the crew, with some stating that the flight attendant was particularly calm and composed during the incident.

George Lucas has chosen Chicago as the location for his first-of-its-kind interactive museum, which will house his extensive collection of artwork and movie memorabilia. The $1 billion museum will be built on a 17-acre site located between Soldier Field and McCormick Place on parking lots. The museum is self-funded by Lucas and has been described as a "history of storytelling" project dedicated to the power of visual images.

Lucas originally wanted to build the museum in his hometown of San Francisco, but site proposals were rejected. Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel moved quickly to secure the project, and the museum's board credited Chicago for providing a larger location, easy accessibility to public transportation, and its reputation as a city renowned for art and architecture.

The museum will open in 2018 and is expected to create hundreds of jobs and bring economic opportunity to the city. However, it has drawn opposition from open-space advocates who are concerned about the potential impact on lakefront parks. The parking lots where the museum will be built may also affect Chicago Bears tailgaters.

Lucas' collection includes valuable Norman Rockwell paintings, examples of special effects he pioneered at Industrial Light & Magic, and memorabilia such as the Darth Vader costume. The works are wrapped around the theme of storytelling, with many pieces predating the arrival of moving pictures

Nathaniel Marston, a former star of One Life to Live, passed away on November 10, 2015, following a car accident on October 30. The 40-year-old actor was not wearing a seatbelt and was ejected from his vehicle during the crash. His mother, Elizabeth Jackson, shared updates of his condition on Facebook, initially reporting that he was in intensive care with broken bones and internal injuries.

Over the following days, it was revealed that Marston had sustained a broken and fractured neck, broken shoulder, broken ribs, and a collapsed lung. Doctors informed Jackson that if he survived, he would likely be paralyzed from the neck down and require a ventilator to breathe. However, on Monday, Jackson reported that Marston was able to communicate and was determined to fight for his life.

Despite these efforts, Nathaniel Marston passed away peacefully on November 11, surrounded by loved ones. Arrangements are being made for memorial services in New York City, Kauai, HI, and Gerlach, NV. The outpouring of support, prayers, love, and kindness from friends and fans has been a source of strength for Marston's family during this difficult time.

The Saturday Night Live episode hosted by Larry David started off with a controversial monologue that included jokes about concentration camps and women, which received mixed reactions on Twitter. Aidy Bryant's impression of Sarah Huckabee Sanders was praised for its accuracy and comedic timing, particularly during a musical number set to Demi Lovato’s “Confident.” The episode also featured a sketch where Donald Trump took a naked shower with Paul Manafort, involving Vice President Mike Pence and Attorney General Jeff Sessions. The sketch ended with a presidential turkey pardon as a solution to save Manafort from prison.

The story takes place five years after Transformers: Dark of the Moon, with the remaining Autobots seeking out Optimus Prime while avoiding capture by Lockdown, a Decepticon who wants to find Optimus.

In terms of acting, Mark Wahlberg is an upgrade on Shia Labeouf but still falls short. The North Korean Foreign Ministry condemned the sanctions, calling them a provocation aimed at depriving the country of its right to self-defense.

Lawmakers criticized Trump for his belligerent comments and tweets, which they believe are exacerbating tensions with North Korea.

Officials said that China is looking the other way as North Korea uses its banking system and front companies to conduct business, while Russian companies continue to provide support to Pyongyang.

In this article from CNN, it was reported that President Donald Trump fired his Chief of Staff Reince Priebus and replaced him with Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly on Friday, July 28th. The change comes after a turbulent six months for Priebus who faced heavy criticism for failing to stem the flow of leaks and struggling to impose order in a chaotic White House.

Priebus told CNN that he submitted his resignation privately to the President on Thursday, but throughout the day on Friday, sources close to him insisted that he was not resigning. However, Trump announced the change on Twitter after landing on Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.

The move follows months of speculation that Priebus would soon be ousted from an administration where he has consistently drawn heavy criticism. Rumors of infighting among Trump's staff eventually devolved into all-out warfare, with incoming communications director Anthony Scaramucci playing a significant role in Priebus' downfall.

John Kelly is expected to begin his tenure as White House Chief of Staff on Monday and will participate in a meeting of Trump's cabinet. Kelly is a Marine who served in the military for nearly five decades, including positions such as chief of Southern Command and senior assistant to the secretary of defense. He also worked as a legislative liaison to Congress and served tours in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Trenton Lewis, a 21-year-old UPS worker in Little Rock, Arkansas, has been walking five miles to work every day for the past seven months due to not having a car. Despite the rain or cold and some rough areas of town, he never missed a shift or was late. His co-workers, Patricia and Kenneth Bryant, learned about his daily trek and collected donations from other UPS workers to buy him a car. Last week, they surprised Lewis with the keys in the parking lot, which he initially found hard to believe. Now, Lewis leaves for work at 3:30 a.m., allowing him to sleep in and giving his legs a break. His co-workers' kindness has resulted in Lewis having a new car, a UPS keychain, and lasting friendships.

The parents of Dylan Noble, an unarmed 19-year-old who was fatally shot by Fresno police during a traffic stop on June 25, denied that he was depressed or unhappy before his death. They held a news conference in Fresno on July 7 to address the matter and announced legal action against the city, alleging excessive force.

On Wednesday, July 7, the Fresno police department released graphic body-camera footage of the shooting incident. The video shows officers repeatedly shouting at Noble to show his hands and firing multiple shots as he lay gravely wounded on the ground. Noble's family launched legal action against the city, arguing that the shooting was an inexcusable use of excessive force.

The police department initially refused to release the footage to the public until the investigation was complete but showed it privately to Noble’s family last Friday. The video provides a much fuller picture of the shooting than the blurry witness video that emerged last week.

During the news conference, Noble's father, Darren Noble, said: "They just wanted to shoot him. They’re just trigger-happy." The family's legal claim against the city argues that officers never had an objectively reasonable basis to shoot Noble and that the police department has shown a disregard for excessive force in encounters with civilians.
