A powerful storm is expected to hit the Northeastern United States starting Friday, potentially dumping up to 3 feet of snow from New York City to Boston and beyond. Residents are preparing for the storm by stocking up on food, water, and other supplies, while road crews are readying salt and sand. Schools have been canceled in several cities, and airlines have announced the suspension of flights through Saturday. The storm could be one of the most significant in recent history, with widespread power failures and flooding in coastal areas a concern. Forecasters warn that this is a dangerous winter storm and advise people to stay indoors and avoid travel if possible.

In St. Johns County, Florida, a father at a teen soccer game was called by a field marshal on duty who accused him of harassment despite the fact that he was only instructing his son from the sidelines. The incident was captured on video and shared on social media with the hashtag #SoccerWhileBlack. The father's identity remains unknown, but witnesses say he was cooperative and attempted to leave the scene in an effort to de-escalate the situation. Deputies arrived and found no wrongdoing, letting the father go without detaining him. This incident is one of several recent cases where white people have called 911 on black individuals who were not committing any crimes.

The hearse carrying the casket of former President George H.W. Bush arrived at the U.S. Capitol on Monday, December 3, 2018 in Washington D.C., marking the beginning of a series of official mourning ceremonies for the late president. President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump paid their respects to Bush's casket on Monday evening at the U.S. Capitol Rotunda, where he will lie in state until Wednesday morning. Trump plans to attend Bush's state funeral at Washington National Cathedral on Wednesday. The body of the nation's 41st president was transported from Houston to Washington on board Air Force One, which was temporarily renamed Special Air Mission 41 in honor of Bush. A motorcade escorted the hearse carrying Bush's casket through downtown Houston for a memorial ceremony, where hundreds gathered to pay their respects. Vice President Mike Pence and House Speaker Paul Ryan delivered eulogies at a ceremony in the Capitol Rotunda on Monday afternoon. Bush died on Friday at his home in Houston at the age of 94.

A high school senior named Evan Murray, known for his exceptional athletic abilities and admirable character, passed away after being injured during a home football game against Summit on Friday night. The news has left the Warren County community in shock and grief. Murray was a three-sport performer, excelling in football, basketball, and baseball. His leadership qualities and kind-hearted nature made him a beloved figure among his peers and teachers.

In response to the tragedy, grief counselors have been made available for students at Warren Hills Regional High School. The specific circumstances surrounding Murray's death have not been disclosed by school administrators. This incident marks another tragic event in the community, following the deaths of Colin Matthew Cudworth Jr., a fellow student, and Kinsey Fredericks-Bishow, a former graduate, within the past year.

The memorial at Warren Hills’ football stadium was adorned with cards bearing a large Superman emblem, symbolizing Murray's heroic status in the community. Students, friends, family, and faculty have gathered to mourn and remember him. Many have expressed their admiration for Murray, describing him as an exceptional individual who will be deeply missed.

In this article, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the Supreme Leader of Iran, addressed heads of state from developing countries during a summit in Tehran, emphasizing that Iran has no interest in nuclear weapons but will continue pursuing peaceful nuclear energy. The summit, hosted by Iran as part of the 120-nation Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), aims to demonstrate that Western efforts to isolate and punish Iran economically for its disputed nuclear program have failed.

During the summit, discord over Syria arose when Egyptian President Mohamed Mursi urged member states to support Syrians striving to overthrow President Bashar al-Assad, whose staunchest regional ally is Iran. This prompted a walkout by the Syrian delegation.

Mursi's visit to Tehran was the first by an Egyptian leader since Iran's Islamic Revolution in 1979, but his uncompromising speech suggested there would be no swift reconciliation between the two countries after three decades of animosity. Diplomatic relations between Cairo and Tehran broke down immediately after Iran's revolution over Egypt's support for the overthrown Shah and over its peace agreement with Israel.

Robert "Joe" Halderman, the CBS news producer accused of attempting to extort $2 million from David Letterman, is due in a Manhattan court on Tuesday for the first hearing in his criminal case. Despite financial struggles and potential plea deals, Halderman has reportedly raised $100,000 for his defense fund, indicating he may not be seeking a plea agreement. The hearing will address legal issues and future proceedings, with defense attorney Gerry Shargel expected to continue attacking Letterman's character. Meanwhile, Levi Johnston, the father of Sarah Palin's grandson, is making headlines this week, receiving Fleshbot’s “Crossover Star Award” for his transition from political figure to sex symbol and potentially appearing on "Saturday Night Live."

The town of San Vitaliano in Italy has temporarily banned traditional wood-burning pizza stoves due to high air pollution levels. The ban, issued by the mayor, aims to reduce pollutants as San Vitaliano has one of the highest rates of air pollution in Italy, with residents spending 114 days last year breathing unsafe air compared to Milan's 86 days. The new legislation came into force on December 17th and will apply until June 30th next year, causing local pizzerias and artisanal bakeries to change their fuel sources or install costly filters to reduce pollution. Those caught breaking the ban will face fines of between €200 and €1,032. However, some locals question whether pizza-making is the true cause of the pollution problem in San Vitaliano.

South Korean opposition lawmakers set a new world record for a combined filibuster, speaking for 192 hours to block an anti-terrorism bill they believed threatened personal freedoms and privacy. The filibuster began on February 23 and was led by the main opposition party Minjoo, joined by other smaller parties. The bill was passed hours after the filibuster ended, with the ruling Saenuri Party controlling a majority of seats in parliament. The legislation allows intelligence services to collect a wide range of personal information, including phone records, which opposition parties argued could be used to stifle political dissent and violate privacy rights. The filibuster was met with increasing public criticism as it delayed the passage of bills on North Korean human rights and electoral districts for April's general election. President Park Geun-hye condemned the filibuster as "nothing more than a dereliction of duty."

The article discusses the tragic murder of Nia Wilson, an 18-year-old Black high school student, who was stabbed on a train in Oakland by John Lee Cowell, a man with a history of violence. The suspect was later arrested and charged with her murder. The article also criticizes local news station KTVU for using a photo of Wilson that depicted her holding what appeared to be a gun during their broadcast about her death. Critics argue that the choice of this image characterizes Wilson negatively, contributing to the narrative that Black people who are victims of violence are "deserving" of violence or "contributing" to the violence against themselves. KTVU later issued an apology for using the inappropriate photo. The article also mentions a vigil held in Wilson's honor and a GoFundMe page set up by her family to raise funds for her funeral expenses.

Joe Wilson planning a live response on Facebook instead. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) has challenged Wilson regarding another stunt, and Republicans have been critical of the president's policies before the speech. Grover Norquist's Americans for Tax Reform has created a mocking State of the Union "Bingo" card featuring phrases like "government subsidized free space" and Obama's favorite phrase "let me be clear."

Michele Bachmann's presidential campaign has been marked by aggressive encounters between her staff and the media, with at least five such incidents reported in less than two months. These confrontations have included pushing, shoving, and allegations of threats of violence towards reporters. Notable instances include ABC News reporter Brian Ross being shoved and CNN's Don Lemon being pushed into a cart. A foreign reporter also alleged that an aide threatened to break his arm, which the Bachmann campaign denied. The campaign justifies these actions as necessary for the safety and security of Bachmann, who tends to draw large, enthusiastic crowds.

In contrast, other high-profile candidates like Rudy Giuliani, Hillary Clinton, and Sarah Palin have managed to distinguish between reporters and threats more effectively during their campaigns. The difference was particularly noticeable at the Iowa State Fair, where Bachmann was guarded more restrictively than other candidates.

Separately, comedienne Kathy Griffin has targeted Michele Bachmann in her stand-up routines, asking the Congresswoman if she was born a bigot during an encounter in Washington. Bachmann responded by saying she would have to get back to Griffin on that question.

Captain Francesco Schettino, the Italian captain of the Costa Concordia cruise ship that capsized near the island of Giglio in January 2012, causing the death of 32 lives, returned to the wreck for the first time as part of his manslaughter trial on February 27, 2014. The ship hit a reef and capsized, and Schettino has been accused of abandoning the ship before all passengers were evacuated. He denies these charges and maintains that he steered the stricken vessel closer to shore to prevent it from sinking in deep water where hundreds might have drowned. His lawyer Domenico Pepe stated that Costa Crociere, his former employer, had shifted the blame towards him. Schettino's return to the island stirred memories of the tragedy among locals, with mixed reactions from the community. The complex operation to salvage the Costa Concordia took 18 hours and followed months of stabilization and preparation work by a team of 500 engineers and divers. Ports in Italy, Britain, France, Turkey, and China are now bidding for the lucrative contract to dismantle it.

The study, published in Neuron, identifies a unique region in the human brain called the lateral frontal pole prefrontal cortex, which seems to be crucial for strategic planning, decision-making, and multi-tasking. This area was not found in macaque monkeys, suggesting it may be exclusive to humans. The researchers used MRI scans to divide the human ventrolateral frontal cortex into 12 distinct areas with unique neural connections, one of which is the lateral frontal pole. Additionally, the study found that auditory parts of the brain were more connected with the human prefrontal cortex compared to macaques, which may contribute to our ability to understand and generate speech. The findings highlight the complexity of the human brain and could lead to advancements in understanding psychiatric diseases.

A 31-year-old teacher named Jillian Jacobson was found dead in her classroom at El Dorado High School in Placentia, California on Monday morning. Students discovered her hanging from the ceiling and emergency services were called, but she was declared deceased at the scene. Investigators suspect that she took her own life, but no suicide note was found. The school community was deeply affected by the incident, with many students and teachers expressing shock and grief. This is not the first time that El Dorado High School has been affected by tragedy; last year a student died after being struck by a van, and in 2009 a teacher also died on campus. Counselors were made available for students and teachers, and school was expected to resume with a normal schedule the following day.

Clinically, Calcific Myonecrosis appears as a gradually enlarging painless mass with occasional tenderness. Radiographs show a fusiform mass with peripheral plaque-like calcification involving the entire compartment, and MRI scans reveal central liquefaction. A differential diagnosis includes soft tissue sarcoma and myositis ossificans.

Pope Francis is set to release an encyclical on Thursday, June 18, focusing on the environment and poverty. The document aims to add moral authority to UN negotiations on new development goals and a 15-year global plan to tackle hunger, extreme poverty, and health.

As of late Sunday, the fault line responsible for the earthquakes had not been identified.

These brain differences could potentially lead to interventions for children at risk of developing psychopathy.

However, the abnormalities in brain structure and function associated with persistent violent behavior are complex, and more research is needed to understand their origins.

Archaeologists from the University of Southampton have discovered what may be one of the largest medieval royal palaces ever found, buried under a vast prehistoric fortress in Old Sarum, Wiltshire. The palace, which dates back to the 12th century, was discovered using geophysical ground-penetrating technology that mapped a long-vanished medieval city beneath grass on the site for over 700 years. The complex, arranged around a large courtyard, had walls up to 3 meters thick and included a probable great hall, substantial tower, and multi-story buildings with columns. The discovery of this royal palace is significant as it was previously thought that only a smaller complex existed on the site. The survey also revealed the foundations of dozens of ordinary houses and gave scholars an unprecedented opportunity to study Norman town planning.

A scheduled wedding had to be canceled on Saturday in Sweden after the groom allegedly assaulted his bride-to-be and threatened to kill her. The incident started at a pub in Örebro, where an argument between the couple continued at their home in Vintrosa, leading to physical violence. The woman reported the groom for assault to the police, who found two wedding rings in his pocket during a search. The groom was arrested and later released on Saturday afternoon but it's uncertain if the wedding will take place. Guests who had traveled to attend the wedding were disappointed as the ceremony did not occur.

Rep. Louise Slaughter, a long-serving Democratic congresswoman from New York, died on Friday at the age of 88 after sustaining an injury from a fall at her home. She was serving her 16th term in Congress and was the top Democrat on the House Rules Committee. Slaughter had been hospitalized since last week due to the fall and was being treated for a concussion but no broken bones. She was originally from Kentucky and held degrees in microbiology and public health. Slaughter was known for her advocacy work, particularly in securing infrastructure funding for her district and fighting for military safety standards. Her death was met with condolences from Democratic leaders, including House Speaker Paul Ryan who ordered the Capitol flag to be flown at half-staff.

China, which produces 95% of the world's rare earth minerals, has tightened export quotas causing global prices to soar. The Chinese government assigns quotas to authorized exporters who often trade them like commodities. The value of remaining quotas has skyrocketed due to rising demand, making it expensive for buyers outside China.

The embargo on rare earth shipments has caused more distress in Japan than in the US or Europe because Japan tends to import raw rare earths and process them into industrial materials, while other countries mainly buy highly processed powders from China. The Chinese government broadened its halt to include the US and Europe on Oct 18, but later resumed shipments only hours before Secretary of State Hillary Clinton raised the embargo issue.

The high cost of quotas has become exorbitant for users of lanthanum, a rare earth vital for catalytic converters in conventional cars, which is mostly produced in Baotou, China's capital of rare earth industry. Such price differences have created a big incentive for companies to move factories to China. The embargo has provided China with some geopolitical leverage, as it was one of several measures taken after Japan detained a Chinese fishing trawler captain.

Ross's penchant for misleading statements extends beyond Forbes, as ten former employees at his private equity firm, WL Ross & Co., confirmed similar stories of fibs, exaggerations, omissions, fabrications, and whoppers. These machinations helped bolster Ross's standing in a way that translated into business opportunities, resulting in millions of dollars in fines, tens of millions refunded to backers, numerous lawsuits, and the failure to initially disclose 19 suits during his confirmation process.

The three-part miniseries titled "Super Cats" airs nationwide on Wednesdays, October 24-November 7 at 8 p.m. on PBS. Each episode will be available to stream the following day on pbs.org/nature and PBS apps. The series, narrated by F. Murray Abraham, explores the secret lives of big cats across four corners of the globe using advanced camera technology and scientific research.

The miniseries showcases various species of cats, including the solitary snow leopard in the Himalayas, elusive swamp tiger of South Asia, and a remarkably efficient Californian bobcat with one blind eye. The series reveals their social sides, complex communication, devoted parental care, courtship rituals, hunting patterns, and more.

Advances in technology allowed for several on-camera firsts, such as the nocturnal pursuits of a black-footed cat in South Africa who hunts more in one night than a leopard does in six months. Remote cameras capture intimate moments between a mother Pallas' cat and her kittens, and low-light technology exposes a puma preying on Magellanic penguins, one of the few successful hunts ever caught on film.

Between October 2nd and 4th, there was a significant increase in heroin overdose cases in Chicago's West Side, with 74 cases reported within 72 hours, more than double the rate of overdoses during the same period last year. The Chicago Fire Department and Chicago Department of Public Health have issued alerts regarding the spike in overdoses.

Authorities suspect that the heroin may be laced with fentanyl, a powerful painkiller that was also involved in a major outbreak of overdose deaths between 2005 and 2007. Police are investigating the source of the dangerous batches of drugs and have recovered a sample from two West Side locations.

The Chicago Recovery Alliance has urged caution, emphasizing the importance of having Narcan (a heroin antidote) on hand and watching out for each other. The overdose victims treated at Mount Sinai Hospital required double and triple the doses of Narcan to revive them.

The DEA is working with Chicago police to trace the source of the dangerous batches, and state-funded drug treatment has been identified as a compounding problem in the Chicago area's heroin crisis. Illinois' heroin overdose deaths have been on the rise since 2011, with 633 heroin overdose deaths occurring in Illinois last year.

A California man named Rodney Harmon has filed a federal class-action lawsuit against Hilton Hotels Corporation for charging him 75 cents for a copy of USA Today that he did not request during his stay at the Hilton Garden Inn Sonoma County Airport. The suit alleges that Hilton hid the newspaper charge in small print on the sleeve of the room key and accuses the hotel chain of deceitful practices, wastefulness, and environmental damage due to the unnecessary distribution of unwanted newspapers. Harmon's lawyer believes there is more at stake than just 75 cents, stating it exemplifies companies taking advantage of consumers every day. Hilton has not yet responded for comment on the lawsuit.

The food tasters lived in barracks and were never allowed to eat meat because Hitler was a vegetarian. Wölk recalls that the food was good but they couldn't enjoy it due to the fear of dying. After the failed assassination attempt on July 20, 1944, security around the Wolf's Lair tightened and the tasters were boarded in an empty school nearby. Wölk was later raped by an SS officer and then saved by a lieutenant who put her on a train to Berlin. She was also saved by a Berlin doctor who lied to SS soldiers searching for the fugitive. After the war, she was raped repeatedly by Soviet soldiers, which left her unable to bear children.

The article discusses two main topics: deliberate forgetting and the potential release of classified documents related to the 9/11 attacks.

Regarding deliberate forgetting, recent studies suggest that people can deliberately forget things under specific conditions. Researchers Jeremy Manning and Kenneth Norman found that when trying to forget something, the brain discards the mental context within which the memory was first learned, effectively letting go of the mental scaffolding that supported the construction of those memories. This study highlights the importance of context in both remembering and forgetting, and suggests that our modern tendency to photograph important moments instead of experiencing them first-hand may diminish our ability to remember experiences directly.

In terms of the 9/11 attacks, former Governor Tom Kean and former Representative Lee Hamilton, who led the independent commission investigating the attacks, have cautioned Americans to be careful when interpreting newly released classified documents related to possible Saudi government involvement in the attacks. They emphasized that these documents are based on raw, unvetted material from the FBI and should be evaluated with care, as they do not necessarily imply Saudi complicity in the mass murder that occurred during the attacks. The article notes that previous investigations found no evidence of institutional or senior Saudi officials funding Al Qaeda, but one Saudi government employee was implicated in the plot and remains a person of interest.

Congress has moved to block President Obama's plan to shift control of the U.S. drone campaign from the CIA to the Defense Department by inserting a secret provision in the government spending bill. This measure, included in a classified annex to the $1.1 trillion federal budget plan, restricts the use of any funding to transfer unmanned aircraft or the authority to carry out drone strikes from the CIA to the Pentagon. The provision represents an intervention by lawmakers into the way covert operations are run and reflects lingering doubts about the U.S. military's ability to conduct strikes against al-Qaeda and its regional affiliates without hitting the wrong targets and killing civilians. Senators John McCain (R-Ariz.) and Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.), who are members of the Appropriations Committee, have expressed concern about the prospect of the CIA ceding responsibility for drone strikes to the military. The spending bill sets budgets for agencies across the federal government for the fiscal year that ends Sept. 30 and is expected to be approved by the Senate this week and delivered to President Obama for his signature as soon as Saturday.

The study by researchers at the University of Illinois suggests that offering frequent travelers free membership to the TSA's expedited screening program, TSA PreCheck, could save money and reduce airport lines for the Transportation Security Administration (TSA). The study found that waiving the $85 enrollment fee for 25 million high-volume travelers would result in a net savings of $34 million annually, due to lower staff and equipment costs. However, the report notes potential issues such as bad feelings among non-frequent fliers who are not offered the fee waiver and backlash from current paying members. The TSA has yet to comment on the study.

The article discusses the death of a 15-year-old Chicago high school basketball player named Steven Rosenthal, who died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound on August 19, 2018. However, his family and community members believe that he was shot by police officers during an encounter on Friday night. The family held a march and protest on Sunday, demanding an independent investigation into Rosenthal's death, the release of footage from the incident, and access to his body for an autopsy. They claim that eyewitnesses saw the events unfold differently than official accounts suggest. Chicago police have stated that there is no evidence that any officer fired a weapon during the encounter with Rosenthal, and no footage has been found that depicts the moment of his death. The family's lawyer, Andrew Stroth, called for authorities to release footage of Rosenthal's death and accused the officers of shooting him without cause or provocation. The Chicago Police Department has stated that the shooting remains under investigation, but no decision has been made yet to release body camera video.

The article discusses a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, which found that reading from electronic devices before bedtime could be negatively affecting sleep patterns and long-term health. The study, conducted at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston, involved 12 participants who read either an iPad or a book for four hours each night before sleep for five consecutive nights.

The researchers found that participants using iPads displayed reduced levels of melatonin, a hormone that helps induce sleepiness, took longer to fall asleep, and spent less time in restorative REM sleep. The iPad readers also reported being sleepier and less alert the following morning, even after eight hours of sleep, and displayed delayed circadian rhythms.

The study suggests that the blue light emitted by electronic devices may be having a greater impact on sleep than previously thought. Although the study used only iPads, other products such as tablets, e-readers, smartphones, laptops, and LED monitors were found to produce similar blue-light emissions. The standard Kindle e-reader was an exception, as it does not emit light and is more akin to a printed book.

A 15-year-old girl who had been missing for over two years reported that she escaped from a home in Washington Park, Illinois, where she claimed she was held captive and repeatedly sexually assaulted. The police raid on the house resulted in the arrest of a 24-year-old man and his mother, with the recovery of the girl's young child. The girl told authorities that her captor forced her to give a false name in medical records during her pregnancy and when the child was born. The teen reported being held against her will, beaten, and sexually assaulted almost every day, and that she had attempted to escape multiple times but was forced back at gunpoint. A neighbor stated they never witnessed anything concerning regarding the girl's situation.

Detroit Tigers outfielder Delmon Young was arrested early on March 15, 2012 in Manhattan for a hate crime and aggravated harassment. The incident occurred outside the Hilton Hotel where he allegedly shouted anti-Semitic slurs at four men, one of whom he pushed and tackled to the ground. Young was intoxicated during the altercation and had to be hospitalized before being processed. He was later released on a $5,000 bond and issued an apology. The Tigers management stated that they will let the legal process take its course. This is not the first time Young has been in trouble; he was suspended for 50 games in 2006 for chucking a bat at an umpire.

The United Nations has released a report predicting that the global volume of discarded electronic waste will nearly triple in weight by 2017, equivalent to approximately eight Great Pyramids of Giza. The report, created by the "Solving the E-Waste Problem (StEP) Initiative," reveals that the U.S. and China are the leading producers of e-waste. Comprehensive data on global e-waste has been hard to come by due to varying definitions among countries. The StEP Initiative has created an interactive e-waste map, which shows data from 184 countries and provides a comparison between purchasing power in different countries. In the U.S., about 258.2 million units of used computers, monitors, TVs, and cellphones were generated in 2010, with 171.4 million collected for recycling and 14.4 million exported. The U.S. is a major exporter of used electronics, particularly CRT monitors and cellphones. Recycling of e-waste is on the rise in the U.S., but it lags behind countries in the European Union. The report also highlights the negative health and environmental impacts of primitive e-waste recycling methods and urges nations to adopt clearer trade descriptions.

The article discusses the benefits of sleep on learning and memory, focusing on its role in improving relearning. Research shows that sleep enhances relearning, enabling individuals to learn twice as quickly and up to three times more effectively. A study led by Stéphanie Mazza at the University of Lyon found that participants who slept between learning and relearning sessions had better long-term memory performance compared to those who did not sleep. The benefits were evident one week and six months after the study, with the sleep group recalling more word pairs than the wake group. The researchers suggest that sleep "transforms" memories, making them stronger and easier to restore during relearning. However, further research is needed to determine if these benefits apply in other circumstances and to address potential issues with varied time experimental designs. Overall, the study suggests that sleeping between study sessions can be an effective learning strategy, particularly when learners repeatedly revisit and practice materials to achieve high performance levels.

In Asheville, North Carolina, two police officers responded to a noise complaint during a Fourth of July block party where a makeshift water slide was set up for children. Upon arrival, they found the noise level acceptable and the slide safe for traffic. Instead of issuing citations, the officers decided to join in the fun and slid down the water slide themselves. Their playful act was captured on video and gained national media attention, including recognition from Good Morning America. The resident, Katlen Joyce Smith, shared that one of the local fathers had built the slide for the children's enjoyment.

Two California men, Hunter Moore and Charles Evens, were arrested by the FBI on charges of computer crimes and identity theft for their alleged involvement in stealing nude photos of hundreds of victims to populate a revenge porn website called isanyoneup.com. The site's operator, Moore, is known for his notorious role in creating and operating the now-defunct website, which was named the "most-hated man on the Internet" by the BBC.

The indictment alleges that Moore conspired with Evens to hack into email accounts of victims to obtain nude photos without their consent, which were then posted on the website. Moore is accused of paying Evens $200 a week via Paypal for the stolen images. The two are charged with 15 counts, including conspiracy, computer intrusion, and aggravated identity theft.

If convicted, they face up to five years in federal prison for each count of conspiracy and computer hacking, as well as a mandatory two-year sentence for each count of aggravated identity theft, which would be served consecutively to any other sentence. The case serves as a reminder for email users to be diligent when setting up passwords and security questions to protect their privacy.

Miss Honduras 2014, Maria Jose Alvarado, and her sister Sofia Trinidad have gone missing four days before the Miss World competition in London. The incident occurred after attending a friend’s birthday party near their hometown of Santa Barbara. Initially, the police did not treat it as a crime but later confirmed that four people, including the owner of the party venue and Sofia's boyfriend, were arrested for questioning. The missing women were last seen getting into a vehicle after the party. Alvarado was crowned Miss Honduras in April and was expected to compete in the Miss World Pageant in London next month. Her disappearance has caused concern in Honduras, known for its high crime rates. The Miss World contest is scheduled to start on Thursday and culminate on Dec 14.

The article highlights that this move could be a response to Senate Republicans blocking numerous executive branch nominees under President Barack Obama as leverage to force changes in the law. The crisis could still be averted if Republicans end their filibusters on pending Obama nominees, but there is concern among senators in both parties that if Reid moves to change the rules by 51 votes, it would further weaken or potentially eliminate the filibuster altogether.

The article also mentions a potential compromise meeting between Democrats and Republicans to discuss the issue, with Senator Bob Corker of Tennessee pleading with Senator Harry Reid for understanding of Democratic grievances. The meeting is set to take place in the Old Senate Chamber on Monday at 6 p.m.

The Greenwich High School football team has come under fire for naming one of its plays "Hitler." The play, which involves an index finger laid across the upper lip as a signal, was used during a game against Trumbull on Thursday. A Trumbull mother, Debbie Levison, whose family suffered atrocities during the Holocaust, was outraged and approached the coach after the game to confirm the play's name. The football team and coaches met with the Connecticut Anti-Defamation League to discuss the offensive nature of the play. Headmaster Chris Winters issued an apology on Friday and stated that the practice has been stopped. Greenwich school officials also reached out to the local Jewish community to express their apology, and Rabbi Mitchell M. Hurvitz of Temple Sholom praised Winters for being "extremely proactive" in responding to the problem. The incident is seen as a teaching moment by Steve Ginsburg, executive director of the Connecticut ADL, who stated that there was a lack of understanding about the offensive nature of using Hitler's name in this context.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to the original versions of pages, even if they are changed or removed from the web. This is aimed at fixing broken links on the internet.

The attack is a significant blow to Tunisia's tourism industry, which depends heavily on foreign visitors. The article discusses an analysis by Data Genetics on the popularity of four-digit passwords and their potential use as ATM PIN numbers. Researchers found that common combinations such as "1234", "1111", and "0000" account for nearly 20% of all four-digit passwords, with those starting with "19" being particularly popular. On the other hand, less common combinations like "8068" appear less than 0.001% of the time. The analysis was based on a database of 3.4 million stolen passwords, and it was suggested that people should be more careful in choosing their PIN numbers to avoid making them easy to guess. The article also includes some interesting anecdotes about password patterns and references to XKCD cartoons.

The article discusses the breakdown of bipartisan negotiations for bank reform legislation in the Senate. Senator Christopher Dodd, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, plans to introduce a revised version of the bill without Republican support due to time constraints and pressure from the White House to pass health care legislation. The bill aims to reform the banking sector by creating a powerful consumer financial protection agency, among other changes.

Corker and Dodd had agreed on several key areas, such as a new structure for a consumer protection division, but disagreements remain on issues like shareholder empowering provisions that Republicans are trying to remove from the bill.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) seized two shipments containing 2,380 counterfeit hoverboards at the Port of Charleston, S.C., due to trademark violations and potential health risks posed by substandard ion lithium batteries. The total estimated value of the confiscated hoverboards is $1.6 million. This incident highlights the growing concern over counterfeit hoverboards entering U.S. ports, with more than 50,000 potentially unsafe boards being seized nationwide. CBP's enforcement of intellectual property rights aims to protect American consumers and businesses from dangerous goods and unfair competition. If you suspect a company or individual of trademark or copyright infringement, report the violation to CBP through their online system or by calling 1-800-BE-ALERT. The American Academy of Pediatrics has released a new policy statement on creating a safe sleeping environment for infants to decrease the risks of sleep-related deaths. The recommendations call for infants to share their parents' bedroom for at least the first six months and, optimally, for the first year of life. Infants should sleep in a separate surface such as a crib or bassinet, never on a couch, armchair, or soft surface. The crib should be bare with no pillows, sheets, blankets, or other items that could obstruct the infant's breathing or cause overheating. Skin-to-skin care is recommended immediately following birth for at least an hour as soon as the mother is medically stable and awake. The University of Virginia has implemented new safety rules for fraternities in response to allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity party. These rules include requiring at least three sober members to monitor behavior at parties, prohibiting pre-mixed alcoholic drinks, and implementing guest lists to control entry to the houses during events. One of the sober monitors must be posted at a staircase leading to bedrooms and have immediate key access to each room in the house to prevent situations that could lead to sexual assault. The rules were announced after a Rolling Stone article depicted a female student saying she was gang-raped at a fraternity house during her freshman year, though the article later unraveled as key elements of the rape allegation fell into doubt. University officials and leaders of Greek organizations pledged to continue a push to improve safety at UVA regardless. The new rules for fraternities will change the party culture at Virginia's flagship public university.

Republican Tim Pawlenty has declined to sign a pledge written by a conservative Iowa group that includes denouncing same-sex marriage rights, pornography, and certain forms of Islamic law. Country music artist Chely Wright, 40, recently married her girlfriend Lauren Blitzer, an LGBT activist, in a ceremony held at Blitzer's aunt's home in Connecticut. The Navy's regional commander postponed a port call for a destroyer in Naples, Italy, keeping it near Syria during the crisis, as it and another destroyer were armed with Tomahawk cruise missiles, potentially first to be used in any military action against Syria if ordered by the President.

Two young cousins, Elizabeth Collins (8) and Lyric Cook-Morrissey (10), have been missing since Friday afternoon after their bicycles were found abandoned near Meyers Lake in Evansdale, Iowa. Over 1,000 volunteers joined authorities in a search over the weekend, but the effort was suspended on Monday as no new clues have been found. The girls' families are hopeful but bracing for the worst, and authorities continue to investigate as tips come in to a designated tip line. The community has shown support during this difficult time, with many offering assistance in the search efforts.

A massive congealed lump of fat, wet wipes, and other non-degradable items, known as a "fatberg," has been discovered in Baltimore's sewer system between Baltimore Penn Station and the 1700 block of Charles St. This fatberg is responsible for two severe overflows in the past two weeks, including one on September 21 that discharged nearly 1.2 million gallons of sewage into the Jones Falls. The Baltimore Department of Public Works (DPW) found the fatberg while investigating multiple sewer overflows in the area. The DPW has a program to prevent fats, oils, and grease (FOG) from entering the sewer system, as they can cause blockages. Private residences are encouraged to keep FOG and non-flushable items out of the sewer system to avoid costly overflows. The DPW is currently repairing and replacing parts of the city's sewers to prevent stormwater infiltration and upgrade the sewer collection and treatment systems under a consent decree.

The Supreme Court heard arguments in the case ABC vs. Aereo, a streaming video service that allows users to watch and record local TV programs over the internet. The case centers around whether Aereo's service violates broadcasters' exclusive rights to transmit works to the public.

Aereo argues that its service is private because each transmission is initiated and controlled by individual users, while the broadcasters argue that it is a public performance due to the use of tiny antennas set up in cities to pick up signals. The justices struggled with understanding the technology involved and expressed concerns about the implications for cloud-based services.

Justice Breyer compared Aereo's service to a rooftop TV antenna that could theoretically pick up every television signal in the world, while Justice Sotomayor questioned why Aereo isn't simply a cable TV company. The broadcasters argued that Aereo is not a content provider like cable operators because it doesn't collect and retransmit programming in bulk to subscribers.

The case could have significant implications for the degree to which innovative companies must seek permission from copyright owners to enable cloud-based services, as well as the future of Aereo itself. The court is expected to issue its decision in the coming months.

Maria von Trapp, the last surviving member and second-eldest daughter of the musical family whose story inspired "The Sound of Music," has passed away at the age of 99 in her home in Vermont. Von Trapp was a key member of the Trapp Family Singers, with her life serving as the basis for Louisa in the 1959 Broadway musical and the 1965 film, which won an Oscar for best picture.

Born to Austrian Naval Captain Georg von Trapp and his first wife Agathe Whitehead von Trapp, Maria was one of seven children whose lives formed the basis for the singing family in the musical and film. "The Sound of Music" is a loose adaptation of a 1949 book by Maria's second wife, who passed away in 1987.

In 1938, the family fled Nazi-occupied Austria and embarked on concert tours throughout Europe before settling in Vermont in the early 1940s, where they opened a ski lodge in Stowe. Maria played accordion and taught Austrian dance at the lodge with her sister Rosmarie.

John Travolta is facing a lawsuit from an anonymous male masseur who claims the actor sexually assaulted him during a massage session. In the aftermath of Osama bin Laden's death, President Obama's approval rating has increased significantly, particularly in terms of dealing with terrorism and Afghanistan. However, there was no overall boost in his approval rating or electoral support, as the economy remains a major concern for Americans. The poll results show that 56% of respondents approve of Obama's job performance, while only 30% think the country is on the right track, and only 27% think the economy is heading in the right direction. Murphy reversed an earlier decision ordering doctors to artificially feed and hydrate the radio icon, who is suffering from Lewy Body Disease. Researchers at UC Berkeley have developed a groundbreaking technique that allows them to reconstruct YouTube videos based on brain activity recorded using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The scientists, led by Shinji Nishimoto and Jack Gallant, were able to create a computer model that matches features of the videos with patterns of brain activity. This technology could potentially offer insights into dreams, memories, and even fantasies, although further research is needed to understand more complex areas of the brain and improve resolution. The potential applications include helping individuals with paralysis control their environment by imagining sequences of movements. However, ethical considerations regarding privacy and the accuracy of memories remain a concern.

North Korea has detained a U.S. student, Otto Frederick Warmbier, from the University of Virginia, for committing a "hostile act" and wanting to "destroy the country’s unity". A Chinese woman named Xiang Liujuan died after being trapped and swallowed by an escalator at a shopping mall in Jingzhou, Hubei province. As they were about to disembark from the escalator, a footplate collapsed under Xiang's feet, creating a gap that threatened to swallow them both. Security camera footage shows Xiang holding her son as she prepares to step off the escalator when the flooring gives way. She pushes her son forward, who is then caught by a shopping assistant standing near the top of the escalator. Apple is launching an iPhone trade-in program this month, partnering with Brightstar Corp., a mobile-phone distributor, to encourage users to upgrade to the iPhone 5 and exchange their older models. This move is part of Apple's efforts to retain loyal customers and increase market share, particularly in overseas markets where the iPhone remains expensive compared to competitors.

In Spain, a professional bullfighter named Victor Barrio was killed during a bullfight in the town of Teruel on Saturday. Another man participating in a village bull-run near Valencia was also killed by a bull's horn, and two other men were gored during the San Fermin festival in Pamplona. The San Fermin festival attracts thousands of revellers and involves bulls chasing runners through narrow streets. Victor Barrio's death was broadcast live on television and stirred widespread reaction from the bullfighting community and well-known politicians. Festivities were immediately suspended following his death, and he is the first professional matador to die during a bullfight in Spain since 1985.

The Obamacare repeal bill in the House GOP received support from two prominent Republican opponents, Fred Upton of Michigan and Billy Long of Missouri, after negotiating a last-minute amendment with President Donald Trump at the White House. The complex weathered past cycles of hostility between the two countries but is now at risk of permanent shutdown due to the current tension.

North Korea has accused Seoul of insincerity, citing ongoing U.S.-South Korean military drills and the spreading of anti-North Korea leaflets at the border as evidence. Both analysts suggest that Pyongyang could confiscate South Korean properties in Kaesong if tensions escalate further, as it did in 2010 at a South Korean-built mountain resort on North Korea's east coast.

A New York City man, Thomas McDonald, is honoring his lifelong friend Roy Riegel by flushing his ashes down ballpark toilets around the country. However, since the recovered bees have been failing and will need to be monitored for diseases or mites before they can be used again. Cunniff's business, Beeline Honey in Choteau, lost about $224,000 worth of bees and equipment in the theft, but about $170,000 worth was recovered. The remaining hives were either damaged beyond repair or never found. Cunniff is planning to truck his bees down to California for the almond pollination season next summer, but will be more cautious about leaving them there for extended periods of time.

The century-old time capsule hidden in a lion statue atop the Old State House in Boston was opened on October 9th, revealing a hardcover book along with expected items such as letters, newspaper clippings, and maps from 1901. The contents of the book remain a mystery due to its fragile condition. The time capsule was sealed inside the lion's head since 1901 and was discovered during the statue's refurbishing. The Bostonian Society is planning to put a new time capsule in the lion's head, made of titanium, and is currently soliciting suggestions for its contents. The society also plans to include a medal from the 2013 Boston Marathon in the new capsule. The Old State House, one of Boston's most popular tourist attractions, has a storied history dating back to the Boston Massacre in 1770 and the first reading of the Declaration of Independence in 1776.

In Richmond, Virginia, a police officer who reported fellow officers for allegedly making inappropriate comments about harming President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama has been fired from the Richmond Police Department. The officer made the initial report to CBS 6 News last May, claiming that a 20-year department veteran suggested an officer "take a couple of shots" and that another voice in the background talked about planting a bomb under the stage during the president's visit.

The Secret Service investigated and found no criminal act, but two officers were fired amidst the furor. The fired officers have been fighting to get their jobs back, with their attorney claiming that the allegations against them were "false and/or greatly embellished" and that Richmond Mayor Dwight Jones pressured then-Police Chief Bryan Norwood to fire the officers before letting an internal investigation run its course.

The whistleblower was fired for violating department policy by doing an interview with CBS 6 about the incident. Employment attorney Thomas Roberts believes the firing may have a chilling effect on other police force members who might be afraid to speak out about matters of public concern. The fired officer is considering legal options.

Lt. Gov. Brian Schatz of Hawaii has been appointed to succeed the late U.S. Sen. Daniel Inouye. Colleen Hanabusa and Esther Kiaaina, a deputy director in the state Department of Land and Natural Resources. Inouye had expressed his wish to have Hanabusa succeed him before his death on Dec. 17, but Abercrombie chose Schatz instead. He will become Hawaii's senior senator heading into the new Congress, which begins on Jan. 3. President Barack Obama invited Schatz to join him on Air Force One as they work on budget issues and other pressing matters before Congress.

For instance, 66% believe information about making explosives should not be allowed on the Internet due to its availability to aspiring terrorists, even if some view this as a form of censorship.

Sen. Ted Cruz argued against Loretta Lynch's nomination as Attorney General, citing her potential continuation of Eric Holder's policies on immigration and executive overreach. Flint, Michigan is currently under a boil-water advisory due to a water main break on Tuesday. The advisory was issued because of concerns about bacterial contamination in the water supply. The advisory will be lifted once water sampling shows that the water is safe to drink.

Google's new photo app has come under fire for mislabeling a photo of two black people as "gorillas." This is not the first time such errors have occurred; similar incidents have been reported with Google Maps and Flickr's auto-tagging system.

The Shroud of Turin, a cloth revered by some Christians as Jesus' burial cloth, has been analyzed using Bloodstain Pattern Analysis, revealing inconsistencies that suggest it might be a fake. Researchers Matteo Borrini and Luigi Garlaschelli found that the blood-like stains on the shroud are inconsistent with each other and cannot be replicated through tests of a standing model. The findings, published in the Journal of Forensic Sciences, indicate that the shroud's bloodstain patterns do not match those expected from a crucified or hanging person, suggesting potential fabrication. However, further investigation is needed to determine the exact origin and creation of the Shroud of Turin.

The first same-sex couple to legally marry in Australia were Jill Kindt and Jo Grant. They married on December 15, 2017, just a week after same-sex marriage became legal in the country. Due to Jo's terminal illness with a rare cancer, they were granted an exemption from the usual 30-day waiting period. Jill Kindt shared that they were only married for 48 days before Jo passed away on January 30, 2018. The details of their wedding and the efforts made to expedite it were revealed in Queensland Parliament by Attorney-General Yvette D'Ath. Staff from Queensland Births, Deaths, and Marriages went to great lengths to ensure the marriage could take place quickly, including driving over 100km to deliver paperwork to the marriage celebrant. Jill Kindt expressed her gratitude for those who helped make their wedding possible, considering themselves married since a commitment ceremony in 2013 but only obtaining legal marriage in 2017. The story was called "inspiring" by Attorney-General Yvette D'Ath, who praised Queensland as a modern and trailblazing state recognizing equal rights.

Workers upgrading water mains under Washington Square Park in Greenwich Village discovered two centuries-old burial vaults, likely part of a Presbyterian church cemetery, containing more than a dozen sets of remains. The vaults were probably built in the late 18th or early 19th century and belonged to one of two area Presbyterian churches. Archaeologists will work to identify the buried individuals using old newspapers, death records, and church archives. Due to New York City policy, project engineers are planning a new route for the water main to avoid disturbing the burial ground further. The discovery is not the first time historical artifacts have been found during planned upkeep projects in the city.

A Pakistani schoolgirl, Malala Yousafzai, who campaigned for education rights, showed signs of improvement on Saturday after being shot in the head by the Taliban. She remains unconscious and on a ventilator but has moved her limbs. The attack has been widely denounced, with Pakistani authorities offering over $100,000 for the capture of her attackers. Malala's condition is stable, and specialist doctors are providing constant care. Two other girls wounded with her are also receiving treatment. The military is investigating the incident, but no details on arrests have been released. There has been a call for renewed vigor in Pakistan's struggle against Islamist militancy following the attack. Schools opened with prayers for Malala, and special prayers were held at mosques across the country. Some groups have cautioned against using the attack as a reason to launch fresh military offensives against militants. The attack has sparked outrage both domestically and internationally, with many viewing it as an attack on human values and national and social values.

David Paterson, New York Governor, appeared on Larry King Live in an attempt to quash sex rumors about him that have been circulating since last Sunday. The rumors were initially sparked by unsubstantiated claims of an upcoming New York Times article containing salacious revelations. However, Paterson's camp and the New York Times have both denied the existence of such an article. Former Army Captain William D. Swenson, who received the Medal of Honor on Tuesday for his heroic actions during a battle against the Taliban in Afghanistan in 2009, has requested to return to active duty in the Army. This is a rare move by an officer who has already received the military's highest award.

Swenson left the military in February 2011 as a captain but could potentially rise to the rank of major upon his return. He will have to pass a physical, drug test, and routine reviews to successfully re-enlist. Officials are optimistic that everything will fall into place.

It is unusual for an officer holding the Medal of Honor to rejoin active duty, and officials are unsure if this has ever happened before. After nearly being overlooked and intentionally forgotten, Swenson received the Medal of Honor at an emotional White House ceremony on Tuesday.

Swenson was honored for his actions during the Battle of Ganjgal in eastern Afghanistan, one of the bloodiest battles of the 12-year war. He braved enemy fire to retrieve bodies and save fellow troops during a lengthy battle against the Taliban.

Swenson has also received a Purple Heart and Bronze Star Medal and lives in Seattle. After his return to active duty, he will likely continue to support the Army and its fallen soldiers, as he did during the ceremony on Tuesday.

On April 22, 2018, a bus accident in North Hwanghae province, south of Pyongyang, resulted in the death of 36 people, including 32 Chinese tourists and four North Koreans. The crash occurred when the tourist bus fell from a bridge. North Korean leader Kim Jong-un expressed "bitter sorrow" over the incident and visited injured passengers at a hospital. He also met with China's ambassador to North Korea, Li Jinjun, at the Chinese Embassy in Pyongyang to express his condolences. The cause of the crash was not mentioned.

China is North Korea's main political ally and largest trading partner, with Chinese tourists making up an estimated 80% of foreign tourists to North Korea. Kim Jong-un's visit to the injured people and the reporting of it may be seen as a way of protecting his image among the Chinese population. Kim earlier this year visited Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, his first known foreign trip since taking office in 2011. China is responsible for virtually all of North Korea's food and fuel aid and can be considered its most important partner. North Korea recently announced it was halting all nuclear and missile tests as it builds up to a major summit with the leaders of South Korea and the US.

A coordinated ATM heist worth approximately $12.7 million was carried out in Japan by an international crime syndicate. The theft involved around 100 individuals who used forged credit cards containing illegally obtained account details from a South African bank, Standard Bank. The thieves made simultaneous withdrawals of the maximum amount allowed by cash machines at 1,400 convenience store ATMs across Tokyo and 16 other prefectures on May 15, 2023. No arrests have been made yet, and the suspects may have left Japan before their crime was discovered. The heist is reminiscent of the blockbuster film 'Ocean's Eleven.' Standard Bank has estimated its losses at $19.25 million but assured that its customers did not suffer any losses. This incident marks the second time Japan has been a victim of a sophisticated ATM heist, with a similar crime occurring between 2012 and 2013.

The incident occurred on May 13 when Paulsen left six dogs, including one of her own, in her truck while she used a public washroom at a Langley dog park. Initially, Paulsen reported the animals stolen, which led to a search by their owners and Petsearchers.com agency. However, the B.C. SPCA later took over the investigation and found that the dogs had died while enclosed in Paulsen's vehicle in Richmond.

Stevenson then fled into the woods and was caught within an hour. This incident highlights the advantage of proximity keys in preventing carjackings, leading to a change in the writer's perspective towards these devices.

The movie "If I Stay," directed by R.J. Cutler and based on Gayle Forman's novel, follows the story of Mia Hall (Chloë Grace Moretz), a 17-year-old cello prodigy who survives a car accident but finds herself in a coma, contemplating whether to continue living. The film is a tear-jerking drama with elements of first love and looming mortality, similar to "The Fault in Our Stars." Mia's life is depicted as idyllic before the accident, with a supportive family and a romantic relationship with Adam (Jamie Blackley). The movie toggles between Mia's hospital vigil and flashbacks of her previous life. Despite some emotional heaviness, the film delivers moments of sweetness and tenderness, with musical sequences adding energy to the narrative. However, critics note that the supernatural element can feel contrived, and Chloë Grace Moretz's character is criticized for being blandly edge-free compared to her roles in tougher films like "Kick-Ass" and "Let Me In." The movie has been rated PG-13.

Army Sergeant Bowe Bergdahl, who was held captive by the Taliban for five years, is en route to San Antonio, Texas, where he will continue his recovery at Brooke Army Medical Center. A lion named Mohawk was shot dead by rangers in Kenya on March 30, 2016, after it strayed from Nairobi National Park and attacked a man. Gillian Bennett, an 83-year-old woman diagnosed with dementia, ended her life on Monday after leaving behind a blog post advocating for assisted suicide. Bennett wrote that she didn't want to lose herself to dementia and leave behind an "empty husk." Her husband was present when she died outside their home on Bowen Island, BC.

Bennett's blog post called for changes in law, religion, and medicine regarding assisted suicide. She argued that the medical profession should mandate the administration of a lethal dose to end the suffering of terminally ill patients in accordance with their living will. Bennett also suggested that everyone over 50 should have a living will specifying how they would like to die.

Bennett's family was aware of her decision, and she spent her last weekend with her children before dying. Her husband, Jonathan Bennett, said Gillian was at peace when she died and did not find death scary.

Gillian Bennett is survived by her husband, two children, six grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren. She left behind a legacy of intellectual curiosity, courage, and grace, as well as a desire to open a conversation about assisted suicide.

The article discusses a new study that suggests weight cycling, or repeatedly losing and regaining weight, may increase the risk of death from heart disease, particularly among postmenopausal women who were of normal weight at the start of the study. The research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2016.

The study classified self-reported weight history from 158,063 post-menopausal women into four categories: stable weight, steady gain, maintained weight loss, and weight cycling. During a follow-up of 11.4 years, they found that women who had a normal weight at the beginning of the study but then lost and regained weight had about three and a half times higher risk for sudden cardiac death than women whose weight remained stable. Weight cycling in the normal-weight women was also associated with a 66 percent increased risk for coronary heart disease deaths.

No increase in either type of death occurred among overweight or obese women reporting weight cycling, nor among women who reported that they gained weight but did not lose it or, in the opposite scenario, that they lost weight without gaining it back. The study has several limitations, including being observational and relying on self-reports.

The incident occurred at the Hyatt Hotel off North Sam Houston Parkway. Ricin is a highly toxic substance derived from castor beans, and there is no specific test for exposure or antidote once exposed. Norway's Prime Minister Erna Solberg has issued an official government apology for the mistreatment of Norwegian women who had intimate relationships with German soldiers during World War II. Approximately 50,000 Norwegian women were labeled as "German girls" and faced reprisals such as job dismissals, detentions, expulsions, and removal of nationality after Norway's liberation in 1945. The apology was based on a report about Norway's post-war actions published by the country's Centre for Holocaust and Minorities Studies. Many of the women were targeted because they were suspected of betraying their country, and some were expelled from Norway to Germany along with their children. The apology comes 70 years after the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights and is based on the conclusion that Norwegian authorities violated the fundamental principle that no citizen can be punished without trial or sentenced without law. The apology was welcomed by families affected by the mistreatment, although many of the women directly involved are no longer alive to hear it.

A strong 6.0-magnitude earthquake struck Northern California on August 24, with the epicenter near Napa Valley's renowned wineries. The quake caused damage to buildings, infrastructure, and precious vintages. More than 170 people were injured, and over 100 homes became uninhabitable.

In the aftermath, volunteers, including Home Depot workers from various Northern California communities, offered their help in cleanup efforts. Residents and outsiders alike found a common calling in assisting each other, with many expressing gratitude for the outpouring of support. Strangers helped Lori Lemieux, a resident whose home was damaged in the quake, by passing her fallen chimney bricks into a waiting truck bed.

Geologists are still investigating the exact fault responsible for the earthquake, but it is believed to have occurred on the West Napa Fault, not the Franklin Fault as initially thought. The earthquake was the largest in California since the 1994 Northridge earthquake and the biggest in Northern California since the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake.

Cleanup efforts are ongoing, with many residents and businesses working to restore normalcy. The recovery will require time and money, but there is a sense of relief that the damage wasn't worse.

The seeds will be sent once paperwork is completed. The vault currently holds over 860,000 samples from almost all nations and is designed to protect crop seeds against catastrophic events such as nuclear war or disease.

Highly fluorinated chemicals (HFCs) are a group of chemicals used in consumer products such as cookware, clothing, outdoor apparel, carpeting, and food packaging to provide nonstick, oil- and water resistant properties. They are also used in some kinds of cosmetics. These chemicals contain carbon-fluorine bonds that make them both incredibly resistant to breakdown and very useful. However, they have been associated with various health problems including testicular and kidney cancer, liver malfunction, hormonal changes, thyroid disruption, high cholesterol, obesity, ulcerative colitis, lower birth weight and size, among others. Due to their resistance to breakdown, these chemicals can persist in our bodies for years and in the environment for millions of years. Scientists from all over the world have expressed concerns about HFCs and are asking for a limit to the production and use of these chemicals. Consumers can take steps to avoid products that contain HFCs by avoiding products that are oil repellant or stain resistant, only purchasing waterproof gear when necessary, avoiding cosmetics with PTFE or any word containing “perfluor” or “polyfluor” on their ingredients list, replacing Teflon nonstick cookware with cast iron, glass, or ceramic, and supporting companies committed to phasing out HFCs.

Archaeologists have discovered evidence suggesting that the people living near Tbilisi, Georgia, 8,000 years ago were the world's earliest known winemakers. The findings, published in PNAS, indicate that these Stone Age farmers produced wine on a large scale as early as 6,000 B.C., using pottery with residual tartaric acid, a chemical "fingerprint" of wine. The researchers found broken pottery, including the rounded bases of large jars, embedded in the floors of the village houses at Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveri Gora. Chemical analysis by University of Pennsylvania archaeologist Patrick McGovern confirmed the presence of wine residues in fragments of pottery from both sites. The evidence adds to our understanding of the Neolithic period, a pivotal time when humans were first learning to farm and settle down. Georgia, which has more than 500 local grape varieties, is still known for its winemaking today.

The breach could potentially have repercussions on the deal, and there is a possibility that the price may be adjusted or the deal may be cancelled due to the security incident. Users are advised to use strong, unique passwords for each account and consider using a password manager app.

The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), a symbol of American capitalism for 220 years, is in discussions to be acquired by IntercontinentalExchange (ICE) in an $8.2 billion merger. A new study has linked certain drugs used to treat Parkinson's disease, such as dopamine receptor agonists, to abnormal behaviors like pathological gambling, hypersexuality, and compulsive shopping. The researchers found that 710 of the cases occurred in people taking these specific drugs, while the other 870 cases occurred in people taking all other types of drugs combined.

The study authors suggest that doctors and patients should be cautious about the side effects of these drugs, as they may lead to impulse control disorders. The researchers also believe that their findings can help scientists better understand how abnormal behaviors develop in general and how they may be related to the brain receptor targeted by the drug.

The dopamine agonist drugs affect a receptor called dopamine D3 receptor, with pramipexole being the most commonly linked drug to such behaviors. The researchers recommend that doctors and caregivers of Parkinson's patients should be on the lookout for these types of behavior and understand that they may be linked to the use of medication.

The study was published in the journal JAMA Internal Medicine, and the authors suggest that a more prominent warning about the potential side effects of these drugs is necessary for doctors who prescribe them. The researchers also note that these behavioral problems usually go away after patients stop taking the medicines.

The main news article discusses a study published in Psychological Science that found people can detect high-power voices based on acoustic properties. They found that high-power voices tend to go up in pitch, become more monotone, and vary more in loudness than low-power voices.

The study suggests that people are perceptive to subtle variations in vocal cues and use them to determine who is in charge during interactions. Vistara, an Indian airline based in New Delhi, has launched a Women Flyer program that offers complimentary services aimed at making female travelers feel safer. The airline claims between 75 and 100 women use the service daily.

The move comes in response to concerns about safety for women travelers in India, particularly on public transportation. In January, Air India introduced female-only rows on its flights following reports of assault cases taking place mid-flight.

The Women Flyer program is believed to be the first of its kind in the airline industry. Vistara hopes to extend the service to international flights once it expands outside of India. The airline is also considering leasing or buying Boeing jets for longer-haul routes.

Chicago residents have filed a lawsuit against the city's controversial tax policy on digital entertainment, claiming it is illegal and could set a precedent for local taxation of Internet companies. The lawsuit alleges that the city's extension of an existing 9% "Amusement" levy to streaming services like Netflix, Spotify, and Xbox Live amounts to a new tax that should have been imposed by a vote of city officials. The plaintiffs argue that the tax violates the federal Internet Tax Freedom Act, which forbids discriminatory internet-only taxes, and treats streaming differently from DVD-by-mail services and imposes a higher rate than various live forms of entertainment. The lawsuit also claims that the city illegally implemented the tax through a decision of its Finance Department instead of submitting the policy change to a city council vote. If the Illinois state court agrees with the plaintiffs, it could set a major precedent for local taxation of Internet companies.

Over the past half-century, linguists and researchers have been intrigued by this "bird language," which adapts standard Turkish syllables into piercing tones that can be heard from over half a mile away. A recent study conducted by Turkish-born German biopsychologist Onur Güntürkün found that the brain processes whistled Turkish differently compared to spoken Turkish, suggesting a more flexible division of labor between the left and right hemispheres in understanding language. The study, published in Current Biology, used dichotic listening to find that both hemispheres played significant roles in comprehending whistled Turkish. However, the opportunity to study this unique dialect is fading as it rapidly disappears from daily life due to modern communication methods like texting offering a level of privacy that whistling never did. Despite this, whistled Turkish still comes in handy when communicating with non-Turkish speakers, such as Güntürkün's secretary who speaks German.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the head of the International Monetary Fund, is currently on suicide watch at New York City's Rikers Island jail complex. He was transferred there after being accused of sexually assaulting a hotel maid in Manhattan. Due to his high profile and potential risk, he has been assigned to a specialized facility with 24-hour guard monitoring, a medical device for sleep apnea, and is housed in a wing that normally houses prisoners with contagious diseases. He is also undergoing mental health evaluations due to concerns raised during the assessment. Strauss-Kahn's lawyer denies the charges against him and he is being held without bail before his next court appearance on Friday. The maid involved in the case is reportedly in hiding following the incident.

The study, published in the journal Science, found that only 39 out of 100 recently published psychology studies could be replicated. This raises concerns about the reproducibility of scientific findings, particularly in the field of psychology. The researchers suggest that this issue is more about the difficulty of designing a reproducible study rather than the accuracy of the studies themselves.

The study aimed to recreate 100 studies published in major psychology journals and found that 61% of the results could not be replicated. This has been attributed to three possible reasons: the original result may not have been real, the researchers failed to detect a real effect during reproduction, or both studies were accurate but their methodologies differed in meaningful ways.

The study highlights the need for more focus on reproducibility in scientific research. The current focus on novelty encourages researchers to publish new results rather than reproduce older ones, which may lead to an overemphasis on findings that are not as reliable as they seem. To move toward more repeatable studies, researchers and journals need to shift their interests away from novelty.
