University of Cincinnati President Santa Ono revealed over the weekend that he had attempted suicide twice in his youth, aiming to erase the stigma attached to mental illnesses and encourage those suffering from depression to seek help. Ono, who has been open about his struggle with depression, was instrumental in arranging for the university to provide five free sessions of mental health counseling following the death of a student by suicide in 2014. His revelation did not surprise Dr. Phil Diller, who oversees the University Health Service, as Ono had confided about his own struggles with depression and suicide attempts during a meeting after the student's death. Ono's revelation was met with praise on social media, with many thanking him for speaking out. Resources for mental health services are provided in the article.

The control of Virginia's House of Delegates remains uncertain after a three-judge panel declined to certify the recount of a key House race, leaving it tied between Democrat Shelly Simonds and Republican Del. David Yancey. The ballot in question contained a mark for both candidates, with an additional mark to strike out Simonds' name. Officials had discarded this ballot during the recount, but Republicans challenged the decision in court, arguing that the voter intended to vote for Yancey. The judges agreed, leaving the race tied at 11,608 votes each. State law dictates that a tied House race will be determined by lot, with a coin toss scheduled for Dec. 27. The outcome of this race could significantly impact the balance of power in Virginia's legislature, as Democrats had previously thought they won the seat by a single vote. Both parties are assessing legal options and the situation remains fluid.

On Wednesday night, a concert by DJ Avicii at the TD Garden in Boston resulted in dozens of concertgoers being hospitalized due to dehydration, drugs, and alcohol. The Massachusetts General Hospital received 13 patients between the ages of 16 and 19. Most patients were treated for heat-related symptoms and underage drinking. Avicii, known for hits like "Wake Me Up," performed as part of his True Tour. This incident follows a series of similar incidents at music festivals, including the Electric Daisy Carnival in Las Vegas and the Electric Zoo music festival. TD Garden has been cited following the mass medical emergency and is taking steps to prevent such incidents in the future.

Burger King is testing a new menu item called the Whopperito, which combines the ingredients of their iconic Whopper burger into a tortilla wrap. The test is currently underway at several locations in Pennsylvania, and it's unclear if the Whopperito will be rolled out to other cities or states. Reactions on Twitter range from disgust to intrigue, with some potential customers expressing excitement about the new offering. The creation of the Whopperito follows the introduction of the Whopper Dog, which replaced the bun of a Whopper with a hot dog. It appears that a similar combination, involving going to both Burger King and Taco Bell for the same meal, has been popular among some diners for several years.

The United States has been urged by China not to allow a delegation from Taiwan to attend President-elect Donald Trump's inauguration on Friday. This request comes amid concerns that Trump may seek to redefine relations between Beijing, Taipei, and Washington.

China's Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Hua Chunying stated that the request had been passed to both Trump's transition team and the current administration of Barack Obama. She emphasized China's opposition to any activities by Taiwan that could interfere or undermine the China-U.S. relationship.

The delegation, led by former premier and ex-ruling party leader Yu Shyi-kun, is scheduled to attend the inauguration and hold talks with politicians, academics, and overseas Chinese community representatives. This is a typical move for Taiwan during U.S. presidential inaugurations.

Tensions between China and Taiwan have risen since Tsai Ing-wen's election last year, with Beijing cutting off contacts and working to deepen Taiwan's diplomatic isolation. Trump's phone call with Tsai Ing-wen in December broke decades of precedent and raised concerns about the future of U.S.-China-Taiwan relations.

Trump has also expressed his willingness to negotiate the "One China" policy, a position that Beijing strongly rejects. The U.S. has no formal relations with Taiwan

The President of Palau, Tommy Remengesau, has proposed a new law that aims to attract high-end tourists by allowing only five-star hotel developments on its islands. This move is part of an effort to reduce the number of tourists and focus on those who spend more money, addressing concerns about overcrowding, damage to coral reefs, and wildlife disturbance. The government will offer tax breaks and exemptions to investors who build their own infrastructure, such as roads and water treatment systems for resorts. Palau, known for its pristine beaches, world-class scuba diving, and forest-covered volcanic islands, relies heavily on tourism for 85% of its GDP. The move appears to have been successful in increasing tourist spending while reducing visitor numbers. The location of the new five-star resorts has not yet been determined, but there are over 500 islands to choose from. The sustainability and harmony with Palau's natural assets of these future developments remains uncertain.

The Supreme Court has upheld a federal law that prohibits individuals convicted of any form of domestic violence, including those committed in heated arguments, from owning guns. The decision was made in response to two Maine men who argued their misdemeanor convictions for hitting their partners should not disqualify them from gun ownership. The ruling was supported by advocates for victims of domestic abuse and opposed by gun rights groups.

Russia won 18 medals, including eight golds, in track and field at the last Summer Olympics but will not be represented under their national flag in Rio. This penalty is more severe than the one imposed on East Germany, which had a notorious doping scheme throughout the 1960s, '70s, and '80s.

The IAAF has given individual Russian athletes a chance to compete as neutrals if they can demonstrate that they have been subject to effective anti-doping systems and are not tainted by Russia's doping program. This feat has not been achieved since 1971 and is shared with Chris Davis (2013), Nelson Cruz (2011), Mark McGwire (1998), and Willie Mays (1971). His impressive performance has earned praise from fellow players and management alike, with Carlos Gonzalez calling him "legendary" and Walt Weiss stating he's never seen anything like it before. A lost species of snake, the Clarion nightsnake, has been rediscovered after nearly 80 years on a remote Mexican island. The snake was first discovered by American naturalist William Beebe in 1936 but was later struck from taxonomic registries due to no further sightings over the years. A team of researchers led by Daniel Mulcahy from the National Museum of Natural History in Washington and Juan Martinez Gomez from Mexico's Ecology Institute rediscovered the snake on Clarion Island, one of the Revillagigedo Islands off Mexico's Pacific coast. DNA analysis confirmed that the snake is genetically distinct from others found in mainland Mexico and exclusively found on the island. The team plans to continue monitoring the species to learn more about its role in the delicate ecosystem of Clarion Island.

In Parsippany, New Jersey, a driver identified as Domingo Moreno, 27, allegedly fled the scene of an accident where he hit a fire hydrant and a mailbox. Gene and Pat Warrington, an Ohio couple who were married for 69 years, passed away eight hours apart in Findlay on December 27, while both were receiving hospice care. After the war, Gene graduated from high school in 1947, a year after Pat's graduation. The couple raised three children together and had seven grandchildren and twelve great-grandchildren. The reality series "Swamp People," airing on The History Channel, focuses on Cajun alligator hunters in Louisiana's Atchafalaya Swamp during the crucial 30-day hunting season. The study conducted by Stanford researchers reveals a growing life expectancy gap between the wealthiest and poorest Americans. Men in the top one percent can expect to live 14.6 years longer than those in the bottom one percent, while women in the top one percent can expect to live 10.1 years longer. However, the authors found that income alone does not fully explain life expectancy; geographical location also plays a significant role. The poor have a higher life expectancy in prosperous urban areas like San Francisco and New York City compared to more rural areas and certain states such as Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Kansas. Factors contributing to this discrepancy include local public health programs and policies, healthier behaviors, higher graduation levels, and government expenditures. The study suggests that discussions about inequality in America should focus more on a local level where disparities have a greater impact on health and lifespan.

The UK general election results show that Prime Minister David Cameron's Conservative Party is poised to retain power, securing a majority in Parliament. A U.K. soldier named David Hart, who was killed by a Taliban bomb while serving in Afghanistan, left £250,000 (approximately $400,000) in his will to be distributed among his friends and charity. Thailand's Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva declared a state of emergency on Wednesday, following anti-government demonstrators storming the country's parliament. The dispute over ownership of the chair predates the current execution crisis, with the DOC claiming ownership and McAlester mayor Steve Harrison suggesting that the chair should be on display for the public to see. As states grapple with a European-led boycott over lethal injection drugs, some have proposed returning to old methods such as the electric chair and the firing squad.

A man named Jason Behrens was arrested in Kearney, Nebraska on Wednesday for drunk driving with his children in the car. This was not the first time he had been accused of driving under the influence with minors in the vehicle. During a family vacation, Behrens' children became nervous as they noticed the car swerving and making close calls, eventually sending text messages to 911. After nearly getting into a head-on collision, they sent texts to Kearney Police, leading them to arrest Behrens at a Burger King. The children, aged 14 and 12, thanked the officers for saving their lives. Behrens blew three times the legal limit when arrested. The children have been placed in the care of their mother, Amy Brooks, who has set up a GoFundMe page for the situation. Buffalo County is one of two counties in Nebraska to offer Text 911 as an emergency service option.

In January 2019, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) along with public health and regulatory officials in several states, Canada, and the FDA investigated a multistate outbreak of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli O157:H7 (E. coli O157:H7) infections. As of January 9, 2019, 62 people infected with the outbreak strain were reported from 16 states and the District of Columbia. Illnesses started on dates ranging from October 7, 2018, to December 4, 2018. Epidemiologic, laboratory, and traceback evidence indicated that romaine lettuce from the Central Coastal growing regions of northern and central California was the likely source of this outbreak. The FDA is continuing its investigation of farms identified in traceback. Consumers were advised to not eat any romaine lettuce due to the ongoing investigation. This outbreak appears to be over as of January 9, 2019. The CDC also provided guidelines on how to clean a refrigerator after a food recall.

The article provides an exclusive update on the ongoing search for the actor to play Captain America in Marvel Studios' upcoming film, "The First Avenger: Captain America." The studio and director Joe Johnston are reportedly considering Chris Evans, who previously portrayed Johnny Storm/Human Torch in two Fantastic Four films. Mike Vogel (Cloverfield) and Garrett Hedlund (Tron: Legacy) remain the top contenders. Hedlund was initially on Marvel's wish list but did not test due to scheduling conflicts and reservations from his representatives over the potential for nine future films and a salary of approximately $300,000. Other actors who tested for the role, including Chace Crawford (CW’s Gossip Girl), John Krasinski (NBC’s The Office), Scott Porter (NBC’s Friday Night Lights), Michael Cassidy (CW’s Privileged) and Patrick Flueger (Brothers), are no longer in contention. Paramount Pictures is set to release the film on July 22, 2011, and a new trailer for Hedlund's upcoming film, Tron Legacy, can be viewed online.

The article discusses a study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association that reveals China has more smokers than ever, despite a decrease in smoking prevalence over the past few decades. In 2012, China had approximately 281 million smokers, accounting for one-third of the world's smoking population. The study was conducted by researchers at the Seattle-based Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation and is among the first to provide a comprehensive global time series on smoking prevalence.

The findings highlight the need for China to address tobacco control due to the significant health, economic, and environmental costs associated with smoking. Despite government measures enacted in recent years to restrict smoking, such as bans in restaurants and public places, these measures are rarely enforced. The overall number of smokers in China has increased, but the gender ratio of smokers has become more skewed towards men, with only about 4% of smokers being female in 2012.

The article also mentions that China is aiming to ban indoor smoking in public areas by the end of the year, and that half of Chinese men smoke. The World Health Organization warns that if tobacco use is not decreased in China, tobacco-related deaths will increase from over a million per year to 3 million by 2050. The latest moves by the Chinese government on tobacco are seen as hopeful

The article reports on a study that found Republicans are slightly more likely to report being happily married than Democrats, even after accounting for demographic differences between the two parties. The study was conducted by W. Bradford Wilcox of the Institute for Family Studies. The researchers suggest that this difference could be due to Republican's cultural emphasis on the importance of marriage or Republicans being more optimistic and charitable in their views of their marriages. However, it is also possible that Republicans are simply less likely to admit to an unhappy marriage. The study found that 67% of Republicans report being "very happy" with their marriages compared to 60% of Democrats. The gap shrinks when demographic differences are accounted for but does not disappear completely. The researchers acknowledge that the causality could work in the opposite direction, with married people being more likely to identify as Republican. The study also found that Republicans are more likely to be married and less likely to be divorced than Democrats.

The study conducted by Kaiser Permanente has found that the HIV-preventing drug Truvada, which was approved in 2012, has been 100% effective in preventing HIV infections among over 600 patients who have been taking it for about three years. The results of this real-world study, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, confirm the drug's effectiveness in a less controlled setting than clinical trials.

Truvada, an anti-retroviral drug originally used to treat HIV, has been shown to reduce the risk of HIV infection by up to 92% when taken consistently. However, it has faced criticism for potentially encouraging unsafe sex due to a false sense of security. Despite this controversy, public health advocates and the CDC recommend Truvada as a prophylactic for high-risk individuals under careful medical supervision.

The study did not have a control group but found no HIV infections among participants, even though many did not use condoms and half were diagnosed with other sexually transmitted diseases within a year. The effectiveness of the drug is attributed to consistent adherence to the medication.

For individuals like Paul Marcelin, who participated in the study while maintaining a relationship with an HIV-positive partner, Truvada offers peace of mind. However, Marcelin acknowledges that its use may not be necessary during all phases of life.

A DreamWorks animator named Young Song, aged 40, pleaded not guilty to a charge of brutally beating and shooting a neighbor's muzzled German Shepherd puppy with a hammer and pellet gun. The incident was captured on surveillance camera but the dog's whereabouts are currently unknown and it is presumed dead. The animator, who has worked on films such as "Kung Fu Panda," "Shark Tale," "Bee Movie," and "Madagascar 2," allegedly scaled a fence into his neighbor's yard in Pasadena on April 20th and chased the defenseless puppy, causing it to become motionless. The Humane Society is investigating the case along with local police, and if convicted, Song could face several years in state prison for animal cruelty and theft of the animal.

The United Nations monitor, Maj. Gen. Robert Mood, stated that the escalating violence in Syria has made it difficult for his mission to observe, verify, and report on the situation, and a ceasefire is necessary for its revival. Syrian President Assad, in an interview with Turkey's Cumhuriyet newspaper, showed no willingness to heed calls for a ceasefire or a transitional government as proposed by Kofi Annan, the special envoy on Syria. The interview provided insights into Assad's views on his domestic situation and regional relationships, including tensions with Turkey following the downing of a Turkish warplane over the Mediterranean last month. Assad also expressed his belief that Islamist militants sponsored by Arab adversaries and hostility from both the West and neighboring Turkey are attacking Syria, aiming to break it up or trigger a civil war. He claimed that he has popular support among Syrians, unlike the Shah of Iran who was overthrown in 1979. Iraq's foreign minister also reported having solid information about al-Qaida militants infiltrating Syria from Iraq to carry out attacks, and Iraq has reinforced security along its border with Syria due to concerns about a spillover of violence.

Nine-year-old Elina Childs sold out of Girl Guide cookies in about 45 minutes outside an Edmonton cannabis store on its opening day. Her father, Seann Childs, came up with the idea to sell the cookies there as they had faced difficulties selling them door-to-door in their neighborhood. The sales were well-received and some cars even stopped on the street to buy a box. Elina's parents used the experience as a teaching moment to discuss cannabis legalization with her, as she has cystic fibrosis and the Girl Guides program helps keep her active. The Girl Guides organization praised Elina's strategy for selling cookies outside of the pot shop.

A 19-year-old individual named Ryan has been arrested by the Metropolitan Police Central e-Crime Unit on suspicion of network intrusions and DDoS attacks against international businesses and intelligence agencies. The investigation involved the FBI, and it's speculated that these attacks may be linked to LulzSec and Anonymous activist groups. However, members of LulzSec and Anonymous have since stated that Ryan is not part of their integral operations and was only running an IRC server for them. There has been some confusion within the AntiSec campaign regarding who was actually arrested, but it's been clarified that Ryan Cleary, a previous target of Anonymous due to his alleged attempts to attack them, is the individual in question. The arrest took place at a residential address in Wickford, Essex, and the teenager is currently being held for questioning at a central London police station.

The document discusses the recent seizure of two major Iraqi cities, Mosul and Tikrit, by Sunni Islamist insurgents led by the Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant (ISIL). The U.S., which has been providing intelligence through unmanned surveillance aircraft, is considering all options, including military action, to help Iraq fight the militants. However, there is no intention of sending ground troops. The insurgents are planning to push further south towards Baghdad and regions dominated by Shia Muslims, whom they consider infidels. If ISIL can hold Mosul and consolidate its presence there, it will have taken a significant step towards creating an Islamist emirate that straddles Iraq and Syria. The success of ISIL could deepen the sectarian conflict between Sunnis and Shias in the Middle East, potentially leading to increased involvement from Iran, which shares a border with Iraq and has close links with some Iraqi Shia militias. The U.S. invasion and occupation of Iraq in 2003 is seen as having contributed to the creation and strengthening of jihadist groups. The insurgent advance has led to increased security measures in Baghdad, and Kurdish forces have claimed control of the oil city of Kirkuk. The failure of the Iraqi parliament to achieve a quorum to vote on emergency powers highlights the fragmented state of Iraqi politics.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has developed a new atomic clock using ytterbium atoms, which is currently the world's most stable clock. This table-sized device ticks with an incredible precision that does not change by more than one part in 10^18, making it about 10 times better than previous atomic clocks.

The new clock could have significant impacts on various scientific explorations and technological advancements, particularly in navigation systems, testing Einstein's theory of general relativity, and improving global positioning systems (GPS). However, the total cost of these clocks is estimated to be around half a million dollars, making them impractical for everyday use.

Researchers are working on shrinking the technology to make it suitable for space travel. Although the clock has demonstrated incredible stability, its accuracy is yet to be determined, and more research is needed to confirm whether these clocks could be the most accurate in the world. The study was published in the journal Science Express.

A woman stole a wedding ring from a deceased person at Sunset Memorial Gardens & Funeral Home in Odessa, Texas on April 8th. The suspect is described as a heavy-set white female wearing a brown long sleeve sweater, black sweat pants, and black sandals. She was driving a red or maroon 4-door Saturn. The family of the deceased has released a photo of the suspect's vehicle and is asking anyone with information to contact the Odessa Police Department or Odessa Crime Stoppers at 432-333-TIPS. The theft occurred after the woman's visitation service, during which several family members were present. The funeral home has video surveillance of the incident, but no arrests have been made and the investigation continues.

The House Intelligence Committee has voted to release a classified memo written by Republicans that alleges improper use of government surveillance during the investigation into Russian election interference and contacts with President Donald Trump's campaign. The memo, which addresses a dossier of allegations against Trump compiled by a former British spy, was written by Trey Gowdy and Devin Nunes, and questions whether it was used to obtain surveillance warrants. Democrats on the committee voted against its release. The White House has not yet decided whether to authorize its release, but President Trump favors "full transparency." Two Republican senators, Lindsey Graham and Susan Collins, have urged special counsel Robert Mueller to review whether Trump tried to fire him last June. The memo has been a source of escalating partisan tension in Congress, with Republicans arguing it shows wrongdoing by FBI officials involved in the surveillance of a Trump campaign aide, while Democrats say it mischaracterizes intelligence and is an attempt to distract from Mueller's probe into Russia's interference in the 2016 election.

This decision comes after Bannon made controversial remarks about Trump's family in a book titled "Fire and Fury: Inside the Trump White House," which led to his resignation from Breitbart. Bannon had been executive chairman of Breitbart since 2012, but his position became untenable due to his comments in the book. He left the White House in August 2017 and returned to Breitbart, but after the release of the book, Breitbart began to distance itself from Bannon. His association with controversial figures like Milo Yiannopoulos and Roy Moore also contributed to his downfall. Bannon's comments about Trump Jr.'s meeting with a Russian lawyer during the presidential campaign enraged Trump, who called him "Sloppy Steve" and accused him of being a leaker. Bannon has since apologized for his comments, but the White House has rejected the overture.

Researchers have proposed a new hypothesis suggesting that microbes, specifically Methanosarcina, may have caused the worst mass extinction in Earth's history 252 million years ago. This event, known as the end-Permian extinction, wiped out up to 90% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrates. Previous theories attributed this catastrophe to asteroids or large-scale volcanism, but the new research suggests that microscopic organisms were the primary culprits.

Methanosarcina is a type of archaea (single-celled organisms distinct from bacteria) that thrives in various environments like oil wells and trash dumps. In this case, it grew rapidly in the oceans, producing large amounts of methane, a potent greenhouse gas. This methane emission led to global warming and ocean acidification, creating unlivable conditions for many species.

The researchers found that volcanic eruptions in Siberia may have played a role by driving up ocean concentrations of nickel, an essential nutrient for Methanosarcina's growth. This combination of factors allowed the microbe to proliferate and cause the mass extinction. The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

U.S. judges in at least five states have blocked federal authorities from enforcing President Trump's executive order restricting immigration from seven Muslim-majority countries. However, some authorities were reportedly unwilling to follow the judges' rulings on Sunday. The orders came after similar decisions by judges in New York, California, Massachusetts, Virginia, and Washington state. The rulings could complicate the administration's effort to enforce the order, which halts travel by people with passports from Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen for 90 days and stops the resettlement of refugees for 120 days. Lawsuits have been filed on behalf of more than 100 individual travelers nationwide, and some have come from large corporate firms including Mayer Brown, Kirkland & Ellis, and Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said it will comply with judicial orders while enforcing the order in a manner that ensures those entering the United States "do not pose a threat to our country or the American people." The growing number of rulings has raised questions about the constitutionality of the order, and attorneys general from several states have condemned it as unconstitutional. Supporters of the order say authorities acted properly in enforcing it.

A passenger plane approaching Heathrow Airport from Geneva was believed to have been struck by a drone while flying at approximately 1,700ft over Richmond Park, London. The British Airways flight, with 132 passengers and five crew members on board, landed safely, but an investigation is underway led by the Metropolitan Police's aviation security unit. No arrests have been made, and no debris has been found. If confirmed, this would be the first such incident in the UK. The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) considers it unacceptable to fly drones near airports, and there are calls for greater enforcement of existing rules. The incident highlights the growing concern about the potential dangers posed by drones to civilian aircraft.

Both Petraeus and Allen appear to know Kelley's sister, and both men have written letters in support of her in a custody battle. The FBI is currently investigating Broadwell for potential unauthorized release of classified information, but it is unlikely she will be prosecuted.

In Tampa, Florida, a serial killing spree has occurred in the Seminole Heights neighborhood over the past 11 days, with three people killed and no arrests made as of yet. Police believe all three victims are connected by proximity and timeframe, but have not released any information about potential connections between the type of weapon or ammunition used in the killings. The shooter remains at large and police have described the situation as frustrating and tragic.

The defendant, Sandra Layne, a 75-year-old Detroit-area woman, has been convicted of second-degree murder for fatally shooting her 17-year-old grandson Jonathan Hoffman last May. The verdict was seen as "vindication" by the victim's parents, Jennifer and Michael Hoffman, who claimed that Layne had portrayed their son negatively during the trial.

Layne testified that she bought a gun due to fear of her grandson and his friends after he moved in with her for his senior year in high school. The jury rejected her self-defense argument, finding her guilty of second-degree murder, using a gun during a felony, and likely facing at least 14 years in prison.

Jennifer Hoffman described her mother as a "monster" and expressed grief over the loss of her son, stating that he was a good person whose reputation had been tarnished throughout the trial. The Hoffmans moved to Arizona due to caring for a daughter with a brain tumor and had offered Layne to take in Jonathan Hoffman for his final year of school in 2011.

The incident occurred on Saturday when Hadley allegedly beat his parents to death before hosting a house party. About 40 to 60 people attended the party, unaware of the grisly events that had taken place earlier in the day.

Hadley's friend, Michael Mandell, recounted seeing the bodies of Hadley's parents when he was asked by Hadley to stay at the party until everyone left. Mandell said that Hadley admitted to taking three ecstasy pills and feeling possessed by the devil before committing the murders.

The police found the bodies of Mary Jo Hadley, 47, and Blake Hadley, 54, with a 22-inch framing hammer between them. Authorities said that Hadley attempted to cover the cadavers in books and towels. Hadley is currently on suicide watch and has been charged with second-degree murder.

In a gruesome discovery near Guadalajara, Mexico, police found 18 mutilated and headless bodies inside two vans on a dirt road near Lake Chapala, a popular tourist spot. The Jalisco state Prosecutor, Tomas Coronado, confirmed that the bodies were dismembered and that handwritten messages were found in the vans, which authorities believe were left by the Zetas drug cartel. This massacre is believed to be part of an ongoing conflict between the Zetas and the Jalisco New Generation gang, allied with the Sinaloa cartel. The Zetas are known for their brutal tactics, including dismembering victims and leaving messages. A woman was detained in connection with a separate kidnapping incident in the same area, which she claimed was retaliation for events in Tamaulipas state, where 23 bodies were found decapitated or hanging from bridges on Friday. The Zetas are currently engaged in a turf war with the Gulf cartel in Nuevo Laredo, on the border with Texas.

The largest genetic study yet on dogs suggests that they were domesticated in Central Asia, specifically around Nepal and Mongolia, contradicting previous theories that placed their origin in Southern China or Europe. The research, led by Adam Boyko of Cornell University, analyzed DNA from thousands of living dogs, including "village dogs" with older lineages than modern breeds. The study found the highest genetic diversity in Central Asia and traced a trail back to "founder" dogs in that region. The researchers speculate that hunter-gatherers in Central Asia domesticated dogs from gray wolves due to climate change, better hunting methods, and increased human population density pushing some wolves towards scavenging. Other researchers have welcomed the tracing of domestication to the neighborhood of central Asia but dispute the precise site. The study is significant as it reaches a clear conclusion that can be tested further, with ongoing research analyzing ancient remains to shed more light on the topic.

In the aftermath of Haiti's earthquake, a local restaurant named Muncheez has transformed into an improvised soup kitchen, serving free meals to over 1,000 people daily. The co-owner, Gilbert Bailly, started this initiative when he realized his ingredients would spoil due to the crisis. Neighbors and other businesses have contributed food and resources, enabling Muncheez to continue its service. Leonce Bell, a recipient of the meals, shared that he had been without food for three days but was saving his meal for his child. World Vision, an international aid group, has recently started delivering sacks of dry food to Muncheez, providing additional support.

The article discusses the city of Mountain View's decision to bar Facebook from fully subsidizing meals inside its new offices, which are part of the Village at San Antonio Center project. This move is in response to local restaurants that claimed Google, the city's largest employer, was hurting their businesses by providing free meals. The rule aims to encourage tech workers to spend money in and integrate with the local community, rather than arriving in a bus each day and never leaving the building. The absence of an in-house cafeteria will help boost local retailers, according to Steve Rasmussen, owner of the Milk Pail Market, a produce market blocks from Facebook’s future office. Similar measures may be implemented in other tech companies' expansions in the North Bayshore area, where Google has its headquarters campus. The article also mentions that cities are clamping down on campus cafeterias to support local restaurants as technology companies come under increasing pressure to deliver more value to the communities they inhabit.

A Spanish bungee jumping instructor's poor English was found to have contributed to the death of a 17-year-old Dutch girl, Vera Mol, during a bungee jump in August 2015. The incident occurred on a highway bridge in Cantabria, Spain, when Mol misunderstood an instruction from her instructor as "Now jump" instead of "No jump." The instructor will face criminal charges for accidental homicide, and the company that organized the event will also be prosecuted for negligent homicide. The court also noted that the instructor should have used the correct terminology "don't jump," and should have checked Mol's ID to ensure she was over 18 years old. Additionally, bungee jumping from the road bridge is allegedly banned under Spanish regulation.

A practitioner of Chinese herbal medicine named Dr. Weidong "Henry" Han, his wife Huijie "Jennie" Yu, and their 5-year-old daughter Emily Han were found dead in their California home on Wednesday evening. The crime does not appear to be random, according to authorities. The incident occurred at a modern neighborhood on winding streets just outside Santa Barbara, where Han owned a gated 7-acre ranchette at the top of a hill off the 101 Freeway.

Han was the founder and owner of the Santa Barbara Herb Clinic since 1991. He had an extensive background in Chinese herbal medicine and Western medicine, and provided traditional treatments including acupuncture, acupressure, and herbal formulas from an on-site Chinese pharmacy.

The investigation is ongoing, with authorities working around the clock to determine who is responsible for this horrific crime. The next update from law enforcement officials will be at noon on Friday. Anyone with information on the case is asked to call the Sheriff’s anonymous tip line at (805) 681-4171.

A Dallas pet-sitting company, Prestigious Pets, filed a $1 million lawsuit against a Plano couple for writing a one-star review on Yelp, accusing them of defamation, business disparagement, and breach of contract. The lawsuit was dismissed by a Dallas County district court after the couple argued that it should be dismissed based on the Texas Anti-SLAPP statute, meant to protect people who speak out about matters of public concern from frivolous lawsuits. Prestigious Pets sought damages up to $1 million, claiming losses in business due to the negative review. The company's attorney stated that they may consider appealing the decision and argued that the family violated a non-disparagement clause in their contract by posting the review, which was found to be false and defamatory. The Duchouquettes' review remains on Yelp, but the site now features a consumer alert reminding reviewers of their First Amendment right to express their opinions.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages as they are created, archiving pages that are referenced and maintaining links to their original versions even if the pages change or are removed from the web. This initiative aims to fix broken links across the internet.

In a separate news article, a tragic incident occurred in Seattle where a University of Washington student was severely beaten by her boyfriend, also a UW student named Casey Henderson. The attack took place on Sunday at an apartment in the 2200 block of NE 50th Street. Henderson was arrested and held on $1 million bail for investigation of domestic violence assault.

The victim was initially undergoing treatment at Harborview Medical Center but later died on Tuesday, making the case against Henderson a homicide investigation. The neighbor reported hearing violent confrontations next door before calling 911. Henderson admitted to police that he and his girlfriend had taken LSD before the attack, during which he became paranoid and believed she was plotting against him.

The Seattle Times generally does not identify suspects until they are charged. The victim's name has not been released.

The practice of payment card skimming at point-of-sale terminals has become more frequent in recent years.

In Paradise, California, three employees from Bigge Crane and Rigging Co. were fired for posting insensitive photos from properties destroyed by the deadly Camp Fire that killed 88 people. The photos, posted on the Town of Paradise's Facebook page, showed workers posing with damaged property and a dead cat with a beer bottle near its mouth. Stephanie Clifford, also known as Stormy Daniels, has expressed concerns about her attorney Michael Avenatti's handling of her legal case regarding her relationship with President Donald Trump. She alleges that Avenatti has ignored her requests for accounting information about a legal defense fund, launched a crowdfunding campaign without her knowledge, and spoke on her behalf without her approval. In this news article, it is reported that House Speaker John Boehner has invited President Obama to address a joint session of Congress on Thursday, September 8th, instead of the originally requested date of Wednesday, September 7th. The change was due to logistical difficulties and potential parliamentary or logistical impediments that might detract from the president's remarks.

The new date conflicts with a Republican presidential debate scheduled for Wednesday night at 8 p.m. EDT, which includes Texas Gov. Rick Perry as a participant. The White House had initially cleared the September 7th date and time with House Republicans before making the formal request. However, Boehner's office denies that the Wednesday date was cleared with the Speaker.

The scheduling conflict has caused controversy, with some accusing the Obama administration of politicking by scheduling the speech simultaneously with the debate. The Republican National Committee (RNC) has called it a "thinly-veiled political ploy," while White House press secretary Jay Carney downplayed the scheduling conflict as an innocent coincidence.

The change in date also competes with the opening night of the NFL season, which traditionally attracts high viewership. This year's opener features the reigning Super Bowl champion Green Bay Packers against the New Orleans Saints, while 32.1 million people watched Obama's speech on healthcare

A person of interest has been arrested in connection with a series of fake bombs planted across Staten Island, New York. The suspect, a 54-year-old man, is believed to have been motivated by jealousy towards his ex-girlfriend's new boyfriend. Three devices were found, the most recent one on Saturday outside a home on Duncan Road in Grymes Hill, which contained a propane container and wires connected to another container of liquid. No explosions occurred as the devices were not rigged properly. The NYPD formed a task force over the weekend in response to these incidents, and all three devices had threatening notes in Spanish attached to them. The suspect is currently being questioned at the 121st Precinct stationhouse, and charges are pending. The NYPD is asking anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers.

The family of Bart Palosz, a 15-year-old student who committed suicide in August 2013 after the first day of his sophomore year at Greenwich High School, is suing the town and its board of education for $15,000 in damages. The lawsuit alleges that school officials were aware of Palosz's years-long history of bullying but failed to protect him. According to court documents, Palosz faced name-calling, teasing, physical violence, and property theft from classmates. School administrators, teachers, and counselors are accused of leaving Palosz "unprotected and unsupported" despite their knowledge of the bullying he endured. The lawsuit claims that Greenwich High School failed to comply with its anti-bullying policy, which requires staff members to provide victims with emotional support, investigate known cases of bullying, file reports on bullying instances, contact the parents of bullying victims, and discipline bullies. The family's attorney stated that the lawsuit is important so that other students in Greenwich don't suffer the same kind of treatment that Bart did and hopes it will result in changes to how the school system responds to students in need of help.

Thomas Piketty, the author of "Capital in the 21st Century," a book that examines income inequality and became a bestseller, has declined France's highest award, the Legion d'Honneur. Piketty, who was once associated with the Socialist Party but has criticized the government of President Francois Hollande, stated that it is not the government's role to decide who is honorable and urged them to focus on reviving economic growth in France and Europe instead. This move is a rare rejection of the award, with notable figures like philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre and radiology pioneers Pierre and Marie Curie having previously refused it.

A homeless man named Glen James in Boston returned a lost backpack containing over $42,000, which led to an outpouring of donations totaling more than $110,000 from across the US. Ethan Whittington, a stranger inspired by James' honesty, started an online fund for him and plans to give him the money. Whittington aims to raise $250,000 so that James can buy a house. The fundraising drive has already garnered over $88,000 in contributions. This act of kindness is seen as a positive statement to everyone in America by Whittington, who hopes it will inspire others to make a difference and change the world one person at a time.

The article discusses updates about Google's Project Glass, also known as Google Glass. Google has provided more details about the user interface and features of the futuristic eyewear through photos and videos on their website. The device doesn't have lenses in front of the eyes but a small screen above and to the right of the wearer's right eye, visible via a mirrored glass block.

Users can interact with Google Glass by saying "OK, Glass," which engages the device's listening mode. The headset is capable of taking photos, recording videos, searching Google, showing reminders, and sharing what the user is looking at through messaging or Google+ Hangouts. Google has also launched a contest for creative uses of Google Glass with the hashtag #ifihadglass. Winners will have the opportunity to purchase their own glasses when they become available for $1,500, plus tax.

Google is accepting applications from individuals who want to test the glasses, which were previously only available to software developers. To apply, applicants must write a post on Google Plus or Twitter with a 50-word explanation of their creative use for Google Glass and include the hashtag #ifihadglass. Those chosen by Google's judges will pay $1,500 for the glasses and attend a pick-up event in New York, San Francisco, or Los Angeles.

A community in Richmond, Indiana held a candlelight vigil on Sunday to support the mother of a 14-year-old boy who died after a shootout with police at Dennis Intermediate School. The boy's mother had called 911 on Thursday to report that her son was armed and headed to the school, potentially posing a threat. The school went on lockdown and officers confronted the boy outside, leading to a shootout. No students were injured. The vigil was organized to show support for the boy's mother, who is being praised for preventing potential loss of lives by alerting authorities. The middle school remains closed on Monday as the investigation continues. The teen's family has stated that he may have been bullied.

In the 2011 Values Voter Summit, Ron Paul won the presidential straw poll with 36.9% of the votes, followed by Herman Cain with 22.5%. Rick Santorum came in third with 16.3%, while Rick Perry and Michele Bachmann trailed behind with 8.4% and 7.9% respectively. Mitt Romney and Newt Gingrich received 4.4% and 2.7% of the votes, and Jon Huntsman received less than 1%. The results suggest that Paul's campaign was well-organized, with a significant number of his supporters attending the event. Herman Cain delivered a well-received speech, but Perry's stance on immigration may have affected his performance. Santorum's showing improved from 2010, but he continues to face criticism for his fiscal conservatism and lack of appeal compared to Cain. The straw poll does not necessarily indicate a clear frontrunner for the Republican nomination, as social conservatives are still divided.

Oliver Stone, a renowned director known for controversial films, has announced plans to write and direct a movie about Edward Snowden, the NSA leaker. The project is based on "The Snowden Files: The Inside Story of the World's Most Wanted Man," a book by Guardian journalist Luke Harding. Stone considers this story one of the greatest of our time and sees it as a significant challenge.

Sony Pictures has also acquired the rights to Glenn Greenwald's "No Place to Hide: Edward Snowden, the NSA and the U.S. Surveillance State." This film is being produced by James Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Stone has been an advocate for Snowden, who currently lives in Russia on temporary asylum after leaking classified NSA documents to the media.

Stone views Snowden as a hero for revealing secrets that violated the Fourth Amendment. Filming for the movie is expected to start before the end of the year. The Guardian, the newspaper where the disclosures were first reported, is collaborating with Stone and his producing partner Moritz Borman on the film.

Charlie Sheen, known for his past support of the 9/11 conspiracy theory, has angered a group of believers due to his recent focus on personal issues such as drug use and sexual exploits. The group, led by Mark Dice from The 9/11 Truth Movement, feels betrayed as they believe Sheen should be advocating for questioning the events of 9/11 instead of bragging about his personal life. Dice has reached out to Sheen but received no response, and if the issue isn't addressed soon, the group plans to protest at Sheen's upcoming live shows.

The article discusses a study that found a significant increase in cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), a neurological condition causing temporary paralysis, in countries affected by Zika virus outbreaks. The increase ranged from 2 to 877 percent compared to the pre-Zika baseline incidence in Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Honduras, Suriname, and Venezuela.

Researchers found that men were more likely to develop GBS than women, and the incidence increased with age. The study suggests a strong association between Zika virus infection and GBS, although only a small proportion of people with recent Zika infections get GBS.

The researchers emphasize that the increase in GBS cases imposes a substantial burden on populations and health services in Latin America and the Caribbean, where approximately 500 million people are at risk for Zika virus infection. The study suggests that monitoring GBS cases could help identify Zika outbreaks.

In related news, Puerto Rico reported its first death from GBS caused by a Zika infection last month. The U.S. government has declared a public health emergency in Puerto Rico due to the Zika outbreak, and federal officials have warned that up to 25 percent of Puerto Rico's nearly 3.5 million people could become infected.

The article discusses minimum wage hikes in ten states that will take effect on January 1, 2013. These increases range from a dime to 35 cents and are primarily due to automatic adjustments designed to keep up with the cost of living, except for Rhode Island where a state law was necessary for the increase. The article highlights the impact of these wage hikes on businesses and workers. For instance, Julio Fonseca, owner of Cafe Zog in Providence, is concerned about the increased costs associated with rewarding his hard-working employees, while Sydonia Lary, a worker at the cafe, welcomes the increase as it will help her make ends meet. The article also mentions that higher minimum wages could potentially harm young workers looking for entry-level jobs, according to Bill Vernon of the National Federation of Independent Business. In total, nearly a million workers in these ten states will benefit from the wage increases. Washington state is raising its minimum wage to $9.19 an hour, which is almost double the minimum wage in neighboring Idaho. The article also discusses the potential impact of these wage hikes on employment and business costs, with some research suggesting that rising minimum wages have no impact on employment and can even reduce turnover.

The article discusses the establishment of Lumos, a charity founded by J.K. Rowling in response to a disturbing photograph of a child locked in a caged bed in a residential institution. The photograph served as the catalyst for Rowling's commitment to ending the unjustifiable incarceration of 8 million children worldwide who are separated from their families due to poverty, disability, and discrimination.

Lumos aims to shed light on these children's lives and work towards closing child institutions and so-called orphanages. The charity was named after a spell Rowling created in Harry Potter to bring light to dark and frightening places.

The article highlights the shocking conditions in many institutions, where children are often caged most of the day and night, malnourished, abused, and traumatized. It is emphasized that the majority of these children have parents who could care for them but are placed in institutions due to poverty or a lack of local education and health facilities, especially for children with special needs.

The article also explains that institutionalization causes children measurable and sometimes irreparable harm, leading to developmental delays, psychological trauma, and a lifetime of poverty and dependency. The solution proposed by Lumos is to eradicate institutions altogether and prioritize keeping families together through investment in inclusive education, health support, fostering, adoption, and other family-based care alternatives

The article discusses the rise in online dating and the concerns surrounding safety on these platforms. With over 20 million Americans using dating sites, there is an increase in encounters with married individuals pretending to be single, sexual predators, and convicted felons. To address this issue, companies like MyMatchChecker offer background checks for a small fee, while mobile apps such as Instant National Criminal Search and Date Check make these checks quick and easy.

State officials are also pushing for safer online dating, with New York and New Jersey implementing regulations requiring sites to post safety tips and inform users about criminal background checks (most do not conduct them). However, the effectiveness of these checks is questionable due to incomplete state and county databases, varying quality, and availability of data.

Critics also point out potential issues with companies conducting background screenings, such as mishandling information and providing personal data to those who may abuse it through mobile apps. Despite these concerns, the Communications Decency Act protects online dating sites from liability for user-generated content, making it challenging to enforce stricter regulations.

Parry Aftab, a lawyer and safety expert, advises singles to exercise caution when using online dating platforms and not to give up their heart too quickly.

In Suffolk, Virginia, a shooting occurred on Thursday morning at a local barbershop following an argument about Halle Berry playing Aretha Franklin in a movie. The altercation started over speculation that Berry would portray Franklin, but she had previously declined the role due to her lack of singing ability. The shooter, identified as 44-year-old Michael Jermell Hatton, shot another man outside the shop. Both individuals received medical treatment and were transported to local hospitals, with the victim, Tony Jonathan Lundy, reportedly in critical condition. Hatton was arrested, treated for his injuries, and is currently held without bond at the Western Tidewater Regional Jail. The investigation is ongoing.

Nancy Reed, a 77-year-old community volunteer from Kingwood, Texas, died on September 15 due to complications from necrotizing fasciitis, a flesh-eating bacterial infection. The infection was caused by blunt trauma to her upper extremity during the flooding from Hurricane Harvey. Reed is the 36th official death in Harris County related to the hurricane and its aftermath. Another case of the bacteria was reported in a rescuer, J.R. Atkins, who survived his infection after being bitten by an insect while assisting flood-ravaged victims in Missouri City. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has documented 700 to 1,100 cases of necrotizing fasciitis annually caused by group A streptococcus, but details on deaths were not immediately available. Reed's memorial service was held at First Presbyterian Church of Kingwood.

The crisis between Russia and Ukraine escalated on March 1st, 2014, when Russian President Vladimir Putin requested permission from the Russian parliament to use military force in Ukraine. This move was intended to protect ethnic Russians and personnel of a Russian military base in Crimea, an autonomous region of eastern Ukraine with strong loyalty to neighboring Russia.

The request came after armed, Russian-speaking forces without insignia took control of key infrastructure sites and airports in Crimea, causing alarm among world leaders. Ukrainian officials have vehemently denied Putin's claim that there is a threat to the lives of Russian citizens and military personnel based in southern Crimea.

The new government in Ukraine, led by Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk, warned of war if Russia intervenes militarily in Crimea, and has put its troops on high alert. The Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Deshchytsya has requested help from NATO to protect the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Ukraine.

The crisis has been escalating since the ouster of President Viktor Yanukovych following bloody street protests that left dozens dead and hundreds wounded, and has put relations between Russia and the United States under strain. Both leaders, Putin and Obama, have expressed their concerns over the mounting crisis during a 90-minute phone call.

A Menifee middle school student, Austin Lacey, wore an Elsa costume from the movie "Frozen" for a Disney-themed school spirit day at Ethan A. Chase Middle School. However, the school principal ordered him to remove his costume, citing it as a disruption. The incident involved a large number of students taking pictures with Austin. Although the school did not discipline Austin for the incident, some students felt that the incident was not disruptive and supported Austin's campaign for ASB president. The Romoland School District Superintendent Dr. Julie Vitale stated that the action was taken in accordance with district policies and that there was no indication that Austin was expressing any particular message.

A sinkhole opened under the National Corvette Museum in Bowling Green, KY on Wednesday, causing eight iconic sports cars to be sucked into a 40-foot deep hole. Security cameras captured the incident and videos of the collapse have been posted on the museum's YouTube channel. At present, there is no timetable for removing the cars or repairing the damaged wing of the museum as engineers need to ensure it's safe to work inside the pit. The National Corvette Museum offers various exhibits, a library and archives, a 50s-themed Corvette Cafe, and more, located at I-65 exit 28 in Bowling Green, KY.

Margaux Sainte-Lagüe, a Parisian entrepreneur, launched Mon Pavé Parisien, an online store that sells real cobblestones from Paris's iconic roads and alleyways. The city of Paris began selling thousands of tons of cobblestones as part of its circular economy initiative to reduce waste and save energy. Sainte-Lagüe bought five tons of these cobblestones and offers three styles: a classic version hand-painted in the colors of France’s flag, one gilded in 22.5 carats of gold, and the May 68 series stone, whose bottom half is sheathed in sand and features the inscription “sous les pavés,” a popular phrase used during the protests of the May 1968 revolution. Customers can also request custom designs. The stones are available on Mon Pavé Parisien’s online store, with prices ranging from $63 to $157. The sales have been steady, with customers coming from far-flung places like China and the US. The city plans to sell as many as 3 million tons of cobblestones, which could potentially last for about three centuries.

The woman accused of driving under the influence and plowing her car into a crowd at an Oklahoma State University (OSU) homecoming parade, resulting in four deaths and numerous injuries, is Adacia Chambers. She is being held on four counts of second-degree murder and one count of DUI. Her attorney, Tony Coleman, claims she was not intoxicated but may be suffering from mental illness. The incident occurred on October 24, 2015, just hours before a scheduled football game between OSU and the University of Kansas. The crash also injured dozens of people, including several children. The victims include Marvin Stone, a retired professor at OSU; his wife Bonnie, who worked for the university; Nikita Nakal, an MBA student from India; and 2-year-old Nash Lucas. Chambers is expected to appear in court on Monday.

In this week's news, actor Robert De Niro made an inappropriate joke about potential white first ladies during a fundraiser with Michelle Obama. The joke was criticized as offensive by various parties, including Newt Gingrich and the press secretary for the first lady. De Niro later apologized for his remarks.

Meanwhile, President Obama's chief political strategist, David Axelrod, used a pun that was perceived as Holocaust and Nazi imagery in a comment about Mitt Romney's advertising barrage in Illinois. The Republican Jewish Coalition demanded an apology from both Axelrod and Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz for the offensive remark.

In a New York Times op-ed, comedian Bill Maher called for an end to the insincere demands for apologies from politicians and celebrities who have supposedly offended them. He argued that Americans should be allowed to express themselves freely, even if their comments are considered offensive by some. However, Maher himself has faced criticism for using vile words to refer to former Alaska governor Sarah Palin and her family in the past.

The article also touches on the issue of incivility in politics and the manipulation of this issue for political gain. The piece ends with a quote from then-Illinois State Sen. Barack Obama, emphasizing the importance of unity in America rather than division.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals has upheld a $25 million settlement between President Donald Trump and students who accused Trump University of fraudulent practices. The settlement, which was first approved in March 2017, will provide restitution to approximately 4,000 former students who paid for seminars and mentorship programs. Florida bankruptcy lawyer Sherri Simpson, who wanted to take Trump to trial over the $19,000 she paid for classes and a mentorship program, challenged the settlement but was unsuccessful in her appeal. The court ruled that the notice sent to participants promised only one opportunity to opt out of the class-action suits, and Simpson's objection was seen as potentially politically motivated. The decision clears the way for students to receive up to 90% of what they paid for Trump University programs.

U.S Senator Bernie Sanders has called on Michigan Governor Rick Snyder to resign over his administration's handling of the lead-poisoning crisis in Flint, Michigan. The crisis began when Flint switched its water supply from Lake Huron to the polluted Flint River in 2014 as a cost-cutting measure. Officials knew that the river water was corroding pipes and causing lead to leach into the drinking water but did not acknowledge this until last fall. Sanders stated that hundreds of children were poisoned, thousands may have been exposed to potential brain damage from lead, and families will suffer from lead poisoning for the rest of their lives due to Snyder's administration's conduct.

The Flint water crisis has a long history, with key events dating back to April 2014 when Flint began drawing its water from the Flint River. Residents immediately complained about the smell, taste and appearance of the water and raised health concerns. Three boil-water advisories were issued in 27 days after positive tests for coliform bacteria. In October 2014, a General Motors engine plant stopped using Flint water due to rusting parts. In January 2015, Flint sought an evaluation of its efforts to improve the water amid concerns that it contained potentially harmful levels of a disinfection byproduct. The document describes the creation of an interactive visualization of military conflicts using data from Wikidata and DBpedia in nodegoat. The authors first highlight the vast amount of structured data available on Wikidata, with over 947 million triples, and note that battles often have a place and date, making them suitable for this project.

To gather battle data, they used SPARQL queries to extract instances of battles with location and date information from both Wikidata and DBpedia. In Wikidata, they found 8049 instances of battles, but after filtering for those with location and date, they were left with 2657 battles. After cleaning the data, they imported it into nodegoat, where users can scroll through time using a timeline and click on dots to open a dialogue with a link to the object in Wikidata.

In DBpedia, they found 12674 instances of MilitaryConflict, of which 4022 had date and location properties. After looking a level deeper for dates and locations, they found 10116 battles that had a place and date reference. They imported this data into nodegoat and combined it with the Wikidata set, highlighting the provenance of each dot.

The authors also note differences between the two datasets, particularly messy dates in DBpedia and a lack of proper references

On May 8 (Americas/Pacific) or May 9 (rest of the world), Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system, will be at opposition, appearing brightest and closest for the year. This event occurs when a planet is directly opposite the sun in our sky, rising in the east as the sun sets and shining all night long. On this occasion, Jupiter will be visible near the constellation Libra, with Zubenelgenubi, Libra's alpha star, nearby. Venus, the brightest planet, will also be visible in the west after sunset. The NASA Juno spacecraft is currently orbiting Jupiter, providing never-before-seen glimpses of its polar regions. This opposition occurs approximately every 13 months, with the dates shifting by about a month each year.

The Robert Gordon University has revoked Donald Trump's honorary degree due to his controversial statements during the US election campaign. Thousands of Britons have signed a petition calling for Trump to be banned from entering the UK, citing his hate speech as grounds. If the petition reaches 100,000 signatures, it could be debated in Parliament. A similar petition was launched earlier by the same author demanding that Aberdeen's Robert Gordon University strips Trump of an honorary degree awarded in 2010. The number of signatories on both petitions is rapidly increasing.

The summary of the article is as follows: The execution of Lawrence Russell Brewer, who was convicted for a hate crime murder over a decade ago, has led to a ban on allowing death row inmates in Texas to choose their final meal. Brewer had requested an extravagant meal which he did not consume. Senator John Whitmire, chairman of the Senate Criminal Justice Committee, finds it inappropriate to grant such privileges to individuals sentenced to death.

The Church of Kopimism, a group of approximately 3,000 Swedish file sharers, has been officially recognized as a religion by the Swedish authorities. The church, which advocates for sharing and data copying as sacred acts, had previously applied for recognition multiple times but was denied until recently. The new status does not make file-sharing legal for Kopimists, but they hope their beliefs will be considered in future legislation. The Church's founder, Isak Gerson, is optimistic that the official recognition will encourage more people to embrace their beliefs and reduce the stigma surrounding file-sharing. The Church has grown from 1,000 to 3,000 members over the past six months and expects to gain even more followers following this news.

Eric Swenson, a co-founder of Thrasher magazine and a significant figure in the skateboarding community, died by suicide on June 20, 2011, at the age of 64. Swenson was a private individual who struggled with a debilitating motorcycle injury, which may have contributed to his decision to end his life. He co-founded High Speed Productions Inc., which includes magazines Thrasher, Juxtapoz, and Slap, as well as Independent Trucks, the manufacturer of skateboard trucks that revolutionized skateboarding by allowing people to skate vertically. Swenson's partner in these ventures was Fausto Vitello, who passed away five years prior to Swenson's death. The pair's work helped establish skateboarding as a subculture with its own music, dialect, and fashion style. Swenson is survived by his wife Linda McKay, sister Rebekah Engle, and sister Sonja Taylor.

China and the US are in contact to address the seizure of a US Navy unmanned underwater glider by the Chinese navy, which occurred in the South China Sea. The incident is one of the most serious incidents between the two militaries in years. The drone was collecting unclassified scientific data when it was seized and is valued at around $150,000. The US has issued a formal diplomatic complaint over the seizure and demanded the return of the drone. China claims virtually all of the South China Sea and considers the waters as sovereign territory, but insists it does not disrupt the passage of other nations' shipping through the area. The incident is likely to further strain already tense relations between the US and China, particularly in light of President-elect Donald Trump's recent comments on Taiwan. Trump has accused China of an "unpresidented act" in seizing the drone and suggested that the US should not want it returned. However, a statement from the Chinese foreign ministry indicated that China intends to return the drone to the US in an appropriate manner.

Some Chinese hoped that a Republican president would do more to encourage freedom of speech in China, but others were concerned about the potential negative impact on Sino-American relations.

The incident sparked demonstrations across the city, but a Cook County judge did not order him held without bail pending trial. Judge Donald Panarese Jr. set Van Dyke's bail at $1.5 million after watching squad car video that showed the shooting. Four hours later, Van Dyke posted bond and was released from jail. The incident led to calls for Chicago Police Supt. Garry McCarthy to resign and plans for a "Task Force on Police Accountability" to review the system of accountability, oversight, and training for Chicago's police officers. The dashcam video of the shooting was made public last week, and hundreds of demonstrators have rallied to mostly peaceful protests across the city since then. An off-duty California Highway Patrol (CHP) sergeant, who wishes to remain anonymous, is being praised for her integrity after finding over $120,000 in cash on a Concord roadway and returning it to its rightful owner. While driving in September, the sergeant had to swerve to avoid two large bank deposit bags and later retrieved them, discovering the large sum of money. She immediately reported the find to authorities and handed over the cash to Concord police. The owner was later located and the money returned. The sergeant, who was raised by a single mother in Los Angeles, said she wanted to set an example for her children and teach them a lesson about honesty. CHP officials praised the sergeant's actions, noting that such acts of integrity are not always recognized.

Hurricane Harvey made landfall as a Category 4 storm on August 25, 2017 near Corpus Christi, Texas. The hurricane caused widespread destruction, knocking out power to nearly 300,000 customers along the coast and dumping nearly 20 inches of rain in some places. Emergency personnel in coastal communities reported loss of cellphone service and other forms of communication. The storm was downgraded to a Category 1 on Saturday, but the threat of sustained rains that could cause catastrophic flooding remained. Rockport, a city northeast of Corpus Christi where Harvey made landfall, suffered widespread damage, with some homes and businesses heavily damaged or destroyed. President Donald Trump commended the head of the Federal Emergency Management Agency for his handling of the hurricane.

Archaeologists are set to conduct a geophysical scan at Waltham Abbey Church in Essex this week, with the aim of determining if King Harold II survived the Battle of Hastings in 1066. The search is being led by amateur historian Peter Burke, who believes that Harold may have lived as a hermit for several decades after the battle and was eventually buried at Waltham Abbey. This theory contradicts the commonly accepted account of Harold's death, which states that he was killed by Norman knights and his body dismembered. The scan will be filmed for a documentary and is being supported by the geophysics team that discovered the remains of Richard III in 2012. If evidence of King Harold's remains is found, it could potentially lead to a rewriting of history books.

Kim Kardashian West was robbed at gunpoint in a private residence in Paris by five armed men disguised as police officers, who made off with millions of pounds worth of jewellery. The incident occurred early on Monday morning local time while Kardashian West was attending fashion week shows. She was "badly shaken but physically unharmed" and has since flown out of France. The robbers escaped on bicycles, and a ring worth €4m (£3.5m) and a jewellery box containing valuables worth €6m (£5.2m) were stolen. The incident sparked a manhunt in Paris, with the perpetrators still at large. Thousands of flights were cancelled and delayed due to this incident, causing a negative impact on the economy. The Air Route Control Center in Aurora, which monitors high altitude aircraft before landing in Chicago or flying through the area, is currently being handled by other facilities in surrounding states, but at a much more limited capacity. Authorities believe this was an isolated incident and that Howard acted alone. He remains hospitalized with self-inflicted stab wounds and is under police guard. The FAA is beefing up staffing at adjacent facilities, and there could be days of potential radar outages at the Aurora facility, which could result in significant flight delays in the Great Lakes region.

United Airlines has updated its boarding process, reducing the number of boarding lanes from five to two in an effort to combat overcrowding at gates and improve efficiency. The new system, which is now in effect, uses color-coded lanes (1 and 2) for passengers to board based on their group number (1 through 5). Elite and priority passengers will board through lane 1, while customers in groups 3, 4, and 5 will use lane 2. The airline is also launching push notifications for those with the United mobile app to inform them when boarding begins. This change follows testing at various gates in Chicago and Houston since June. Additionally, United has announced a joint business agreement (JBA) with Copa Airlines and Avianca, pending government approval, which aims to provide benefits for customers, communities, and the air travel market between the US and 19 countries in Central and South America. The JBA is expected to offer integrated, seamless service in more than 12,000 city pairs, new nonstop routes, additional flights on existing routes, reduced travel times, and drive economic benefits for consumers and communities.

In a historic referendum, Ireland legalized same-sex marriage by a landslide vote of 62% to 38%, making it the first country to do so via a popular vote. The capital city, Dublin, showed particularly strong support for the measure, with over 70% of voters approving it. The archbishop of Dublin acknowledged the result as a "social revolution" and called for the Church to do a reality check. The referendum was backed by all political parties, championed by big employers, and endorsed by celebrities. This marks a significant transformation in Ireland's social conservatism and sends a message of progress to the rest of the world.

The shooting occurred after Bello was reportedly unable to find the doctor he blamed for his dismissal from the hospital two years earlier.

Before the shooting, Bello sent an email to the Daily News blaming colleagues for forcing him to resign. Bello had a history of aggression, loudness, and threats towards his former colleagues. He had warned them that he would return someday to kill them.

Bello died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, and the six injured individuals were hospitalized. Authorities searched Bello's home and found the box where the gun was purchased at a gun shop in Schenectady on June 20.

Weinstein was abducted from his home in Lahore and was believed to have been passed through various criminal and terrorist organizations before being held by Al-Qaeda. The call took place before Trump entered office and discussed sanctions against Russia. Flynn's resignation came quickly, just 24 days into his tenure in the White House, and has raised questions about what the president knew and when. The incident also highlights ongoing uncertainty about the relationship between the Trump administration and Vladimir Putin's Russia. Conservative radio host Rush Limbaugh claimed that the media helped force Flynn out of his position.

On June 27, 2017, a police helicopter attacked the Venezuelan Supreme Court and Interior Ministry in what President Nicolas Maduro described as a "terrorist attack" aimed at ousting him from power. The helicopter was reportedly piloted by Oscar Perez, who identified himself as part of a coalition of military employees, policemen, and civilians seeking to combat the government's impunity and tyranny. The incident occurred during ongoing anti-government protests in Venezuela that have left at least 75 people dead and hundreds injured over the past three months. Some critics accused Maduro of staging the attack to justify a crackdown against his opponents, while others suggested it may have been carried out by rogue policemen with links to the CIA. The whereabouts of Oscar Perez are unknown.

In a sensational turn at the trial of Captain Francesco Schettino, who is facing multiple charges including manslaughter and abandoning ship following the 2012 Costa Concordia disaster that killed 32 people, a Moldovan dancer named Domnica Cemortan testified that she was his lover. She admitted to being on the bridge with him when the cruise ship ran aground off the north-west Italian coast.

Ms. Cemortan had dinner with Captain Schettino before he invited her to join him on the bridge, and local press speculated that the captain may have been distracted by her presence or even showing off. She acknowledged their romantic involvement after being pressed in court. Ms. Cemortan boarded the ship as a non-paying passenger hours before the crash, stating "When you are someone's lover, no-one asks you for a ticket."

The trial is expected to hear evidence from about 1,000 surviving passengers and crew during Capt Schettino's trial. Earlier in the day, ship maitre d' Antonello Tievoli testified that he had asked the captain to sail close to the island of Giglio because he has family there, which the captain obliged.
