The Utah bill, currently awaiting final approval from the governor, could criminalize miscarriages and some instances of induced abortions. The bill, unique for its punitive approach towards pregnant women rather than abortion providers or third-party attackers, allows for punishment up to life in prison for an "intentional, knowing, or reckless act" that leads to a miscarriage or abortion without medical supervision.

The bill's broad language could potentially prosecute women for various actions such as drinking too much alcohol, failing to wear a seatbelt, falling down stairs, and staying with an abusive partner, if these actions are believed to have caused a miscarriage. The bill applies throughout pregnancy, unlike most other states' fetal homicide laws that only apply in the third trimester.

Critics argue that this law could make pregnant women vulnerable to arrest, particularly those suffering from substance abuse or domestic violence, and may discourage them from seeking necessary treatment or help. The bill has been met with concern by women's rights advocates who believe it is designed to punish women rather than protect fetuses.

Lindsay Lohan's court hearing regarding her DUI case has concluded. She is currently inside the courtroom, discussing matters with her lawyer and completing paperwork related to a SCRAM bracelet. Outside, media are waiting for reactions from both parties. In an exclusive interview with Hollywood.TV, Lohan addressed various rumors about her recent "cocaine" photograph, her DUI case, her father Michael Lohan, alleged drug use, and missing her brother's graduation.

The article discusses the ongoing electricity crisis in Pakistan, which is causing widespread power outages and affecting millions of people. The crisis is due to a combination of factors including decrepit power plants, crumbling transmission lines, decades-old policy mistakes, and unpaid bills totaling $5 billion known as "circular debt." This debt affects various sectors of society, from government departments to wealthy politicians to slum dwellers.

The crisis has been a major political issue in Pakistan, with the public galvanized by it more so than Islamist militancy. Nawaz Sharif, who swept to victory in the May 11 election on promises to deliver a "shining Pakistan" and end the darkness, is now faced with the challenge of making tough decisions to change the system. Analysts question whether he has the political will to do so, as some of his own supporters are among the bill defaulters who need to start paying their fair share.

The article highlights that easing the $5 billion "circular debt" is the principal problem, but money is only part of the solution. Deep-rooted structural issues, exacerbated by political interference and systemic graft, lie at the heart of Pakistan's power crisis. Electricity theft, both by rich and poor, is common, with slum dwellers stealing power through illegal connections and powerful politicians and government departments simply refusing to pay their bills. Two Northwestern University freshmen, Anthony Morales and Matthew Kafker, are accused of vandalizing a campus chapel by spray-painting racist, homophobic slurs, swastikas, penises, and the word "Trump." The incident occurred around 12:45 a.m. on Friday at the Alice Millar Chapel. University President Morton Schapiro called it an "abhorrent act of vandalism" in an email to students. The freshmen are each being held on $50,000 bail for charges including institutional vandalism, hate crime to a place of worship, and criminal damage to property. Judge Peggy Chiampas expressed her disgust towards the defendants during a bond hearing at the Leighton Criminal Court Building. The university estimated the damage to be over $300, and workers wiped away most of the graffiti over the weekend, including the "Trump." Prosecutors have not yet stated why the students allegedly targeted the chapel or how they accessed it after hours.

A Belgian woman named Florence Heene, aged 71, has found her biological father after a lifelong search. She discovered that he was a Canadian soldier named Herbert Louis Hellyer who served during World War II and was stationed in Ghent, Belgium. His surviving family members in British Columbia recognized him from a CBC News story and contacted Heene. The family has provided a picture of Hellyer to Heene, which matches the only clear picture she had of her father. Herbert Hellyer died by suicide in 1948 after suffering a head injury during the war. Florence Heene is glad to have found a "new family" in Canada and hopes to meet her half-sister Thelma Janes, one of Hellyer's daughters. The family has shared details about Herbert Hellyer's life, including his English birth and Canadian upbringing before he became a printer by trade in British Columbia. He had five children, including three surviving ones who live in B.C.

Astronauts who have gone on spacewalks consistently report an extraordinarily peculiar odor in space, which they describe as metallic, reminiscent of welding fumes, seared steak, and hot metal. This distinctive smell is attributed to atomic oxygen and other particles that cling to their suits, helmets, gloves, and tools. NASA astronaut Kevin Ford described the odor as something he hadn't ever smelled before but would never forget. The interior of the International Space Station has a more mundane smell, with a mix of machine-shop, engine-room, laboratory, and cooked food aromas. During Discovery's recent mission to deliver fresh supplies and new science gear to the space station, astronauts were surprised by the life aboard the station, which is a $100 billion product of 16 different countries. The crew was also impressed by the variety of food from various international partners available on the station.

A woman identified as Snochia Moseley, aged 26, fatally shot three co-workers and injured three others at a Rite Aid distribution center in Harford County, Maryland on Thursday before killing herself. The incident occurred at the facility near Aberdeen where Moseley was a temporary employee.

The shooting took place both inside and outside the building, with the motive for the attack still unknown. Moseley used a 9 mm Glock pistol that she owned legally. No law enforcement officers fired shots during their response, and multiple agencies are investigating the incident.

Four victims were taken to Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center in Baltimore, two of whom were reported as stable, while two remain seriously injured. One victim was also taken to Christiana Hospital in Newark, Delaware. The names of the victims and the shooter have not been released yet, as next of kin are still being notified.

This shooting marks the third high-profile incident in U.S. workplaces within 24 hours and comes less than a year after a gunman killed three fellow employees at another Harford County business. The investigation is ongoing to determine the motive behind the attack.

The New York Police Department is investigating a theft of two high-value photograph prints from MoMA PS1 Annex in Long Island City, Queens last month. The stolen photographs, worth $55,000 and $50,000 each, were part of the exhibit "Carolee Schneemann: Kinetic Painting." A facilities manager discovered the missing gelatin-silver prints on Monday, October 30, but there was no sign of forced entry or witnesses. The photographs were anonymously mailed back to the museum on November 3.

Surveillance footage from a shipping store in Williamsburg, Brooklyn shows a woman mailing the photos in a large box. The NYPD is asking for the public's help in identifying the woman, who is described as white, in her twenties, wearing a dark cap, glasses, black overcoat, tan pants, and tan shoes. If connected to the theft, the suspect could face charges of criminal possession of stolen property and grand larceny. The museum does have video surveillance, contrary to initial reports.

An orca named J35, also known as Tahlequah, has carried her deceased calf for at least 17 days and over 1,000 miles off the Pacific Northwest coast, in an unprecedented display of mourning that garnered international attention. J35 is a 20-year-old member of the long-studied J Pod of Southern Resident Killer Whales, which inhabits a vast territory including waters off Seattle, Vancouver, and Victoria, British Columbia.

Researchers were concerned that J35's prolonged effort could endanger her health, but she appears to have made it through physically unscathed. The death of another calf is a significant blow to the J Pod, which hasn't seen a successful birth in three years, and experts worry about the population's viability. Ken Balcomb, founder and principal investigator at the Center for Whale Research, estimates that the population has five more years of reproductive life to ensure its survival.

The new guidelines for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis, released by the National Institute on Aging and the Alzheimer's Association, expand the definition of the condition to include patients with earlier stage symptoms. The guidelines recognize that Alzheimer's is not just end-stage dementia but a continuum that can start in the brain five to ten years before symptoms appear.

The new guidelines divide Alzheimer's into three stages: a phase when dementia has developed, a middle phase with mild problems, and an early phase without symptoms. The drive behind these changes is to diagnose Alzheimer's earlier, ideally before it progresses into profound dementia.

The guidelines also emphasize the importance of biomarkers, such as proteins in patients' blood and tissue, for earlier diagnosis. However, these methods are not yet ready for widespread use due to a lack of standardization and unclear cutoff points for normal results.

The new guidelines aim to encourage more research to develop drugs that can attack early brain changes and identify people who might benefit from such drugs when they become available. The ultimate goal is to extend the range of our ability to investigate Alzheimer's disease and find treatments to avoid an impending epidemic over the next 40 years.

Previously, Thatcham in Berkshire held the record for the longest continuous settlement, but Amesbury's longevity has now been recognized by the Guinness Book of Records. The dig also unearthed 31,000 worked flints and remains of big game animals such as aurochs and red deer. The findings suggest that Stonehenge, rather than being a Neolithic new-build, should be viewed as a response to long-term use of the area by indigenous hunters and home-makers.

He married Barbara Pierce after returning from the war and finished his education at Yale. Instead of pursuing a career in finance like his family intended, he moved to Texas to become a businessman in the oil industry.

Bush began his political career as chairman of the Harris County Republican Party and was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1966. He lost a Senate race but was appointed ambassador to the United Nations by President Nixon, leading to a series of top appointments within the Republican Party.

Bush ran for president in 1980 but lost to Ronald Reagan. However, he became Reagan's vice president and succeeded him in the White House after winning the 1988 election. He lost his bid for re-election to Bill Clinton in 1992 due to a disappointing economic performance and opposition from conservatives within his own party over a decision to raise taxes.

The study published in the British Medical Journal suggests that following a Mediterranean diet may contribute to a longer lifespan by keeping people genetically younger. Researchers found that nurses who adhered to the diet had fewer signs of aging in their cells, specifically longer telomeres. Telomeres are protective structures at the ends of chromosomes that prevent the loss of genetic information during cell division. As we age and our cells divide, our telomeres get shorter, which can lead to cell death and various age-related diseases such as heart disease and cancer. The study followed over 4,000 nurses for more than a decade and found that those who closely followed the Mediterranean diet had longer, healthier telomeres. The researchers believe that the key components of the Mediterranean diet, including an abundance of fresh fruits and vegetables, poultry, fish, and a low intake of red meat, butter, and animal fats, all have beneficial effects on the body that may protect our DNA. The findings reinforce advice to eat a balanced and healthy diet to reduce the risk of developing heart disease. However, experts caution that while the results are interesting, they are not conclusive and further research is needed to confirm the causal relationship between the Mediterranean diet and telomere length.

The study published in PLOS ONE suggests that domestic cats do not generally perceive their owners as a focus of safety and security like dogs do, indicating that they are more independent in their relationships with humans. The research, led by Professor Daniel Mills at the University of Lincoln's School of Life Sciences, used an adapted version of the Ainsworth Strange Situation Test (SST) to observe the relationship between cats and their owners.

The study found that while cats might prefer interacting with their owner, they do not rely on them for reassurance in unfamiliar environments. This is likely due to the nature of cats as largely independent and solitary hunters. The research also suggests that what we interpret as separation anxiety in cats might actually be signs of frustration rather than a need for safety and security from their owners.

The study's findings challenge the notion that cats develop social preferences or close relationships based on a need for safety and security, unlike dogs. The researchers believe alternative methods are needed to characterize the normal psychological features of the cat-owner bond.

Two capybaras, nicknamed Bonnie and Clyde, have been missing from the High Park Zoo in Toronto since May 24th. The capybaras escaped when zoo workers were moving a third capybara into their enclosure. Capybaras are the world's largest rodents, reaching over four feet in height and weighing up to 140 pounds. They are semi-aquatic animals that enjoy swimming and do not like children. The escape of the capybaras has led to a search party, a parody Twitter account, an online video game, and joking comments from Mayor John Tory. However, the zoo could face charges under the Ontario Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act due to its history. This is not the first time an animal has escaped from the High Park Zoo; a peacock and six other animals have also run free in the past. The missing capybaras are still at large, and their survival in Toronto's winter could be in question due to their lack of fat reserves and thick coats.

"Bob" Haldeman, who would later spend 18 months in prison for his role in the Watergate scandal. He went on to serve as supreme allied commander of NATO and secretary of state under Ronald Reagan, but his tenure was marked by controversy and he was dismissed from his position in 1982.

Walter Samuel Radford failed to appear for a final divorce hearing on Wednesday in Bartow County court, resulting in the divorce being finalized at 12:04 p.m. Approximately two hours later, Radford allegedly shot and killed his ex-wife's attorney, Antonio Benjamin Mari, in his Cartersville office. Thieves stole a solid gold replica of the Lunar Excursion Module, which was given to astronaut Neil Armstrong, from the Armstrong Air & Space Museum in Wapakoneta, Ohio. The replica is one of only three made and has an unknown value due to its historical significance. The theft occurred late Friday night, and police are investigating with help from the FBI and Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation. The museum stated that the theft robbed visitors of their opportunity to experience history. The replicas were commissioned by French newspaper Le Figaro in 1969 and given to Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins during a visit to Paris. Only one other replica has been recovered, which was bought back by the jeweler Cartier in a 2003 auction for $56,000. The lunar module model is only 5 inches tall and 4.5 inches wide. Retired NASA agent Joseph Gutheinz Jr. believes the thief or thieves intend to melt down the gold replica for its value rather than trying to sell it as a collectible worth millions of dollars.

A new documentary suggests that William Shakespeare's skull may have been stolen from his grave in Stratford-upon-Avon, England. Archaeologist Kevin Colls and his team used ground-penetrating radar to investigate Shakespeare's grave at Holy Trinity Church without disturbing the remains. They found an apparent repair to the head end of the burial site, indicating a previous disturbance that could suggest the skull was stolen by trophy hunters in 1794.

The team also investigated another legend that Shakespeare's skull was sealed in a crypt at St. Leonard's church in Worcestershire, but found it belonged to an unknown woman. They discovered that Shakespeare and his wife Anne Hathaway were buried in shallow graves beneath the church floor, and not in a family vault as previously thought. The GPR scan found no indication of metal, suggesting Shakespeare was wrapped in a shroud rather than buried in a casket.

The findings will be part of a television program airing on Channel 4 in the U.K. to mark the 400th anniversary of Shakespeare's death. The Holy Trinity Church vicar is not convinced that there is sufficient evidence to conclude that Shakespeare's skull has been taken, and the mystery remains as to what lies beneath the stone.

The study conducted by researchers at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business suggests that a person's voice can significantly influence job prospects, even surpassing the importance of a resume and professional experience. In various experiments, it was found that when job candidates' qualifications were presented as spoken pitches rather than written ones, they were perceived as more competent, thoughtful, and intelligent. This positive evaluation led to increased interest in hiring the candidate. The study, titled "The Sound of Intellect: Speech Reveals a Thoughtful Mind, Increasing a Job Candidate's Appeal," will be published in The Journal of Psychological Science. The findings indicate that when conveying intelligence, it is essential for one's voice to be heard.

Spanish speakers have encountered difficulties navigating the site, with some reporting technical glitches and long wait times on the Spanish hotline. Legendary mountaineer and author Fred Beckey, known for his numerous first ascents on North America's tallest peaks, died at the age of 94 due to congestive heart failure. Born in Germany and raised in Seattle, Beckey was a member of The Mountaineers club and made hundreds of first ascents throughout the Pacific Northwest, Alaska, Canada, and Wyoming. He also climbed in the Himalayas and China. Beckey authored over a dozen books on mountaineering, including the three-volume "Cascade Alpine Guide." Despite his age, he continued to plot routes and climb until his death. Beckey is survived by his younger brother Helmut, and a public memorial service will be held in November.

A team of UCLA geochemists have found evidence suggesting that life likely existed on Earth at least 4.1 billion years ago, which is 300 million years earlier than previous research suggested. The discovery indicates that life may have begun shortly after the planet formed 4.54 billion years ago.

The researchers analyzed more than 10,000 zircon crystals from Western Australia, and found two locations containing graphite - pure carbon - in one of the crystals. The graphite has a specific ratio of carbon-12 to carbon-13 that indicates the presence of photosynthetic life.

The researchers are confident that their findings represent 4.1 billion-year-old graphite, and believe that this discovery challenges scientists to think about how ancient the biosphere could be and find new ways to explore for a cryptic record of it. The research was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The United States is currently experiencing a critical shortage of sodium bicarbonate, also known as baking soda, due to issues with two major suppliers, Pfizer and Amphastar. This essential drug is used in various treatments including chemotherapies, organ failure treatments, open-heart surgery, and emergency situations. The shortage has forced hospitals to postpone surgeries and chemotherapy treatments, and some have even turned away patients or sent them to other hospitals.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is working with the suppliers to mitigate the effects of the scarcity, exploring temporary importation as a solution. The shortage is just one example of inexpensive, essential generic medicines hitting alarming lows, with similar shortages occurring in 2012 for sodium bicarbonate and in 2014 for saline solution.

The shortage is due to a combination of factors including problems getting raw materials, issues with aging facilities where many old drugs are manufactured, consolidation in the industry that reduces the number of potential suppliers, and the fact that generic drugs are unlikely to drive profits, leading drug companies to not make necessary investments to maintain supplies.

Hospitals and pharmacies are conserving their supplies without resorting to drastic measures such as delaying surgeries or treatments. The shortage is expected to continue for another month, but may last longer.

Brussels Airport is set to partially reopen for short-haul passenger service on Sunday, April 3, following a terror attack that occurred 12 days prior. The airport will initially only offer three flights by Brussels Airlines and will have stringent security measures in place, including vehicle screenings, luggage checks outside the main building, and increased patrols of armed police and military. The airport aims to return to full capacity before the start of summer holidays at the end of June or early July. The closure of the airport has resulted in significant losses for Brussels Airlines and a drop in overnight stays for hotels in the city. Alternative airports are being used by the busiest airlines until passenger services resume fully at Zaventem.

The study published in Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking in October 2012 examined the relationship between Facebook usage and postbreakup adjustment. The research found that continued online exposure to an ex-partner through Facebook, including remaining friends or engaging in surveillance, was associated with greater current distress, negative feelings, sexual desire, longing for the ex-partner, and lower personal growth. This effect was observed even after accounting for offline contact and well-established personality and relational predictors. The findings suggest that weak-tie contact with an ex-partner through Facebook may contribute to poorer postbreakup functioning over and above strong-tie contact. Contrary to expectations, people who remained Facebook friends with an ex-partner were lower in negative feelings, sexual desire, and longing for the former partner but were also lower in personal growth. The study highlights the challenges of avoiding exposure to an ex-partner online and emphasizes that cutting off contact with an ex may be beneficial for emotional recovery following a breakup.

Big names such as Michelin, KPMG, and Nestle have also been victims of this type of fraud. The study published in Science this week confirms that Dickinsonia, an early complex life form discovered in 1946, is among the earliest known animals on Earth. This flattened, ribbed oval creature, which can grow over four feet across and sports a distinct ridge down its center, had previously been classified as various types of organisms including fungi, protists, and even algae.

In this latest study, researchers used modern techniques to analyze the ancient creatures' molecular biomarkers, specifically sterols. The results showed an abundance of cholesterols in Dickinsonia's trace remains, pointing to its classification as an animal. This evidence supports the hypothesis that Dickinsonia was one of the earliest forms of life on Earth, predating the Cambrian explosion of life that took place 541 million years ago.

The Ediacarans, a group that includes Dickinsonia, are evolutionary oddballs first discovered in the Ediacara hills in South Australia. More than 50 types of Ediacarans are now known and they have been found on every continent except Antarctica. Studying these ancient life forms can provide insights into the makings of complex creatures and potentially yield clues about how life arises on far-flung worlds.

Astronomer Mike Brown, known as the "Pluto killer," has announced new evidence suggesting a ninth planet in our solar system, which he calls Planet Nine. U.S.-based astronomers initially announced the discovery of a new planet in the system with a mass three times that of Earth and orbiting at a distance suitable for liquid water. However, Swiss astronomers, who have been observing the same star using the HARPS instrument, could not confirm the existence of Gliese 581(g) in their data.

The Swiss team expanded their published data set from 6.5 years and 180 measurements to challenge the U.S. findings. Despite this, they acknowledge that they cannot definitively prove the absence of such a small exoplanet due to limitations in observation precision.

Yahoo filed a lawsuit against Facebook on Monday, alleging that Facebook violated 10 patents related to messaging, news feed generation, social commenting advertising display, preventing click fraud, and privacy controls. The complaint was filed in the U.S. District Court in San Jose, Calif., and Yahoo is seeking unspecified damages. This lawsuit comes at an awkward time for Facebook as it prepares for an IPO in May to raise $5 billion. Yahoo claims that Facebook's growth has been based on its patented technology and quotes Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg as acknowledging that "getting there first is not what it's all about." The lawsuit follows failed negotiations between the two companies over patent claims, with Yahoo threatening a lawsuit if Facebook did not pay licensing fees. This is Yahoo's first major legal battle against a big technology company in social media and they have retained the same law firm as Google and other manufacturers in many Android-related smartphone patent cases. Only two of the 10 patents at issue are directly related to social networking technology, most focus on online advertising, including methods for preventing "click fraud," as well as privacy and technology for customizing the information users see on a Web page. Yahoo has never initiated offensive patent litigation against such a large publicly traded company before.

In response to a massive earthquake in Japan, all nuclear reactors at various plants shut down as designed. Control rods were lowered to stop the nuclear reaction, and enormous pumps were activated to cool the fuel rods to prevent melting. However, the diesel backup generators were destroyed by the tsunami, causing a loss of power for the cooling system. Neutron-absorbing boron and seawater were used as a last resort to avoid a nuclear meltdown, but an explosion occurred in one reactor building. Radiation was released, but Japanese officials stated it was at minimal levels that do not harm human health.

The U.S. media has focused on the nuclear accident, while the natural destruction of Earth and sea from the earthquake and tsunami have been far more devastating. The crisis seems to have been triggered by the failure of diesel generators to provide electricity for cooling the reactors once they were shut down. New nuclear plant designs have corrected this weakness, but political obstacles and delays have increased costs, making it difficult for new plants to be built in the U.S.

The Japanese response to the earthquake has been admirable, while the reaction in the U.S. has been characterized as an overreaction about the risks of modern life and technology. The crisis should serve as a lesson about measuring and mitigating risk, but continuing to take risks is necessary for future progress

The EPA has reached a settlement with Magnolia Waco Properties, LLC, also known as Magnolia Homes, over alleged violations of the Toxic Substances Control Act's Lead Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule (RRP Rule) during home renovations depicted on the television show Fixer Upper. The violations included failing to comply with requirements such as obtaining firm certification, assigning a certified renovator, providing homeowners with an approved pamphlet about lead-based paint hazards, and following specific work practice standards.

Magnolia has agreed to pay a civil penalty of $40,000, become an EPA certified renovation firm, obtain training and renovator certification for staff, implement a compliance management program, create educational content about lead-based paint safety, and perform a supplemental environmental project (SEP) to abate lead-based paint hazards in homes or child-occupied facilities in the Waco, Texas area. The settlement also includes steps for Magnolia to ensure compliance with lead-based paint regulations in future renovation projects and to educate the public about lead-based paint hazards and appropriate renovation procedures.

The ruling also stated that Disneyland has a duty to warn disabled guests that they could become stuck on the ride for an extended period if it breaks down. The award consisted of $4,000 for "pain and suffering" and the rest was for a violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act. Disneyland expressed disappointment with the ruling

The other individuals arrested during the sting were Tia Booth, 32, Tammy Glautney, 45, Paul Alan Leys, 35, and Felipe Reuben Manuel, 22.

In a news conference, LAPD Chief Michel Moore announced that during a shootout with suspect Gene Evin Atkins in Silver Lake, Los Angeles, a Trader Joe's store assistant manager, Melyda Corado, was accidentally killed by police gunfire. The investigation revealed that one of the officers' rounds struck Corado as she was exiting the market and was in close proximity to Atkins. Atkins is facing multiple charges, including murder, for his crime-spree that resulted in Corado's death. The Trader Joe’s store remained closed following the incident, with a memorial growing outside, and a GoFundMe page set up to help cover Corado's funeral expenses. The officers involved are "devastated" by their actions, and the LAPD has released body camera and dash camera footage leading up to the chase.

The annual Canadian UFO Survey for 2015 was released, showing an increase in UFO reports compared to 2014. There were 1,267 reported sightings of UFOs, the second-highest number since the survey started in the 1980s. The survey defines a UFO as any object in the sky that people cannot explain. Most sightings can be explained by stars, planets, fireballs, aircraft, and police helicopters, but about 12% remain unexplained despite further investigation. One notable "high-quality" unexplained case was a silent, triangular object with bright lights seen in Manitoba. The survey also revealed that Quebec had the most UFO sightings, followed by Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver. Many of the reports involved strange lights, while a few included claims of alien beings. Researchers suggest that the increase in UFO reports may be due to growing public interest and the popularity of space-related topics.

The Wolfman is a horror film released in 2010, starring Benicio Del Toro, Anthony Hopkins, Emily Blunt, and Hugo Weaving. Directed by Joe Johnston, the movie is a remake of the 1941 screenplay by Curt Siodmak and follows Lawrence Talbot (Del Toro), who returns to his family's estate in rural England after his brother disappears. After being attacked by a werewolf, Talbot becomes cursed and transforms into one himself during the next full moon, going on a bloody rampage.

The film attempts to blend gothic storytelling with modern horror elements but is criticized for its uneasy fusion of traditional makeup and CGI effects. The portrayal of Lawrence Talbot by Del Toro is compared unfavorably to Lon Chaney Jr.'s iconic performance in the original, as Del Toro's character lacks emotional depth and generates little empathy from viewers. The supporting cast, including Anthony Hopkins and Emily Blunt, is also criticized for underutilization.

The action takes place in the 1890s on the moors of rural England, with the estate of Sir John Talbot (Anthony Hopkins) serving as a central location. The film had been searching for a director before Joe Johnson was brought on board, but the results are mixed, with the effects

Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the supreme leader of Iran, has criticized U.S. President Donald Trump for pulling out of the 2015 nuclear deal, calling his statement "ludicrous and shallow." Khamenei claimed that Trump's speech contained more than 10 lies and threatened both Iran's people and its government. Hardliners in Iran have seized on this opportunity to consolidate their power over reformists who championed the pact. The commander of Iran's Revolutionary Guards congratulated the nation on the US exit, while at the opening session of the Iranian parliament, hardline MPs set fire to a paper US flag and the text of the JCPOA. The nuclear deal, known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), was a landmark agreement that ended a 12-year deadlock over Tehran's nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief. Under the deal, Iran unplugged two-thirds of its centrifuges, shipped out 98% of its enriched uranium, and filled its plutonium production reactor with concrete. The JCPOA is enshrined in a UN security council resolution that incorporated it into international law. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is set to vote on net neutrality rules on Thursday, aiming to preserve an open internet and prevent internet service providers from discriminating against content creators. The rules, if approved, would regulate broadband providers as utilities under Title II of the Communications Act, giving the FCC the authority to prohibit "fast lanes" for companies that pay for priority access. The vote is expected to pass, but it could face challenges in court and from Congress. The debate over net neutrality has been polarizing, with Republicans expressing concerns that the regulations are excessive, while strong net neutrality proponents argue that they are necessary to prevent internet providers from curtailing access, services or content. The rules could affect the entire internet, but some argue that the FCC should focus on consumer protection rather than regulating the industry as a whole.

The First Step Act, a bipartisan bill aimed at reforming federal criminal justice sentencing laws, has gained support from President Donald Trump and various law enforcement organizations. The proposed legislation includes improvements in prison conditions, preparation for prisoner re-entry into society, and incentives such as time credits for good behavior and participation in job-training programs.

The bill also addresses the treatment of incarcerated women by prohibiting shackling pregnant inmates and requiring the Bureau of Prisons to locate prisoners near their homes when possible. However, opposition remains from some law enforcement officials and conservative politicians who argue that sentencing changes could pose a risk to public safety.

The bill has been under negotiation since 2015, with two components: prison reform and sentencing reform. Prison reform enjoys broad bipartisan support, while sentencing reform is favored by Democrats but has divided Republicans. The bill passed the House in May with only prison reform included, but a Senate version that includes sentencing reform has recently earned support from the Fraternal Order of Police and other influential figures.

The First Step Act aims to reduce crime, improve conditions in federal prisons, and provide re-entry opportunities for prisoners. A 19-year-old surfer named Lucas Ransom died after being attacked by a shark off the Santa Barbara coast in California. The attack occurred around 9 AM on October 22. It is believed that the shark was likely a great white, as a shark expert suggested that only a dozen out of the world's 400 shark species could inflict such a bite, and great whites are known to be present off the coast of California. Ransom was attacked while boogie boarding with a friend about 100 yards offshore, and it is believed that he died before reaching shore. Three nearby beaches were immediately closed following the attack, and federal and state wildlife officials are working to identify the type of shark involved. Ransom was a chemical engineering major at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and was from Riverside County outside Los Angeles.

HBO Now, a standalone version of HBO without the need for a cable subscription, has officially launched exclusively on Apple devices including Apple TV, iPhone, and iPad. The service costs $14.99 per month with a free 30-day trial available this month. Users can access content on any computer at HBONow.com or through Cablevision's Optimum Online. Although the app is currently exclusive to iOS, it is expected to expand to other devices in the future. The service offers over 2,000 titles and will be particularly useful for watching the fifth season of "Game of Thrones" which premieres this month. Some users have experienced issues during setup, but the service overall is functioning as expected with no noticeable buffering or freezing issues.

Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump has refused to endorse House Speaker Paul D. Ryan and Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) in their primary races, citing a need for strong leadership. This move is unusual as both leaders have endorsed Trump but have criticized some of his policies and statements. Trump's comments come after President Obama denounced Trump as "unfit to serve as president" and challenged Republican leaders to withdraw their support of their nominee. The divisions within the GOP were further highlighted when Rep. Richard L. Hanna (N.Y.) announced he will vote for Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton in the upcoming election. Trump's comments about Ryan are seen as a response to Ryan's criticism of his remarks about the Khan family, who spoke at the Democratic convention and criticized Trump's knowledge of the Constitution. Trump also expressed his intention to start super PACs to savage Republicans or Democrats of his choosing in future elections if he loses the election.

The Associated Press reports that during his confirmation hearing, Judge Brett Kavanaugh was questioned about various topics including abortion, presidential power, and sexual misconduct allegations against a former mentor.

On the topic of Roe v. Wade, Kavanaugh called it an "important precedent" that has been reaffirmed many times over the past 45 years. He also noted that a 1992 decision, Planned Parenthood v. Casey, didn't just reaffirm Roe v. Wade in passing but became "precedent on precedent." However, Kavanaugh did not reveal his stance on the issue.

Regarding presidential power, Kavanaugh declined to answer questions about the extent of a president's pardon power and whether a sitting president can be forced to testify in a criminal case, citing them as hypothetical questions he cannot answer.

In response to questions about sexual misconduct allegations against former federal appeals court judge Alex Kozinski, who was a friend and mentor of Kavanaugh's, the nominee said he knew nothing about the allegations before they became public and felt a "gut punch" when they did.

The hearings were marked by numerous protests from both audience members and Democratic senators who called for a delay in the hearing.

A 26-year-old student named Marcela Franco has died from injuries sustained in a shooting rampage that took place on Friday at Santa Monica College. The shooting also claimed the life of her father, Carlos Navarro Franco, who was a groundskeeper at the college. John Zawahri, aged 23, is identified as the shooter and was killed by police during a confrontation in the college's library. Marcela had registered to attend summer classes at Santa Monica College and was with her father when the shooting occurred. The school has set up a memorial fund for the Franco family. The suspected motive behind the shooting is still under investigation, but it appears that Zawahri may have suffered from mental health issues.

Keith Urban and Nicole Kidman, married for seven years, maintain a hot relationship by sexting each other when their work commitments keep them apart. Urban is currently touring and taping American Idol in the US, while Kidman is filming a movie in London. In an interview with Ellen DeGeneres, Urban mentioned that they only communicate via phone calls, which he prefers.

In a separate interview with Vanity Fair, Kidman reflected on her marriage to Tom Cruise at 23 and her growth since then. She discussed the intense fame she experienced during her marriage to Cruise, stating that it brought them closer but was intoxicating. Kidman now lives in Nashville with Urban and their two daughters, and she expressed gratitude for stepping away from Hollywood's fame and finding a more idiosyncratic path.

Kidman also discussed the challenges of balancing her love for her husband and children with her artistic desires, stating that it is an ongoing struggle. She emphasized the strong bond between her family, describing them as very close and protective. To read the full interview, download Vanity Fair's digital edition.

A scheduling glitch at American Airlines has left thousands of flights without pilots assigned during the busy holiday travel period next month. The airline is offering pilots 150% of their hourly pay to work those dates, but some 15,000 flights may still be affected. The problem occurred when pilots loaded up their schedules with flights in early December and took days off around the holidays after the system allowed it. American Airlines says it is working diligently to address the issue and expects to avoid cancellations this holiday season by using reserve pilots and offering extra pay to those who pick up open trips. However, the pilots' union has filed a grievance, claiming that the airline's solution violates the pilots' contract. The scheduling problem may result in higher labor costs, which have concerned investors in the past. American Airlines shares tumbled after the airline announced pay raises for pilots and flight attendants earlier this year.

Jacob Brundage, a professional poker player from Lakeland, Florida, experienced an emotional jackpot when an Uber driver returned his lost bag containing $7,000 in cash and playing chips during the World Series of Poker. Brundage realized he had left the bag in an Uber minivan he took from The Venetian to the Rio around 9 p.m. on June 1st. After failing to reach the driver through the app, he enlisted help from a group of Uber employees at the Rio who successfully tracked down the driver and the lost bag. The driver returned the bag after his cellphone battery died, and Brundage rewarded him with $200. This incident is likely the most expensive item ever left in an Uber car in Las Vegas, according to Uber spokeswoman Maui Cheska Orozco.

On October 24, 2015, Academy Award-winning filmmaker Quentin Tarantino joined hundreds of demonstrators in New York City to protest police brutality nationwide. The protesters marched from Washington Square Park to Sixth Avenue, chanting slogans and waving signs with photos of the dead, mostly young black men, who were killed by police. Speakers at the event called for justice for those killed by police.

Notable attendees included activist Cornel West, who organized the protest along with Carl Dix, and Marion Gray-Hopkins, whose son Gary Hopkins Jr. was killed by police in 1999. The event was part of a series of demonstrations organized by RiseUpOctober this week.

The protest came at a time of heightened awareness of the relationship between police officers and the people they serve. While the day was peaceful, it followed the shooting death of New York Police Officer Randolph Holder while chasing a bicycle thief. A suspect has been charged with murder and robbery in the case.

The city's police union called for a boycott of Tarantino's films after he referred to cops as "murderers" during the rally. Patrick Lynch, president of the Patrolmen’s Benevolent Association, criticized Tarantino for glorifying crime and violence in his

A New Jersey man named Joe Hornick is facing potential fines or jail time for flying a Donald Trump campaign flag on his property, which violates a local ordinance that limits political signage to 30 days before an election. The American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey has stated that the ordinance may be unconstitutional as it discriminates against political speech and cannot limit political signs. Hornick, who has been flying the flag since February, is prepared to face a judge and potentially serve jail time if necessary. This incident occurred in West Long Branch, New Jersey.

Two men, Dereck James "D.J." Harrison (22) and his father Flint Wayne Harrison (51), were taken into custody following a day-long manhunt in Wyoming. The arrests came in connection with the alleged kidnapping and assault of a Utah woman and her four daughters aged 13 to 18.

The incident occurred on Tuesday when the family was lured to a home for a barbecue, where they were allegedly tied up with wire and duct tape. The women and some of the girls were assaulted with a baseball bat as they tried to break free. However, the suspects had fled before police arrived.

The manhunt centered on Half Moon Lake Lodge in Pinedale, Wyoming, where authorities found a makeshift campsite. Both father and son are believed to have been armed and made threats against law enforcement officials. Dereck Harrison was found without incident on Saturday night, while Flint Harrison had turned himself in earlier.

The younger Harrison is suspected of using methamphetamine and the motive appears to be retaliation against the mother. Both men will be extradited to Utah to face charges, but it's unclear if they will face additional charges in Wyoming due to Flint Harrison's past as a registered sex offender there.

Dennis Hastert, former U.S. House speaker and alumnus of Wheaton College, had his name removed from one of the college's programs following federal charges against him for lying about illicit payments to a man from his past. The J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy at Wheaton College was re-designated as the Wheaton College Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy. The college stated that it would pray for all involved, including Speaker Hastert, his family, and those who may have been harmed by any inappropriate behavior. The arraignment for Hastert is scheduled for June 4, 2015, in a Chicago federal court. Additionally, the Illinois state legislature scrapped plans to construct a statue of Hastert due to his recent indictment.

A 19-year-old named Jonathan Brussow from Michigan was killed in the Bahamas while on vacation with his girlfriend's family. The incident occurred when a large wave swept him away during a hike. Brussow and his girlfriend, Athena Williams, had been together since they were in eighth grade and had recently discussed getting married. The couple was on vacation in the Bahamas, where Brussow asked Williams' family for permission to propose. Despite extensive search efforts, Brussow's body was recovered four days later. The community is now raising funds to install safety devices near the Glass Window Bridge, where the incident occurred, and to help the local hospital obtain new equipment.

Assemblyman Bill Nojay, a conservative Republican from New York, died by suicide on Friday morning at the Riverside Cemetery in Rochester. The news came after reports that Nojay had failed to appear in court for fraud charges and was being investigated by the FBI for possible fraud in a business deal related to a $1.3 billion school modernization program. Nojay was also under investigation in Cambodia for a fraud case involving a dentist who accused him of defrauding her of $1 million. He was 59 years old and represented the 133rd Assembly District, which includes Livingston County and parts of Monroe and Steuben counties. Nojay was known for his outspoken conservative views and was a vocal critic of gun control laws in New York. He worked as a talk radio host and held positions with Commodity Resource Corp. and the Empire Page.

In summary, a news gathering technique used by several hundred Bloomberg reporters has come under scrutiny for potentially invading user privacy on their own platform. This technique allowed reporters to view lists of subscribers at a firm, access background information including contact details and usage statistics, and monitor chat logs between subscribers and customer service representatives. The practice involved using the "Z function" and "UUID function," both of which have since been disabled in the newsroom.

The issue was initially raised by Goldman Sachs last month, leading to assurances from Bloomberg that they would address the problem. Similar concerns were also raised by JPMorgan Chase regarding a reporting technique used by Bloomberg reporters that questioned whether traders responsible for a multibillion-dollar trading loss had been fired.

Bloomberg has since taken steps to centralize data security efforts, appointing Steve Ross as client data compliance officer and reminding reporters of the company's policy about terminal use and employee confidentiality agreement. However, concerns remain about the potential misuse of this information, with some suggesting that nothing on the Bloomberg terminal is private.

Thomson Reuters, a competitor, has seized on the headache faced by Bloomberg, emphasizing that their reporters have no access to nonpublic data on its customers. The incident has raised questions about the boundary between journalism and business interests in the financial industry.

The White House has indicated that President Donald Trump currently has confidence in Veterans Affairs Secretary David Shulkin, despite reports suggesting his potential dismissal this week due to allegations of excessive spending on travel and staff purges. However, the White House deputy press secretary Hogan Gidley stated that the president reserves the right to make changes when he sees fit, implying that Shulkin's tenure could still be in jeopardy. The administration is reportedly considering several candidates as potential replacements for Shulkin, including Pete Hegseth and former Rep. Jeff Miller, among others. The situation remains fluid, with no official announcement having been made yet.

A human heart intended for donation was accidentally left on a Southwest Airlines flight bound for Dallas, causing the plane to return to Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. The heart was meant to be unloaded in Seattle but was overlooked during the initial flight. The heart's destination and purpose remain unclear, as do details about whether anyone's life was ever in danger. The airline confirmed that the heart was a "life-critical cargo shipment" and that it made the decision to return because it was necessary to deliver the shipment quickly. The incident caused a five-hour delay for passengers before the flight took off again for Dallas. The heart was eventually delivered safely, according to Sierra Donor Services, which organized the donation.

Sarah Palin, a prominent American figure, visited Paul Revere's house in Boston this week and provided an unusual account of Paul Revere's famous midnight ride during the Revolutionary War. Instead of warning John Hancock and Samuel Adams about the approaching British army as historically documented, Palin suggested that Revere was actually trying to warn the British by ringing bells and sending warning shots. However, it is historically inaccurate that Paul Revere used bells during his mission or warned the British, who were America's adversaries at the time.

The cybersecurity firm Trend Micro has reported that hacking groups Fancy Bear, APT 28, and Pawn Storm have launched similar phishing attacks on French presidential candidate Emmanuel Macron and German political parties, using tactics similar to those used in the Democratic National Committee (DNC) email breach. The attackers are believed to be Russian espionage operations, and one of the domains used against Macron's campaign was "onedrive-en-marche.fr," which appeared to be a fake account for Microsoft's OneDrive service associated with Macron's political party. Trend Micro also reported that the hackers targeted German political groups Konrad Adenauer Stiftung and Friedrich Ebert Stiftung, both of which are associated with major German political parties. The report has raised concerns about potential Russian interference in the French presidential election, as Macron faces right-wing nationalist Marine Le Pen in a contentious race that has been compared to the 2016 U.S. election. Macron's digital campaign manager confirmed that there had been attempted hacks on the campaign, but said they were unsuccessful and no party supporters' information was compromised.

The Heartland Institute, a conservative think tank known for promoting climate skepticism, has come under criticism for an ill-judged billboard campaign launched in May 2012. The campaign featured infamous criminals such as Ted Kaczynski (the Unabomber), Charles Manson, and Fidel Castro, who had expressed beliefs in man-made global warming. The billboards were designed to question viewers about their own beliefs regarding global warming.

The campaign drew criticism for its association of climate change advocates with criminals and madmen. Critics argued that the campaign was a misguided attempt to discredit those who believe in man-made global warming, portraying them as radical fringe elements rather than scientists or mainstream thinkers.

The billboard campaign followed Heartland's announcement of a digital billboard featuring an essay by Joseph Bast, and it ran from May 5 through the Institute's conference on May 23. The campaign sparked questions about whether sponsors and speakers would continue to support the Institute in light of the controversy.

One notable speaker, Roger Helmer, a British politician known for his climate skepticism, defended the campaign and encouraged people to attend the conference or follow it online. The Gulf of Mexico is experiencing an oil slick, with officials considering a controlled burn as it approaches sensitive ecological areas in the Mississippi River Delta. The spill is estimated to be one of the worst in U.S. history, with oil leaking at a rate of approximately 42,000 gallons per day from a well located 50 miles off the coast of Louisiana. Efforts to seal the leak using remote-controlled submarines and other methods have been unsuccessful so far. The slick is currently within 20 miles of land, and if it makes landfall, it could have serious ecological repercussions. Controlled burns may be conducted as soon as Wednesday, but they could produce a black plume of smoke that puts soot and other particulates into the air. The incident has intensified political reaction, with government officials expanding their investigation of the explosion that caused the oil rig disaster and considering possible criminal or civil violations by the operators of the drilling rig and related companies.

Vulfpeck, a small-time funk band, released an album called Sleepify consisting of silence to generate royalties from streaming services like Spotify. The idea is for fans to stream the "songs" continuously, with the profits intended for touring expenses. This project serves as a publicity stunt and commentary on the digital age's music valuation.

The album has garnered over 1 million plays on Spotify, earning the band between $6,700 and $9,400. Vulfpeck member Jack Stratton acknowledges that while Spotify is beneficial for promoting their music, they make less on YouTube. The silent tracks have boosted traffic to the band's actual music.

Spotify views the stunt as clever but prefers earlier albums from Vulfpeck. If the band wants to maximize digital earnings, it should focus on avoiding bot-driven traffic, a common issue in digital advertising that results in brands losing millions annually. However, Spotify did not discuss dealing with bot-driven traffic due to technical barriers and potential attention capture.

Using bots for streaming could potentially harm other honest bands trying to make money on the platform. The project highlights the complexities of music royalties and digital revenue streams in the modern era.

The body of former White House chef Walter Scheib, who served under Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush from 1994 to 2005, was found on Sunday night near a hiking trail in the Taos area of New Mexico. Scheib went missing last weekend after going for a solo hike in the mountains near Taos Ski Valley. His vehicle was found parked at a canyon trailhead on Tuesday. The cause of death and further details about the discovery are not yet known. Scheib recently moved to New Mexico and is the author of "White House Chef: Eleven Years, Two Presidents, One Kitchen."

Federal Election Commission decision, which granted corporations First Amendment free speech rights and allowed unlimited donations for electioneering, on the 2012 U.S. presidential election. The ruling led to the rise of super PACs, independent political action committees that can receive unlimited corporate contributions and make unlimited expenditures for federal candidates.

The article focuses on the Iowa caucuses as the first presidential battleground where the influence of super PACs was evident. One super PAC, Restore Our Future, which supports Mitt Romney, spent $2.8 million on negative attack ads against Newt Gingrich, contributing to his decline in polls and Mitt Romney's rise. The ads were created and paid for by people with deep knowledge of the Romney campaign's strategic thinking, close relationships with Mr. Romney's most generous donors, and even research on what television viewers like and dislike about Mr. Romney himself.

Despite the political carnage suffered by Republican presidential candidates at the hands of super PACs in Iowa, conservatives show no signs of buyers' remorse after supporting the Supreme Court decision that opened the floodgates for unlimited campaign money. In an unexpected turn of events, two-time Oscar winner Tom Hanks played a role in the resolution of a domestic assault case in Los Angeles. Hanks served as a juror in the trial since it began last week. On Tuesday, the prosecuting attorney revealed that another lawyer had interacted with Hanks outside the courtroom, thanking him for his service. This led to a request for a mistrial by the defense, citing prosecutorial misconduct.

In a hearing on Wednesday, both sides agreed to a reduced charge for the defendant: disturbing the peace and a $150 fine. The City Attorney's Office confirmed the interaction with Hanks, stating that they will be reviewing the situation.

During jury selection, defense attorney Andrew Flier initially expressed concern about Hanks' celebrity status potentially influencing the case's outcome. However, after interviewing Hanks, Flier decided he was a fair juror. Hanks' presence outside the courthouse also drew a crowd of photographers and fans.

If the case hadn't ended in a plea, it is unclear how Hanks would have voted. The alleged victim's reaction to the resolution was not available due to privacy reasons. This report was contributed by CNN's JD Cargill.

Jane Fonda, a renowned actress and activist, recently discussed her controversial activism during the Vietnam War on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. In 1972, Fonda visited Hanoi and was photographed sitting on an anti-aircraft gun used against American soldiers, causing decades of outrage from critics who labeled her "Hanoi Jane." During the interview, Fonda admitted that she regretted the incident, stating it was a lapse in judgment. She also mentioned that despite the controversy, she doesn't regret going to Vietnam as she learned a lot during her visit. The discussion revolved around Fonda's activism and its impact on her career, which is detailed in the HBO documentary "Jane Fonda in Five Acts."

Sacha Maujean, a single parent, is currently in Brisbane with her two daughters, Romany and Rumer, after Rumer was diagnosed with stage 3 neuroblastoma cancer. The tumor measures 11cm long and Rumer has a 50% chance of recovery. The family is looking at a potential 2-year stay away from their home, family, and friends. They have set up a GoFundMe page to help with expenses during this difficult time.

In a separate story, Adam Koessler, the father of Rumer Rose, was arrested for administering medicinal cannabis oil to his daughter after she was diagnosed with stage 4 Neuroblastoma. His bail conditions prohibit him from having direct or indirect contact with his child who is in the Lady Cilento Children's hospital. Adam and his family are advocating for the decriminalization of medicinal cannabis oil in Australia due to its beneficial effects for cancer patients without harmful side effects.

The second quarter of 2012 has been particularly challenging for CNN, with ratings for prime-time shows plummeting by 40% compared to last year. This decline was the worst ever recorded by CNN for a second quarter, likely due to a lack of major news events during this period compared to the previous year.

All three cable news networks experienced declines among viewers aged 25-54, the demographic most valuable to news advertisers. Fox News saw a 14% drop, MSNBC a 18% drop, while CNN suffered a more significant decline of over double these figures.

CNN's 9 p.m show, hosted by Piers Morgan, experienced a particularly steep decline, dropping 32% from last year to just 137,000 viewers in the 25-54 age group. This is the worst performance ever for a quarter by a 9 p.m show on CNN.

In terms of total viewers, Fox News led easily with 2.14 million, followed by MSNBC with 817,000 and CNN with only 470,000. This represents a 35% decline for CNN compared to the same quarter last year.

A group of approximately 15 armed, battle-hardened thieves ambushed two secure vans carrying jewels worth €9m (£6.3m) on a French highway, forcing out the drivers and escaping in four vehicles. The incident occurred on the A6 highway connecting Paris and Lyon, with no injuries reported. The perpetrators are currently being hunted by French authorities in the Burgundy region southeast of Paris. This latest heist is part of a string of big jewel thefts that have occurred in France over the past few years. The jewels remain missing, and investigations are ongoing, with authorities focusing on organized crime connections. Notable previous jewelry heists in France include the 2007 and 2008 Harry Winston boutique robberies in Paris, which netted over €100m in total.

A student was fatally shot at Butler High School in Matthews, North Carolina on Monday morning during a fight in the hallway. The suspect, another male student, was quickly arrested by a school resource officer and the weapon used has been secured. The victim's name and age were not immediately released, nor was that of the suspect. The shooting occurred as crowds of students arrived for the day, causing many witnesses. Counselors and psychologists were made available for affected students.

School officials implemented a lockdown for about two hours after the incident, during which parents rushed to the school to ensure their children's safety. Classes resumed for students who remained on campus once the lockdown was lifted. The diverse student body of approximately 2,000 at the school consists of one-third white, one-third African American, and one-quarter Hispanic.

Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools Superintendent Clayton Wilcox expressed concern over a young person obtaining a handgun in North Carolina and stated that the system would review its security procedures. The type of gun used has not been confirmed by police. Emotional footage showed students leaving the school, crying and hugging their parents.

Andy Roddick, a prominent figure in tennis for the past decade, announced his retirement from the sport after the US Open, which coincides with his 30th birthday. In a press conference, Roddick stated that he felt it was time to retire due to physical and emotional concerns about his ability to compete at the top level anymore. He will face Bernard Tomic of Australia in the second round of the tournament.

Roddick has had an impressive career with a 610-212 record, including 32 singles titles, and career prize money of over $20 million. He won the 2003 US Open, marking the last time a North American male tennis player won a Grand Slam singles title. Throughout his career, Roddick has been known for his competitiveness, determination, work ethic, and witty retorts, serving as a mentor to up-and-coming players such as Sam Querrey and Ryan Harrison.

Roddick plans to stay busy post-retirement with philanthropic efforts, part-time radio work, and family life with his wife, actress and model Brooklyn Decker. However, he expressed that he may not completely abandon tennis, stating that he still loves the game and might continue to play casually. The US Open will provide one last opportunity for fans to witness Roddick's talents on the court.

The U.S government has shut down for the first time in 17 years due to a dispute over President Obama's healthcare initiative. The shutdown affects more than 800,000 federal workers, with certain agencies requiring unsalaried employees to continue working, such as those dealing with national security and managing benefits like Social Security payments. Essential services like the U.S Postal Service will remain unaffected.

The Senate rejected House amendments to a short-term spending bill on Monday, pushing the government towards its first shutdown in nearly two decades. With no agreement on a funding bill in sight, Republicans and Democrats continue to spar on Capitol Hill while federal workers are furloughed and services are closed. The shutdown could also impact negotiations over raising the federal debt limit, with the Senate-rejected House amendments seeking to undermine the Affordable Care Act by delaying enforcement of the individual mandate.

Active-duty troops will continue to receive their paychecks, but other workers may face delayed payment. Many congressional hearings, including one scheduled for Tuesday on last month's Washington Navy Yard shootings, have been postponed. Vint Cerf, one of the inventors of the Internet and a current Vice President of Google, warned at the American Association for the Advancement of Science annual meeting in San Jose, California that future archaeologists might struggle to interpret the 21st century civilization due to the potential erasure of our digital trace. He expressed concern about relying solely on digital data storage for books, texts, and photographs, as they may become unreadable or disappear over time, creating an "information black hole."

Cerf compared this situation to the post-Roman period in Western Europe, where relatively little is known due to the lack of written records. He suggested that future generations might have great difficulty understanding our civilization because of the uninterpretable bits of information we leave behind. Cerf recommended creating physical copies of important photographs and documents to ensure their preservation.

Cerf also pointed out that historians may struggle to reconstruct conversations between contemporary luminaries due to missing or unreadable digital records. He proposed a concept called "digital vellum," which involves taking a digital snapshot at the time an item is stored, capturing all the processes needed to reproduce it in the future. This snapshot could then be used to reproduce games, picture files, or spreadsheets on a modern computer, even centuries from now.

Italy's national statistical agency, Istat, announced on Thursday that it will include the economic value of prostitution, illegal drug sales, and trafficking in contraband cigarettes and alcohol in its calculation of the country's 2014 Gross Domestic Product (GDP). This update to the methodology follows guidelines provided by Eurostat, the EU's statistical agency.

The move aims to reflect a more accurate representation of Italy's economy, including elements of the underground economy. Istat acknowledges that measuring these illegal activities will be challenging. The inclusion of these sectors is expected to add between 1% and 2% to Italian GDP.

This expansion could positively impact the national government, particularly when calculating the ratio of the deficit to GDP. Prime Minister Matteo Renzi's commitment to reducing Italy’s deficit to 2.6 percent of GDP this year may benefit from this boost to the country's GDP.

Additionally, research and development (R&D) and arms will also be included in the GDP calculation for the first time. R&D was previously excluded due to being classified as an intermediate cost.

The change in methodology does not yet have official comment from the Finance Ministry. The revised figures will be applied retrospectively, affecting prior-year measurements as well.

In an interview with The Huffington Post, Senator Rand Paul defended his aide Jack Hunter, who has been criticized for past comments critical of Abraham Lincoln and sympathetic to the Confederacy. Paul stated that he opposes such views, many of which have been recanted by Hunter, and emphasized that he has a zero tolerance policy for discriminatory behavior. However, he also defended Hunter as a talented conservative writer, stating that he would not shy away from hiring him based on his past writings. Jack Hunter has since left Paul's office to resume his career as a political pundit, citing the desire to clear his name and avoid being a distraction for Paul. The controversy over Hunter's past writings and radio broadcasts has been seen as a drag on libertarian-leaning Republicans' mainstream political ambitions and a reminder of the elder Paul's newsletters.

Scientists have discovered the most distant galaxy ever confirmed, named z8_GND_5296, which is approximately 13.1 billion light-years from Earth. The discovery was made using the Hubble Space Telescope and Keck Observatory in Hawaii. Light from this ancient galaxy began its journey when the universe was about 700 million years old. The find could help researchers better understand the early universe, particularly the era of reionization when newborn hot, massive stars transformed the opaque hydrogen fog into the transparent intergalactic space we see today. The discovery of this distant galaxy is expected to push back the record for the most distant object ever detected. However, further confirmation and remeasurement are required to verify its distance.

The article discusses the reactions of various political figures to President Barack Obama's expected nomination of former Senator Chuck Hagel as Secretary of Defense. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell has stated that Hagel should receive a fair confirmation hearing, but he will review Hagel's past statements and qualifications before making a final decision.

Senators Ted Cruz, Tom Cotton, and Lindsey Graham have expressed concerns about Hagel's views on Israel, Iran, and terrorism, while Senate Majority Whip Dick Durbin has defended Hagel as a "serious candidate." Actress Ashley Judd is reportedly considering challenging McConnell in the 2014 elections, but he has stated that he will focus on current Congressional issues rather than potential challenges.

The United Nations Security Council has voted to impose a no-fly zone over Libya, authorizing military action to prevent a humanitarian disaster caused by Colonel Moammar Gadhafi's escalating violence against rebels. However, experts and Libyan rebels suspect that Gadhafi's sudden promise of a cease-fire is a tactical move aimed at buying time and confusing the West. Reports from Misrata indicate that the city is still under bombardment despite the cease-fire announcement. The West, led by Britain, is preparing for military action, with naval forces stationed off the Libyan coast and air bases in Italy and Cyprus ready for operation. The intervention is a high-stakes gamble, with concerns about potential long-term consequences if it fails to succeed quickly. The hope is that the UN's resolution will lead to Qaddafi's regime collapsing and creating conditions for a rapid political process to change the regime without actual use of military force. However, there are unanswered questions about what comes next, and concerns about the potential impact on other countries in the region, such as Bahrain and Yemen.

In summary, violent protests continued in Bahrain for a second day on February 18, 2011, with security forces opening fire on anti-government demonstrators, resulting in at least 50 injuries. President Barack Obama condemned the violence and urged Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa to show restraint, hold those responsible accountable, and respect the universal rights of its people while embracing meaningful reform. The crown prince subsequently ordered the military to withdraw from the Pearl Square roundabout and appealed for all political factions to join in a dialogue for political reforms. However, the outcome of the uprising remains uncertain due to disunity within the opposition over ultimate goals and the protesters' determination to continue demonstrating. The violence in Bahrain, along with similar incidents in Yemen and Libya, prompted sharp criticism from President Obama and led Britain and France to announce a halt in arms sales to these countries. Clashes also erupted across other Middle Eastern countries, including Jordan and Djibouti, on the same day.

The Academy Award nominations for 2014 were announced this morning, with notable omissions and controversies surrounding the films Selma and Force Majeure. Selma, directed by Ava DuVernay, was snubbed in major categories such as Best Director and Best Acting, despite critical acclaim and box office success. The film's absence from these categories is particularly disappointing given its importance as a black-centric historical drama told from the perspective of its black protagonists. Force Majeure, a Swedish film, was also overlooked in the Best Foreign Language Film category, highlighting the Academy's tendency towards shortsightedness and lack of recognition for difficult or foreign films. The nominations this year have sparked criticism for their lack of diversity, as no black woman has ever been nominated for a Best Director Oscar, and only three black men have ever been nominated in the best director category. This year marks the Academy's 87th award show, and the absence of DuVernay from the Best Director nominees sends a brutal message about the Academy's apparent disregard for diversity.

The mayor of Kharkiv, a city in eastern Ukraine, was critically wounded after being shot in the back by an unknown gunman while jogging on Monday. The shooting comes amid ongoing unrest in the region, where pro-Russian separatists have seized government buildings and called for greater autonomy or outright annexation by Russia. The US has expanded sanctions to include targets linked to Russian President Vladimir Putin's inner circle, including seven new individuals and 17 companies. The European Union is also expected to announce new sanctions against Russia. Western nations accuse Moscow of supporting separatist gunmen who are occupying official buildings in cities across eastern Ukraine. The separatists continue to hold seven Western military observers who were seized last week in the region. Pro-Russian separatists also seized a local government building in Kostyantynivka on Monday, and there have been reports of kidnappings by pro-Russia militants in Slovyansk. The mayor of Kharkiv, Hennadiy Kernes, was previously a supporter of the former pro-Moscow President Viktor Yanukovych but dropped his support for the ousted president in favor of a united Ukraine. The Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), led by Joseph Kony, has reportedly weakened as his son Salim Saleh, who is believed to be 22 years old, has been named deputy leader. This change indicates that Kony may have lost control over his commanders, with some killed by Ugandan forces and others in disarray. The LRA, infamous for its extreme violence, continues to operate in remote forest regions of Central African Republic, Sudan, South Sudan, and Democratic Republic of the Congo despite international efforts to capture them.

Ugandan General Sam Kavuma claims that Salim Saleh is now responsible for field command, suggesting that Kony's control over the LRA has been weakened. The United Nations Regional Office for Central Africa reported a significant reduction in the activities of the LRA but emphasized the need to capture Kony to ensure peace for displaced people and refugees.

Recent reports suggest that Kony may be seeking refuge in an area known as Kafia Kingi, controlled by Sudan. The Security Council has praised the progress made against the LRA but called for continued efforts until they are no longer a threat.
