The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Michigan has accused Detroit police of forcibly removing homeless individuals from the Greektown entertainment district and abandoning them miles away, sometimes outside the city. This practice, which the ACLU calls "kidnapping," is described as inhumane, callous, and illegal. The ACLU claims that these individuals are told they are not welcome in Greektown and are forced into vans, driven away, and deserted, often late at night in unfamiliar neighborhoods. The police allegedly take their money and force them to walk back to Detroit with no guarantee of safety.

The ACLU's investigation found five individuals who were subjected to this abusive treatment on multiple occasions. One of the individuals, Andrew Sheehan, has been picked up several times while sitting on a manhole in Greektown to keep warm and driven anywhere from 5 to 8 miles away. Another individual, Dennis B., was dropped off on the Detroit's eastside or in Dearborn on several occasions.

The ACLU has demanded an end to this practice and filed a complaint with the U.S. Justice Department. Detroit Police Chief Chester Logan has promised to look into the matter. The ACLU plans to continue investigating and documenting these incidents.

The Supreme Court has declined Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli's request for a fast-track review of the constitutionality of President Obama's healthcare law. Instead, the legal challenge will continue in federal appeals courts. The case could still reach the high court by early summer 2012.

Virginia and several other states have challenged the requirement that virtually all Americans buy health insurance, claiming it is unconstitutional. Two federal judges have agreed with the states, while three others have found the law constitutional. The cases are moving through the appeals courts quickly, with hearings scheduled in May and June.

The Supreme Court's decision means that all nine justices will hear the case when it reaches the court, though there were calls for Elena Kagan to recuse herself due to her previous role as solicitor general. Governor Bob McDonnell of Virginia expressed disappointment at the court's decision not to expedite the case.

Mischa Barton has filed a lawsuit against her mother and former manager Nuala Barton, alleging financial exploitation and fraud over the course of her career. According to the lawsuit, Nuala withheld earnings from various acting roles, including "The Hoarder," and took a 10% management fee without properly compensating Mischa. The suit also claims that Nuala lied about Mischa's salary for "The Hoarder" and pocketed the difference, as well as using her daughter's name to pimp out a handbag line and fashion boutique in London without compensating her. Additionally, Nuala allegedly structured the purchase of Mischa's Beverly Hills home to give herself co-ownership and then kicked her out of the property. The suit seeks unspecified damages, triple the amount found to have been withheld, and legal fees. Nuala's attorney has not yet responded to the complaint.

The Global Slavery Index 2013 reports that approximately 29.6 million people worldwide are enslaved, with Mauritania and Haiti having the highest proportions of slaves. India, Pakistan, China, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Russia, Thailand, Democratic Republic of Congo, Myanmar, and Bangladesh have some of the highest absolute numbers of enslaved individuals. The forms of bondage include sexual exploitation, debt bondage, forced marriage, and unpaid labor in various industries such as fishing boats and domestic work. Many victims are tricked or kidnapped, while others are born into hereditary slavery, particularly in West Africa and South Asia. The report also states that slave numbers in wealthy countries like Iceland, Ireland, Britain, New Zealand, Switzerland, Sweden, Norway, Luxembourg, Finland, and Denmark are higher than previously thought. The 10 countries with the highest number of enslaved or exploited workers, according to Walk Free, are India, China, Pakistan, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Russian Federation, Thailand, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Myanmar, and Bangladesh. Mauritania, with about 150,000 slaves, retains the highest proportion of enslaved people in the world, with aspects of "chattel slavery" that resemble the American experience of the institution.

On April 1, 2016, a new record high temperature for Alaska was set in southeast Alaska at 71 degrees Fahrenheit, breaking a record that had stood since 1915 (69 degrees). The record-breaking temperature was recorded in Klawock, located on Prince of Wales Island. Several other locations in the region also set new record high temperatures for March 31, including Juneau, Yakutat, Sitka, and Ketchikan. This marks the warmest official temperature ever recorded in Alaska during the month of March. The previous record was held by Ketchikan's temperature of 69 degrees in 1915.

In the sixth Democratic presidential debate, Hillary Clinton was praised for her strong performance, particularly in challenging Bernie Sanders's health care and immigration reform proposals. She also effectively positioned herself as a loyal supporter of President Obama, which is expected to resonate with black voters. On the other hand, Sanders struggled to differentiate himself from Clinton, particularly on domestic policy, and was criticized for his response to questions about race relations and his comments regarding President Obama's leadership. The debate also highlighted the importance of police reform, with both candidates emphasizing the need for change in policing. Overall, Clinton was deemed the winner of the debate, while Sanders faced criticism for his performance.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp has sold a majority stake in three of its Chinese television channels to China Media Capital (CMC), a private equity fund backed by the government in Beijing. This sale marks a shift in News Corporation's strategy in China and could potentially signal a broader retreat from the country, where the company has struggled to break through despite a long-standing commitment.

The deal includes the transfer of control over Xing Kong, Xing Kong International, Channel [V] Mainland China, and its Fortune Start Chinese film library. News Corp will retain a significant stake in the business but did not disclose the exact percentage. The combined assets of the three channels and the film library are valued at $300m, making the deal worth about $160m.

The move is seen as an attempt by News Corp to develop the business further and explore new growth opportunities while partnering with local state-owned operators. CMC's main interest is believed to be gaining access to overseas distribution channels that could help Chinese media groups internationalize.

This decision comes after a series of concessions made by Murdoch to the Chinese government, including barring the BBC from his satellite platform broadcasting in the region and being turned down for requests to make and broadcast programs in China. In October last year, Murdoch expressed frustration about his operations in China and called for a more open media industry.

A white tiger named Riku attacked and killed a zookeeper, Akira Furusho, at the Hirakawa Zoological Park in Kagoshima, Japan. The incident occurred while Furusho was cleaning the tiger's enclosure, which is against the zoo's manual that requires the tiger to be moved into its sleeping chamber before a keeper enters the display cage. Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the attack and the zoo's care of the four white tigers it keeps. The zoo remains open, but the area around the tigers' display cage is restricted. This tragic incident echoes similar attacks in 2017, where a British zookeeper was killed by a tiger in Cambridgeshire and a Russian keeper survived a tiger attack in Kaliningrad.

In this article, it is reported that Republicans are making gains in both the House and Senate, with one potential Republican presidential candidate, Governor Scott Walker of Wisconsin, surviving a challenge from Democrats. The article notes that Walker has been a target for Democrats due to his actions reducing the power of public sector unions, which angered labor groups.

Additionally, the article highlights GOP gains in the House, including victories over veteran Democratic lawmakers such as Nick Rahall in West Virginia and John Barrow in Georgia. The article also mentions that Republicans are advancing toward a Senate majority.

Hillary Clinton, the presumed Democratic front-runner for the 2016 presidential nomination, was targeted with a shoe and papers during a speech at the annual Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries convention in Las Vegas. A woman threw multiple objects at Clinton, who had to dodge a projectile near her head. The woman was escorted out by security and police were called. Clinton handled the situation professionally and continued with her speech without announcing any plans for the 2016 presidential race. The rest of her address went smoothly and she touched on various topics including the recycling industry, international trade, the civil war in Syria, and U.S. relations with Russia. The incident was not related to the organization and the woman was not credentialed for the event. Clinton's visit to Las Vegas was part of a cross-country tour where she is giving paid speeches to industry organizations and appearing before key Democratic Party constituents.

A suspected gunman, Eulalio Tordil, is in custody after two people were killed and three injured in separate shootings at a mall and grocery store in Montgomery County, Maryland, on Friday. The shootings may be linked to a deadly domestic shooting in the area on Thursday.

Tordil was arrested in the Aspen Hill area, where police believe he ate at the same restaurant as the DC Beltway snipers during their rampage in 2002. He is an employee of the Federal Protective Service and had been placed on administrative duties after a protective order was issued against him in March.

The first shooting occurred outside Montgomery Mall, where three people were wounded, one of whom died. The second shooting took place at a Giant grocery store in Aspen Hill, where a woman was killed. Police believe that Tordil may have targeted Friday's victims after killing his estranged wife outside a high school in Beltsville on Thursday night.

Prince George's County police charged Tordil with first-degree murder and related charges for the fatal shooting of his wife, as well as assault for shooting a bystander who tried to intervene. Charges are pending against Tordil in connection to the Montgomery County shootings. He was in custody on Friday night at Montgomery County police headquarters being interviewed.

China has released over two years worth of high-definition photos taken by its lunar rover, Yutu or "Jade Rabbit," as part of the Chang'e-3 mission. The rover, which landed on the moon in December 2013, had initially faced problems but continued to transmit data until October 2015. Despite being immobile for nearly 20 months, Jade Rabbit still holds the record for the longest operational period of a lunar rover, surpassing that of the Soviet Lunakhod rover. The newly released photos show detailed images of the moon's surface and are a testament to China's space program's progress. This release marks a rare instance of openness from China's usually secretive space program.

The Aurora Borealis, also known as the Northern Lights, is expected to be visible in most of Canada and northern parts of the United States on Sunday night, July 16, 2017. This spectacle is due to a geomagnetic storm from the sun that occurred late Thursday into early Friday. The solar flare released charged particles, known as a coronal mass ejection, which will reach Earth in a couple of days. NOAA has issued a geomagnetic storm watch for the event and expects a "moderate" storm. Auroras are visible in both the northern and southern parts of the world, with the southern lights known as aurora australis. The lights form when charged particles from the sun interact with molecules of atmospheric gases, causing the glowing red and green colors.

Brian Williams, during the GOP debate, asked Rick Perry about executing innocent individuals, but did not directly reference Cameron Todd Willingham's case. Perry maintained that Texas has a fair and clear process for capital punishment cases. Later in the night, Anthony Graves, who spent 18 years on death row for a crime he didn't commit, was exonerated by the district attorney. Williams also asked Perry about audience applause for his execution record, to which Perry responded that Americans generally support capital punishment for heinous crimes. The article also includes a detailed account of the Cameron Todd Willingham case, where he was accused and executed for arson that resulted in the death of his three daughters. However, scientific evidence later suggested that the fire might have been accidental, raising questions about Perry's role in the execution.

In Robertsville, Missouri, a UPS driver played a crucial role in rescuing a woman who was being held captive and sexually assaulted by her husband, James Tyler Jordan. The driver noticed "Contact 911" written on a package at Jordan's home during a scheduled delivery. He immediately contacted the police, leading to a SWAT team intervention and Jordan's arrest. The woman told authorities that Jordan had refused to let her leave, physically assaulted her, and threatened to kill her and himself. During the standoff, Jordan allegedly held a gun to the woman's head while she communicated with the UPS driver. Jordan has been charged with several crimes, including domestic assault, sodomy, felonious restraint, unlawful use of a weapon, and endangering the welfare of a child. The toddler in the home was found unharmed.

Brad Pitt clarified his previous remarks about his ex-wife Jennifer Aniston, stating that they were taken out of context. He emphasized that he has nothing but positive feelings towards Aniston and that his comments were not meant to be critical of her. Pitt also discussed his upcoming movie "Moneyball," for which he is receiving Oscar buzz, and distanced himself from any speculation about awards. Additionally, there have been rumors suggesting that Pitt's comments were prompted by jealousy towards Jennifer Aniston's current boyfriend Justin Theroux, but these claims remain unverified.

Israeli police have arrested a woman accused of setting a petrol pump on fire at a gas station in Jerusalem. CCTV footage shows the woman approaching a man refueling his car, asking for a cigarette, and then allegedly igniting the fuel pump with a lighter when he refused. The fire quickly spread to the man's car, but he and his brother, who was inside the vehicle at the time, were not harmed. The suspect has been denied bail and undergone psychological evaluations while under investigation.

Two New York City schools have banned Rainbow Loom bracelets due to their potential distraction during recess and classroom time. The colorful bracelets, made using a crochet hook and multicolored rubber bands, have become popular among elementary school students. Some parents see the ban as counterintuitive given the lack of arts education budgets, while others applaud the schools for taking action due to disruptions caused by the bracelets. The Rainbow Loom defies traditional gender norms, with both boys and girls being equally interested in making, trading, and giving away the bracelets. However, some schools have started banning the wearing and trading of Rainbow Loom bracelets during school hours. The trend for Rainbow Loom bracelets began three years ago and has gained popularity among children across the country.

French chef Sébastien Bras, who has been running Le Suquet restaurant in Laguiole for the past ten years, has requested to be removed from the prestigious Michelin guide due to the immense pressure of maintaining his three-star rating. This is the first time a French chef has made such a request without major changes to their restaurant or business model. Bras believes that the constant inspections and expectations associated with the three-star ranking are causing undue stress, and he wants to continue cooking excellent local produce without worrying about Michelin's anonymous food judges. The Michelin guide has acknowledged the request but stated that it will be given due consideration, and Bras may not automatically be removed from the list. This decision has significant implications in France, where Michelin stars hold major cultural significance, particularly for renowned chefs like Joël Robuchon.

A hacker is attempting to sell the account information, including emails and passwords, of approximately 117 million LinkedIn users. The data was stolen during a breach in 2012, which initially resulted in the exposure of around 6.5 million encrypted passwords. However, it appears that the number of affected accounts was much higher than previously believed. The hacker is selling the data for about $2,200 on a dark web marketplace called The Real Deal. LeakedSource, a site that maintains a database of compromised accounts, also claims to have obtained the data. LinkedIn has confirmed the legitimacy of the new data and is working to invalidate passwords and contact affected users to reset them. Users are encouraged to use strong passwords and two-factor authentication to keep their accounts secure.

The Obama administration is planning to introduce a fee on banks as part of the upcoming budget to help recoup costs from the government's bailout of financial firms and the auto industry. This move aims to address public anger towards banks that have benefited from taxpayer support while continuing to profit during economic struggles.

The specific details of the fee, such as who will pay, when it will be implemented, and how much banks will have to contribute, are still under discussion. The administration is considering placing a fee on a bank's liabilities or targeting bank profits. Auto manufacturers and American International Group (AIG) are not currently being targeted for the fee.

The proposal comes amid ongoing tension between the administration and banks over their role in revitalizing the economy. The fee is expected to cost large banks billions of dollars, potentially impacting both institutions and individual investors. However, efforts are being made to ensure that the fee does not disproportionately affect community banks or be passed on to struggling bank customers.

The administration has been discussing ways to recoup costs from the $700 billion Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), with estimates of losses ranging from $120 billion to a lower, unspecified amount. The fee would require congressional approval and could potentially impact banks that have already repaid their TARP funds.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg expressed her intention to continue serving on the court until she is 90 years old, stating that she has at least five more years left. This announcement comes after the retirement of another conservative justice and Trump's nomination of Brett Kavanaugh to replace him, potentially shifting the court further right. Ginsburg made these comments during a speech in New York following a production of "The Originalist," a play about her late colleague Antonin Scalia. She also spoke about her friendship with Scalia and their intellectual debates, comparing it to a ping-pong game. Ginsburg has gained notoriety for her vehement dissenting opinions and is the subject of a new documentary, RBG.

The article discusses the controversy surrounding country sports tourism, particularly hunting, in Scotland. A report shows that it contributes around $200 million to the Scottish economy annually. However, the display of animal trophies by well-heeled individuals on social media has sparked criticism and outrage, with some citing the killing of Cecil the lion in 2015 as a notable example.

Recently, American media personality Larysa Switlyk, who hosts the online hunting show "Larysa Unleashed," faced backlash after sharing photos from a hunting trip in Islay, Scotland, where she posed with the head of a wild goat she had shot. Many found these images disgraceful and offensive, leading to calls for a review of the current laws and potential changes.

Both the First Minister Nicola Sturgeon and Secretary for Environment Roseanna Cunningham acknowledged the concerns raised but confirmed that hunting wild animals like deer and goats is not illegal in Scotland. They have promised to review the laws and consider if changes should be made.

Switlyk responded to the backlash by stating she was on her way to her next hunting adventure and would be out of service for two weeks, prompting further criticism for her perceived insensitivity towards the issue.

Robin DiMaggio, a professional drummer and former musical director for The Arsenio Hall Show and the United Nations, has been charged with embezzling $750,000 from a charity concert organized by the Bulgaria-based Peace for You Peace for Me Foundation. The funds were intended to help homeless and displaced children from conflict zones worldwide. DiMaggio allegedly used the money for personal expenses, including purchasing a home in Calabasas for his ex-wife. He was arrested on Friday and could face up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted. DiMaggio has performed with numerous A-list artists throughout his career spanning over 30 years. The case is being investigated by the FBI.

Andrew Gillum, a progressive Democrat from Tallahassee, won the Democratic primary for governor of Florida on August 28, 2018. He will face Ron DeSantis, a Republican backed by President Trump, in the general election. Gillum's victory sets up a closely watched gubernatorial race in a key political battleground state. DeSantis gave credit to Trump for his win, saying that one supportive tweet from the president "kind of put me on the map." Gillum is the third black gubernatorial nominee this year, along with Stacey Abrams in Georgia and Ben Jealous in Maryland. The winner of the Florida governor's race will give their party an advantage heading into the 2020 presidential campaign as incumbent Rick Scott vacates the governor's mansion to run for Senate. In Arizona, primary contests were shadowed by the death of Sen. John McCain. Among those on the Arizona ballot was former state Sen. Kelli Ward, who tried unsuccessfully to unseat McCain in 2016. The winner of the GOP primary is likely to face Democratic Rep. Kyrsten Sinema, who had only token primary opposition. The contests in both Florida and Arizona were being closely watched for signs of how the political battlegrounds might tilt in the 2020 presidential election.

Relatives of California Highway Patrol Officer Mark Saylor, who died in a high-speed crash in 2009 that was later linked to safety flaws in Toyotas, have filed a lawsuit against Toyota Motor Corp., Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A., other Toyota U.S. entities, and El Cajon Luxury Cars, Inc. The lawsuit, filed in San Diego County Superior Court, alleges product liability against Toyota and negligence against the dealership that provided Saylor a loaner car the day of the crash. The family seeks unspecified damages and "responsibility and change." The crash led to a wave of recalls by Toyota, totaling millions of cars for floor mats and gas pedals that were found to potentially cause the accelerator to jam. The lawsuit does not specify an amount of money, but the family is also seeking accountability and changes in the automaker's practices.

The article describes ongoing clashes between police and protesters in Egypt, marking a significant challenge to the nation's military leaders. The unrest stems from frustration over the lack of progress towards democracy since the ousting of President Hosni Mubarak earlier this year. Protests have occurred in Cairo, Suez, and Alexandria, resulting in five deaths and over 1,000 injuries since Saturday. Security forces have used batons, birdshot, and armored vehicles to disperse demonstrators, who are demanding an end to military rule. The military council has called for calm and crisis talks with political parties to find a resolution. The violence has raised international concern and casts uncertainty over Egypt's upcoming parliamentary elections, which are scheduled to begin on November 28th. Some protesters have called for the formation of a new national salvation government to manage the country during the transition period.

The article discusses Olive, a dog who is portrayed as having a hipster lifestyle, complete with listening to Radiohead, wearing vintage clothing, and napping on Paste magazine issues. This is compared to websites like Hipster Puppies and Hipster Kitty, which feature pets dressed in hipster-inspired attire and make fun of the hipster culture. The article also mentions other popular sites such as LOLcats and Fail Blog, and a new site called Hipster Puppies meets Bingo that has gained popularity quickly. The article concludes with the author jokingly suggesting starting a blog called Republican Babies.

A customer in Hialeah, Florida purchased Powerball tickets for Wednesday's drawing on August 22, 2017. The winning ticket for the $758.7 million jackpot was actually sold at a convenience store in Chicopee, Massachusetts, making it the largest grand prize won by a single lottery ticket in U.S. history. Mavis Wanczyk of Chicopee has been identified as the winner. The winning numbers were 6, 7, 16, 23, and 26, with the Powerball number being 4. The store that sold the winning ticket will receive $50,000. This is the fourth time a Powerball jackpot winning ticket has been sold in Massachusetts.

In Portage, MI, Democratic state House candidate John Fisher accused the Michigan GOP of sending out campaign mailers directing voters to call him at a number for his 91-year-old mother's room at a local nursing home. The mailers urged voters to complain about Obamacare and the health care policies supported by Democrats. Fisher's campaign manager stated that the number is registered under Fisher's name but is a direct line to his mother's room, where she is currently receiving hospice care for congestive heart failure. Fisher expressed outrage over the tactic, stating it was beyond the pale and questioned the ethics of the Republican Party. Kalamazoo County Commissioner Brandt Iden, Fisher's opponent in the 61st state House District race, distanced himself from the tactics and apologized for any distress caused. The Michigan Republican Party has not yet commented on the matter.

A new study has traced the origin of the AIDS pandemic to the 1920s in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo. The researchers used genetic sequencing and historical records to find that a combination of factors including population growth, sex trade, unsterilized needles used in health clinics, and Belgium-backed railways allowed HIV to spread from the city to neighboring regions. The study adds insights into the early phases of the HIV-1 pandemic, which has infected nearly 75 million people worldwide since it came to global attention in the 1980s. The virus is a mutated version of a chimpanzee virus that probably made the species-jump through contact with infected blood while handling bush meat on multiple occasions. Only one cross-species jump, HIV-1 subgroup M, went on to infect millions of people across every country in the world. The answer to why this happened lies in the era of black and white film and the tail-end of the European empires, with Kinshasa being a large, rapidly growing area during Belgian colonial rule where there was a high incidence of various sexually transmitted diseases.

The report from the U.S. Department of Education shows a 50% increase in reported forcible sex crimes on college campuses over the past decade, with 3,300 reports in 2011 compared to 2,200 in 2001. This rise is considered positive by some as it suggests more students are coming forward to report sexual assault, which has historically been an underreported crime.

The increase in reports may not necessarily indicate a rise in actual assaults but rather a greater willingness of survivors to report incidents. The White House has responded to the issue by releasing guidelines urging universities to combat sexual assault and change reporting structures to make victims feel safer coming forward.

One example of a school taking action is the University of Michigan, which offers training sessions on preventing sexual assault for first-year students and teaches "bystander education" to show students how to intervene in dangerous situations. However, the university has faced controversy over its handling of sexual misconduct allegations against a football player, highlighting the challenges schools face in addressing this issue.

By next fall, all schools will be required to comply with the Campus SaVE Act, which demands more assault prevention education and better investigations.

A quadriplegic man named Jamie Merrett, who was paralyzed from a 2002 road accident and able to communicate using a voice-activated computer, suffered brain damage after a nurse accidentally switched off his ventilator in January 2009. The incident was captured on a camera that Merrett had installed due to concerns about the quality of his care.

Nurse Violetta Aylward, who worked for an agency contracted by the NHS Wiltshire Primary Care Trust, has been suspended while an investigation is ongoing. The trust has apologized for the incident and implemented measures to prevent such occurrences in the future.

A confidential report by Wiltshire social services found that the agency was aware it should provide a nurse trained in ventilator use but lacked adequate systems to verify staff training. Aylward's solicitor described this as the worst case of negligence on the part of a nurse, and legal action is being considered.

Jamie Merrett's sister, Karen Reynolds, claimed that health authorities did not act on her brother's e-mails expressing concerns about errors involving nurses operating his ventilator. The Simon Fraser University in British Columbia has developed a new bedbug bait and trap after eight years of research led by biologist Regine Gries. The trap uses chemical attractants, or pheromones, to lure bedbugs into traps and keep them there. Regine Gries endured 180,000 bites from the team's bedbug colony during the study as she is immune to the bites.

The research began eight years ago when the team initially isolated a pheromone mix that attracted bedbugs in lab experiments but not in infested apartments. They realized they were missing a crucial component and brought in chemist Robert Britton to help figure out why human skin is appealing to bedbugs. After two years, Britton and the Gries discovered the answer is histamine, a chemical that signals "safe shelter" to the bloodsucking pests.

The team then began analyzing airborne chemicals from bedbug feces and discovered three new compounds that had never before been reported for bedbugs, completing the combination of attractants needed for the trap. The trap has been successfully tested in infested apartments in Metro Vancouver and is now being developed commercially with Victoria-based Contech Enterprises Inc. Unfortunately, this means Regine Gries must continue to feed the bedbug colony every week.

Israel has mobilized up to 75,000 reservists and is preparing for a possible invasion of Gaza after Palestinian militants fired rockets towards Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, marking the first such attacks in decades. A cloud of radioactive pollution over Europe in late September indicates a potential nuclear accident in Russia or Kazakhstan, according to the French nuclear safety institute IRSN. The incident is believed to have occurred at a nuclear fuel treatment site or center for radioactive medicine, and not in a nuclear reactor. Ruthenium 106, a radioactive nuclide that does not occur naturally, was detected in high levels across Europe.

The IRSN estimates that the quantity of ruthenium 106 released was significant, between 100 and 300 teraBecquerels. If an accident of this magnitude had happened in France, it would have required evacuation or sheltering of people within a few kilometers of the accident site.

The Russian authorities have stated they are not aware of any accidents on their territory, and IRSN has not yet been in contact with Kazakh authorities. The most plausible zone for the release lies south of the Ural mountains, between the Urals and the Volga river, which could indicate Russia or possibly Kazakhstan.

The concentrations of ruthenium 106 in the air recorded in Europe were of no consequence for human health and the environment. The probability of importing foodstuffs, notably mushrooms, contaminated by ruthenium 106 near the site of the accident is extremely low.

The study published in Circulation Research, an American Heart Association journal, indicates that long-term use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), a commonly used heartburn medication, may accelerate the aging of blood vessel cells in laboratory testing. This finding could potentially explain the link between long-term PPI use and several serious illnesses such as heart disease, kidney disease, and dementia.

The research suggests that PPIs impair acid production by the lysosomes in blood vessel cells, causing a buildup of waste products that lead to rapid cell aging. However, clinical studies are still necessary to determine if these effects occur within the human body.

Despite their effectiveness for short-term use, PPIs are not meant for extended treatment due to potential risks. The authors of the study suggest that physicians should consider PPIs only for short-term use for relief of symptoms of GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease), and they recommend other approaches such as H2 antagonists, lifestyle modifications, or surgical approaches for long-term treatment.

The study has limitations, including the fact that it was conducted in a laboratory setting and did not show how PPIs actually impair the lysosome's ability to produce enough acid to clear waste within the human body. Long-term clinical trials are necessary to confirm these findings.

In a study published in JAMA, researchers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) found that approximately 30% of all outpatient oral antibiotic prescriptions written in the United States are unnecessary. Of the 184,032 outpatient visits included in the data, 12.6% resulted in an antibiotic prescription, with sinusitis, suppurative otitis media, and pharyngitis being the top three diagnoses associated with the most prescriptions per 1000 population. The researchers estimated that 353 of the 506 antibiotic prescriptions written annually per 1000 population were appropriate. The study highlights the need for establishing goals for outpatient antibiotic stewardship, as a 15% reduction in overall antibiotic use would be necessary to meet the goal set by the White House's National Action Plan for Combating Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria of reducing inappropriate antibiotic use in outpatient settings by 50%

The world's major central banks, including the European Central Bank (ECB), US Federal Reserve, Bank of England, Bank of Canada, Bank of Japan, and Swiss National Bank, have coordinated to ease strains on the global financial system. They are making it cheaper for banks to get U.S. dollar liquidity when needed, starting from next Monday. This move is aimed at enhancing their capacity to provide liquidity support to the global financial system.

The ECB has announced a reduction in the cost of temporary dollar loans (liquidity swaps) by half a percentage point, effective from December 5, 2011. The banks have also agreed to establish temporary bilateral liquidity swap arrangements to provide liquidity in any currency if necessary. Stocks surged following this news, with Germany's DAX trading 4 percent higher and Dow futures in New York also rising.

The financial system has been showing signs of another credit crunch due to Europe's debt crisis spreading. Fears of a possible default by one or more European governments have raised concerns about a shock to the global financial system, leading to severe losses for banks and a contraction in lending. The central banks' actions are intended to mitigate these effects and foster economic activity.

Dustin Snyder, a 19-year-old with terminal cancer, will marry his high school sweetheart Sierra Siverio this weekend after a community outpouring of support. The couple met in middle school but lost touch until they reconnected when Snyder was working at a Steak 'n Shake. Snyder was diagnosed with synovial sarcoma three years ago and has been through multiple rounds of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation. Despite his dire prognosis, the couple is focusing on their upcoming wedding, which has been made possible by donations of a wedding dress, tuxedo, venue, flowers, and more. A GoFundMe page set up to cover additional costs has raised over $14,000. The couple will be married this Sunday at The Big Red Barn surrounded by friends and family.

The IPO is the biggest U.S. Internet debut since Google Inc., and it will begin trading on the Nasdaq on Friday under the ticker symbol ZNGA.

The pricing of the shares was at the high end of the expected range for the deal, indicating strong investor demand for Zynga. The company plans to use the proceeds from the offering for general corporate purposes and potential acquisitions. About $83.6 million will be allocated towards satisfying tax-withholding obligations related to the vesting of restricted stock units.

Zynga's total market value is just under $7 billion, making it one of the larger game publishers in the industry. The company expects to have approximately 699.4 million total shares outstanding following the debut, including Class B and C shares that won't be offered to the public.

In a video posted on YouTube, Unger criticizes Obama for failing to advance the progressive cause in the United States and for focusing solely on financial confidence and food stamps as solutions to the country's economic problems. He also accuses Obama of subordinating the broadening of economic and educational opportunity to the issue of access to healthcare and of evoking a politics of hand-holding. Unger, who is a renowned politician in his native Brazil, has taught at Harvard Law School since 1976 and was one of the founding members of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party. The video has been viewed over 22,000 times.

The article discusses a study conducted by South African researchers using state-of-the-art forensic technology to analyze residue from tobacco pipes found in the garden of British playwright William Shakespeare. The analysis, performed at the Transvaal Museum in Pretoria, revealed that eight pipe fragments contained traces of cannabis, two had cocaine, and some were laced with tobacco, camphor, and hallucinogenic nutmeg extracts. This suggests that a variety of substances were smoked during Shakespeare's time, including cannabis and possibly cocaine. The findings also hint at the possibility that Shakespeare may have used cannabis for creative inspiration, as suggested by his sonnet 76, which mentions "invention in a noted weed." The study was published in the South African Journal of Science in July 2015.

The article discusses the persistent imbalance in household chores between men and women, with a focus on cleaning tasks. Arlie Hochschild argues that cleaning is not just physical work but also emotional work, and women are often judged more harshly for messy homes than men. Despite both partners caring about maintaining a clean home, the responsibility often falls on women. David Michael Perez notes that even when men do the majority of housework, they are still not always recognized or rewarded for it.

Jessica Grose's piece in The New Republic highlights that while men may be taking on more childcare and cooking responsibilities, they still do less housework than women. The article suggests several solutions to address this imbalance, such as dividing tasks according to comparative advantage, lowering filth thresholds, making cleaning more enjoyable, and practicing cultural relativism regarding cleanliness standards.

The author of the piece shares their personal experience of handling more household responsibilities than their wife but argues that not all work can be equated, as some tasks are more stressful or enjoyable than others. The article concludes by suggesting that feminists should consider living like men to better understand and address the imbalance in household chores.

Caitlyn Jenner, formerly known as Bruce Jenner, underwent facial feminization surgery in March 2015 after years of living in secrecy due to gender dysphoria. The surgery included procedures such as hairline correction, forehead contouring, and jaw and chin contouring. Jenner had already been taking hormones and had undergone other physical changes prior to the surgery. The decision to transition was not an easy one for Jenner, who feared the reaction of his four children from his first two marriages, but he ultimately decided to go through with it. The surgery took about 10 hours and was followed by a period of recovery. Despite some initial panic and self-doubt, Jenner has expressed satisfaction with the decision and hopes to use her platform to help others in the transgender community. The story is significant as it highlights the challenges faced by transgender individuals and the importance of acceptance and understanding.

In response to the devastating aftermath of Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico, Google's parent company Alphabet Inc.'s Project Loon has been deployed to provide internet connectivity to remote areas where cellphone towers were damaged. Two balloons, HBAL199 and HBAL237, are currently over Puerto Rico, enabling texts, emails, and basic web access for AT&T customers with 4G LTE handsets.

More balloons are on their way from Nevada, and the FCC has authorized Alphabet to send up to 30 balloons to serve the hard-hit area. Project Loon is an experimental technology that uses algorithms to navigate and ride wind currents, providing signal during daylight hours. The company aims to keep the balloons over areas with needed connectivity for as long as possible, as they learn how best to adapt to the constantly shifting winds in Puerto Rico.

Project Loon has been tested since last year in Peru following flooding, but its effectiveness in Puerto Rico is still uncertain. The disaster has left Puerto Rico's 3.4 million residents with less than a fifth of electricity, half their cellphone towers not functioning, schools closed, and more than 4,000 in shelters. In response to mounting public relations issues, President Barack Obama has taken action to address the Benghazi attack and the IRS scandal. He directed his Treasury Secretary to request the resignation of the acting IRS commissioner, which was granted, and released 100 pages of emails and documents related to the Benghazi attack. However, Republicans are not satisfied and have called for Obama to apologize to the American people. The White House plans to appoint a new acting IRS commissioner this week. The administration is under investigation by Congress on all three fronts - Benghazi, IRS, and the Justice Department's seizure of phone records from the Associated Press. Republicans are urged to lead the investigations but be cautious not to rely solely on scandal for election victories in 2014 and 2016. The president is facing challenges in his second term, including a shrinking agenda and controversies that could harden an impression of an Obama presidency that has expanded government further than many Americans would like.

Justin Bieber, known for his pop music career and occasional legal troubles, recently had a video call with Malala Yousafzai, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate and activist for girls' education rights. Bieber expressed admiration for Yousafzai's inspiring story and shared his intention to support her work through the Malala Fund. The exact nature of their collaboration remains unclear. This interaction comes amidst a controversy involving Bieber and actor Orlando Bloom, who were reportedly involved in a disagreement over Bloom's ex-wife, model Miranda Kerr. Yousafzai, on the other hand, continues to advocate for education rights, particularly focusing on the plight of the kidnapped Nigerian school girls and participating in the Africa Summit.

The star KIC 8462852, which was initially thought to exhibit unusual light patterns suggesting possible extraterrestrial life, has been found to likely be surrounded by comets according to a study led by Massimo Marengo of Iowa State University. The research used data from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope and addressed the mystery that had been under scrutiny since its unusual light fluctuation was discovered by users of the online astronomy crowdsourcing site Planet Hunters. NASA also confirmed that the Kepler Telescope only viewed the star in visible light, while the new study searched by infrared light. The comets are believed to be traveling on a long, eccentric orbit around the star and may have caused the star's light dimming incidents in 2011 and 2013. More observations are needed to confirm this explanation completely.

Starbucks is set to release a new limited-time drink, the Unicorn Frappuccino, on April 19. The drink, which has been leaked online, reportedly has a sweet and sour flavor with notes of raspberry and Skittles. The news has been shared on social media platforms such as Twitter and Reddit, with some individuals having already tasted the drink. The Unicorn Frappuccino is part of a trend of colorful, Instagram-friendly food and drinks that have become popular in recent times. The latest GOP attempt to repeal Obamacare has been dealt a significant blow with Senator John McCain's announcement that he will oppose the bill. Republicans are still pushing for repeal before the September 30 deadline, but it is highly unlikely due to opposition from McCain and other senators like Rand Paul and Susan Collins.

Democrats are pushing for bipartisan talks in the Senate Health Committee, with key issues being the cost-sharing reductions that help insurers provide coverage to low- and middle-income people. Trump has threatened to cancel these payments, which could lead to premium increases.

Beyond the repeal effort, ObamaCare will remain on the books, providing coverage to roughly 20 million people. However, Democrats are concerned about Trump's threats to "sabotage" the law, both with his threats on the insurer payments and a 90% cut to funds used to advertise and enroll people in the insurance exchanges.

McCain's opposition is seen as a major blow to the seven-year effort to repeal the law, but it is of course still possible that Republicans could make another attempt at repeal either before or after September 30.

Thousands of documents, allegedly leaked from inside ISIS, have been obtained by several media organizations, including NBC News and Sky News. These documents provide a detailed picture of ISIS' personnel and recruitment process. The documents include a 23-question form that appears to be a job application for the terror group, with an ISIS logo in the top right corner. The questions start off mundane but then shift to more sinister topics such as previous fighting experience, special skills, level of obedience, and interest in fighting or becoming a suicide attacker. The forms also ask for "countries traveled" to clarify the route to ISIS' caliphate and who can vouch for the recruit. More than 22,000 jihadis are named in the files and some 51 nationalities represented. The documents could offer critical information to intelligence agencies, including routes taken by foreign fighters, previously unknown recruits and recruiters. The leak and its origin deal a blow to ISIS itself, signaling weakness at a time when the organization has been coming under increasing pressure. The documents were obtained from a man who claims to be a disillusioned ISIS fighter who recently defected.

The article discusses PizzaNet, an online pizza ordering system launched by Pizza Hut in Santa Cruz, California in 1994. Customers needed computers with Internet access and Mosaic, an early web browser, to participate in the pilot program. Using the World Wide Web, customers could view a customized menu for ordering pizzas and enter their vital statistics along with orders for pizza and beverages. The data was transmitted back to Pizza Hut headquarters in Kansas, then relayed via modem and conventional phone lines to the local restaurant. To minimize risks of digital pranksters, the local restaurant would telephone customers to verify orders. Money changed hands only at the point of delivery.

The article argues that while the on-line ordering system was technically innovative, it missed the opportunity to create value for customers by allowing them to design their own pizzas online. The author suggests that Pizza Hut could have offered a more interactive and customizable experience by presenting a palette of toppings and letting people place their mushrooms and green peppers and pepperoni anywhere on the pizza they wanted, with the real pizza being customized accordingly. The author argues that this would have added value for customers and potentially increased sales.

In Kansas City, Missouri, approximately 10 individuals were reported sick after receiving a suspicious package at an IRS building. The victims complained of symptoms such as vomiting and sweating, with two being hospitalized. Both victims are currently in good condition. The Fire Department is investigating the package for potential gasses or fumes, but the contents have not been identified yet. The building was not evacuated and has since returned to normal operations. The investigation has been handed over to the IRS and other federal authorities. This incident is part of an effort by the Internet Archive to preserve web pages and fix broken links on the internet.

Tiger Woods, a renowned golfer and high-profile celebrity, has faced backlash from several sponsors following allegations of multiple extramarital affairs. Golf Digest suspended monthly articles under Woods' name until his return to the PGA Tour. The decision was made due to the widespread marketing problems Woods is facing, which have significantly damaged his endorsement earnings estimated at $110 million annually by Forbes.

Accenture, Gatorade, and Gillette have already distanced themselves from Woods, while AT&T is reevaluating their business relationship. Despite the controversy, Swiss watchmaker TAG Heuer publicly supported Woods, re-posting images of him on its website with the headline "TAG Heuer stands with Tiger Woods."

Woods has been in a long-standing relationship with Golf Digest, and despite suspending his articles, they have kept him on the masthead. The magazine has not commented on the compensation for Woods' exclusive agreement.

The U.S. Under-23 national team was eliminated from Olympic qualifying after a 3-3 tie against El Salvador on Monday night. Despite being heavy favorites, the Americans struggled to establish their usual possession-dominating rhythm and were plagued by injuries, particularly keeper Bill Hamid who tweaked his ankle in the first half and was replaced by Sean Johnson. El Salvador took advantage of Hamid's absence to score twice, taking a 2-1 lead before the U.S. fought back to take a 3-2 lead in the second half. However, El Salvador equalized in the very last minute of extra time to eliminate the U.S. from the tournament. The U.S. had only a handful of seconds left to run out the clock and advance, but failed to do so, resulting in a disappointing end to their Olympic qualifying campaign.

Rebel forces have been targeting military aircraft and air bases in an attempt to deprive President Bashar al-Assad's regime of a key weapon used against opposition strongholds. In the past months, there have been reports of rebels occupying parts of a military air base in northern Syria and shooting down a military helicopter in the east, killing eight government troops on board. The Syrian conflict started with anti-government protests in March 2011 and has since claimed an estimated 70,000 lives and forced over 1.2 million Syrian refugees to flee. Israel has been involved in the conflict as well, carrying out air strikes around Damascus to prevent Hezbollah from receiving hi-tech weaponry.

British scientists from Imperial College London have discovered that human intelligence may be influenced by two networks of genes, possibly controlled by a master regulatory system. The research suggests that these networks, known as M1 and M3, play a role in neurodevelopmental disorders such as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and autism. Approximately 40% of the variation in intelligence is explained by inheritance, with the other factors yet to be determined. The discovery could potentially lead to ways to modify human intelligence and help people with learning disabilities reach their full potential. The research was conducted using evidence from mouse brains, human brain samples, and data from a family health study called "Generation Scotland." The scientists hope that this research will provide new insights into better treatments for neurodevelopmental diseases such as epilepsy and ameliorate or treat the cognitive impairments associated with these disorders.

The article by Thom Hartmann argues that the Second Amendment was ratified to preserve slavery and slave patrol militias in the southern states. The article cites historical evidence from the ratifying convention in Virginia in 1788, where Patrick Henry expressed concerns about the federal government's power over state militias under the proposed Constitution and the potential for emancipation of slaves through military service. James Madison, who is known as the "Father of the Constitution," later changed his draft of the Second Amendment to address these concerns by changing the word "country" to "state." The article also discusses the ongoing debate over gun control in modern times and suggests that the real purpose of the Second Amendment is to protect citizens from tyranny, including their own government.

Senators Joe Lieberman and Susan Collins announced their intention to introduce a new stand-alone bill to repeal the policy, with Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid promising to support it. The failure of the bill is a setback for President Obama and Democratic leadership, who have made repealing the Clinton-era policy a key priority. Supporters of the policy criticized the vote as a result of political squabbles in Congress, while opponents accused Republicans of blocking the defense bill and the provisions to repeal "Don't Ask Don't Tell." The new stand-alone bill faces challenges, including the possibility that supporters of the policy may seek to offer numerous amendments during debate.

These players include winners of Grand Slam titles, and more than half of them will compete at the Australian Open on Monday. The last person in Iowa tested for the parasite got sick on June 28, but it's unclear what's happening in other states. Some believe there may be more than one outbreak going on. The investigation is ongoing, and officials are working to eliminate potential sources and provide more information soon.

Michael Bloomberg, the former New York City mayor and billionaire media owner, has expressed interest in running for President of the United States as an independent candidate. His potential entry into the race would significantly impact the 2016 election, which has already been disrupted by the anti-establishment campaigns of Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders.

Democratic National Committee Chairwoman Debbie Wasserman Schultz suggested that Bloomberg's priorities are already addressed in the Democratic platform, while Republican National Committee leader Reince Priebus welcomed the idea but views Bloomberg as a potential spoiler who would siphon votes from the eventual Democratic nominee.

Bloomberg has criticized the level of discourse and discussion in the current presidential race and expressed concerns about both major party candidates, particularly Donald Trump. If no candidate clinches a majority of electoral votes in the general election, the tiebreaker would be put in the hands of the House of Representatives, potentially placing House Speaker Paul Ryan and his GOP colleagues in the position of choosing the next president.

Bloomberg's potential candidacy has received mixed reactions from both parties, with some viewing him as a threat to their nominee and others welcoming the opportunity for an independent voice. However, experts believe that an independent candidate would face significant challenges in a system heavily skewed towards the two main parties.

The study published in the journal Translational Psychiatry suggests that older men tend to have "geekier" sons who are more aloof, have higher IQs and a more intense focus on their interests than those born to younger fathers. The findings emerged from a study of nearly 8,000 British twins, with researchers defining geekiness as high IQ, strong focus on the subject of interest, and social aloofness. The study found that children born to older fathers tended to score slightly higher on the geek index, with the effect being strongest in boys. The age of the children's mothers seemed to have almost no effect on the geek index. The researchers also found that having a high IQ, a tendency to focus intensely and social aloofness were all linked to children taking more technical GCSEs, with the effect being even more pronounced when all three traits co-occurred in the "geek" cluster. The study suggests that delayed fatherhood may have benefits for children, boosting their performance in technical subjects at secondary school. However, the authors caution that the findings do not mean men should put off having children until they are older in the hope of having more intelligent sons.

Bernie Sanders, a Democratic Senator from Vermont, is considering running for President in 2020. He believes his ideas are the best for the country and that he is well-positioned to win, but is also aware of the potential risks involved. Sanders has been mulling over this decision all year as he travels across the country. In the past, he has faced criticism from both Democrats and Republicans, but his popularity among progressives has grown since his 2016 campaign for President. He has experimented with using social media to reach a wider audience and has successfully pushed for changes on issues such as healthcare and income inequality under the Trump administration. However, some worry that another presidential campaign may not be the best vehicle for his cause and that he can be difficult to work with. Sanders is also aware of the potential negative attacks he may face during a campaign due to his age and past comments.

Mike Evans, a wide receiver for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, donated $11,000 to the family of Gregory Hill Jr., who was fatally shot by a St. Lucie County deputy in 2014. The jury in a federal court trial found that Hill was 99% responsible for his death and the county sheriff's office 1%, awarding the family $4 (one dollar for each of Hill's children and one dollar for funeral expenses). However, due to the 1% liability ruling, the Sheriff's Office only had to pay 4 cents. The family initially received just 4 cents from the jury award but has since raised nearly $100,000 through a GoFundMe page, with Evans' donation helping push the total. Gregory Hill Jr., who was 30 at the time of his death, had a blood alcohol content of 0.40 when he was shot while listening to music in his garage. Nintendo, the video game company known for its iconic characters such as Mario and Zelda, has forecasted a surprise annual loss of 25 billion yen ($240 million) due to weak demand for the Wii U console. This led to a significant drop in the company's share price, with Nintendo American depositary receipts falling 17% to $14.90 in New York, marking its biggest decline since September 2001.

The company had initially projected a profit of 55 billion yen for the year ending March, but has now cut its forecasts for Wii U console sales to 2.8 million units from 9 million and for Wii U game sales to 19 million units from 38 million. The poor performance is attributed to a shift in the gaming market towards mobile devices, with casual gamers migrating away from Nintendo's family-focused content due to delayed titles and hardcore players preferring faster consoles like Sony's PlayStation 4 and Microsoft's Xbox One.

Nintendo's refusal to offer games featuring its characters on mobile devices is also limiting its ability to profit from the surging demand in this area. In response, Nintendo President Satoru Iwata has stated that the company is considering a new business model, with a focus on how smart devices can be used to grow the game-player business.

European scientists have determined that if Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko could be brought to Earth, it would emit a strong odor of rotten eggs (hydrogen sulphide), horse stable (ammonia), formaldehyde, bitter almonds (hydrogen cyanide), alcohol (methanol), vinegar (sulphur dioxide), and sweet aromatic scent of carbon disulphide. This discovery was made using the Rosina-DFMS instrument aboard the European spacecraft Rosetta, which is preparing to drop a lander onto the comet's icy surface on November 12. The detection of so many different molecules at this stage has been a surprise as scientists initially believed only the most volatile molecules would be released as the comet's icy surface started to warm. The Rosetta mission is an ambitious attempt to shed light on the origins of comets, ancient travellers of the Solar System. Rosetta caught up with Comet 67P/C-G after a six-billion-kilometer trek that required four flybys of Earth and Mars, using their gravity as a slingshot to build up speed. The appeal also argues that the judge considered allegations for which Fogle did not face criminal charges, including discussions about possible sexual contact with minors and collecting pornography of children as young as 6 years old.

These substances are sold and used recreationally under various names such as herbal or liquid incense, K2, Spice, Black Mamba, Bombay Blue, Genie, Zohai, among others.

Spain's Crown Prince Felipe was formally proclaimed as King Felipe VI on Thursday, following his father Juan Carlos' abdication after nearly four decades of rule. The ceremony took place in Madrid before the Spanish Parliament, with Felipe promising to lead a modernized monarchy that unifies the nation and works with political leaders. He expressed gratitude towards his parents and acknowledged the country's economic struggles while emphasizing the need for transparency and sobriety in royal dealings. The proclamation ceremony was more subdued compared to traditional coronations, without foreign dignitaries or elaborate ceremonies. Felipe's elder daughter, Leonor, became Princess of Asturias, first in line to the throne. A 23-year-old man named Gregory Arthur Weiler II, originally from Illinois, was arrested and charged with planning to bomb approximately 48 churches in Oklahoma. Archaeologists have recovered a bronze arm from an ancient Roman-era shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, where at least seven more priceless statues from the classical world are believed to be buried. The ship, which was sailing from Asia Minor to Rome in 1BC, foundered near Antikythera and is now located under half a metre of sediment on a boulder-strewn slope.

The project team, led by the Greek Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities and Lund University in Sweden, discovered the arm using a bespoke underwater metal detector. They believe there are at least seven more bronze statues still waiting to be found. The operation is overseen by Ageliki Simosi, director of the Greek Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities.

During the 2017 excavation season, divers also recovered a patterned slab of red marble, a silver tankard, sections of joined wood from the ship's frame, a human bone, and last year, they found the skull, teeth, ribs, and other bones of an individual who perished on the wreck. They have since extracted DNA from the skull and learned the individual's sex and origin.

Luca Guadagnino's film "Call Me By Your Name" is a lush and vibrant masterpiece about first love set in northern Italy during the summer of 1983. The story revolves around two young men, Elio (Timothee Chalamet) and Oliver (Armie Hammer), who develop an unexpected romance amidst the sensual delights of the Italian countryside.

Their initial interactions are prickly, but their electric connection is evident from the start. The film takes its time establishing the characters and their dynamic, with long takes and expert use of silence to create a melancholic atmosphere that underscores the transient nature of their romance.

Hammer's portrayal of Oliver balances swagger and vulnerability, making their love scenes heartbreaking yet intensely erotic. The film's visual beauty is heightened by the tactile quality of cinematographer Sayombhu Mukdeeprom's 35mm images, which enliven all senses and build an inescapable tension.

The article discusses the death of Toughie, the last known Rabbs' fringe-limbed tree frog, at the Atlanta Botanical Garden. Toughie was at least 12 years old and was collected in 2005 during a rescue mission due to the deadly chytrid fungus. His species, Ecnomiohyla rabborum, wasn't described until 2008. The frog's death marks the extinction of his entire species, as it is unlikely that any survived in the wild. Toughie was named by Mark Mandica's son and gained popularity due to being the last of his kind. He was silent for most of his life at the botanical garden until 2014 when his call was recorded. Photographer Joel Sartore photographed Toughie as part of the Photo Ark project, which aims to showcase biodiversity and inspire people to fight extinction. The loss of species like Toughie compromises healthy ecosystems necessary for everyone's survival.

This 15-year episode of above-average moisture likely contributed to high grassland productivity, providing resources for Genghis Khan's war horses and potentially facilitating the formation of his political and military power.

The study also indicates that the early 21st-century drought in central Mongolia was the hottest drought in the last 1,000 years, consistent with projections of warming over Inner Asia. Future warming may lead to similar heat droughts, potentially having severe consequences for modern Mongolia. The research was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

A group of 37 college students and three staff members from La Salle University in Pennsylvania were lost during a hiking trip in Kentucky on March 8th. The incident occurred near Bad Branch Falls, Pine Mountain, Letcher County. The students called for help around 7 PM EST and were found by 11 PM. They stayed together near a campfire and maintained contact with rescuers via cellphone.

The hikers had to walk down the mountain due to the difficult terrain, which took until 3:45 AM Friday. All 40 of them were taken to Whitesburg Appalachian Regional Hospital, where one remained hospitalized for observation due to a pre-existing condition. The rest were treated for possible hypothermia, dehydration, and exhaustion.

Hospital staff provided the cold, wet students with chicken noodle soup, dry hospital scrubs, and pajama pants. They also loaned them cellphones so they could contact their families. The group is expected to return to Pennsylvania on Saturday as scheduled. The incident occurred during an annual mission trip called Project Appalachia.

The article by Derek Miller for SmartAsset identifies the worst cities in the US to own a car, based on factors such as traffic congestion, cost of time spent in traffic, motor vehicle theft rates, and availability of non-driving options like walking or public transportation. The top 10 cities include Newark, NJ; San Francisco, CA; Washington, D.C.; Oakland, CA; Arlington, VA; Portland, OR; Anaheim, CA; New York, NY; Seattle, WA; and Boston, MA. These cities were chosen due to their high traffic congestion, high cost of idling in traffic, and low availability of non-driving options. The study considered data from the Texas A&M Transportation Institute 2014 Mobility Score Card, Walkability.com, the FBI's 2015 Uniform Crime Reporting Program, and the U.S. Census Bureau's 2014 Business Patterns Survey. The methodology for ranking the cities involved giving double weight to non-driving options and half weight to motor vehicle theft rates, repair shops per driver, and parking garages per driver, with all other factors receiving single weight. The city with the highest average ranking received a score of 100, while the city with the lowest average ranking received a score of 0.

The USA leads the world with the highest number of obese individuals at 87 million, representing 13% of the global total despite having only 5% of the population. However, obesity is a growing issue worldwide, affecting both rich and poor countries, according to a new report published in the Lancet medical journal. The study, which covers 188 countries over the past several decades, reveals that nearly 30% of the world's population is now either obese or overweight, with rates rising among men, women, and children in all regions.

The researchers attribute this trend to factors such as increased calorie intake, changes in diet composition, decreased physical activity, and the availability of cheap, unhealthy food. The report notes that population-wide weight gains generally correspond with income gains, suggesting that affordability may play a significant role in obesity rates.

The study highlights countries like Tonga, Kuwait, Kiribati, Micronesia, Libya, Qatar, Samoa, and Egypt, where obesity rates exceed 50% among men and women. In the USA, about one-third of adults are overweight (BMI of 25 or above), and another third are obese (BMI of 30 or above).

A three-year-old child fell approximately 15-16 feet into a jaguar exhibit at the Little Rock Zoo in Arkansas on Friday morning. The incident occurred around 10:45 AM, and initial calls for help were made by a primate zoo keeper who saw one of the jaguars with its mouth around the child's neck.

The child was being treated for extensive scalp lacerations, a depressed skull fracture, and minor puncture wounds. The condition of the child is currently stable and expected to improve. Zoo staff used a fire extinguisher to keep the cats away while another staff member climbed into the exhibit with a ladder to retrieve the child.

The Little Rock Police Department and Arkansas Children's Hospital have confirmed that an investigation into the incident is ongoing, and the child's name and additional information are being withheld at the family's request. The Little Rock Zoo remains open following the incident.

A Bend day care operator, January Neatherlin, was sentenced to 21 years and four months in prison for abandoning numerous young children at her unlicensed day care while she went for a tan or to work out, giving them melatonin to sleep. The sentence came after an emotional day of testimony from tearful parents who spoke about the lingering issues their children have faced with sleep cycles, trust, and more. Neatherlin apologized to the parents, saying she thought of the children as her own but admitted to making a poor decision that has forever changed their lives. The judge noted the "carnage" left by the case and said it was good that Neatherlin had taken responsibility for her actions but still has a "very long way to go."

Existing Tidal subscribers will not experience any changes in their service. The announcement comes amidst reports that Tidal had been inflating subscriber numbers and rumors of a potential acquisition by Apple. Jay-Z bought Tidal from Swedish company Aspiro AB for $56 million in 2015.

A man named Michael Briggs has pleaded guilty to the murder of a retired nun, Mary Greco, in December 2012. The crime was discovered on New Year's Day 2013. Briggs admitted to strangling Greco in her apartment and had shoveled snow for her around the time of the murder. At the time, he was on parole for a burglary and robbery in Long Island.

Evidence that led to Briggs' guilty plea included fingerprints found on a toilet seat, coffee mugs, and a glass in Greco's kitchen, as well as his DNA on a blanket covering her body. Video surveillance footage also showed Briggs leaving his home with a snow shovel and walking towards Greco's apartment just before the murder.

Greco was a spiritual woman who volunteered as a teacher on international mission trips. She lived alone near Vale Cemetery, where Briggs also resided. A Gold Coast lifeguard named Nick Malcolm rescued Denmark's 10-year-old Prince Christian from a dangerous underwater current at Mermaid Beach on the Gold Coast in Queensland on Thursday. The prince was swimming with his family, and his mother, Princess Mary, had heeded her childhood message to swim between the flags. Mr Malcolm paddled out to pull the prince to safety after spotting him in trouble. The lifeguard's supervisor, Stuart Keay, confirmed that Mr Malcolm saved the youngster's life. Prince Christian's father, Prince Frederick, personally thanked Mr Malcolm for the rescue. Nick Malcolm is originally from New Zealand but is based on the Gold Coast while he trains full-time in surf lifesaving sports and works as a lifeguard. This was not the first time Mr Malcolm has saved someone's life; in January 2014, he helped save another tourist at the same beach. The Danish Royal Family has been holidaying on the Gold Coast for the past few days, with Princess Mary and Prince Frederick spotted with their brood at theme park Dreamworld and shopping at Marina Mirage.

The white iPhone 4 will be available for purchase starting tomorrow, April 30, through Apple, Verizon, AT&T, and Apple's other authorized resellers. It will come in both 16- and 32-gigabyte versions at prices of $199 and $299, respectively, with a two-year wireless contract.

Apple has also addressed concerns about the gathering and use of location information by iOS devices. The company states that it never tracks or will track the location of a customer's iPhone and admits to several bugs related to location data that it plans to fix in an upcoming software update. This update will reduce the size of the Wi-Fi hotspot and cell tower database cached on the iPhone, encrypt and stop backing up this cache, and delete it entirely when Location Services is turned off by the user.

A class action suit was filed earlier this week accusing Apple of invasion of privacy and computer fraud, and regulators in France, Germany, Italy, and South Korea had started investigating the location collection feature on Apple devices following a researcher's report. It remains to be seen whether Apple's response will be deemed credible by all parties involved.

In a seaside sand dune in Peru, archaeologists have discovered the remains of 42 children and 76 llamas who were sacrificed in a ritual dating back 600 years. The site was part of the Chimú state, which dominated coastal Peru from around 1100 to 1470 AD. Tulane University physical anthropologist John Verano, who has spent summers in Peru for the last 30 years, is leading the study of these remains. The researchers believe that the sacrifice may have been an offering to the sea or a response to severe flooding caused by an El Niño event, with the llamas possibly intended to transport the victims to the afterlife. More details on this exciting discovery will be released as further analysis is conducted.

In a tweet that was later deleted, Nir-Mozes wrote "Do you know what Obama coffee is? Black and weak." The D.C. Council Committee on the Judiciary and Public Safety passed a bill lowering the voting age to 16 in Washington D.C., making it the first municipality in the country to allow minors to vote in all elections, including presidential races. The bill will now be voted on by the full council later this month. If passed, approximately 10,400 16- and 17-year-olds in D.C., with nearly 80% identified as youth of color, would be added to the voting rolls. The bill was introduced by Ward 6 Councilmember Charles Allen and has been supported by eight members of the council. If approved by the full council and signed by Mayor Muriel Bowser, the bill will undergo a 30-day congressional review period before becoming an official act.

Archaeologists have discovered a stone tool in eastern Oregon that could potentially be older than any known site of human occupation in western North America. The find was made at the Rimrock Draw Rockshelter outside Riley, and was announced by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management. The tool, a hand-held scraper chipped from orange agate, was found about 8 inches below a layer of volcanic ash from an eruption of Mount St. Helens that has been dated to 15,800 years ago. If the age of the site holds up, it would be the oldest west of the Rockies and predate the so-called Clovis culture, once believed to be the first people to migrate from Asia into North America. The find is still under investigation and has not been published in a scientific journal yet.

Paige was hospitalized and later died. The family is grieving, and a GoFundMe page has been set up to support them. Paige's mother shared detailed accounts of the incident on the GoFundMe page.

The current flu season, which may extend until May, has already resulted in at least 30 pediatric deaths as of January 13, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). This number is expected to rise as the season continues, with health experts predicting more deaths than usual this year. The best way to protect children from catching the flu is to vaccinate them, even though the vaccine's effectiveness this year has been estimated to range from 10 to 30 percent. The CDC recommends vaccination as the best option to reduce the chances of getting the virus by up to 60 percent, but it can take up to two weeks to become effective. Symptoms such as a fever that does not go away, difficulty breathing, or trouble staying awake should prompt individuals to seek medical attention. The flu season shows no signs of slowing down and it is unclear when it will end.
