The discovery of two stone rings in a French cave, known as Bruniquel Cave, suggests that Neanderthals were more sophisticated than previously thought. The rings, made from stalagmites, are estimated to be around 176,500 years old, making them the oldest known well-dated constructions by humans. The structures were found deep inside the cave and show traces of fire, indicating that Neanderthals had mastered the underground environment. The purpose of these oval structures is still a matter of speculation, but they may have served some symbolic or ritual purpose. The discovery challenges long-held assumptions about Neanderthal behavior and suggests that they were capable of complex behavior and possibly even rituals.

A female Aldabra giant tortoise named Abuh, who weighs approximately 121 pounds and measures around one meter in length, escaped from the Shibukawa Animal Park in Okayama prefecture, Japan on August 1st. After a two-week search, Abuh was found just 140 meters (460 feet) from the zoo by a local bounty hunter or a family, depending on the source. The tortoise is known for her gentle disposition and popularity among children. This marks Abuh's second escape attempt in less than a month. The zoo plans to implement new measures to prevent future escapes.

The study conducted by a team from the University of Nottingham and the Finnish National Institute for Health and Welfare found evidence of respiratory viruses on 10% of surfaces tested at Helsinki-Vantaa airport in Finland during winter 2016. The plastic trays used at airport security checkpoints were found to have the highest levels of viruses, with further viruses detected on shop payment terminals, staircase rails, passport checking counters, children’s play areas, and in the air. The most common virus found was rhinovirus, which causes the common cold, but influenza A virus was also detected. The study emphasizes the importance of hand washing and coughing hygiene in public areas with high volumes of people passing through to control contagious infections. The findings add weight to previous studies showing that microbes are commonly found on surfaces in public transport vehicles and will strengthen public health advice in preparation for future flu pandemics.

In a legal dispute, the Walton family, founders of Walmart, are suing Helen Huff, the widow of Robert A. Huff, a photographer who took hundreds of pictures of the Walton family from 1950 to 1994. The Waltons claim intellectual property rights to more than 200 photographs in six boxes, including those shot at Bob's Studio of Photography and photos taken to the studio for restoration. However, Huff argues that she holds the copyright to the photos as her husband and father-in-law were independent contractors who used their own equipment, controlled the positions of their subjects, chose and developed the film or hired the processing company, and provided a copyright notice to the Walton family notifying them that they owned "exclusive rights to reproduce" the pictures. The Professional Photographers Association (PPA) supports Huff's claim, stating it would set a terrible precedent if the Waltons were allowed to take ownership of the photographs without paying for them. A federal judge will hear the case on July 7, 2015.

A self-proclaimed email prankster in the UK, going by the Twitter handle @SINON_REBORN, deceived several White House officials by impersonating various members of the Trump administration, including Jared Kushner and Reince Priebus. The prankster managed to convince Homeland Security Adviser Tom Bossert to reveal his personal email address during an exchange where he posed as Kushner.

The prankster also successfully tricked White House Communications Director Anthony Scaramucci, who was fired on Monday, into believing he was Priebus in a series of heated emails. The prankster's emails to Scaramucci were accusatory and baiting, leading to a back-and-forth exchange that included references to Shakespeare's Othello.

The White House has acknowledged the incidents and is investigating them further. The email prankster described his actions as humorous rather than malicious. He has previously deceived Scaramucci into thinking he was Ambassador to Russia-designate Jon Huntsman, and tricked Huntsman himself into believing he was President Trump's son Eric Trump. He also briefly convinced Eric Trump that he was Donald Trump Jr., but the prankster never heard from law enforcement regarding his email to Eric Trump.

The study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that sea levels rose faster during the 20th century than during nearly any of the previous 27 centuries, with a rate of 1.4 millimeters per year from 1900 to 2000. This rapid rise is attributed to global warming caused by human activities, as the study found that without human-induced warming, it's very unlikely that seas would have risen so much during the century. The study used a combination of geological sea-level indicators and tide gauge data from around the world to reach its conclusions. They can also charge fees to websites that want quicker content delivery, potentially slowing down poorer sites that cannot afford to pay. This is bad for small businesses and indie retailers, as well as for consumers who may experience slower load times on certain websites.

In addition, ISPs can now force websites to pay for faster content delivery, potentially favoring partner sites over competitors. The algorithm was able to correctly identify a user's spouse 60% of the time and predicted relationships 50% accurately, significantly higher than random guessing. Additionally, the researchers found that relationships with high dispersion are more likely to last, although this is not necessarily causal. The article discusses a study conducted by behavioral researchers Jason Rogers and Abbe Macbeth from Noldus Information Technology regarding the phenomenon known as Resting Bitch Face (RBF). The study aimed to understand why some faces are perceived as expressionless, while others are seen as off-putting or inexplicably negative.

Using software called FaceReader, which can analyze facial expressions based on a catalogue of over 10,000 human faces, the researchers found that while most faces register around 97% neutrality, those with RBF have approximately 6% underlying emotion, primarily contempt. This is due to subtle signals such as one side of the lip being pulled back slightly and the eyes squinting a little.

Interestingly, the study revealed that FaceReader detected RBF in male and female faces equally, suggesting that the perception of RBF as a predominantly female phenomenon may be more related to social norms than facial physiology. The researchers also noted that women are often expected to smile more and appear happier than men, which could contribute to the observation of RBF in women more frequently.

The study's findings have sparked public interest, with people now able to submit their own photos for analysis to determine if they exhibit RBF. The researchers emphasized that there is no need to worry about having RBF and that it does not necessarily reflect one's personality or emotions.

A piece of potential debris from missing Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 has been found on a beach in Madagascar by one of the relatives of a passenger who lost their loved one on the flight. The debris found on Madagascar's beaches is thought to have been carried there by ocean currents and winds, as scientists have shown that these currents would carry small, floating parts across the Indian Ocean to the coasts of South Africa, Tanzania, Madagascar, Mozambique, and Reunion Island. "Mirror Mirror" is a fantasy film directed by Tarsem Singh, opening on March 30 in major theatres. The film takes a lighter approach to the classic fairytale of Snow White, with a modern girl-power twist and references to Disney's animated version. Julia Roberts delivers an entertaining performance as the vain and self-absorbed Queen, while Lily Collins shows promise in her first leading role as Snow White. A 30-year-old man named Michael Rotondo was ordered by a New York State Supreme Court judge to vacate his parents' home in Camillus, near Syracuse, after refusing to leave despite multiple notices and offers of financial assistance. Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi is considering an appeal to the state Supreme Court, while public defender Manuel Alvarez filed an emergency request to release Connolly immediately, which was denied later that day.

Bilour made this announcement at a news conference on Saturday, but clarified that he was speaking as a private citizen and not as a government representative. A curling team led by Olympic gold medallist Ryan Fry, who won gold for Canada at the 2014 Winter Olympics, was disqualified from a Canadian tournament, the Red Deer Curling Classic in Alberta, due to poor behavior and drunkenness. The team, which includes Jamie Koe, Chris Schille, and DJ Kidby, reportedly broke brooms, damaged locker rooms, and were extremely drunk during the event. In a statement, Fry apologized for his behavior and promised to improve. The Red Deer Curling Classic is part of the World Curling Tour and counts towards rankings of the best curling teams in Canada.

Beijing authorities have taken drastic measures to combat air pollution by destroying over 500 outdoor barbecues, which are said to contribute significantly to the city's air pollution. This action is part of a three-month operation targeting illegal barbecues, many operated by ethnic Uighur Muslims from Xinjiang province. The destruction of these barbecues aims to reduce PM2.5 levels, harmful particulate matter that can penetrate deep into the lungs.

However, this action has received criticism online, with citizens suggesting authorities should focus on larger sources of pollution. Beijing's air pollution often reaches hazardous levels and is a cause for concern due to its potential long-term health effects, including an increase in lung cancer rates among residents. The city government has implemented emergency measures such as odd-even car restrictions and school closures when smog levels are high.

The smog in Beijing is largely caused by emissions from factories, heating plants, vehicles, and winds blowing in from the Gobi Desert. Last winter, Beijing experienced severe smog that was dubbed the "airpocalypse", and there are concerns about a repeat this winter.

The New York Times has excluded Senator Ted Cruz's memoir, "A Time for Truth," from its bestselling books list despite strong sales numbers provided by the book's publisher, HarperCollins. The Times claims that the book's sales were mostly strategic bulk purchases, a claim disputed by Cruz's campaign and HarperCollins. The controversy has generated significant publicity for Cruz's book, which has also been successful in fundraising, with Cruz raising at least $51 million for his 2016 presidential campaign. On August 13, 2013, an American Airlines pilot died during a flight from Phoenix to Boston due to a medical emergency. The incident occurred about four hours into Flight 550, causing the plane to divert and land in Syracuse. The co-pilot took over and informed air traffic control that the captain had become incapacitated. The nature of the pilot's sudden illness has not been disclosed. Researchers have discovered the earliest known prehistoric ancestor of humans, a microscopic sea creature named Saccorhytus coronarius, which lived approximately 540 million years ago in central China. The species is new to science and is considered the most primitive example of a deuterostome, a broad biological category that includes vertebrates (backboned animals) and other invertebrates such as starfish and sea urchins.

Saccorhytus coronarius was about a millimeter in size and likely lived between grains of sand on the seabed during the early Cambrian period. The creature had a large mouth, which it used to engulf food particles or even other creatures, and small conical structures on its body that may have allowed water it swallowed to escape, potentially serving as an early version of gills.

One of the most intriguing aspects of Saccorhytus coronarius is that it does not appear to have had an anus, suggesting that any waste material would have been expelled through its mouth. The study was carried out by an international team of researchers from the UK, China, and Germany, including Professor Simon Conway Morris from the University of Cambridge.

A Russian passenger plane carrying 71 people (65 passengers and six crew members) crashed near Moscow shortly after taking off from Domodedovo Airport on February 11, 2018. The plane, an Antonov An-148 operated by Saratov Airlines, disappeared from radar screens a few minutes after departure en route to Orsk, a city about 1,500 kilometers southeast of Moscow. Fragments of the wreckage were found in the Ramenskoye area, about 40 kilometers from the airport. No on-ground casualties were reported. The Transport Minister confirmed there were no survivors and DNA tests will be needed to identify the dead. Investigators are looking into all possible causes, including weather conditions, human error, and the plane's technical condition. President Vladimir Putin expressed his condolences and ordered a special investigative commission to be set up. The last large-scale crash in Russia occurred on Dec. 25, 2016, when a Tu-154 operated by the Russian Defense Ministry crashed into the Black Sea minutes after takeoff from Sochi, killing all 92 people on board.

A 14-year-old boy named Joseph "Seph" Ware from West Monroe, Louisiana, who has Duchenne muscular dystrophy, has gained attention online after his service dog, Presley, was included in his school's yearbook. Seph's service dog, Presley, a 5-year-old golden doodle, assists him with daily tasks due to his weakened muscles. The school officials decided to include Presley in the yearbook alongside the other students, and Seph gave his permission. Presley has been with Seph for four years, including when he attends classes at Good Hope Middle School. The school administrators' gesture has garnered positive feedback on social media, and Seph has been drawing a paw print in his classmates' yearbooks on behalf of Presley. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a genetic condition that causes progressive muscle weakness, leading to physical impairment, heart, and respiratory issues. Advances in cardiac and respiratory care have expanded patients' life spans, making survival into their 30s more common, with some cases living into their 40s and 50s.

The most wanted suspect from the November 2015 Islamic extremist attacks in Paris, Salah Abdeslam, was arrested alive in Brussels, Belgium on March 18, 2016 after a four-month manhunt. The arrest took place during a major police operation in the Molenbeek neighborhood of Brussels following a tip-off to police. Abdeslam, who is a Belgian asylum seeker and childhood friend of suspected ringleader Abdelhamid Abaaoud, was among the attackers who killed 130 people at various locations in Paris on November 13, 2015. The Islamic State group claimed responsibility for the attacks, in which Belgian nationals played key roles.

The arrest came after Belgian authorities found Abdeslam's fingerprints in an apartment raided earlier this week in another Brussels neighborhood. In that raid, a man believed to have been an accomplice of Abdeslam — Mohamed Belkaid — was shot dead by police, while two men escaped from the apartment, one of whom appears to have been Abdeslam. Belgian authorities initially said Belkaid had no known background in radical Islamic activities, but later issued a statement saying he was "most probably" an accomplice of Abdeslam who had been using a fake Belgian ID card in the name of Samir Bouzid.

A baby girl named Vanellope Hope Wilkins, born with her heart outside her body due to a rare condition called ectopia cordis, has survived after undergoing three surgeries at Glenfield Hospital in Leicester, England. The surgery was the first successful procedure of its kind performed on a newborn child in Britain, although similar cases have been reported in the United States. Vanellope's parents, Naomi Findlay and Dean Wilkins, were initially advised to terminate the pregnancy due to the low survival chances, but they chose to continue with it. The baby is now doing well and has a long road ahead, with the major risk being infection. The family named her after a character in the Disney film "Wreck-It Ralph" who is also a fighter.

Researchers have made a significant advance towards replacing large pieces of human bone, specifically for facial reconstruction, by growing pig's own cells into bone in the lab. The study, led by Gordana Vunjak-Novakovic from Columbia University, involved 14 pigs with facial bone damage. The team crafted scaffolds out of cow leg bone and seeded them with mesenchymal stem cells isolated from the pigs' fat. The cells were grown in a bioreactor for three weeks before being implanted into the pigs to replace missing jawbone pieces.

Results showed that regrowth was more complete in the seeded grafts, and they could withstand the same stress as the original bone. The unseeded scaffolds shrank over time, suggesting faster degradation of bone matrix than formation. The technique holds advantages but will need to prove its advantages over other experimental bone regeneration approaches, including currently used autografts. Clinical trials in humans are planned within three years.

The article discusses the development of a new method called targeted error correction sequencing (TEC-Seq) for detecting early-stage tumors using cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in the blood. This approach allows for ultrasensitive direct evaluation of sequence changes in commonly altered cancer genes without prior knowledge of alterations in the tumor. The study analyzed plasma from 44 healthy individuals and 200 patients with colorectal, breast, lung, or ovarian cancer, detecting somatic mutations in the plasma of 71, 59, 59, and 68% of patients with stage I or II disease, respectively. The method demonstrated high concordance between alterations in the circulation and those in tumors of the same patients, suggesting its potential use for cancer screening. The development of this noninvasive liquid biopsy method could lead to earlier detection and intervention for human cancer, reducing morbidity and mortality.

Firefighters near Grande Prairie, Alberta, successfully rescued ten horses that broke through ice-covered slough on Sunday. The herd had wandered onto thinning ice due to warmer temperatures and fell through. About 35 firefighters and a search and rescue team responded to the call, using chainsaws to create pathways to shore and slings and boards to extract the horses from the melting ice and mud. Seven horses were saved, but three died later from exhaustion or injuries sustained during the incident. The remaining seven horses are reportedly in good condition. Regional Fire Chief Trevor Grant is urging landowners to be cautious with their animals around sloughs due to the changing conditions. The rescue was particularly challenging due to the wild broncing horses involved, which are not domesticated and used in rodeos.

Ruth Ann Steinhagen, who was 19 at the time, shot and nearly killed former Cubs first baseman Eddie Waitkus in 1949. The incident, which put a spotlight on stalking crimes, inspired the book and movie "The Natural." After undergoing psychiatric treatment for three years, Steinhagen disappeared into near obscurity and lived quietly until her death at the age of 83 from an accidental fall in December 2012. Her death went unreported until it was discovered during a search for another story. On October 19th/20th, there will be a lunar occultation where the moon passes in front of Aldebaran, one of the brightest stars in the sky. This event is classified as either "total" or "grazing." In the total occultation, the star vanishes behind the moon and reappears an hour or so later, which will be visible for most of the eastern and southern U.S. The grazing occultation, where the star appears to slide along the edge of the moon, will only be visible in a few hundred yard-wide line running through Los Angeles, Denver, about 50 miles southeast of Las Vegas, about 30 miles southeast of Minneapolis, and northeast to Ishpeming Township, Michigan, and continuing to George's Island, Labrador. This series of Aldebaran occultations has been happening since January 2015 and will end in September 2018, with the next one not occurring until 2033. Binoculars or a telescope are needed to fully enjoy the spectacle, and skies should be mostly clear across the southern tier of the U.S. late Tuesday and early Wednesday.

The document discusses the development of a clinical decision aid called CrisTAL (Criteria for Screening and Triaging to Appropriate aLternative care) to help identify patients nearing the end of life, who are often high users of hospital services. The tool is intended to assist clinicians in recognizing these patients, initiating discussions about end-of-life care preferences, and making more appropriate management plans.

The CrisTAL checklist includes 29 items covering demographic, physiological, and diagnostic predictors of short-term death, such as age, frailty, illness, cognitive impairment, previous hospitalizations, and specific health conditions. The tool is designed to be easily collected in routine practice and does not require specialist clinical judgement or value judgments.

The aim of CrisTAL is to improve care by enabling doctors to have honest conversations with patients and families about the inevitability of death and provide them with more choices regarding end-of-life care, such as going home or saying goodbye to loved ones. The tool may also prevent futile and expensive medical treatments that merely prolong suffering.

The CrisTAL checklist is being trialed in selected hospital emergency departments in Sydney, Australia, and includes communication training for medical staff to sensitively discuss end-of-life care options with patients and their families. The researchers hope the tool will eventually be used for all hospital admissions.

This article reports on a study where researchers used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and an implicit attentional processing procedure to establish communication with four patients suffering from advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), who were in a completely locked-in state (CLIS). The patients learned to answer personal questions with known answers and open questions requiring a "yes" or "no" by using frontocentral oxygenation changes measured with fNIRS. Three patients completed more than 46 sessions spread over several weeks, and one patient completed 20 sessions. Online fNIRS classification of personal questions with known answers and open questions resulted in an above-chance-level correct response rate over 70%. The results are potentially the first step towards abolition of completely locked-in states, at least for ALS patients. The work was funded by several grants from various organizations.

On December 18, 2017, an Amtrak train derailed in Washington, resulting in the death of three passengers and injuries to over 70 people, with several still in critical condition. The deceased individuals were identified as Jim Hamre, Zack Willhoite, both from Tacoma area rail enthusiasts, Benjamin Gran from nearby Auburn, and an Amtrak fan. The train was on its inaugural run of a new route aimed at improving safety and reducing travel times south of Tacoma.

Preliminary findings from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) revealed that seconds before the derailment, the engineer informed the crew about traveling too fast. The train's final recorded speed was 78 mph, within the approach limit but exceeding the 30 mph speed limit at the crash location, which followed a curve. The train was not equipped with positive train control, a safety system that can prevent derailments caused by excessive speed.

The NTSB's investigation into the incident is expected to last up to two years. The crew was found not to have been using personal electronic devices during the accident. Additionally, there were no reports of the crew's use of cellphones leading up to the crash.

Researchers at Queen Mary University of London have shown that bumblebees can learn to pull a string to retrieve a reward, and they can also learn this trick from other bees. This study challenges the notion that large brains are necessary for new skills to spread and suggests that insects may possess the essential cognitive elements for cultural transmission. The findings could hint at a rudimentary form of culture in bees, as the insects demonstrated the ability to pass on knowledge through observation. The researchers trained bumblebees by placing a flower with a string attached under a table and rewarding them with sugar water when they successfully pulled the flower out. More than half of the 40 bees tested learned what to do, and untrained bees that watched others retrieve the sugar water were able to pull the string when it was their turn. The study was published in PLOS Biology.

The proposed changes include reducing the boundaries of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante preserves in Utah, reopening protected oceans to commercial fishing, and altering several other monuments. The proposed adjustments aim to ease restrictions on mining, timber cutting, and recreational activities, while maintaining public access for uses such as hunting, fishing, or grazing. If adopted by Trump, these recommendations could significantly reduce the size of national monuments, particularly those created by Obama, potentially leading to lawsuits from conservationists concerned about lost protections for historic and natural sites.

The photographs, which date mostly from the early to mid-1930s, show Hitler in relaxed poses and with his guards on duty.

The auction was competitive, attracting bidders from various countries, including Britain, the United States, Germany, China, and South Africa. The buyer is generally historians who collect Nazi memorabilia out of fascination rather than political affiliation.

Memorials dedicated to preserving the historical context of the Holocaust have called for donations of personal items from survivors or collectors.

In conclusion, the auctioned photograph album offers a rare glimpse into Hitler's private life and is a valuable historical artifact, but its sale raises ethical concerns about the ownership and provenance of Nazi memorabilia.

This research suggests that simple reciprocal activities trigger high degrees of altruism in 1- and 2-year-old children, while friendly but nonreciprocal activities do not. The findings challenge the dominant claim that young humans are naturally and spontaneously altruistic and that socialization cannot account for their altruistic actions.

The study involved four experiments with different age groups of children. In the first experiment, reciprocal play led to more helping behavior than parallel play in 1- and 2-year-olds. In the second experiment, the effects of a single reciprocal interaction carried over to affect how much children helped a new person. In the third experiment, reciprocity promoted greater generosity in preschool-age children. Finally, in the fourth experiment, reciprocal interactions triggered an important belief in the mind of a child: the perception of benevolence in that situation.

The researchers argue that these findings suggest that simple reciprocal interactions are a potent trigger of altruism for young children and that these interactions lead children to believe that their relationships are characterized by mutual care and commitment. The study has implications for adult-child interactions, as caregivers may engage in simple reciprocal activities to foster both the enactment of altruism in children and their expectation of altruism from others.

Researchers at Leiden University Medical Center in the Netherlands found that watching horror movies can increase levels of blood clotting agents in viewers' blood, supporting the centuries-old metaphor that horror is "bloodcurdling." The study recruited 24 healthy volunteers aged 30 and under who watched either the movie Insidious or a documentary called A Year in Champagne. Blood samples were taken before and after each movie, with levels of coagulating factor VIII increasing in 57% of participants during the horror movie compared to just 14% during the documentary. The researchers believe this increase is the body preparing to heal itself as a physical response to fear. They advise a "truly relaxing and merry Christmas" without exposure to frightening situations to prevent venous thrombosis.

The study published in Molecular Psychiatry suggests that there may be a genetic link between the use of cannabis and the development of schizophrenia. Researchers found that individuals with a higher genetic risk for schizophrenia were more likely to use cannabis and use it in greater quantities than those without any schizophrenia risk genes. This finding suggests that the causal relationship between cannabis use and schizophrenia may not be straightforward, as there may be some genetic overlap between the two. The study adds to the ongoing debate about the relationship between marijuana and schizophrenia, with some scientists arguing that cannabis can worsen the course of schizophrenia in those genetically predisposed to the disorder. However, others are skeptical of the findings and argue that more research is needed to confirm the genetic link between the two.

The Senate passed a bill on Thursday that allows states to withhold federal family planning funds from Planned Parenthood and other abortion providers, with Vice President Mike Pence casting the tie-breaking vote in a 51-50 roll call. The bill reverses an Obama-era rule that prevented states from denying funding to such organizations. The measure was opposed by Democrats who criticized it as an attack on women's health and reproductive rights, while Republicans argued that it gives states more freedom to decide how to spend family planning funds. The bill now goes to President Trump for his signature.

A new study published in the journal Heart suggests that eating chocolate may help reduce the risk of atrial fibrillation, a type of irregular heartbeat. The study found that adults who ate chocolate at least once a month had rates of atrial fibrillation that were 10 to 20 percent lower than those who ate chocolate less frequently. The strongest effects were seen in men and women who ate one to six ounces of chocolate per week, with the biggest risk reduction for women being tied to eating one serving per week and for men being tied to eating two to six servings per week. The study did not prove a cause-and-effect relationship between eating chocolate and a lowered risk of atrial fibrillation, but it is possible that compounds in chocolate called flavonoids may play a role. The findings suggest that moderate intake of chocolate, particularly with higher cocoa content, may be a heart-healthy snack option. However, the study's limitations include the fact that the participants were generally healthier and more similar to each other in race and ethnicity than people in other countries.

The article tells the story of Harold Hayes, a medic who was part of the 807th Medical Air Evacuation Transport Squadron during World War II. In November 1943, while traveling to Italy on a transport plane, their aircraft crash-landed in Nazi-occupied Albania due to bad weather and German attacks. Hayes and his fellow passengers, which included nurses and other medics, traversed more than 600 miles of harsh terrain, evading German troops, facing hunger, illness, and cold, before eventually crossing Allied lines.

The group was forbidden from discussing their experiences due to concerns about protecting the people who helped them and maintaining secrecy for future downed airmen. Now, almost 70 years later, Hayes, the only living member of the group, is sharing his story with Cate Lineberry, author of the new book "The Secret Rescue: An Untold Story of American Nurses and Medics Behind Nazi Lines." The book was published this month.

In Eastern Ghouta, a rebel-held enclave near Damascus, Syria, hundreds of civilians have been killed over two days due to intense violence by forces loyal to President Bashar al-Assad. The Syrian civil defense reports 61 people killed on Tuesday alone, while the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights states that 194 people have died in the last 48 hours. In a recent study, researchers from University College London claim to have discovered what they believe are the oldest direct evidence of life on Earth, dating back at least 3.7 billion years. The findings come from rocks in Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq belt, which contain tiny tubes and filaments filled with hematite, an iron oxide mineral. These structures resemble iron-oxidizing bacteria found at hydrothermal vents today, suggesting a biological origin.

The researchers also found carbon-rich material around these structures, with a ratio of carbon isotopes that falls within the biological range, although not unambiguously. Additionally, they discovered blobs ringed with magnetite, which have been seen in other rocks containing fossils. The multiple lines of evidence presented make a strong case for a biological origin, but the findings are subject to scientific debate and further study.

If confirmed, this discovery would support the hypothesis that hydrothermal vents could have been a logical place where life on Earth began. This makes hydrothermal vents on other planets more attractive targets in the search for extraterrestrial life. The Nuvvuagittuq rocks might even be older than those previously studied in Greenland, South Africa, and Australia, representing a different marine environment that could provide new insights into the origins of life on Earth.

The suspected Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, was arrested after a 40-year manhunt, thanks to the use of genealogy websites. The investigators used GEDmatch, a website that pools raw genetic profiles from users, to find a distant relative of DeAngelo's, which led them to his arrest at his Citrus Heights home. DeAngelo is suspected of conducting a reign of terror in California between 1976 and 1986, including 12 homicides, 45 rapes, and over 100 residential burglaries. The genetic information used to identify DeAngelo came from a public database on the website, which pools data from users who voluntarily share their genetic profiles for free. This case highlights the potential use of genetic information in criminal investigations, raising concerns about privacy and the exposure of relatives to scrutiny by law enforcement. The arrest sheds light on a little-known fact that even if we've never spit into a test tube, some of our genetic information may be public and accessible to law enforcement.

The article discusses a proposed regulation by California water officials that would allow local communities to decide their own water conservation targets, ending strict rules imposed during the drought. The proposal would allow cities and water districts to compare their water supplies with anticipated demand if the drought continues for three more years. Local districts will set conservation targets based on the difference between supply and demand, and some may set strict conservation goals while others could lift mandates.

Bans on wasting water, such as washing sidewalks with a hose or washing cars without a shut-off nozzle, would become permanent under the proposed regulation. Californians are encouraged to continue practicing their conservation habits, as the drought remains critical.

The article discusses a potential breakthrough in the development of a blood test for Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the Scripps Research Institute in Florida have developed a technology that harnesses the immune system to detect Alzheimer's by identifying specific antibodies in the blood.

The study, published in the journal Cell, showed that three laboratory-made molecules called peptoids reacted strongly with the blood of six patients with Alzheimer's but not with healthy individuals. The technology has been licensed to Miami-based OPKO Health Inc., which plans to develop diagnostic kits within six to seven months.

The test could potentially be used for other diseases as well, such as cancer. However, the findings need to be confirmed in larger numbers of patients before it can be considered a reliable diagnostic tool. The researchers believe that early diagnosis of Alzheimer's will be crucial for developing effective treatments against the disease.

The Belgian royal family is set to start paying taxes for the first time since Belgium's independence in 1830, following a government reform approved on Wednesday. A four-foot American alligator was found in Lake Michigan off Waukegan Harbor on October 8, 2018. The discovery was made by a kayaker who initially thought it was a dead salmon but upon closer inspection saw an alligator head. The animal had its mouth taped shut and appeared thin. The family reported her missing and provided a detailed description including distinct tattoos. The medical examiner performed a cursory death investigation and tagged her as Jane Doe 10-3047 with an undetermined cause of death. The settlement, worth A$497.4 million, will be distributed over 12 to 18 months following final court approval.

The lead plaintiff, Carol Matthews, expressed relief at the settlement, acknowledging the ongoing pain but also feeling a sense of justice. A total of 173 people died in the Black Saturday fires.

The polar vortex, a high-speed, high-altitude wind system that typically pins Arctic cold in the North Pole, is currently stronger than average. According to Andrea Lang, an assistant professor of atmospheric and environmental science at the University of Albany who studies the vortex, it should keep Arctic cold penned in through the start of the Christmas season or so. However, there's a statistical likelihood that the vortex could become more volatile later in winter, potentially leading to late blasts of cold air and snow in some southerly regions.

The stronger-than-average polar vortex aligns with national long-range weather forecasts, which credit a stronger El Nino warming effect in the Pacific Ocean for a warmer winter. In New York, homeowners who heat with propane can expect a 18% decrease in their heating bills compared to last year, while those using heating oil and natural gas can expect a 25% and 10% decrease respectively. In a tragic incident in Florida's Everglades, three people were killed and eight others were injured in a chain reaction crash involving a black bear. The initial accident occurred when a woman driving an SUV hit and killed the 300-pound black bear on a remote road, leaving her stranded. Three good Samaritans stopped to help but were struck by another car, resulting in their deaths.

The first vehicle involved was a Cadillac SUV, and the second car that stopped to assist was not identified. The third car, a Mercedes, was the one that caused the fatal collision. The identities of the victims have not been released yet.

The crash occurred along Snake Road in Alligator Alley on the Big Cypress Seminole reservation. Six patients were transported to Broward Health Medical Center in Fort Lauderdale, and two others were taken to Memorial Regional Hospital in Hollywood. Two passengers from the three cars managed to walk away uninjured.

This is a rare incident as authorities have not previously recorded a case of a bear being involved in a traffic accident. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Commission confirmed that the Everglades is the natural habitat of black bears.

She was not issued a ticket prior to the arrest, and the only explanation she received was a complaint from the Village of Cahokia. This incident is part of a larger issue where individuals are being arrested for similar violations in various locations, including Prichard, Alabama, Riesel, Texas, and Pagedale, Missouri.

In Pagedale, Missouri, residents have been facing excessive fines for minor code violations such as chipped paint, mismatched curtains, and walking on the left side of a crosswalk. From 2010 to 2014, the number of non-traffic tickets issued to residents increased by 495 percent, making up a significant portion of the city's revenue.

The Institute for Justice (IJ) has teamed up with some Pagedale residents to challenge these ticketing practices, claiming they are unconstitutional. The case involves plaintiffs like Vincent Blount and Valarie Whitner, who have accumulated thousands of dollars in fines due to the city's demands, leading to a cycle of more fines and potential home demolition or arrest.

A student at the United States Air Force Academy was responsible for racial slurs posted outside the dorm rooms of five black students, as confirmed by the academy on November 7th, 2017. The student is no longer attending the school, but their status (whether they withdrew or were expelled) remains confidential due to privacy laws and their name was not released.

The incident occurred at a dormitory that houses students attending the academy's prep school, which helps promising students meet the academy's entrance requirements. Academy superintendent Lt. Gen. Jay Silveria gave a stern speech to cadets shortly after the slurs were reported, emphasizing the importance of treating everyone with dignity and respect.

The racial slurs appeared in the aftermath of racial violence in Charlottesville, Virginia, and amid a debate about NFL players kneeling for the national anthem. This incident marked a rare public discussion of racial issues at the academy, which has previously faced problems with sexual misconduct but few racial incidents. The Air Force Academy, located outside Colorado Springs, has approximately 4,000 students, and the prep school usually accepts about 240 students.

A 3-year-old girl named Mariah Woods has been missing since Sunday night from her home in Jacksonville, North Carolina. Her mother, Kristy Woods, reported her missing on Monday morning at around 6:45 a.m. Authorities have launched ground and air searches for Mariah, who is 2 feet 9 inches tall with brown hair and blue eyes. As of Tuesday, the Onslow County Sheriff's Department and multiple agencies including the FBI are still searching for her. The investigation is ongoing, and authorities declined to elaborate on details of the case. Mariah wears braces on her legs to help her walk, and her mother believes she wouldn't have left the house on her own. Authorities have released surveillance pictures taken Monday morning of a woman and child at a North Carolina Walmart, and are asking for the public's help in identifying both the woman and child. Mariah is described as a white female with brown hair and blue eyes, about 2 feet, 9 inches tall and weighing 30 pounds. Her mother has pleaded to be reunited with her child. Anyone with information about Mariah should call the Onslow County Sheriff's Office at 910-989-4070.

Dennis Lee Thian Poh, a 47-year-old businessman from Kuala Lumpur, has been missing since April 5 during a trek in Ampurna, Nepal. His family is anxiously awaiting his return as they hope to celebrate their second wedding anniversary on Saturday. Search efforts have intensified with rescue teams combing the areas between Khopra and Bayeli as well as Dobasto and Tadatani. SAR Dogs Nepal, an independent Nepali search-and-rescue team, is leading the efforts, but the family has urged experienced volunteers to help with on-ground search efforts. Lee was last seen between Ghorepani and Ghundrung on April 5, as he was descending from Khopra Danda, heading to Bayeli. Those who can help in Nepal may contact rescuers at +977 9856025679 or email any information to finddennis@yahoo.com. Lee's friends have also set up a Facebook page called Find Dennis for the public to share information or express their support. The area where he disappeared is known for its dangerous terrain and weather conditions, making it difficult for rescue operations.

In this summary, Iranian lawmaker Hossein Naqvi Hosseini stated that Tehran no longer needs more 20 percent-enriched uranium, which is a significant concession sought by Western powers in negotiations over Iran's nuclear program. Hosseini also mentioned that Iran is prepared to convert its stockpile of 20 percent-enriched uranium into fuel rods to alleviate concerns about non-peaceful use. The comments were published online by ICANA, and while Hosseini is not a government spokesman or a member of the nuclear negotiation team, his remarks are seen as progress in the ongoing negotiations between Iran and the West.

The negotiations aim to ease economic and oil sanctions placed on Iran's government over its contested nuclear program. Last week, Iranian diplomats met with negotiators from the United States, Russia, China, Britain, France, and Germany in Geneva. The next round of talks is scheduled for Nov. 7-8.

However, there are obstacles to reaching a deal, including concerns about Iran's underground facilities and the skepticism of some world powers, particularly Israel, regarding Iran's nuclear intentions. Additionally, Iran's recently elected president, Hassan Rouhani, faces growing criticism from hardliners in his country for conceding too much to the US.

Jack Ma, the CEO of Alibaba Group, spoke at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, where he discussed the U.S. economy and its relationship with China. Ma expressed his belief that globalization has been beneficial for American multinational companies like IBM, Cisco, and Microsoft, but criticized the U.S. government for mismanaging the wealth generated by these companies. He suggested that instead of spending over $14 trillion on wars in the past 30 years, the money could have been used to improve infrastructure and help American workers. Ma also urged the world to give Donald Trump time before passing judgment on his impact on Sino-US trade relations, stating that he is open-minded and listening. Additionally, Alibaba announced a deal with the International Olympic Committee to supply technology for organizing the Games, support a new shopping platform for merchandise, and run a Chinese version of the Olympic internet TV channel.

The document summarizes the release of a trove of documents by WikiLeaks, which alleges to contain hacking secrets of the CIA. The documents detail various methods used by the CIA to hack into everyday devices such as smartphones, televisions, and computers, potentially allowing them to record conversations, access private messages, and even control vehicle systems. The documents also suggest that the CIA has developed tools to bypass encryption used by popular messaging apps like WhatsApp and Signal. The source of the documents is unclear, but some experts have suggested that they may have been stolen by a foreign state, most likely Russia. The Obama administration reported that HealthCare.gov, an online marketplace offering subsidized private health insurance to uninsured individuals, is functioning well during the second sign-up season. Secretary of Health and Human Services Sylvia Burwell stated that 100,000 new applications were submitted via the federal website serving 37 states in the first few days, a significant improvement compared to last year's launch with technical issues. Additionally, half a million people who already have coverage through the program were able to log into their accounts this time.

President Barack Obama noted the improvements made to HealthCare.gov. The Congressional Budget Office has projected a total of 13 million enrollments for 2015, and Burwell expects to grow that by 2 million more or so. However, some states, such as Washington, experienced problems with their respective exchanges, including inaccurate subsidy calculations.

With Congress under Republican control, the administration cannot afford another website meltdown. Premiums appear to be stable this year, but experts warn of potential significant cost increases for customers who already have coverage and advise them to shop around during the enrollment period.

Mark Herzlich, a rookie linebacker for the New York Giants, recently arrived in Indianapolis for Super Bowl XLVI against the Patriots. He tweeted his gratitude for being able to walk after overcoming Ewing's sarcoma, a rare type of bone cancer he was diagnosed with in 2009. Herzlich chose to continue aggressive treatment instead of surgery to save his football career, increasing the likelihood that the cancer could return. Despite this, he played for Boston College in 2010 and went undrafted. He later signed as a free agent with the Giants and is now playing in the Super Bowl, an achievement that seemed nearly impossible just three years ago.

The study compares the cost of a school's degree to the average earnings of its graduates, providing a measure of a school's value.

The top 13 schools with the highest ROI scores are highlighted in the article, with California Institute of Technology (Caltech) having the highest ROI of $1,713,000 and Shaw University having the lowest ROI of $15,480. PayScale's complete list, including a breakdown of public and private schools with the highest ROIs, can be found on their website.

The case represents an escalation in the long-running battle between the Trump administration and California over issues such as immigration and climate change.

The Justice Department is asking for a preliminary injunction to block these three laws.

SOLD's services range from waiting for the latest tech releases, designer sample sales, and even brunch reservations.

SOLD's clientele varies from middle-class individuals to wealthy customers, with a significant number being busy professionals or parents who cannot wait in lines due to their schedules. The business has gained popularity as an alternative to waiting in long lines for popular events and products, joining other "Uber"-like services such as Lugg, Doughbies On-Demand, Minibar, and Breather.

Pfizer's erectile dysfunction drug Viagra has been approved for over-the-counter (OTC) sales in the U.K., making it the first country to allow such a change. The OTC version, named Viagra Connect, will be available at pharmacies starting in spring 2018. Men seeking the medication will need to have a conversation with a pharmacist before purchasing it, as its supply will depend on the pharmacist's assessment of its suitability for each individual.

Viagra has been one of the most successful prescription drugs since its launch in 1998 and achieved peak worldwide sales of over $2 billion in 2012. However, sales have declined due to patent expirations, prompting Pfizer to explore extending its brand value as a non-prescription drug.

The U.K.'s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) made the decision to deregulate Viagra after a public consultation, hoping it would reduce the number of people buying counterfeit versions of the drug, which can be dangerous. The MHRA has seized over £50m ($67m) of unlicensed and counterfeit erectile dysfunction medications in the past five years.

Peter Kassig, a former U.S. Army Ranger who served in Iraq, has been taken hostage by the Islamic State militant group and is believed to be the next victim in their series of beheadings. Kassig started a humanitarian aid organization called Special Emergency Response and Assistance (SERA) in 2012, which provides medical assistance, supplies, and food to Syrian refugees in Lebanon and Syria. He also worked as an employee for TYR Solutions LTD, a British firm that provides security and consulting services for individuals planning to go to war zones. Kassig enlisted in the Army in 2006 and served with the 75th Ranger Regiment from October 2006 to September 2007, deploying to Iraq from April to July 2007. He traveled to the Middle East after leaving the Army and while on spring break from Butler University in Indiana, where he wanted to learn about the humanitarian crisis in Syria firsthand and raise awareness about it. Kassig's family confirmed that he was being held hostage by ISIS but provided no further details.

At least 12 people were killed, and 46 were wounded in these attacks. The assaults targeted significant symbols of Iranian ideology, with ISIS claiming responsibility for the violence.

ISIS has been fighting against Iranian forces in Iraq since its founding in 2006. The attacks were intended to punish Iran for meddling in Iraq, force Iran to commit more resources to the conflict, create sectarian warfare, and push the Iranian government into cracking down on Sunnis inside Iran.

The attacks occurred during a time when ISIS is losing territory in Iraq and Syria, including its stronghold of Raqqa. The group may have carried out these attacks to demonstrate that it remains a threat, recruit new members, and attract attention during the Muslim month of fasting, Ramadan. It is believed that ISIS has wanted to carry out an attack in Iran for a long time but was discouraged by its parent organization, al-Qaeda, until their split in recent years.

The Indian authorities have put on hold efforts to retrieve the body of an American missionary, John Allen Chau, reportedly killed by members of the Sentinelese tribe on North Sentinel island in the Andaman and Nicobar islands last week. The decision was made due to concerns about disturbing the protected tribe and potential danger for both sides. Chau was trying to convert the tribespeople to Christianity when he was allegedly killed with arrows. His body is still on the island, and attempts to retrieve it have been unsuccessful due to the hostility of the Sentinelese people towards outsiders. The authorities are in a quandary about how to proceed further as they do not want to escalate tensions or put the tribe at risk of contracting diseases from the outside world. The fishermen who ferried Chau to the island have been arrested, and Indian anthropologists and researchers have expressed concern that search teams going to the island may further antagonize the Sentinelese.

The article discusses a new calculation that challenges the long-held belief that it would take 42 minutes for an object to fall through the Earth from one side to another, assuming a uniform density throughout. A graduate student at McGill University in Canada, Alexander Klotz, used seismic data to create a more realistic mass distribution of Earth and found that it would take 38 minutes and 11 seconds for an object to fall through the planet. Interestingly, Klotz also discovered that if gravity were assumed to be constant throughout the journey, the time taken would still be approximately 38 minutes. This new calculation provides a more accurate answer to the classic physics question and offers insights into the importance of considering realistic assumptions in calculations.

Israel's security forces have thwarted a large-scale terrorism network planned by Hamas, with at least 30 members arrested and weapons, ammunition, and bomb-making equipment seized. The network aimed to carry out attacks against Israeli targets including the Teddy soccer stadium, light rail system in Jerusalem, car bombings, kidnappings, and infiltrations of Israeli communities. The nerve center of the network was situated in Hamas’s headquarters in Turkey. The plot involved the assembly of multiple terrorist cells in the West Bank, as well as the training of Hamas members overseas. The Shin Bet uncovered the plot in September after explosive devices were detonated in the West Bank. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu praised the security services for their work in foiling the attacks, which could have resulted in many casualties.

A mysterious piece of space junk named WT1190F, which contains letters forming an unprintable expression of bafflement, is expected to collide with Earth on November 13th. This object was initially discovered in early October and is believed to be three to six feet long and man-made, possibly a spent rocket or moon mission debris. Scientists have been tracking it, predicting it will land in the Indian Ocean off the southern tip of Sri Lanka, but will likely burn up before reaching Earth. This event offers a scientific opportunity and tests plans for coordinating astronomers' efforts when a potentially dangerous space object appears. WT1190F is one of the few space objects whose impact can be accurately predicted, and it represents a rare breed of space object with only 20 known in distant orbits. However, there are likely many more pieces of space junk orbiting Earth, but they remain undiscovered due to lack of funding and attention for their tracking.

Phil Mickelson, a professional golfer, was not criminally charged for allegedly profiting off an insider stock tip from sports gambler Billy Walters. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) alleged that Mickelson made $931,000 after purchasing stock based on a tip from Walters in 2012, and used some of the money to repay Walters, whom he allegedly owed money. Mickelson has agreed to pay back "all ill-gotten gains," which totals $1.03 million, including interest. He was charged as a relief defendant for profiting without evidence of knowledge concerning the origin of the illegal tip. Billy Walters was arrested by the FBI and charged with insider trading. The case is part of a broader investigation involving former chairman of Dean Foods Thomas Davis, who allegedly received $1.1 million in loans from Walters that went unpaid. Mickelson has a history of gambling and is also tied to a federal money laundering case. He has not been charged with a crime in the laundering case.

The Lion's Gate Sanctuary in Agate, Colorado, has euthanized all 11 of its exotic animals after the Elbert County planning commission denied their request to move due to safety concerns. The sanctuary, which houses lions, tigers, bears, and wolves, had been facing flooding issues that made it difficult to continue operations at their current location. The owners of the sanctuary, Peter Winney and Joan Laub, stated that they were devastated by the loss of the animals, many of whom were seniors with disabilities. Elbert County commissioners expressed shock and sadness over the decision, stating that they had offered to care for the animals if Lion's Gate was unable to do so. The sanctuary has faced criticism in the past due to Winney's previous legal trouble involving wild animals and licensing issues.

Ninety-one-year-old Walter Thomas from Woodstock, Illinois, fulfilled an unusual bucket list dream by intentionally backing a car through a garage door with his family's help. The garage was scheduled for demolition, and the SUV used for the stunt was donated. Thomas, who has a passion for automobiles, collected antique cars over the years and owned four gas stations in Woodstock. His granddaughter Becky Goers shared his dream with her brother Andrew Thomas, a deputy and accident reconstruction officer, who made it happen by finding an old car and a suitable garage for the stunt. The event took place on Sunday, with Walter Thomas' wife of 70 years, Dorothy, watching. The crowd cheered as the car burst through the wooden garage doors, causing some excitement but no injuries.

A cookbook co-authored by Australian chef Pete Evans titled "Bubba Yum Yum: The Paleo Way For New Mums, Babies and Toddlers" has been put on hold due to concerns raised by health officials. The book, which includes a recipe for a "DIY baby milk formula" made from chicken liver and bone broth, is being investigated by the Federal Health Department as some of its recipes are considered potentially dangerous for infants.

The DIY formula recipe has been criticized for containing more than ten times the safe daily intake of vitamin A for babies and inadequate levels of other nutrients. The book also includes recipes with runny eggs and added salt, which health experts claim contravene national health guidelines for babies.

Health officials have expressed grave concerns over the potential health ramifications of the DIY formula and have alerted the Federal Government's Department of Health to their fears. The department is investigating further due to concerns about the inadequate nutritional values of some of the foods, particularly for infants.

The cookbook was co-authored by Evans, nutritionist Helen Padarin, and blogger Charlotte Carr. None of the authors have medical qualifications. The book was due to be published by Pan MacMillan but health officials claim it would be negligent of the publishers to release the book.

A school bus carrying sixth-grade girls from Pembroke Hill in Kansas City overturned on southbound Kansas Highway 7 near Kansas Highway 32, resulting in multiple injuries for the students and driver. The bus slid off the highway and rolled down an embankment after the driver took a turn too quickly. The driver, Elmer Scott Jr., was trapped and had to be extricated. He and the students were taken to various hospitals with minor injuries. The bus was operated by Durham School Services, who are working with the Kansas Highway Patrol to determine the cause of the crash. The southbound ramp was closed until 3:45 p.m., and an administrator from the school said the sixth-graders were heading to a camp out at Tall Oaks in Linwood, KS. Students who weren't injured were taken to Bonner Springs High School to meet their parents, and staff took good care of them to make them as comfortable as possible. The incident caused some disruption, but no one was seriously hurt.

Laverne Cox, known for her role in Orange is the New Black, has been announced as Madame Tussauds' first transgender wax figure. The figure will be unveiled at San Francisco's museum on June 26, coinciding with the city's Pride Festival. Cox expressed her honor and hope that her inclusion would inspire others to believe in their dreams. Madame Tussauds praised Cox's achievements, aligning with the theme of equality without exception. Pope Benedict XVI's decision to resign has sparked discussions within the Vatican regarding his future status. The former pope will continue to live in the Vatican after his retirement on February 28, but questions remain about his role and title. He is expected to write and pray while maintaining a low profile to avoid any potential rivalry with his successor. The Vatican has yet to decide on the color of his vestments or whether he will hold audiences with potential admirers. Pope Benedict has made it clear that he will not interfere with his successor's work, giving up all formal powers of his office. This is the first time in six centuries that a living ex-pontiff will exist within the Roman Catholic Church.

A mother of triplets named Rachel Park died unexpectedly at home after spending her first Christmas with her children. The triplets, Poppie, Mollie, and Evelyn, were born prematurely in March and spent several months in hospitals in Newcastle and Whitehaven. An online appeal has been launched to help her husband Steven care for the youngsters who were born 14 weeks early. Tributes have poured in for Rachel, with many describing her death as "totally tragic and heartbreaking." The family had hailed their children as Christmas miracles after they were allowed home for the first time in ten months. Following Rachel's death, a GoFundMe page has been set up to help Steven care for the triplets.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is set to implement new rules requiring cleaner gasoline and lower-pollution vehicles nationwide, which is one of President Obama's most significant air pollution initiatives. This move faces opposition from the oil industry, who argue that the rules will create billions of dollars in compliance costs while providing little benefit. The automakers, however, support the rule as it aligns with California's emissions standards and would help them meet stricter emissions standards already in place in California. The proposed standards are estimated to add less than a penny per gallon to gasoline prices but could reduce the amount of sulfur in U.S. gasoline by two-thirds and impose fleet-wide pollution limits on new vehicles by 2017. The EPA estimates annual health benefits of up to $23 billion by 2030, while critics argue that the costs will be much higher due to the flexibility provided in complying with the standards.

A teenager celebrating his 18th birthday in Taree, New South Wales, died on Christmas Eve after his legs were severed by a train four days earlier. The accident occurred at a railway crossing near Taree during the early hours of December 21. The driver managed to stop the train soon after the accident and was taken for mandatory tests. Police are investigating the actions of several party-goers who allegedly tried to block paramedics from treating the teenager and threw rocks at police and the train driver. The group's actions may lead to criminal charges. The deceased is believed to have been visiting Taree with his family, and the cause of his presence on the tracks is still under investigation. The tragedy has been met with condemnation by local authorities, who expressed their sympathy for the family while also emphasizing that such disruptive behavior towards emergency services will not be tolerated.

Harold "Butch" Knight, a 67-year-old man, is wanted for the murder of his wife Sarah Knight in Allegan County, Michigan. The police believe that Knight confessed to the murder during a 911 call he placed himself. Sarah's body was found at the couple's home on January 13, 2015, and since then, authorities have been searching for Knight. He has been spotted in rural locations in Maine, and there is speculation that he may be hiding out in an Amish community in Maine due to his interest in Amish communities and books found in his pole barn. The search for Knight has reached the 10-month mark, and his stepdaughter Roxanne Cameron-Harris believes he is playing a calculated game while on the run. A GoFundMe page has been set up to raise funds for a reward for information leading to Knight's arrest, and pink t-shirts with the phrase "No Evil Goes Unpunished - Justice for Sara Lee" are being sold as part of the fundraiser.

This is aimed at preserving links to archived pages when the original pages are changed or removed, thereby fixing broken links on the web. Additionally, the archived pages may be used as replacements for broken links or as companion links to show the original intended content of a page.

In a separate news item, Edgar Latulip, who had been missing from Kitchener, Ont., for nearly 30 years, was found in St. Catharines, Ont., and has been confirmed as the missing man through a DNA test. He had suffered a head injury shortly after his disappearance and effectively forgot who he was. In January of this year, he told a social worker in St. Catharines that he remembered his name, leading to his eventual return home. A reunion with his family is planned, and they are reportedly very happy about his return. Edgar's mother has not yet spoken with him.

In the October 11, 2015 presidential election in Belarus, President Alexander Lukashenko was expected to win a fifth term with ease, but he stated that anything less than 80% of the vote would indicate a decline in his support. The election was boycotted by the opposition and faced criticism from international observers due to concerns about ballot box security and early voting procedures. Lukashenko, who has been in power for over two decades, is known for his authoritarian rule, suppression of dissent, and cultivation of an image as a strong leader. Despite criticism, he faces no serious competition in the election.

The document discusses the potential consequences if President Obama and Congress fail to reach an agreement to raise the federal borrowing limit by August 2, 2011. If no deal is reached, the government would run out of cash on August 3, forcing President Obama to make difficult decisions about which obligations to prioritize for payment. The shortfall in August alone would be $134 billion.

The president would have to balance priorities between paying Social Security checks, military salaries and veterans' benefits, unemployment benefits, student loans, and other government programs, as well as making payments to investors in U.S. government bonds. A default could lead to a downgrade of the U.S.'s top-of-the-line credit rating, which would destabilize the financial system and potentially increase interest rates on mortgages, credit cards, and other types of debt.

The Bipartisan Policy Center's analysis suggests that the government would have to cut 44% of spending immediately if the debt ceiling is not raised. This would include eliminating all other federal spending, including pay for veterans, members of the armed services and civil servants, as well as funding for Pell grants, special-education programs, the federal courts, law enforcement, national nuclear programs, and housing assistance.

Ohio State Troopers arrested Daniel Yates, a 31-year-old resident of Eureka, California, on November 23, 2016, after pulling him over for following too closely. During the traffic stop in Millbury, Wood County, a drug-sniffing police dog alerted troopers to marijuana hidden in Christmas present-wrapped boxes in the trunk and back seat of Yates' rented Ford Expedition. The seized items included approximately 71 pounds of marijuana, 360 THC pills, and a pound of hash wax oil, with an estimated street value of $330,000.

Yates was charged with drug possession and trafficking, both felonies, and faces up to 16 years in prison and a fine of up to $30,000 if convicted. The traffic stop took place on Interstate 80 near milepost 71.

In August 2016, Compassion Over Killing released a graphic undercover video alleging mistreatment of chickens by Tyson Foods employees in Virginia. The video shows workers throwing, punching, kicking, and suffocating chickens, as well as sticking plastic rods through their beaks and leaving injured birds to die. Tyson Foods, the largest chicken-processing company in the United States, called the behavior "inexcusable" and fired 10 employees depicted in the video. The company also discontinued the practice of "boning," a historical method used to keep males from eating food intended for females. Compassion Over Killing condemned the workers' behavior and questioned whether there is any way to humanely kill and eat animals. Two of the facilities shown in the video are in Virginia's Mecklenburg County, one is in Buckingham County, and one is in Lunenburg County. Animal Control officials in Mecklenburg and Buckingham counties confirmed that they were investigating the allegations but declined to comment further. An Animal Control official in Lunenburg County did not return a request for comment. Tyson Foods has since retrained all of its live poultry workers on animal welfare policies in response to the new allegations of abuse.

Hurricane Irma made landfall in Florida on September 10, 2017, causing widespread damage across the state. The storm initially hit the Florida Keys as a Category 4 hurricane with winds of up to 130 mph (215 kph). It later moved north and struck Naples, but other parts of the eastern coast were also affected by the almost 400-mile-wide storm. In Miami, high winds snapped construction cranes and water flooded streets like rivers. In Palm Bay, a tornado destroyed six mobile homes. Water rose by 4 feet in 30 minutes in some places.

In Miami-Dade County, about 850,000 homes were without power, prompting Mayor Carlos Gimenez to impose a 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. curfew. Looting was reported as thousands of businesses and homes were empty due to evacuations.

Millions of Floridians evacuated ahead of the historic storm, and more than 3.4 million power customers – about 7 million people – were without electricity on Sunday. Governor Rick Scott said, "We're going to get through this."

Irma was expected to roll Monday into Georgia, where a state of emergency was declared for all 159 counties. Atlanta claimed the dubious distinction of receiving its first tropical storm

The Australian Prime Minister Julia Gillard has caused controversy by knitting a toy kangaroo as a gift for the royal baby, due next month. A 16-year-old girl is being charged as an adult for the murder of her 7-year-old nephew, Jordan Vong, who went missing from their home in Denver's Montbello neighborhood on August 6. The girl allegedly intentionally killed Jordan, wrapped his body in a blanket, and hid it in a portable closet in her basement bedroom.

According to court documents, the girl was upset about an argument with her girlfriend when Jordan came down to ask if she wanted to play video games. She told him to go upstairs but he refused, laying on her bed instead. The girl then pushed Jordan off the bed, causing him to hit his face on the floor. When Jordan began to cry, the girl allegedly covered his mouth and nose, holding him down until he stopped moving.

The girl later moved Jordan's body under her bed before wrapping it in a blanket and placing it in one of the two portable closets in her room. She did not tell any family members what she had done to Jordan out of fear. Jordan's body was found two days later, on August 8, after police obtained a search warrant for the house. The cause of death is still undetermined, but the coroner's office has ruled it a homicide.

The defendant's first appearance in district court has not yet been scheduled.

He aims to position himself as a key adversary of Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader, who also spoke in Lyon on the same day. Both politicians have similar views on the EU and globalization but differ sharply on migration. The French presidential election is set for April 23 and May 7, with Marine Le Pen leading in polls, followed by Emmanuel Macron, François Fillon, Benoit Hamon, and Jean-Luc Melenchon. Facebook has targeted 30,000 fake accounts linked to France ahead of the election as part of a worldwide effort against misinformation. The French will go to the polls this weekend and again on May 7 to pick their new president, with the outcome being closely watched by many, given the recent surprises of Brexit and the U.S. presidential election.

On September 28th, a four-CD box set titled "An American Treasure" will be released by Tom Petty's family and former collaborators. The collection includes previously unreleased studio recordings, live performances, deep cuts, and alternate versions of popular songs spanning over 40 years of Petty's career. The first single from the set is a bouncy, organ-heavy cut called "Keep a Little Soul" from 1982.

The box set will include a total of 60 tracks, with each CD featuring a mix of previously unreleased and rare tracks, as well as popular songs from throughout Petty's career. Dennis Oland's defense team ended their case in his second-degree murder trial for the 2011 bludgeoning death of his father, Richard Oland. The jury is expected to receive the case as early as Dec. 16. Oland testified in his own defense on Tuesday and Wednesday, stating he did not kill his father and that he loved him. The trial has been ongoing since September 16 and includes testimony from nearly 50 witnesses. Richard Oland was found dead in his Saint John office with 45 sharp and blunt force injuries to his head, neck, and hands. No weapon was ever found. Dennis Oland, the last person to see his father alive, has been standing trial since September. The defense called only two other witnesses and dismissed the remaining potential witnesses. Judge John Walsh warned jurors that deliberations will be mentally exhausting and emotionally draining. One juror will be dismissed by random draw as a precaution in case of sickness or emergencies. Oland acknowledged inconsistencies between his testimony and statements to police, including wearing a brown sports jacket instead of a navy blazer on the night in question and visiting his father's office three times instead of two. The trial is one of the longest in New Brunswick history.

Snap Inc., the parent company of Snapchat, is expected to go public as early as March 1, with shares priced between $14 and $16. This would give the company a total market value of $20 billion. The IPO is anticipated to be one of the hottest in years. However, the lead-up to the IPO has been rocky due to concerns about Snap's slowing user growth and lack of profits. Despite these issues, investors may be warming up to Snap as they begin to view it as a serious media company with potential for ad revenue. The question remains whether Snap can bring in considerable ad revenue like Facebook has done post-IPO, or if it could face the same fate as Twitter, which has struggled since its IPO. Some investors are hesitant due to their lack of understanding of the app and Snap's decision not to issue voting rights to investors. The IPO is expected to take place on March 1, with trading beginning the next day.

The average pay for CEOs rose by 17.6% to $18.9 million, while worker wages stalled with a minimal increase of 0.3%.

The gap between CEO and worker compensation has been growing since the 1990s, with the ratio peaking in 2000 at 344-to-1. Despite fluctuations, CEO pay has been increasing rapidly since 2009, surpassing even the top 0.1% earners.

The report highlights that the rise in CEO compensation cannot be solely attributed to stock market growth or corporate profits. Between 1978 and 2017, CEO compensation increased by 979%, outpacing both stock prices and corporate profits.

Notable examples include McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook earning $21.7 million while the median wage for McDonald's workers was just $7,017, resulting in a CEO-to-worker pay ratio of 3,101-to-1. Similarly, Walmart CEO Doug McMillon took home $22.8 million compared to an average worker

Yelp Inc., a consumer review website based in San Francisco, made a successful market debut on September 23, 2011, with its stock closing at $24.58, up 64% from its IPO price of $15 per share. The company is now worth approximately $1.47 billion, about 17 times its 2011 revenue. Yelp's stellar debut follows similar successful public listings by other Internet companies like LinkedIn Corp, Groupon Inc and Zillow Inc. However, unlike these companies, Yelp is still unprofitable and generates revenue through advertising on its sites that feature more than 25 million reviews of local businesses.

Yelp competes with Angie's List, which charges for memberships, but has a smaller user base due to its subscription model. The company faces stiff competition from Facebook, Google Inc (through its acquisition of restaurant reviewer Zagat), and others like Groupon and Angie's List. Jeremy Stoppelman, co-founder and CEO of Yelp, testified before a Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on Capitol Hill on September 21, stating that he was not fazed by competition from larger companies.
