A massive and mysterious bloom of pyrosomes, often referred to as the "unicorn of the sea" or "sea pickles," has occurred on the west coast of America. These translucent, tubular creatures have swarmed in their millions, causing havoc for fishermen by ruining their nets and baffling scientists who are racing to study them. The pyrosomes, which can grow up to two feet long, are usually found in warm tropical seas far from the coastline but have unexpectedly appeared along the west coast of America this year in unprecedented numbers. Researchers are scrambling to learn more about these creatures, their impact on the ecosystem and fisheries, and what has caused the bloom. Some theories suggest it could be due to warming sea temperatures caused by climate change or unusual sea currents. Scientists are concerned that if all the creatures die off at once, they could create a dead zone for marine life by depleting oxygen as they decompose.

Facebook announced on Wednesday that it found evidence of a Russian-based group spending $100,000 on political ads promoting divisive social and political messages during a two-year period through May 2017. The ads, which were spread by 470 "inauthentic" accounts and pages, focused on topics such as immigration, race, and gay rights, rather than backing a particular political candidate. Facebook's chief security officer, Alex Stamos, stated that the company is cooperating with federal inquiries into influence operations during the 2016 U.S. presidential election. The ads were mostly national in scope and did not appear to target political swing states as voting neared. Facebook did not release the names of any of the suspended pages, but some included words such as "refugee" and "patriot." The findings support US intelligence agency conclusions that Russia was actively involved in shaping the election. Facebook previously published a white paper detailing techniques used by countries and organizations to spread misleading information for geopolitical goals, including content seeding, targeted data collection, and fake accounts used to amplify one particular view, sow distrust in political institutions, and spread confusion. The company stated that it found no link between the Russian-purchased advertising and any specific presidential campaign. Two former Hooters employees, PJ Cagnina and Scott Peterson, have filed a lawsuit against the restaurant chain and their male supervisor, Rick Leukert, alleging years of sexual harassment. The men's attorney, Jason Oliver, did not immediately return a call for comment. Neither man currently works for Hooters. The lawsuit seeks to prevent similar behavior from happening again.

Kennedy International Airport on April 1, 2014, for allegedly attempting to smuggle nearly two pounds of heroin into the U.S., worth over $70,000. Customs and Border Protection officers became suspicious when Charles appeared nervous during a bag inspection and noticed his awkward gait. Upon further search, they discovered two plastic packages containing a brown paste-like substance in Charles' underwear, which tested positive for heroin. Charles was ordered held without bail and faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of drug smuggling charges. The incident was described as another example of Customs and Border Protection officers being vigilant in protecting the U.S. from illegal drug distribution.

NASA's Curiosity rover has delivered significant findings from its exploration of Mars, providing evidence of an ancient Martian lake that could have supported life as we know it for long periods. The lake likely existed about 3.7 billion years ago and covered a small portion of Gale Crater, which the rover has been exploring since landing in August 2012.

The lake's sedimentary rocks, known as mudstones, contain clay minerals that formed in the sediments of an ancient freshwater lake. The rover also detected key chemical ingredients for life, including sulfur, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and carbon. These findings suggest that the lake could have potentially supported a class of microbes called chemolithoautotrophs, which obtain energy by breaking down rocks and minerals.

The new results confirm and extend Curiosity's landmark discovery, painting a more complete picture of the Yellowknife Bay area long ago. The rover's analysis of these findings has provided a new understanding of early Mars, suggesting that it was in many ways similar to Earth. However, the mission has also faced challenges, such as high levels of radiation on the Martian surface and complications in identifying organic compounds.

Two Ohio men, Ricky Jackson and Wiley Bridgeman, were exonerated and released from prison after spending nearly four decades for a murder they did not commit. They were convicted in 1975 for the shooting death of Harold Franks, a Cleveland-area money order salesman, based on testimony from a 12-year-old witness, Edward Vernon. However, last year, Vernon recanted his testimony, stating that he was coerced by detectives and never saw the murder take place. The Ohio Innocence Project took up the case, and Jackson was released on Friday, making him the longest-held U.S. prisoner to be exonerated. Wiley Bridgeman was also released later in the day. The men expressed gratitude towards the Ohio Innocence Project, county prosecutors, and Vernon for showing courage in admitting his lies. Eddie Vernon had testified against Jackson and the Bridgeman brothers, claiming that he saw the slaying, but it was later discovered that he wasn't close to the crime scene and was fed information by detectives. The case against Ronnie Bridgeman is still ongoing as he seeks to have his record cleared.

The news article discusses an ongoing investigation into the death of musician Prince, who was found dead at his home in suburban Minneapolis on April 21, 2016. Law enforcement officials are looking into whether Prince died from an overdose and whether a doctor was prescribing him drugs in the weeks before his death. One possibility is that he overdosed on the powerful painkiller Percocet or something similar.

Investigators are also examining prescription drugs found at Prince's home, and they are trying to determine how he obtained them. Prince's plane made an emergency stop in Moline, Illinois, on April 15, and he was given a shot of Narcan, which is used in suspected opioid overdoses.

An autopsy has been performed, but the results are not expected for three to four weeks. The search warrant for Prince's Paisley Park home and studio was filed under seal at the request of investigators who said it would hamper their investigation if contents were public.

The investigation is reminiscent of Michael Jackson's death, as his doctor was convicted of involuntary manslaughter for his role in prescribing a powerful anesthetic that contributed to the pop star's death in 2009. It is unclear where the investigation into Prince's death is heading at this time.

In November, Ohio voters will decide on a constitutional amendment to legalize marijuana, making it the sixth jurisdiction in the nation to do so if passed. The initiative, led by ResponsibleOhio, has collected over 320,000 signatures, surpassing the necessary threshold for the ballot.

Opposition to the plan includes the Ohio Farm Bureau Federation and some activists who argue it creates an unfair edge for the wealthy.

The US has accused seven Russian spies of involvement in a series of cyber-plots across the globe, including targeting the global chemical weapons watchdog, anti-doping agencies, and a US nuclear company. This is part of an organized pushback against alleged Russian cyber-attacks worldwide. Russia dismissed the allegations as "Western spy mania."

House Majority Whip Steve Scalise, the third-ranking Republican in the House of Representatives, spoke at a white supremacist group's event in 2002 while he served as a state representative. The group was founded by former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke. Scalise acknowledged speaking to the group but said it was "insulting and ludicrous" to think he shared their views. House Speaker John Boehner and other GOP leaders have expressed support for Scalise, saying they stand by him as whip despite the controversy surrounding his appearance before the group. Some conservatives have criticized Scalise for not taking full responsibility for the incident and for attending the event without knowing about the group's white-supremacist leanings. The controversy comes just days before Republicans take full control of Congress, with Scalise poised to play a key role in shepherding through conservative legislative priorities.

During the 90-minute ride of terror, Tamerlan Tsarnaev kept talking and detailed his hatred of Americans while asking Danny about his heritage and family. He emphasized that ending high-end tax cuts is crucial to address societal priorities and reduce the deficit, portraying those who oppose this as unserious about the issue.

Obama also brought up the GOP's opposition to raising revenues by ending a corporate jet tax break worth $3 billion, which he used to provoke a response from Republicans and position them as defenders of the wealthy. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has expressed dismay after 28 Russian athletes had their lifetime bans from the Olympics overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). This ruling means that the athletes' results from the 2014 Winter Olympics will be reinstated, returning Russia to the top of the medal table. The IOC is bracing itself for a fresh legal challenge from some of these athletes who now want to compete in the upcoming Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang.

The CAS decision partially upheld 11 other appeals and said that evidence was "insufficient" to prove doping in 28 cases. However, for the 11 athletes whose appeals had been partially upheld, evidence "was sufficient to establish an anti-doping rule violation." The IOC stated that it would consider its own appeal to the Swiss Federal Tribunal.

The overturned bans include Alexander Tretiakov, who won gold in men's skeleton at Sochi but was later banned for life by the IOC. Britain's four-man bobsleigh team from Sochi may also be upgraded to a bronze medal due to the disqualification of two Russian sleds that finished first and fourth.

The Badlands National Park's official Twitter account posted tweets about climate change contradicting President Trump's administration's stance, stating that carbon dioxide levels are currently higher than in the last 650,000 years. The tweets were deleted after a few hours and the National Park Service attributed them to a former employee who was not authorized to use the account. The NPS stated that they deleted the tweets on their own accord and encouraged social media managers to continue using Twitter for public safety and park information, excluding content related to national policy issues.

The baby dinosaur skeleton named "Joe" is the smallest, youngest, and most complete Parasaurolophus ever found. Discovered in 2009 by high-school student Kevin Terris during a field trip with The Webb Schools, the fossil was initially overlooked by professional paleontologists Andrew Farke and Don Lofgren.

Parasaurolophus is known for its distinctive tube-shaped head crest, which may have served as a visual display or amplifier for calls. "Joe" had a small bump on its head that would have grown into the crest, indicating that Parasaurolophus youngsters started growing their crests earlier than previously thought.

The skeleton was excavated and analyzed over four years, with students from The Webb Schools participating in the process. "Joe" is now on display at the Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, California, and a digital exploration of the skeleton is available online at dinosaurjoe.com.

Kevin Terris, the student who discovered "Joe," is currently studying geology in college. The research team's findings were published in the journal PeerJ on October 22, 2019.

A tragic road rage incident occurred in East Oakland, California on October 27, 2014, resulting in the death of Perla Avina, a mother of four. The shooting took place as Avina and her husband, Luis Lopez Gallegos, were driving home from shopping for ingredients to prepare posole for the Raiders game. An angry motorist sprayed gunfire into their car, hitting Avina in the head. Despite efforts by Gallegos and emergency responders, she died in their driveway. The shooting happened on 98th Avenue between the 400 to 600 blocks, and police are still searching for the suspect. The couple had been high-school sweethearts, with Avina working as a medical clerk at a pain rehabilitation center in Emeryville. Police and CrimeStoppers of Oakland are offering up to $30,000 in reward money for information leading to the arrest of the shooter. The family has set up a GoFundMe page to help with funeral expenses.

A Harvard student named Aran Khanna developed a Chrome extension called Marauder's Map, which capitalized on a privacy flaw in Facebook Messenger that allowed users' locations to be shared with anyone they messaged. The app showed the locations of users within three feet accuracy and was downloaded over 85,000 times before it was disabled. Facebook became aware of the issue and asked Khanna to disable the app, deactivated location sharing from desktops, and rescinded his summer internship offer, citing a violation of their user agreement. The incident sparked discussions about privacy concerns on social media platforms and the need for greater transparency in how companies handle user data.

The study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences suggests that adopting expansive postures, such as spreading limbs and having a stretched-out torso, can increase romantic interest in speed-dating situations and online dating platforms. Researcher Tanya Vacharkulksemsuk found that people who sat or posed in expanded postures were deemed more attractive, with this strategy working particularly well for men. The study also found that expansive postures convey dominance and a willingness to share resources, potentially making individuals more appealing to potential romantic partners. However, the findings should be taken with skepticism, as previous studies on power poses have been met with controversy due to inconsistent results.

The report, titled "‘Just Don’t Call It a Militia': Impunity, Militias and the ‘Afghan Local Police'," released by Human Rights Watch in April 2011, found that the Afghan government and US-backed Afghan Local Police (ALP) are committing serious human rights abuses, including killings, rape, arbitrary detention, abductions, forcible land grabs, and illegal raids. The report documents these abuses in various provinces of Afghanistan, such as Kunduz, Baghlan, Herat, and Uruzgan. The Afghan government has failed to hold these forces accountable, fostering future abuses and generating support for the Taliban and other opposition forces. Human Rights Watch called on the US and Afghan governments to sever ties with irregular armed groups, create properly trained and vetted security forces that are held accountable for their actions, and investigate all allegations of abuse by militias and the ALP. The report is based on over 120 interviews with victims, witnesses, government officials, foreign military officials, journalists, and Afghanistan analysts.

Barack Obama, upon entering the U.S. Senate in 2005, sought a deeper understanding of foreign affairs due to his limited experience and academic background. To achieve this, he reached out to various foreign policy experts, including academics, journalists, and politicians like Susan Rice and Samantha Power. Power's book "A Problem from Hell" influenced Obama significantly, as it advocated for liberal interventionism in preventing genocides and massacres.

Obama invited Power to dinner and later hired her as a foreign policy fellow in his office. During this period, he was determined to learn the institution and acquire substance over celebrity, especially in foreign affairs. However, Obama's approach to foreign policy has been criticized for being passive and indecisive, with some labeling it "leading from behind."

This style is said to be based on two unspoken beliefs: that the relative power of the U.S. is declining, as rivals like China rise, and that the U.S. is reviled in many parts of the world. Critics argue that this approach is a non-sequitur, as it does not logically follow from China's rising GDP or widespread anti-American sentiment.

Overall, Obama's foreign policy has been characterized as ad hoc, erratic, and confused, with a tendency towards hesitation, delay, and indecision.

The article discusses the end of former Florida governor Jeb Bush's presidential campaign, which he announced on February 20th after a disappointing fourth-place finish in South Carolina's primary. The article highlights several reasons for Bush's failure to gain traction in the race, including his perceived lack of energy and his association with the unpopular Iraq war. Additionally, the article notes that Bush was outmatched by Donald Trump, who became the front-runner in the Republican primary and took much of the media attention away from other candidates. The article also mentions the role of Bush's family name in his campaign, as some voters were hesitant to support another member of the Bush family after the presidencies of George W. Bush and George H.W. Bush. Overall, the article suggests that Bush's campaign was poorly managed and failed to adapt to the changing political landscape of 2016.

The article discusses the use of castoreum, a chemical compound derived from beavers' anal glands, in food and perfume industries. Castoreum is used as a flavoring agent, particularly for its vanilla-like scent, and has been in use for at least 80 years. It is considered safe by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and can be found in various foods without being explicitly listed on ingredient labels, often under the term "natural flavoring." The process of extracting castoreum involves anesthetizing the beaver and milking its anal glands, which is described as unpleasant. Annual consumption of castoreum is relatively low due to this process, with approximately 292 pounds (132 kilograms) being used each year. The article also mentions that men may find the vanilla scent attractive, but it originates from beavers' unique diet rather than reminding them of childhood as commonly believed.

A 14-year-old boy named Stephen J. Brumby died accidentally at High Noon Gun Range in Sarasota, Florida, on July 3rd. The incident occurred when his father, William C. Brumby, was shooting and the spent shell casing deflected off a wall and fell into Brumby's shirt. In an attempt to remove it, he accidentally pointed the gun behind him and fired, hitting his son. The investigation is ongoing, and there are currently no charges against Brumby. A memorial fund has been set up on GoFundMe to help the family with expenses. This is not the first fatal incident at a local gun range; last August, a man in his 70s killed himself at Take Aim Gun Range.

Taylor Swift's new album "1989" is projected to sell over one million copies in its first week, making it her third consecutive set to achieve this milestone and the first pop act to do so in history. The album is currently performing exceptionally well on iTunes and Target, with a bonus track exclusive at Target. If the sales figures hold, "1989" will be the 19th album since 1991 to sell over one million copies in its first week, surpassing other popular albums released this year such as Frozen soundtrack, Beyoncé's self-titled album, Lorde's Pure Heroine, and Coldplay's Ghost Stories. Taylor Swift has been promoting the album extensively, appearing on multiple talk shows and participating in various events to support its release. Final sales figures will be announced on November 5th.

Dr. George Doodnaught, an anesthesiologist, was sentenced to 10 years in prison for sexually assaulting 21 sedated women during surgeries at North York General Hospital in Toronto between 2006 and 2010. The judge described his conduct as "reprehensible in the extreme" and noted that the victims suffered lasting emotional damage, including feelings of betrayal, anger, bitterness, shame, panic attacks, loss of self-worth, distrust of doctors, and an inability to form intimate relationships. Many of the victims were present in court during the sentencing and wiped tears from their eyes. Doodnaught intends to appeal his convictions, and a bail hearing for his release pending the appeal is scheduled for Wednesday at the Court of Appeal. The hospital has apologized for the impact of Doodnaught's crimes on the victims' lives and has made changes to how it addresses and tracks patient complaints.

In an evening press conference, NYPD, Mayor Bill de Blasio, and Brooklyn Borough President Eric Adams announced that Daniel St. Hubert is the suspect accused of stabbing two young children in the elevator of their NYCHA building in East New York. The public was implored to contact 1-800-577-TIPS or 911 if they have any information about St. Hubert, who is considered "armed and dangerous." St. Hubert has nine prior arrests and has been on parole since May 23 for a domestic violence incident. BP has agreed to the Obama administration's request to broadcast the "top kill" procedure, a tricky method aimed at stopping the oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico, starting as early as Wednesday morning. The process involves forcing drilling mud and cement onto the leak. This is the latest attempt to plug the oil leak, which has been ongoing since April.

BP had initially refused to show the "top kill" procedure live, but after discussions with Coast Guard Adm. Thad Allen and pressure from lawmakers, they have agreed to broadcast it. The company warned that significant changes in the appearance of the flows at the seabed may occur during the two-day long procedure, but these changes may not indicate the overall progress or success of the operation.

In addition to the live feed of the "top kill" procedure, multiple live streams from various underwater robots are available for viewing, although they may freeze or become unavailable at times. These live streams provide a visual representation of the ongoing efforts to contain and clean up the oil spill.

The couple took Gammy's healthy twin sister back to Australia but faced criticism for abandoning the disabled child. As commercial surrogacy is outlawed in Australia, many couples turn to clinics in Thailand and India. Thailand has no clear legal framework for surrogacy, but a draft law banning commercial surrogacy has been submitted to the military government. Jeff Bezos' spaceflight company, Blue Origin, successfully landed its New Shepard rocket back on Earth for the first time after flying it to the edge of space during an uncrewed reusability test on Monday. The rocket reached a maximum speed of Mach 3.72 and brought the spacecraft's capsule about 100.5 kilometers into the air. The capsule landed back on Earth using parachutes, while the rocket made a soft touchdown using its landing legs after its engine reignited at 5,000 feet above the landing pad. Blue Origin plans to offer suborbital flights to space aboard New Shepard and eventually build an orbital rocket for carrying people and cargo to space from Florida. The aim is to lower the cost of access to space by reusing rockets multiple times. Elon Musk, founder of SpaceX, congratulated Blue Origin on their achievement but clarified the difference between "space" and "orbit." Both companies are working towards creating a fleet of reusable rockets for private space launches.

Miranda July, the filmmaker and author known for her work "You And Me And Everyone We Know," has confessed to a history of shoplifting in The New Yorker. Her first theft was during college when she stole Neosporin, leading to a public embarrassment as she wet her pants upon being caught. July continued to shoplift at grocery stores and even at Goodwill, including stealing from charity. This article also mentions other female celebrities who have (allegedly) shoplifted. July describes her shoplifting as a casual, almost compulsive habit that became part of her livelihood when she moved to Portland, Oregon. She stole various items from supermarkets and even Goodwill, and involved friends in the act by stealing luggage from airport baggage carousels. July's shoplifting ended after she entered a relationship, leading her to question the need for criminal behavior as an artist. The article ends with July reflecting on the feeling of being an adult and the sense of secret fraudulence that comes with it.

In this news summary, several ballot measures were considered in six states on Tuesday, with Colorado being a notable state where voters approved a 15% excise tax and a 10% sales tax on marijuana to fund school construction and law enforcement efforts. The measure passed with 65% support and is expected to generate nearly $70 million in additional state tax revenue next year.

In Colorado, secession measures were also proposed in 11 counties, aiming to form a 51st state known as North Colorado. However, the plan has no chance of becoming reality due to requiring statewide and congressional approval.

Other noteworthy measures included Washington voters considering a hotly contested initiative that would require labeling all foods containing genetically modified ingredients. New Jersey voters were asked to amend their constitution to raise the state minimum wage from $7.25 to $8.25 per hour, while New York voters considered revising their constitution to allow the legislature in Albany to authorize seven casinos.

The news article also highlighted an increasing trend of out-of-state funding in local races and ballot measures, with large contributions from out-of-state groups being seen in SeaTac, Kitsap Peninsula, and Whatcom County. This trend has raised concerns about the core promise of the initiative process and representative democracy.

The wedding had a Great Gatsby theme and featured a cigar and scotch bar. Snooki wore two dresses for the occasion - an off-white traditional lace gown for the ceremony and a more extravagant one for the reception. In summary, President Donald Trump has expressed support for a boycott of Harley-Davidson due to the company's decision to move production of motorcycles sold in Europe to facilities outside the U.S., citing tariffs imposed by the European Union as the reason. This decision was made in June and has resulted in Harley-Davidson expecting new tariffs to cost the company up to $100 million annually. Trump's statement came after a meeting with "Bikers for Trump" supporters at his golf course in Bedminster, New Jersey over the weekend. Harley-Davidson did not respond to requests for comment on Sunday.

Steve Vogelsang, a former broadcast personality and Red River College journalism instructor, has been charged with two counts of bank robbery in Medicine Hat, Alberta. The incidents occurred on October 19th at the Royal Bank and October 20th at the Bank of Montreal. Vogelsang was arrested at a hotel in the area on Saturday.

Vogelsang worked as a news director and sports anchor at CTV Winnipeg from the early 1990s to 2002, and later became a journalism instructor at Red River College until 2011. He faced financial difficulties, including missing mortgage payments on a home in Winnipeg and being accused of forging his ex-wife's signature to renew the mortgage.

Earlier this year, a former student he had dated off and on since 2004 was granted a protection order against him due to harassment through text, emails, and voicemails despite police requests to leave her alone. Vogelsang is fighting those allegations next month.

Vogelsang remains in custody in Alberta to face the robbery charges and is expected in court tomorrow. He has also faced other legal issues, including a sexual assault charge that was stayed in October 2017 and three charges of disobeying a court order, which are expected to be dealt with in court next year

South Korean film legend Choi Eun-hee, who was once abducted and forced to make movies for North Korea, has died at the age of 92. Born in Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province, in 1926, Choi began her film career in 1947 and became one of the three most celebrated actresses of her time. She married Shin Sang-ok, a leading film director, with whom she established Shin Film and made many films that led the Korean film industry in the '60s and '70s. In 1978, Choi was kidnapped by North Korean agents and taken to North Korea where she was forced to make movies for the regime. She won the best actress award at the Moscow Film Festival in 1985 for a movie made in North Korea. After eight years, she and her ex-husband escaped from North Korea to the United States. Choi is survived by two sons and two daughters. Her health deteriorated quickly after her ex-husband's death in 2006, and she had been receiving kidney dialysis three times a week until her death. The kidnapping and forced filmmaking by North Korea have been widely reported and are the subject of a recent film titled "The Lovers and the Despot." Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter was taken to a hospital in Winnipeg on Thursday after experiencing dehydration while working on a Habitat for Humanity house. The incident occurred during a two-day build, where Carter and his wife Rosalynn were assisting with the construction of 25 homes as part of Canada's 150th anniversary celebration.

Carter, who is 92 years old, was working in the sun for about an hour when he appeared to feel faint and collapsed. He was rehydrated at St. Boniface Hospital, with his wife Rosalynn by his side. The former president has since informed build leaders that he is feeling "OK" and encouraged volunteers to continue their workday.

Jimmy Carter and Rosalynn arrived in Winnipeg earlier in the day for their first public appearance since 1993, where they led a morning prayer service and worked on sawing boards for a staircase. The couple has been longtime supporters of Habitat for Humanity and have volunteered with the organization since 1984.

Any further updates on Carter's condition will come from the Carter Center, a not-for-profit organization founded by the ex-president.

An Ohio man named Matthew B. Matheny, aged 40, was found alive on Mount St. Helens in Washington state after six days of being lost in the wilderness. He sustained himself by eating berries and bees during his time lost. Matheny had set out for a hike last Thursday but got lost and couldn't find his way back to the car he had borrowed from a friend. His friends reported him missing, prompting a search that ended successfully when Matheny was airlifted to a hospital on Wednesday. He was being treated mostly for dehydration and is expected to stay overnight at the hospital as a precaution. Matheny's parents described him as a former Boy Scout with a sense of humor, who got himself into humorous situations. About 40 people participated in the search for Matheny, including search-and-rescue personnel, helicopters, tracking dogs, and a drone operated by the sheriff's office. The search focused on a 1-square-mile area based on cellphone signals and a computer model that sought to predict Matheny's movements.

Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney spoke at the NAACP annual convention on Wednesday, promising to work towards job creation for African Americans if elected and criticizing President Obama's health care overhaul. However, his speech was met with jeers from the predominantly black audience, particularly when he pledged to repeal Obamacare. Romney's appearance at the convention was seen as a bold move aimed at reaching out to diverse audiences and demonstrating inclusivity, but it was also criticized for being tone-deaf to the concerns of African Americans. Romney's speech came after President Obama declined an invitation to speak at the convention this year.

Oprah Winfrey's Harpo Studios in Chicago is closing after 25 years, with production moving to OWN headquarters in Los Angeles by December. The decision was made to consolidate everything under one roof on the West Coast. Approximately 200 employees will be impacted, but some may have the opportunity to continue working on shows on a freelance basis. Winfrey held an emotional meeting at Harpo Studios to address staffers and thank them for their contributions. The closure of Harpo Studios may be a tipping point for TV production in Chicago, with doubts about whether there will be enough jobs to absorb the influx of talent. OWN, co-owned by Winfrey and Discovery Communications, has posted three consecutive years of growth and ranked as the No. 20 ad-supported cable network among women. Winfrey plans to continue pursuing interests outside of the executive suite, including film projects, international speaking engagements, and acting roles in scripted shows at OWN.

Madonna's teenage son, Rocco, has been living with his father Guy Ritchie in London instead of celebrating Christmas with his mother due to her controlling ways. The source close to Madonna stated that she is a strict disciplinarian and very controlling, which has led to tension between the two. Despite their close relationship, Rocco has expressed a desire to stay with his father. A New York judge ruled that Rocco must return home to Madonna before school begins in January, but it remains unclear if he will comply. She shared a moving message with her audience and asked for a moment of silence for the victims.

The document is a transcript of a speech given by President Trump at a lunch with leaders from various African countries including Cote d'Ivoire, Ethiopia, Ghana, Guinea, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, Uganda, and South Africa. The purpose of the meeting was to discuss economic partnerships, job creation opportunities, health initiatives, peace, and security issues between Africa and the United States.

President Trump highlighted the business potential in Africa and praised some African countries for their impressive economic reforms, such as Cote d'Ivoire. He also mentioned that several American firms are investing in Africa in various industries like agriculture, energy, transportation, healthcare, travel, and tourism.

The Miss World pageant, established in 1951, has announced that it will no longer feature a swimsuit round in its competition for the first time in 63 years. This decision comes as part of an effort to modernize and shift focus from physical appeal to "beauty with a purpose," emphasizing charity work, service projects, and intellectual abilities. The pageant aims to position its contestants as spokespersons and ambassadors rather than beauty queens. Miss World will continue to feature challenge events like sports, dance, talent, top model gown, Beauty with a Purpose video, and several interviews but will replace the swimsuit round with a beachwear competition. The final event featuring contestants in bikinis was held on Dec 14, 2014, with Rolene Strauss of South Africa being crowned the winner. This marks a significant change in the pageant's history and direction.

In a tragic incident, a father and son from Brooklyn died of a double opioid overdose while celebrating a family birthday party on Sunday. The father, Joseph Andrade, 44, was known to be an addict, while his 22-year-old son, Carlos, was not known to use drugs. The younger man reportedly joined his father in taking a mix of heroin and fentanyl after excusing themselves from the party to go for a smoke. Carlos was found dead just inside the foyer of his father's building, while Joseph was found outside the building. Both men were administered Narcan but died at Lutheran Medical Center. The incident is under investigation, and it is believed that over 1,300 people may have succumbed to drug-related deaths in 2016. This incident highlights the ongoing opioid epidemic in the United States, which was declared a public health emergency in October 2017.

In a recent interview with CNN, Donald Trump expressed the belief that the world would have been better off if dictators like Saddam Hussein and Moammar Gadhafi were still in power. A protein called cardiotrophin 1 (CT-1) discovered by Ottawa researchers might offer a potential treatment for heart failure. CT-1 can stimulate the heart to grow healthily, improving its ability to pump blood, similar to what happens during exercise or pregnancy. The growth is reversible and could potentially replace the need for heart transplants.

The team of researchers from The Ottawa Hospital, the University of Ottawa, the University of Ottawa Heart Institute, Carleton University, and private industry have been studying CT-1's mechanisms for over two decades. They found that it promotes heart repair and blood flow improvement in animal models with right heart failure and myocardial infarction (heart attack).

Heart failure is a leading cause of death and disability in high-income countries, often resulting from heart muscle damage following a heart attack. The new study represents a step forward in regenerative medicine, offering hope for patients diagnosed with heart failure.

CT-1 treatment could be ready for clinical trials in two to three years, potentially becoming available to the general population within a decade. If successful, it could vastly improve the prognosis for patients with heart failure. The researchers already have patents pending for using CT-1 to treat heart conditions and hope to partner with others to test the protein in human patients.

Pearson was one of 64 people charged in March as part of "Operation Usual Suspects," an investigation into a drug gang that allegedly bought drugs from New York and California and sold them on the streets of Baltimore. Pearson was caught on a wiretap conspiring with others to store drugs and money at her apartment, and was also implicated in a kidnapping and ransom case. Pearson has stated that she is moving to Los Angeles to avoid legal trouble in the future. This is not Pearson's first brush with the law; she served five years of an eight-year sentence for second-degree murder committed when she was 14.

Renowned film critic and television co-host Roger Ebert, known for his trademark thumbs up or thumbs down reviews that could make or break a movie's success, died on Thursday at the age of 70 in Chicago. He had worked for more than 40 years at The Chicago Sun-Times, where he was the best-known and most trusted film reviewer of his generation.

Ebert battled cancer since 2002, but continued to write reviews, commentary, and publish a cookbook despite losing his ability to eat, drink, and speak due to operations on his thyroid, salivary glands, and chin. In recent years, he became prolific on social media platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and his blog, where he engaged with millions of followers on various topics including movies, television shows, sports, and literature.

President Obama reacted to Ebert's death by stating that "for a generation of Americans — especially Chicagoans — Roger was the movies." Mick LaSalle, movie critic for The San Francisco Chronicle, wrote that Ebert occupied a unique space in film criticism, being both influential and esteemed while having widespread influence.

Ebert popularized television film criticism with his collaboration with Gene Siskel, beginning in 1975. Despite initial reservations about working together, their partnership became iconic and changed the face of film criticism.

In a groundbreaking study, researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to scan the brains of infants at high risk for autism, those with older siblings diagnosed with the disorder. By analyzing brain growth patterns between 6 and 24 months, they were able to predict 80% of these infants who would later be diagnosed with autism at 2 years of age. The study suggests that early brain development biomarkers could help identify high-risk babies before symptoms appear, potentially allowing for earlier interventions and improved outcomes. The technology is not yet ready for clinical use but could pave the way for a tool to predict autism in high-risk infants before their first birthday.

Apple has filed a patent for a protective mechanism aimed at preventing damage to electronic devices, particularly the iPhone, during accidents such as drops. The system involves a sensor that detects when a device is falling and how it's positioned relative to the ground. It uses data on the position and speed of the fall to make decisions on how best to land the device to avoid damage.

The patent suggests several methods for this, including reorientating the device mid-air using weighted masses, aeroplane-like foils, or gas propulsion devices. The system also explores the possibility of ejecting cables when rapid movement is detected to prevent the device from being pulled to the ground.

The patent was filed in 2011 and credits Nicholas V. King and Fletcher Rothkopf as its inventors. However, it's unclear whether this system will be integrated into an iPhone anytime soon due to the handset's trend towards a thin-and-light design.

The bill is expected to face a difficult battle in both chambers of Congress, particularly in the House where narrow margins could make passage uncertain.

The Nobel Peace Prize for 2012 was awarded to the European Union, recognizing its contributions to peace and reconciliation, democracy, and human rights over the years. The EU's unique structure as a supranational group of states has allowed it to integrate most European countries, including former military dictatorships and communist states. Despite criticisms of bureaucracy and undemocratic practices, the EU's laws support integration and offer a structured way for legal redress.

The decision to award the prize to an organization is not unprecedented, but it has been met with mixed reactions due to the current economic turmoil in Europe. The prize of $1.2 million has been seen as both a mockery given the financial crisis and a pep talk for a continent that needs encouragement. The decision was leaked early by Norway's NRK public radio, despite Norway not being part of the EU.

The awarding of the prize to an organization like the European Union is considered one of the more unusual choices in the history of the Nobel Peace Prize, alongside recipients such as Yasser Arafat, Henry Kissinger, and Barack Obama. The decision was made by the Norwegian Nobel Committee, which selects the laureates for the Peace Prize.

The University of Granada scientists have discovered a phenomenon they've named 'The Pinocchio Effect,' where the tip of the nose heats up due to anxiety, particularly when lying. This effect was found using thermal imaging cameras on volunteers. The researchers also claim that thermal imaging can detect sexual desire and arousal in both men and women, as well as identify distinct types of dance such as ballet through specific temperature changes in the body. The scientists reached these conclusions by observing changes in the brain's insular cortex when volunteers lied about their feelings. When someone dances Flamenco, for example, the temperature in their buttocks lowers and rises in their forearms, creating a unique thermal footprint for that dance style.

Chicagoans were praised for their witty banter and observational humor, particularly their ability to poke fun at the city's weather and public transportation. However, the study found that despite their funny ranking, Chicagoans are not great joke tellers as they prefer to mine humor from their everyday situations. The top 10 cities, according to the study, also include Boston, Atlanta, Washington D.C., Portland, Ore., New York, Los Angeles, Denver, San Francisco, and Seattle. The study was led by Peter McGraw, an associate professor at CU-Boulder's Leeds School of Business, and is part of his new book, "The Humor Code: A Global Search for What Makes Things Funny."

The study conducted by Dr. Meghan Azad and her team at the University of Manitoba suggests that artificial sweeteners, commonly found in diet drinks, do not aid in weight loss but are linked to an increased risk of weight gain, obesity, high blood pressure, diabetes, and other health issues. The research, published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ), is a meta-review of 37 previously published studies that looked at the diet habits of over 400,000 people.

The study found no significant evidence supporting weight loss from regularly consuming artificial sweeteners. Longer observational studies showed a link between the sweeteners and higher risks of weight gain, obesity, high blood pressure, diabetes, and other health issues. However, the researchers noted that most studies were observational, which means they can show a link but cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship.

Among the seven randomized controlled trials (RCTs), regular consumption of sweeteners had no significant effect on weight loss. The team found that regular use of sweeteners was associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure, and modest increases in weight and waist circumferences.

Krzysztof Szczypiorski, a Polish cybersecurity researcher, has developed a method of hiding secret messages in dance music, specifically Balearic techno, which is popular in Ibiza. He uses subtle changes in tempo to encode Morse code-like messages that can be decoded by analyzing the beats per minute or listening closely. Szczypiorski calls this system StegIbiza, a play on the term steganography, and has conducted two experiments with it, one involving twenty participants and another at an open-air summer party. In both cases, the manipulated tempo was not noticeable to most listeners, but caused issues when it was too extreme and disrupted the overall enjoyment of the music. Music steganography is an old practice, but Szczypiorski's work is unique in its application to club music. However, it seems that Szczypiorski may have learned a lesson about not overcomplicating the tempo too much for a dance floor audience.

British restaurant chain Pret a Manger is under scrutiny after a second customer died from an allergic reaction to food containing undisclosed allergens. The first incident occurred in 2016 when 15-year-old Natasha Ednan-Laperouse died after eating a baguette containing sesame, which was not listed on the label. Following this, Pret promised to improve its labeling.

Pret has been in a dispute with the vegan brand CoYo, a supplier of its dairy-free yogurt, over the cause of the second death. CoYo denies any responsibility and accuses Pret of hindering their investigation by failing to provide crucial information.

Natasha's parents, who have been campaigning for allergy awareness and changes in food labeling laws since her death, expressed their condolences over the second incident. They urge all parties to work together to find the true cause of the deaths and improve food safety measures.

This legislative achievement is a significant victory for Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and GOP leaders, who struggled all year to push through an Obamacare repeal measure. A mountain lion broke into a home in Boulder, Colorado, killing a family's cat named Klondike. The big cat likely entered through a window and roamed around the house for over an hour before animal control officers used non-lethal rounds to scare it out. Neighbors watched from their windows as the incident unfolded. The mountain lion was later found near Boulder Canyon, uninjured. The homeowner has expressed concern but was reassured by authorities that the mountain lion is unlikely to return after being hit with bean bags. The incident has prompted residents to be more vigilant in securing their homes, especially at night.

Rutgers University has announced a 2.3% increase in undergraduate tuition and fees for the 2015-2016 academic year, amounting to an additional $300 for in-state students on the New Brunswick campus. This brings the total annual tuition and fees to $14,131. Room and board costs are also increasing by about 2.6%. The average student living on campus will pay a total bill of $26,185, a $624 increase from last year.

The Rutgers Board of Governors approved the tuition hike during a meeting on the New Brunswick campus, also approving a new $3.8 billion budget for the 65,000-student university. The increase is necessary to cover rising costs, including new contracts with unions and a 3.7% cut in state funding for Rutgers operations.

Similar increases have been approved for most graduate students, with out-of-state students seeing a slightly higher increase of about 3.4%. However, undergraduate tuition varies by campus and school within the Rutgers system.

The report also mentions that Rutgers University has one of the highest tuition rates among state universities in the nation but is considered a high aid state where low-income students receive generous financial aid packages to help cover costs

In April, the U.S. economy added 160,000 new jobs, which is below market expectations of 205,000 jobs. The unemployment rate remained steady at 5%. Over the past three months, employers have averaged adding 200,000 new positions. Hourly earnings showed growth of 2.5% over the past year, while the labor force participation rate decreased to 62.8%.

The economy has been experiencing mixed signals recently. While the stock market and consumer confidence have shown signs of improvement, the bond market indicates stagnation with a drop in 10-year Treasury bond yields from 2% at the start of the year to 1.8% now. The Federal Reserve has held off on raising interest rates after doing so for the first time in nearly a decade last December due to the unevenness in the economy.

The jobs report for April is causing complications for the Fed, as it was weaker than expected and follows a period of slow economic growth. There will be another jobs report before the next Fed meeting in June, which could further impact their decision-making process.

On June 25, 2017, an oil tanker explosion occurred on a highway near Bahawalpur, Pakistan, resulting in the death of at least 153 people and injuring over 100 others. The victims were primarily local residents who had gathered to collect leaking fuel from the accident site. Many of the injured suffered severe burns, and some may require DNA testing for identification. The tanker was en route from Karachi to Lahore when it lost control and crashed. Authorities believe that the fire started after someone attempted to light a cigarette near the spilled fuel. Pakistan's Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif has expressed his condolences and is returning to Pakistan to address the incident.

A United Airlines passenger was forcibly removed from a flight in Chicago on Monday after refusing to be "voluntarily" bumped from an overbooked flight. The incident, which was captured on video and went viral, has caused widespread outrage and embarrassment for the airline. United's initial response to the publicity was criticized as insincere and Orwellian, with CEO Oscar Munoz issuing a statement that was seen as defensive and lacking in empathy. It is unclear how United's rules regarding "refusal of transport" and "denied boarding compensation" apply to this incident, as the passenger was already seated and instructed to deplane. The airline has been accused of poor treatment of passengers in the past, with incidents including refusing to allow three young girls to board a flight because they were wearing leggings and diverting a flight to kick an autistic child off. The incident has sparked calls for a boycott of United Airlines.

The National Park Service (NPS) has proposed increasing entrance fees during peak seasons at 17 highly visited national parks to fund infrastructure improvements. These parks include Yosemite, Grand Canyon, Yellowstone, and others. If implemented, the new fee structure would be as follows: $70 for a private non-commercial vehicle, $50 for motorcycles, and $30 for pedestrians or cyclists during peak season. An annual pass for any of these parks would cost $75. The proposal aims to generate an estimated $70 million in additional revenue per year, with 80% remaining in the park where it is collected.

The public comment period on this proposal will be open from October 24, 2017, to November 23, 2017, on the NPS Planning, Environment and Public Comment (PEPC) website. Written comments can also be sent to the National Park Service at a specified mailing address. The proposed fee increases would not affect the $80 annual America the Beautiful pass that provides entrance to all federal lands.

The Amtrak train that derailed in Philadelphia on Tuesday, resulting in eight deaths and over 200 injuries, was reportedly struck by an object before the crash, according to a conductor who overheard radio transmissions between the Amtrak engineer and a Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA) train engineer. The SEPTA engineer had reported a broken windshield and placed his train into emergency stop after being hit by a projectile. The NTSB is investigating this report, interviewing the Amtrak engineer Brandon Bostian, and examining damage to the lower portion of the Amtrak train's windshield. Bostian had no recollection of anything that happened after passing the North Philadelphia station, where he sustained a concussion. The NTSB is also reviewing outward-facing video from the SEPTA train and radio transmissions. Investigators are considering various factors including speed, track conditions, and human error as they try to determine the cause of the derailment. Passengers aboard other trains reported being struck by objects before the crash, adding to the mystery of what happened. The Philadelphia District Attorney's office is closely monitoring the investigation but has not found any conclusive evidence indicating criminal recklessness on the part of Bostian.

A paraplegic man named Ricky Gilmore, 49, was left stranded in the New Mexico desert for three days after he hitchhiked with a couple who later abandoned him without his wheelchair. Gilmore dragged himself about four miles down a dirt road to survive, sustaining injuries to his skin, wrist, and kidneys from dehydration and lack of food and water. He was found by a motorist on Tocito Road, near Shiprock, NM, and is currently being treated at the Northern Navajo Medical Center for acute kidney failure, a sprained wrist, and a blood infection. Gilmore filed a police report with the Shiprock Police Department, but no details have been confirmed yet. The incident has raised concerns about the treatment of people with disabilities and the lack of empathy shown by those who passed by without helping.

The Thai authorities, equipped with tranquilizer guns, are attempting to capture and remove approximately 137 tigers from a controversial Buddhist temple in Kanchanaburi Province, west of Bangkok. The temple, known as the "Tiger Temple," has been criticized for mistreating the animals and posing a danger to visitors.

On Monday, wildlife officers arrived to remove the tigers but were initially refused entry by temple officials. After a standoff, eight tigers were sedated and transported to three government animal refuges across Thailand. The authorities are expected to continue this operation for a week.

The Tiger Temple has been accused of illegal breeding and trafficking of the animals, and it has resisted previous efforts to remove the tigers. The temple was planning to operate as a zoo, but the plan fell through due to insufficient resources. Animal rights activists have long criticized the temple for its inadequate care of the animals and flouting of regulations restricting their trade.

A 25-year-old woman named Lauren Mann from Colorado, United States, was found dead in her apartment in Vienna, Austria on Tuesday, January 28, 2016. The cause of death has not been determined yet, as an autopsy did not reveal any immediate cause and toxicological tests are pending. Mann had been working as an au pair in Vienna and was reported missing by her employer after she failed to show up for work. She graduated from the University of Colorado-Boulder's College of Music in 2012. The police are treating the case as a homicide, but no specific suspect has been identified yet. Mann's friends and neighbors have been contacted by the police for information. The U.S. Embassy in Vienna is providing consular assistance.

Norway is set to become the first country to transition completely to digital radio, starting on January 11, 2017. The government's decision to switch off FM radio channels is aimed at saving money and improving radio quality by eight times through Digital Audio Broadcasting (DAB). This move is expected to save Norway approximately 200 million Norwegian Krone annually, which is about $23.5 million.

However, the transition has been met with opposition from a majority of the population, with 66% opposing the switch and only 17% in favor. Critics argue that the move could lead to missed emergency alerts for drivers who don't upgrade to DAB or aren't within the area of receiving a local FM radio signal. Additionally, those without digital-ready cars will need to purchase a digital adaptor for their FM car radios at around 1,500 Norwegian Krones ($176).

The transition has been planned for years and Norway's DAB network already has 25 national radio channels, with the potential to support 20 more. Other countries such as Britain, Switzerland, and Denmark are also considering a similar move towards digital-only radio by 2020. The switch-off will begin in the northern city of Bodø on January 11 and is expected to be completed by the end of the year.

A taxi driver named Wang Mingqing from southwest China will be reunited with his daughter Qifeng, who went missing in 1994 when she was three years old, on Tuesday. The reunion comes after a 27-year-old woman named Kang Ying contacted the Wangs via social media and took a DNA test that confirmed she was their long-lost daughter.

Wang and his wife Liu Chengying ran a fruit stall in Chengdu, Sichuan province, when Qifeng went missing. They spent years searching for her, but to no avail. In 2015, Wang became a taxi driver and used the opportunity to ask his passengers to help spread the word about his search on social media. He also distributed thousands of fliers with details about Qifeng's case.

Over the past three years, Wang was contacted by numerous women who suspected they might be his daughter, but DNA tests ruled them out. However, a breakthrough came late last year when a police sketch artist produced a drawing of what Qifeng might look like as an adult. Kang Ying saw the picture and realized she resembled it.

However, the opposition boycotted the election and denounced it as illegitimate due to widespread irregularities. The United States, along with several other countries, rejected the results of the election, with US Deputy Secretary of State John Sullivan stating that they would not recognize the result and were considering oil sanctions against Venezuela. The opposition leaders Henri Falcon and Javier Bertucci called for a new election, claiming vote buying and electoral fraud. Maduro dismissed the criticisms and vowed to stabilize Venezuela's economy amidst a calamitous economic meltdown that has seen millions flee the country since 2015.

Fresh clashes have erupted in South Sudan's capital, Juba, resulting in at least 66 soldiers being killed. The US embassy has advised all citizens to depart immediately due to the ongoing violence. The fighting between army factions is reportedly a bid for power by former vice president Riek Machar, who was sacked by President Salva Kiir in July. The two men, from different ethnic groups with a history of conflict, have long been political rivals. A Canadian sniper from Joint Task Force 2 has set a new world record for the longest confirmed kill shot in military history at a distance of 3,540 meters during an operation in Iraq within the last month. The shot was made using a McMillan TAC-50 sniper rifle while firing from a high-rise and took under 10 seconds to hit the target. The Canadian Armed Forces confirmed the record-breaking shot, but did not disclose specific details about when and how it occurred for operational security reasons. The previous world record was held by British sniper Craig Harrison, who made a shot from 2,475 meters away in 2009. Canada's JTF2 special forces are primarily tasked with counterterrorism, sniper operations, and hostage rescue.

In the Republican primary race, Newt Gingrich has decided to continue his campaign despite back-to-back losses in Alabama and Mississippi, aiming instead to prevent Mitt Romney from securing the nomination before the convention. 1. Level I (0.7 for Earth according to Carl Sagan): Civilizations that harness all resources of a planet.
2. Level II: Civilizations that harness all radiation from a star.
3. Level III: Civilizations that harness all resources from a galaxy and then move on to another one.

The Pew Research Center's recent analysis shows that 60% of Americans believe in evolution, while a third reject it, stating that living things have existed in their present form since the beginning of time. This percentage remains steady compared to 2009.

The survey found that about half of those who believe in evolution attribute it to natural processes such as natural selection, while many Americans believe God or a supreme being played a role in guiding the evolution of living things. Approximately a quarter of adults believe that a supreme being guided the evolution of living things for the purpose of creating humans and other life in their current form.

White evangelical Protestants are particularly likely to believe that humans have existed in their present form since the beginning of time, with 64% holding this view. The gap between Republicans and Democrats on beliefs about evolution has grown, with only 43% of Republicans believing in human evolution compared to 67% of Democrats.

The survey was conducted March 21-April 8, 2013, among a representative sample of 1,983 adults in all 50 states and the District of Columbia, with a margin of error of +/- 3 percentage points.

An Egyptian woman named Eman Ahmed Abd El Aty, believed to be the world's heaviest woman at 500kg (1,102lb), will soon travel to Mumbai, India for weight reduction surgery. The Indian embassy initially denied her visa request due to her inability to travel to Cairo for fingerprinting. However, after a Twitter appeal by the surgeon Dr Muffazal Lakdawala, India's Minister of External Affairs Sushma Swaraj granted the medical visa. Abd El Aty will be flown on a chartered plane to Mumbai where Lakdawala plans to operate. The surgery is expected to help her lose at least 200 to 300 pounds and she may need to remain in Mumbai for months as she recovers.

Two balloon pilots, Troy Bradley from New Mexico and Leonid Tiukhtyaev from Russia, set off from Saga, Japan on January 25, 2015, aiming to break the world records for both distance and duration in a gas-filled balloon. On Thursday, they surpassed the distance record of 5,209 miles (8,383 km) set by the Double Eagle V in 1981, and are now heading towards a landing in Mexico's Baja California on Saturday. They are also expected to break the duration record of 137 hours aloft set in 1978 by another team crossing the Atlantic. The balloon is equipped with monitoring instruments and can stay aloft for up to 10 days, but weather conditions have forced changes in their flight plan. Their records must be officially certified by aviation authorities.

The article discusses the accidental destruction of an ancient Neolithic tomb in northwest Spain, which was believed to be around 6,000 years old and had heritage status. Workers mistook the tomb for a broken stone picnic table and repaired it by pouring concrete into the burial chamber and placing a new picnic table on top. An investigation is underway, and officials were not aware of the site's existence, including the town's mayor. The archaeologist who discovered the error described it as a "monumental error."

The article also mentions that similar incidents have occurred in other countries, such as China and Belize, where ancient remains have been destroyed intentionally or unknowingly. However, it is noted that mistakes like this are not common in Spain, where monuments over 100 years old are preserved by law. The article concludes by mentioning a previous incident where workers destroyed a 2,300-year-old Mayan pyramid in Belize for road repair without knowing it was a Mayan ruin.

The article discusses a survey by OfficeTeam that found office workers spend an average of 56 minutes per day using their cell phones for non-work activities, amounting to nearly five hours of lost productivity each week. Personal email and social media were the primary distractions, followed by sports sites, mobile gaming, and shopping. Additionally, employees spend an average of 42 minutes a day attending to personal tasks such as errands, totaling 3.5 hours of lost productivity per week.

Younger workers (ages 18-34) were found to be the biggest offenders, spending an average of 70 minutes on mobile devices and 48 minutes on personal tasks each workday, equating to almost 10 hours of lost time per week. OfficeTeam's survey included responses from over 600 workers employed in office environments and senior managers at U.S. companies with 20 or more employees.

The survey also found that 58% of office workers use their personal devices to access websites blocked by their companies, but only 39% of managers think this happens frequently. Men were more likely than women to frequently access blocked websites using their cellphones (68% vs. 43%). OfficeTeam suggested that employees take advantage of breaks during lunch and throughout the day to catch up on non-work email or errands to manage their time effectively.

Researchers used 3D computer tomography to examine Ötzi's mouth and found evidence of accidents that led to tooth loss and a broken molar potentially caused by a stone in his food. The gruel he consumed may be the cause of his cavities and gum disease.

In addition, an international team sequenced Ötzi's entire genome, which revealed several interesting findings. Ötzi had a genetic predisposition to arteriosclerosis despite having no known risk factors such as being overweight, inactive, or a smoker. The genome sequencing also placed Ötzi in the rare G2A4 haplogroup, linking his paternal genes to a population that migrated from the Near East to Europe at the beginning of the Neolithic era.

Ötzi's genetic profile suggests he was most closely related to small populations living on the islands of Sardinia and Corsica, as well as some remote areas of Georgia and Russia. Rapper T.I., whose real name is Clifford Harris, was arrested early Wednesday on charges of disorderly conduct, public drunkenness, and simple assault after an argument with a security guard at his gated community outside Atlanta. The incident occurred when T.I. lost his key and the guard refused to let him in. He was released on bail following the arrest.

T.I., who has previously served time in prison for federal gun charges and drug-related probation violations, believes he was unfairly targeted by white police officers due to being an affluent African-American celebrity. According to T.I., the argument started because the security guard was allegedly asleep on duty. He claims that the guard refused to apologize for his actions and that he plans to take legal action against his Homeowners Association (HOA) over the incident.

T.I.'s attorney has released a statement supporting his claim of wrongful arrest, and he spent some time with his family after being released, celebrating his son Major's 10th birthday. The rapper is one of the biggest names in hip-hop, with multiple platinum-selling albums and singles, production credits, and roles in films like "ATL" and "American Gangster."

The shooting of two police officers in Ferguson, Missouri early Thursday morning has been strongly condemned by Attorney General Eric Holder who described the incident as an "ambush" and a "pure act of violence." The officers, one from St. Louis County and another from Webster Groves, were shot during a protest that followed the resignation of Ferguson's police chief in response to a Justice Department report finding racial bias within the force. Both officers are currently in serious condition at a local hospital. A manhunt is underway to find those responsible for the shooting, and rewards are being offered for information leading to an arrest. The shooting has intensified tensions in Ferguson, which has been rocked by protests since last August following the shooting of unarmed black 18-year-old Michael Brown by a white police officer. The city's police force is almost entirely white, while a majority of its residents are black. The shooting is the latest in a series of incidents targeting police officers in the wake of the Brown case.

The article discusses an online auction of personal effects belonging to Ted Kaczynski, also known as the Unabomber, who carried out a mail bombing campaign between 1978 and 1995, resulting in three deaths and 23 injuries. The auction is being held by the U.S. Marshal's office to raise funds to pay off a $15 million restitution order to his victims and their families. Some of the items attracting attention include Kaczynski's handwritten manifesto, his iconic hoodie, Smith-Corona typewriter, and hand-bowed wood saw. The auction ends on June 2, and there is debate over whether it is a sad sign of the times or if there is historical value in the items being sold. Crime memorabilia collector Scott Michaels believes there is value in owning items belonging to infamous criminals, while art historian Elyse Luray dismisses most of what is being sold as only valuable to "weird" collectors.

The jury found that Oculus, which Facebook bought in 2014, had breached a contract with Zenimax when launching its own VR headset, the Rift. Oculus said it would appeal against the ruling.

The case threatened to overshadow Facebook's latest results, which showed strong growth for the fourth quarter. Montana Congressman-elect Greg Gianforte pleaded guilty to misdemeanor assault for body-slamming a reporter during last year's election campaign. He was sentenced to 180 days of deferred sentence, 40 hours of community service, 20 hours of anger management, and a $300 fine. President Trump praised Gianforte despite the incident, causing controversy among some who view it as an attack on press freedom. The incident is also personal for Trump as he is campaigning to unseat Democratic Senator Jon Tester, whom he believes was responsible for allegations against White House physician Adm. Ronny Jackson that led to his failed nomination for the Department of Veterans Affairs. The midterm elections are seen as an election of Kavanaugh, immigration, law and order, and common sense by Trump.

Thousands of farmed Atlantic salmon were accidentally released into the waters between Anacortes and the San Juan Islands after a net pen at Cooke Aquaculture's fish farm near Cypress Island collapsed, causing concern among tribal fishers and environmental groups. The Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) is urging the public to catch as many of the fish as possible, with no limit on size or number. It is estimated that between 4,000 and 5,000 fish escaped, but the exact number is unknown. Officials believe the collapse was caused by high tides and strong currents, although some experts question this explanation. The Atlantic salmon are non-native to the Pacific Northwest and have been fraught with controversy due to concerns about their impact on native salmon populations and potential for disease transmission. Cooke Aquaculture is also proposing a larger net pen in the Strait of Juan de Fuca, which has been met with opposition from fishers and environmental groups.

The world's cheapest smartphone, the Freedom 251, is set to be delivered by Ringing Bells Pvt Ltd starting from June 30th, despite initial skepticism and allegations of an elaborate scam. The company has managed to produce nearly two lakh units of the phone, which was initially planned to deliver 25 lakh handsets before June 30th. The Freedom 251 features a 4-inch dual-SIM screen, 1GB RAM, 8GB internal memory, and runs on Android 5.1 (Lollipop). It will be available in black and white colors and offers an 8MP primary camera with flash, a 3.2MP front camera for selfies, and a 1,800 mAh battery. The company is also planning to launch a 32-inch HD LED television called "Freedom" next month, priced at less than Rs 10,000. Despite taking a loss of Rs 140-Rs 150 per unit, the CEO Mohit Goel feels vindicated and plans to sell around 200,000 Freedom 251 every month. The company has faced criticism and doubts over its ability to produce such an affordable phone, but it has managed to gather a whopping 70 million registrations for the device.

On August 13, Shanann was reported missing by a friend after returning from a short work trip to Arizona. Emmanuel Macron has been elected as the President of France, defeating far-right candidate Marine Le Pen in a decisive victory. The result was welcomed by leaders across the world, particularly within the EU, who saw it as a significant victory for a strong and united Europe. German Chancellor Angela Merkel congratulated Macron, stating that his win was a victory for a European future. European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker also offered his congratulations, saying the French had chosen "liberty, equality and fraternity."

One of Macron's new responsibilities as French president will be negotiating the terms of Britain's exit from the EU along with other leaders. British Prime Minister Theresa May called Macron to congratulate him on his election victory and discuss Brexit. US President Donald Trump also offered his best wishes to the new French president, despite earlier praising Le Pen over her security policy.

Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau was quick to telephone France's election winner, stating that he looked forward to working closely with Macron on a progressive agenda. Brazil's President Michel Temer and Australia's prime minister also congratulated Macron on his victory.

The U.S. military will continue to allow transgender individuals to serve openly until further direction from President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Jim Mattis, according to a memo from Gen. Joseph Dunford, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The memo was issued in response to Trump's tweet announcing that the U.S. government will not "accept or allow" transgender people to serve in any capacity in the military. The Pentagon has been unable to explain Trump's announcement and has stated that there will be no modifications to current policy for now. Criticism for Trump's action was immediate and strong from both political parties, with many expressing concern about the impact on transgender service members and the potential disruption to military readiness and unit cohesion.

On Saturday, two men skiing in Alaska's Rainbow Mountains were caught in an avalanche. One man, identified tentatively as Eric Peterson of Delta Junction, was killed, and the other, Michael Hopper from Fairbanks, survived after digging himself out for 2-3 hours. The body of the deceased has not been recovered yet. Hopper, who is the owner of Black Rapids Lodge, is known to be well-versed in mountain safety. A motorist named Kimberly McRoberts found Hopper near the road and helped him call for help. Responding agencies included Alaska State Troopers, military members from Black Rapids, Fort Greely Fire Department, and Rural Delta Fire and Rescue. The avalanche site is considered unstable and deteriorating due to additional snowfall. Recovery of the body will be attempted when weather conditions improve. This is an ongoing story; updates can be found on KTUU.com and Channel 2 newscasts.

The report by Human Rights Watch reveals that in 2012, only 3% of U.S. drug defendants in federal cases chose to go to trial instead of pleading guilty. This low percentage is attributed to the threat of mandatory minimum sentences and the power held by prosecutors to offer smaller sentences as part of a deal. The report argues that prosecutors essentially coerce defendants into pleading guilty due to the risk of longer prison sentences if found guilty after trial.

In 1980, the percentage of federal drug defendants who pleaded guilty was slightly over 60%, and it has steadily increased since then, largely due to mandatory-minimum sentencing laws enacted in the mid-80s. These laws require harsh predetermined sentences for drug distribution and possession, while giving prosecutors the ability to offer defendants smaller sentences as part of a plea deal.

The report found that defendants who took their case to trial faced prison sentences on average 11 years longer than those who pleaded guilty. The study also uncovered numerous cases where defendants received extremely long prison sentences, including one case where a woman was sentenced to over 45 years for first-time drug offenses.
