Researchers from the Czech Republic have found that people can predict a man's intelligence by looking at his face, but not a woman's. The team found that faces perceived as highly intelligent are longer with a wider distance between the eyes, a larger nose, an upturned mouth, and a sharper chin. By contrast, faces perceived as less intelligent have broader, more rounded features and a shorter nose. However, these facial characteristics were not correlated with actual IQ scores. The team used static facial photographs of 40 men and 40 women to test the relationship between measured IQ, perceived intelligence, and facial shape. Both men and women were able to accurately evaluate the intelligence of men by viewing facial photographs, but not women. The researchers suggest that this may be due to the fact that attractiveness clouds judgement or that women are judged according to their attractiveness, preventing an accurate assessment of their intelligence. The study was published in the journal PLoS One.

The Jamaican bobsled team, returning to the Winter Olympic Games after a 12-year absence, has a new theme song titled "The Bobsled Song" to accompany their run at the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi. Composed by Sidney Mills and Jon Notar, the catchy reggae tune syncs with the twists and turns of the Olympic bobsled track. An 8-bit music video is also available for the song on YouTube. The Jamaican team qualified for the two-man bobsled competition without racing in any World Cup events but accumulating enough points in lower-tier races in North America. Despite being considered a long shot to win a medal, their journey echoes the story depicted in the film "Cool Runnings." Fans can download and play the song on BobsledSong.com at the exact moment the Jamaican team begins their race on Feb 16, 2014.

Derrick Henry, Alabama running back and Yulee native, is expected to enter the 2016 NFL Draft if he wins or loses the Heisman Trophy on Saturday. His college workload has been a concern for some analysts due to his high number of carries in three seasons, with only 78 times in NFL history having a running back had at least 340 attempts in a season. However, Henry's balance, vision, and patience have been praised by former scout Dan Hatman, who believes he is more reliant on scheme and blocking to be effective. Hatman predicts that Henry will be drafted in the fourth round (100-150 range) and compares him to current rookies Matt Jones and Karlos Williams. He also suggests that Henry would fit better in teams with a zone blocking system, such as Oakland, San Francisco, Pittsburgh, and Carolina. The draft stock of Henry and other running backs could be impacted by how many NFL teams feel they are set at the position.

The small community of Sutherland Springs, Texas was rocked by a mass shooting at its downtown church on Sunday, November 5th. At least 26 people were killed and over 20 injured when a gunman opened fire during a service at the First Baptist Church. The shooter has been identified as Devin Patrick Kelley, a 26-year-old from New Braunfels. He was later found dead in his vehicle after a brief chase north into neighboring Guadalupe County. The victims ranged in age from 5 to 72 years old and included several members of the same family. The church is both a religious center for the town and a provider of community services, offering free meals and working with local nonprofits. The shooting has devastated the small community and sparked calls for increased gun control measures.

The Navy has its first female candidates for two elite special operations jobs previously closed to women, including a prospective SEAL officer and a special warfare combatant crewman. These candidates are currently undergoing training and will have to complete the same rigorous training as their male counterparts without any allowances for physical differences. The path ahead for them is challenging, with attrition rates in these programs being high. It may take months or even years before a woman graduates from these elite Navy positions. Additionally, the Navy has also admitted a transgender person into the special warfare combatant crewman role.

The article discusses the success of a creationist campaign in South Korea, where efforts have been made to remove references to evolution from high school textbooks. The antipathy towards evolution in South Korea is partly due to strong Christianity in the country, where about half of citizens practice a religion, mostly split between Christianity and Buddhism. A 20-year-old nursing student named Holly Bobo from Parsons, TN has been missing since April 13, after being taken away by an individual dressed in camouflage clothing. A similar incident occurred in Centerville, TN, where a woman named Heather Sullivan was approached by a tall, skinny man outside her home in January. Both incidents happened near wooded areas. Heather Sullivan and Mark Gwyn, director of the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, have suggested a possible connection between the two cases. An $80,000 reward has been offered for information related to Holly Bobo's case, with hundreds of area residents searching the woods near her home. Holly's family continues to hold out hope that she is alive.

The Nielsen Company's Women of Tomorrow Study, which surveyed 6,500 women across 21 countries from February to April 2011, found that Indian women are the most stressed globally, with 87% reporting feeling stressed most of the time and 82% claiming they have no time to relax. Mexican (74%) and Russian (69%) women also reported high levels of stress.

The survey revealed that Indian women were more likely to spend disposable income on themselves, particularly on health and beauty products and clothes. Women in developing economies tended to spend more on these items, groceries, and education for their children, while those in developed economies spent more on vacations, savings, and paying off debt.

The study found that women worldwide are under pressure due to their multiple roles but that the social infrastructure allowing them to navigate these roles differs between emerging and developed markets. Women in emerging markets tend to be more stressed than women in developed countries due to factors such as rapid social change in emerging economies compressing what took half a century to evolve in developed countries into five years.

McDonald's has launched its nationwide all-day breakfast menu, but with some limitations. The menu varies by location and does not include popular items like McGriddle sandwiches, bagel sandwiches, cinnamon melts, "Big Breakfast" platters, Egg White Delight McMuffins, steak, egg and cheese McMuffins, or southern style chicken biscuits.

In markets offering biscuits, customers can order bacon, egg and cheese biscuits, sausage biscuit with egg, and sausage biscuits.

The all-day breakfast menu is available in addition to the regular morning breakfast menu, which includes the signature Egg McMuffin and other favorites. Menu items may vary by location.

The unclaimed body of Tamerlan Tsarnaev, one of the Boston Marathon bombers, has been taken by a funeral home in Worcester, Massachusetts. His relatives have demanded an independent autopsy before burial. Despite opposition from some cemeteries due to safety concerns, Peter Stefan, the owner of the funeral home, plans to find Tsarnaev a resting place in Massachusetts. The second autopsy is scheduled after which a grave site will be sought if none is found, even by asking the government for assistance.

Tsarnaev died on April 19 from gunshot wounds and blunt trauma caused by police and being run over by a car. His younger brother Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, who is being held at a federal prison, is charged with using a weapon of mass destruction in the bombing that killed three and injured more than 260 on April 15.

Investigators found explosives residue in the apartment Tamerlan Tsarnaev shared with his family, and believe that the marathon was not the original target. The brothers had initially planned a suicide attack on the city's Independence Day celebration but changed their plans due to an earlier readiness of the bombs.

The Oakland general strike called by Occupy Oakland drew thousands for rallies and marches on Wednesday. The event turned chaotic early Thursday after protesters took over a vacant building and police moved in, firing tear gas and flashbang grenades.

The protests disrupted the Port of Oakland as protesters blocked truckers from entering the port, causing scuffles with some truckers. Some protesters remained near the police line, but most dispersed by 3:30 a.m. The general strike had a significant impact on the city, with many businesses closed and traffic disrupted. The event ended with dozens of arrests and injuries.

During his 24-hour run from the law, he allegedly stole a total of four vehicles. He was arrested in Kankakee Township in rural LaPorte County, Ind., and was arraigned there on auto theft charges.

Elliot led deputies on a short chase in one of the stolen vehicles before Stop Sticks were deployed, causing him to lose control and crash into a snowbank. Elliot was wearing jeans that were too big and "a couple of jackets" during his arrest. He appeared tired, like he had not slept in days. Michigan Governor Rick Snyder thanked law enforcement agencies for their efforts in the search and capture of Elliot.

In the New Hampshire Republican primary, Donald Trump finished first, while Ohio Governor John Kasich presented himself as a compassionate alternative to the negative campaigning that has dominated the race so far. Kasich, who is in second place, believes his strong finish will help him gather momentum for future primaries. Bernie Sanders won the Democratic primary, defeating Hillary Clinton and delivering a convincing victory that could force her campaign to reassess its operations. Sanders' win was attributed to an enthusiastic and aroused electorate, and he plans to continue his campaign in New York City. Clinton conceded the race and vowed to fight for every vote in upcoming contests. Both Democratic candidates have been facing criticism over their foreign policy proposals and preparedness to be Commander-in-Chief.

President Trump attacked one of the women accusing Brett Kavanaugh, his Supreme Court nominee, with harsh language on Tuesday, dismissing Deborah Ramirez's account of sexual misconduct as she was "totally inebriated and all messed up." Trump accused Democrats of playing a "con game" to derail his nomination. Kavanaugh has strongly denied the allegations from two women. The Senate Judiciary Committee is scheduled to vote on Kavanaugh's confirmation this Friday, with the full Senate voting next Tuesday. Republicans are under pressure to confirm Kavanaugh amid warnings that failure could cost them in November's midterm elections. A third accuser may come forward soon, according to lawyer Michael Avenatti. Democrats have criticized the Republican's handling of the hearings and called for an FBI investigation into the allegations.

The preliminary report from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) regarding a fatal plane crash in East Haven, Connecticut on August 9th describes the aircraft as being "inverted" and traveling at a high rate of speed before the crash. The multi-engine propeller-driven plane, which had taken off from Teterboro Airport in New Jersey, struck two homes on Charter Oak Avenue and killed four people: pilot William Henningsgaard, his 17-year-old son Maxwell, 13-year-old Sade Brantley, and her 1-year-old sister Madisyn Mitchell.

A student pilot traveling on Interstate 95 near the crash site saw the airplane at the end of a right roll, inverted and traveling at a high rate of speed, nose first towards the ground in the vicinity of Tweed-New Haven Airport. Jimmy Kimmel, a late-night talk show host, has been criticized by Senator Bill Cassidy for his understanding of health care policy. In a seven-minute monologue, Kimmel accused Cassidy of lying about his proposed Obamacare repeal and replace bill, which he co-authored with Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). Kimmel claimed that the bill would not live up to promises made by Cassidy to protect people with pre-existing conditions like Kimmel's infant son, who was born with a serious heart condition. Experts agree that Cassidy and Graham’s bill can't guarantee those protections, as it gives states flexibility to set up their own health care systems, potentially allowing insurers to hike premiums for patients with pre-existing conditions if their states obtain waivers from Obamacare regulations. The bill would also roll back the Affordable Care Act’s Medicaid expansion and make other funding changes that could disproportionately affect children and lead to dramatic reductions in coverage for adults. Former University of Illinois graduate student Brendt Christensen has been charged with kidnapping resulting in the death of Yingying Zhang, a visiting scholar from China, in a superseding indictment filed on Tuesday. The new charge could potentially lead to the death penalty if convicted, although the decision on whether to seek it will be made at a later date by U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions. Christensen is also facing two counts of making false statements to FBI agents. The charges come after Zhang's disappearance in June, which sent shockwaves through the university and China. Prosecutors allege that Christensen approached Zhang in his car and lured her inside, and surveillance footage captured the exchange. Police believe they have evidence against Christensen, including audio recordings and visits to a sadomasochism fetish website with discussion threads on kidnapping fantasies found on his phone. Christensen is currently being held without bond and is tentatively set to go to trial on February 27.

This new assessment contrasts with earlier statements suggesting the attack grew out of a spontaneous protest over an anti-Islam video. The U.S. has sent operatives to Libya to assist in the investigation, and several individuals have been arrested in connection with the attack. The attack posed a challenge to President Obama's foreign policy record just weeks before the November election. The intelligence community continues to investigate the attack, with unanswered questions about whether it was planned in advance and who exercised overall command and control of the attack. The administration has faced criticism for its shifting accounts of the attack, but officials maintain that they have conveyed what facts they knew at the time.

Sofia Vergara, known for her role in Modern Family, and Joe Manganiello, star of True Blood, are engaged after six months of dating. The proposal took place during their Christmas vacation in Hawaii, where Vergara has been spotted wearing a large diamond ring. The couple's whirlwind romance began after they were introduced at the White House Correspondents Dinner in May. Manganiello had previously expressed his admiration for Vergara, calling her his "dream girl." Vergara's ex-fiance Nick Loeb has congratulated them on their engagement, expressing that Vergara deserves happiness. The couple celebrated Manganiello's 38th birthday during the vacation and have been enjoying a luxurious stay at the St. Regis Princeville Resort in Kauai.

Skye McCole Bartusiak, who played Mel Gibson's daughter in the 2000 film "The Patriot," passed away at her home in Houston on Saturday at the age of 21. Her mother reported that Bartusiak had been suffering from epileptic seizures in recent days and believes she may have died from a seizure while sleeping.

Bartusiak began her acting career as a child, appearing in films such as "The Cider House Rules" in 1999 and "Don't Say a Word" opposite Michael Douglas in 2001. She also had roles on popular TV shows like "24," "Lost," and "House M.D."

In recent months, Bartusiak was preparing to produce and direct her first feature film. Her boyfriend found her unresponsive in a garage apartment adjacent to her parents' home, and despite CPR efforts by her mother and paramedics, she could not be revived.

Bartusiak had been dealing with epileptic seizures since she was a baby, although they disappeared for a few years before returning last week. Her mother spent Sunday morning looking through photos of Bartusiak for the funeral, which include images with Presidents George W. and George H.W. Bush, Mel Gibson, Dennis Hopper, and Michael Douglas.

Johnny Strange, a renowned adventurer from Malibu known for his daredevil stunts, died at 23 following a wingsuit BASE jumping accident in the Swiss Alps on Thursday. The crash occurred a few seconds after takeoff from Mt. Gitschen, and strong winds were reported on the mountain that day. Strange had discussed his trip to Switzerland on KROQ-FM’s Kevin and Bean show just days before the incident. He was best known for wingsuit BASE jumping, which involves leaping from mountains, ledges, and buildings while wearing a suit that allows extended flight time. The inherent dangers of this extreme sport were highlighted by the deaths of Dean Potter and Graham Hunt in Yosemite National Park earlier this year. Strange acknowledged these risks on his social media accounts but continued to pursue the activity. At 17, he became the youngest person to climb the "seven summits," the world's highest mountains in seven continents.

Donald Trump is set to moderate a presidential debate hosted by Newsmax and airing on Ion Television on Dec 27 in Iowa. This event is expected to be a memorable moment in the Republican primary season, known for its unconventional nature. Trump's influence with the party's conservative base, particularly the Tea Party wing, is significant due to his perceived independence from the Washington and media establishments. The debate will not focus on a specific topic like national security or economy, and it is scheduled just a week before the Iowa caucuses. Newsmax invited several candidates for the debate, with some having already met Trump privately. Despite potential initial reservations about appearing in a debate moderated by Trump, candidates may find it hard to refuse due to his ability to command media attention and his influence among conservatives. Newsmax has a broad reach into the conservative base, making it a powerful player itself. Trump's involvement in the debate follows his flirtation with running for president this year, which coincided with a new season of his popular reality TV show "Celebrity Apprentice." However, Trump's presidential ambitions have been uncertain in the past, with similar flirtations in 1987 and 1999 that ultimately did not lead to a campaign.

Mexico's President Enrique Peña Nieto has reiterated that Mexico will not pay for Donald Trump's proposed border wall, but has not yet cancelled a planned meeting with the new US president. The Mexican government is considering cancelling the visit due to Trump's executive orders on building the border barrier, but no decision has been made. Mexicans have reacted with confusion and some have called on Peña Nieto to cancel the meeting. The president's personal popularity ratings currently languish at 12%, and he is facing sustained criticism for failing to come up with a decisive strategy to deal with Trump's combative policies. Analysts say the president has few strong options in confronting an American administration considered the most hostile to Mexico since the Mexican-American war of the 1840s.

Lady Gaga's album "Born This Way" debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart, selling 1.11 million copies in its first week. This marks Gaga's first No. 1 album and the highest sales week since 2005. The album's strong sales were attributed to a promotional offer by Amazon.com Inc., which sold the digital download version of "Born This Way" for just 99 cents on two separate days, resulting in an estimated 440,000 downloads. The last album to sell more copies in a week was rapper 50 Cent's "The Massacre," which notched 1.14 million copies its first week out, in 2005. This is one of only 17 albums since SoundScan began tracking sales data in 1991 to sell a million copies in a week. The decline in music sales due to digital piracy and other factors has made such high-selling weeks increasingly rare.

The article reports on the arrest of Ross Ulbricht, a 29-year-old man from San Francisco, who is accused of being the mastermind behind the online drug marketplace known as Silk Road. Ulbricht, also known by the pseudonym "Dread Pirate Roberts," was arrested at the Glen Park library branch on Tuesday. He is charged with narcotics trafficking, money laundering, and attempting to murder a witness among other crimes. The FBI alleges that Ulbricht ran Silk Road from San Francisco and facilitated the sale of drugs like heroin and cocaine through the website since at least 2011. He is accused of collecting tens of millions of dollars in commissions and ordering two hits on people who threatened his empire. Ulbricht did not resist when he was taken into custody, and a complaint filed in New York and a grand jury indictment handed down in Maryland detail the charges against him. His attorney declined to comment. The Silk Road website was seized by the FBI before Ulbricht appeared in court on Wednesday. The site had many of the trappings of popular online retail sites and featured wares like "amphetamine paste" and "high quality #4 heroin." Undercover agents made over 100 purchases from Silk Road vendors from 10 countries during the investigation. To pay for items, buyers used Bitcoins, an anonymous digital currency with no central

The study conducted by Stanford University researchers analyzed body-worn camera footage from Oakland Police Department traffic stops in 2014, revealing that police officers spoke less respectfully to black community members compared to white ones. The research used computational linguistic techniques to automatically measure levels of respect based on officer language during routine traffic stops. The findings showed that white community members were more likely to hear respectful utterances like "please" and "thank you," while black people were more likely to be called by their first names or informal terms. The study aims to use body-cam footage to improve police-community relations, as these routine interactions can affect public trust in law enforcement. The researchers are releasing their computational linguistic models for others to use and plan to analyze the actual footage for further insights into improving police training and interactions with the community.

Daniel Sickles, a U.S. Congressman, shot and killed Philip Barton Key, the son of the author of the "Star-Spangled Banner," on February 27, 1859, in Washington D.C., after discovering an affair between his wife Teresa and Key. Sickles was charged with murder but successfully pleaded temporary insanity, becoming the first American to do so. The trial was sensational and garnered public support for Sickles, who was later appointed as ambassador to Spain.

Sickles's life was marked by scandals and audacious behavior, including seducing a married daughter of Lorenzo Da Ponte, Mozart's librettist, and blackmailing her husband. He was a rising star in the pro-slavery wing of the Democratic Party before the Civil War, but his hubris led to his downfall when he shot Key in broad daylight near the White House.

Sickles's successful insanity plea set a precedent that would be known as the "Twinkie defense" and later reformed by Congress in 1984 after John Hinckley Jr.'s attempted assassination of President Ronald Reagan. The National Liberation Front of Corsica (FLNC), a militant group seeking independence for the island since 1976, has announced an end to its armed struggle against France after nearly 40 years. The decision was made without preconditions and involves a process of demilitarization. This development comes following several recent advances via conventional means, such as property-owning restrictions aimed at ending real estate inflation on the island. The FLNC stated that these measures mark the beginning of constructing a true Corsican political power. The group has been responsible for numerous attacks in Corsica and the French mainland over the years, including murders, bombings, and rocket attacks. This decision by the FLNC follows a similar one made by Eta, the Basque separatist organization, earlier this year.

In a tragic incident, two twin sisters aged 29 from Australia made a suicide pact and shot each other at a gun range near Denver, Colorado. One sister died, while the other is now in stable condition. The incident occurred at the Family Shooting Center inside Cherry Creek State Park, where the women had been firing small caliber handguns for nearly 90 minutes.

The Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office believes this was a suicide pact, based on physical evidence, the surviving sister's statement, and video surveillance footage. The women were visiting on cultural visas and had traveled to the U.S. and Canada regularly. Their family and friends are at a loss to explain their actions.

The surviving twin has been uncooperative about revealing the reasons for their suicide pact during an emotional interview with investigators. Her parents are scheduled to arrive in Colorado on Friday. The authorities have not released the names of the women, pending confirmation from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

This incident marks at least the seventh suicide involving rented guns at US shooting ranges this year, and the third at the Family Shooting Center since 2004. The Denver Post has more details on the story.

Adele's second album, titled '21', was released recently and it is a breakup album written entirely about one heartless ex-boyfriend. The album, which serves as "cheap therapy" for Adele, features deeply personal songs like 'Someone Like You' and 'Rolling in the Deep'. Inspired by her own painful breakup, the album is a reflection of Adele's emotions and struggles. She plans to explore American musical traditions such as country and bluegrass in her future work. The album has been well-received for its raw emotion and candidness, with Adele's voice being particularly praised.

Kim Cattrall, known for her role as Samantha Jones in Sex and the City, has stated that she is not friends with her co-stars Sarah Jessica Parker, Kristin Davis, and Cynthia Nixon. In an interview with Piers Morgan, Cattrall claimed that they have only been colleagues and that there's a clear line between their professional and personal lives.

Recent reports suggested that Cattrall's "outrageous demands" were the reason for the cancellation of a third Sex and the City film, but Cattrall has denied this claim. She asserted that she never asked for any money or projects and finds it absurd to be labeled as a diva.

Sources have reported that Cattrall made significant demands to rejoin the movie franchise, which allegedly led Warner Bros. to cancel the film. However, Cattrall maintains that these reports are untrue. The third Sex and the City film, which was expected to follow the 2008 and 2010 films, is now officially off the table according to Sarah Jessica Parker.

During the interview with Morgan, Cattrall also discussed her decision not to have children due to her busy shooting schedule for Sex and the City. She expressed a sense of maternal instinct but acknowledged that she never pursued motherhood because of the demands of her career. Instead, she found fulfillment in mentoring young actress

LulzSec, a hacker group known for its high-profile cyberattacks, has announced its retirement after 50 days of hacking various corporate and governmental targets. In their final statement, they released a data dump containing information from AOL, AT&T, Battlefield Heroes, FBI, Hackforums.net, NATO bookshop, US Navy, corporate office networks, private investigators, gaming forums, and routers with default passwords. The group's sudden retirement is unexpected as they had previously indicated an ongoing campaign of looting servers and posting the booty. It remains unclear whether this is a permanent retirement or a temporary gag, as law enforcement agencies are likely to be mobilized in response to their actions.

Senator Rand Paul is exploring the possibility of running for both the U.S. Presidential election in 2016 and re-election to the U.S. Senate. To facilitate this, Kentucky Senate Majority Leader Damon Thayer is considering filing a bill that would clarify a state law prohibiting candidates from holding or running for two offices simultaneously. The bill aims to make it clear that Rand Paul or anyone in a similar situation in Kentucky can run for both offices in the same year. However, the bill's passage is uncertain due to opposition from the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives. If the bill passes and Paul wins both elections, he would become President while relinquishing his Senate seat, or remain a second-term Senator if he loses the presidential election but wins the Senate re-election race. This move by Rand Paul comes as his fellow Kentucky Republican, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, faces a serious challenge from the political right in his own party.

A Tennessee high school student, Emily Gipson, created an anti-bullying video titled "Welcome to Lebanon High School" which received nearly 700,000 views on YouTube. The video criticized the school's culture and administration for their handling of bullying and suicide prevention. Gipson was given a two-day in-school suspension by the principal, Scott Walters, who claimed it was due to her recording the video without teacher's permission in a classroom. However, Gipson disputes this and claims she had two coaches' permission. The controversy has sparked discussions about bullying and school administration at Lebanon High School in Tennessee.

The article discusses the disparities in workers' compensation benefits for similar injuries across different states, using the cases of Jeremy Lewis and Josh Potter as examples. Both men, aged 27 and 25 respectively, were married with two children and lived within 75 miles of each other. They both worked at industrial plants and lost a portion of their left arms in machinery accidents. However, due to differences in workers' compensation laws between Alabama (where Lewis lived) and Georgia (where Potter lived), they received vastly different benefits: $45,000 for Lewis and potentially over $740,000 for Potter. This highlights the geographic lottery that governs compensation for workplace injuries in America, as each state determines its own benefits with no federal minimums. The article also mentions the impact of these benefits on workers' lives, citing examples of dehumanizing calculations and insurers offering benefits for individual fingers instead of the entire hand. The article concludes by discussing the history and politics behind these benefit tables, stating that they are often the result of political expediency rather than medical wisdom or economic analysis.

The article discusses two separate issues related to Wells Fargo. Firstly, the bank's executive, Estrada, announced a plan to offer premium checking accounts for Latino immigrants, which would allow them to send money across borders at no charge. However, customers would need to have at least $25,000 on deposit within three months or pay a $30 monthly charge if they only deposit $50 to open the account.

Secondly, the article highlights concerns about unethical practices within Wells Fargo's business operations. Siham El-Dahan, a former employee who worked for the bank for more than 20 years, claimed that her managers played favorites, denied employees their legal breaks, and threatened them about meeting sales quotas. In response, some employees allegedly opened bogus accounts for customers without their consent.

Another customer, Frank Ahn, reported repeated instances of unwanted account openings and unnecessary fees despite his protests. Despite his efforts to cancel these accounts and reverse the fees, he was left with multiple accounts that he found difficult to manage due to his business's complex payment systems. Ahn expressed frustration over the time spent dealing with these issues, which he felt detracted from improving his business's productivity.

Wells Fargo declined to comment on both El-Dahan's and Ahn's stories.

The marine engineer, Saddam Hussain from Jamshedpur in Jharkhand, has been struggling to find a job due to his namesake, the former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein. Despite ranking second in his batch at Tamil Nadu’s Noorul Islam University and being unemployed for two years, he has faced rejections from multinational shipping companies due to concerns about potential complications with immigration officials across international borders.

Saddam legally changed his name to Sajid to avoid the issue but encountered further obstacles when his university refused to change his name on educational certificates until he got his Class 10 and 12 exam certificates changed first. He approached the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) for a name change, but they have not acted yet. Saddam moved the Jharkhand high court with a plea to direct the CBSE to change his name, and the court has set a hearing date on May 5.

Saddam remains fond of his grandfather, who gave him the name, but feels he is paying for his folly as one by one his batchmates secure jobs while he spends sleepless nights. The situation highlights the challenges faced by people with names similar to Saddam Hussein, both in India and Iraq, where some have faced discrimination, job loss, and even violence due to their names.

In a unique approach to recruit interns, Emmis Digital held a social media contest dubbed "Intern Games" for a single unpaid internship position at their River North office. Over 25 college students applied, with the top 10 candidates interviewed and the field narrowed down to three finalists. The finalists, Kelsey Halverson and Jake Bouvy, were pitted against each other in a two-week social media battle under hashtags #TeamJake, #TeamKelsey, and #TeamKatie. Both contestants showcased their digital skills, with Bouvy focusing on technical abilities and social media success promoting indie music videos online, while Halverson excelled in driving traffic and attracting Facebook "likes" for Emmis. In the end, both were declared winners due to their complementary skills, marking a shift towards unconventional methods in the competitive job market.

The missing Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, which disappeared three days ago with 239 people on board, is still untraceable. The search for the Boeing 777 has involved teams from nine countries, including the U.S., China, and Vietnam, but no wreckage or debris has been found yet.

Investigators are considering various possibilities, including hijacking, terrorism, pilot error, or mechanical failure, but have not ruled out any theories. Two passengers were traveling on stolen passports, one from Austria and the other from Italy, raising concerns about possible illegal immigration or terrorist involvement. The FBI is running their thumbprints through a database to identify them.

The area being searched has grown, now covering hundreds of miles in the Gulf of Thailand and the South China Sea. Authorities have warned that crucial time is passing as the search continues. Family members of passengers are being told to prepare for the worst, but some relatives remain hopeful due to a lack of answers. The mysteries surrounding the identities of some of the passengers and the circumstances of the stolen passports remain unsolved.

In January and February of 2017, Chicago experienced an unprecedented record of no snow on the ground for 146 years, as documented by the National Weather Service. This record was broken due to small amounts of snow that melted before being recorded at O'Hare International Airport. The weather service measures snow at 6 a.m., and on Feb. 25, there was a trace of snow, while Jan. 30 had 0.1 inch. However, this record-breaking near-snowless start was overshadowed by severe storms moving through the state on Tuesday, which brought large hail, winds, localized flooding, and tornadoes. A tornado hit Ottowa on Tuesday evening, killing one person. More stormy weather was forecast for the week, including possible snow.

Climate scientists have mixed opinions about the cause of this warm spell. While some, like WGN-TV meteorologist Tom Skilling, believe it is part of climate change, others argue that blips of weather are too short a time period to assign a true cause. Meteorologists also point out that there are natural variances in weather over time that have nothing to do with climate change.

In this summary, Queen Elizabeth II delivered her annual pre-recorded Christmas message to the nation, emphasizing the importance of family and friendship. The royal family gathered for a Christmas service at St. Mary's church on the Sandringham Estate, with Prince Philip absent due to his hospitalization following a heart procedure. Notable attendees included Prince William, Kate Duchess of Cambridge, Prince Charles, Camilla Duchess of Cornwall, and Prince Harry. The Queen's message, recorded on December 9 before Philip's hospitalization, highlighted the strength family provides during hardships and how friendships are often formed in difficult times. She also pointed to the Commonwealth nations as an example that family can extend beyond blood relatives to a community. The royal family later returned to their residence for lunch, followed by the Queen's annual address to the nation focusing on family and community.

Thieves have stolen an estimated €250,000 (£230,500) worth of fine wine from a private residence in Paris by exploiting the city's vast underground tunnel network, specifically the catacombs. The thieves reportedly broke into the catacombs through one of its secret entrances and drilled a hole into the cellar wall of the apartment near the Luxembourg gardens, which houses the French Senate. After stealing around 300 bottles of grands crus, they disappeared back underground, leaving the police baffled.

The catacombs, originally mines, were converted into ossuaries in the late 18th century due to overflowing cemeteries in Paris. They house between six and seven million human remains and are a popular attraction for some Parisians known as 'Cataphiles', who often explore the tunnels at night despite the risks of fines and potential dangers. The police have a special branch, called the 'Cataflics' or Catacops, to deal with intruders in the catacombs.

The theft is currently under investigation by the 3rd District of the Parisian Criminal Investigation department, who have so far refused to comment on the matter. The specific wines stolen remain unnamed. This incident highlights the intricate and sinister allure of the Paris Catacombs, a

Two men, Joseph E. Van Wert (65) and Randy W. Lambach (45), were arrested in Pittsfield, Massachusetts on charges related to running a citywide prostitution ring involving multiple women, some of whom may have been as young as 15 years old. The investigation began in the spring of 2017 after police received calls and complaints regarding increased prostitution activity in the area. Most of the activity seemed to be centered around First, Adam, North, Linden, and Wahconah streets.

Lambach allegedly recruited women with drug addictions, photographed them, and posted advertisements online for sexual services. He would then arrange meetings with clients, collect money, and keep a significant portion of it, sometimes paying the women in drugs instead. Some of the women were reportedly formerly his foster children.

Van Wert allegedly allowed some of these meetings to take place at his third-floor apartment in a senior living facility. Both men have pleaded not guilty to various charges including human trafficking and maintaining a house of prostitution. The investigation is ongoing, with additional charges possible.

A woman named Alexandria Duval, who is accused of killing her twin sister Anastasia by driving their SUV off a cliff in Hawaii, is fighting her extradition from New York to face a murder charge. Duval was arrested in Albany, NY on Nov 11th and appeared in court on Nov 18th. A grand jury in Hawaii indicted her on a second-degree murder charge last month. The sisters were involved in a fight over the steering wheel of the SUV when it crashed into a rock wall and plunged about 200 feet, resulting in Anastasia's death. Duval's attorney claims the crash was a tragic accident and that Duval had returned to upstate New York to grieve, not to avoid justice. An extradition hearing is scheduled for Dec 16th.

A woman named Semantha Bunce, a member of the U.S. Army's 105th Engineer Battalion, was seriously injured in a shootout at her Charlotte, North Carolina home on Tuesday. The incident occurred when intruders forced their way into her home and exchanged gunfire with her. Semantha was shot several times but is recovering at Carolinas Medical Center. Her baby was not harmed during the incident.

Reco Latur Dawkins Jr., 23, has been charged with attempted murder, felony breaking and entering, and conspiracy in connection with the shooting. He turned himself in to the Charlotte-Mecklenburg police's violent criminal apprehension team on Sunday morning. Dawkins has a history of criminal charges, including several for breaking and entering.

The case has received national attention, and a Go Fund Me site has been established to help pay for Bunce's expenses such as utility bills, child care, travel expenses, home repairs, medical bills, and missed wages. Paul Bunce III, Semantha's husband, believes her training as a combat medic helped her stay focused during the incident. The public is being asked to call 704-432-TIPS with any information that could lead to the identification of other suspects involved in the shooting.

A 14-year-old boy was fatally shot by his father in their East Price Hill home on Tuesday morning, after the father mistook him for an intruder. The incident occurred around 6:30 a.m., and the father, whose name has not been released, had recently dropped his son, Georta Mack, off at school but the teen returned home. After hearing a noise in the basement, the father grabbed a handgun to investigate, and Georta startled the man, leading to the accidental shooting. The father called 911, begging police to hurry as he held a cloth to his son's neck to slow the bleeding. Georta was taken to Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center but died shortly after 8:15 a.m. Neighbors expressed their grief over the tragic incident, and Cincinnati Police Chief Eliot Isaac called it a "terrible, terrible tragedy." The father is being interviewed by police and is cooperative, but it is unclear if he will be charged in the case.

In Baltimore, Toya Graham, a single mother of six, was praised for her actions after she was caught on video repeatedly smacking her 16-year-old son during riots. Graham confronted her son after spotting him among the protesters, concerned that he would become another victim like Freddie Gray, who died mysteriously in police custody earlier in the month. The incident has been widely circulated and drew praise from Baltimore Police Commissioner Anthony Batts, who wished for more parents to take charge of their children during such situations. Graham hopes this incident will serve as a teachable moment for her son, emphasizing the seriousness of the ongoing violence in Baltimore.

British Prime Minister Theresa May survived a no-confidence vote from her Conservative Party, but more than a third of her lawmakers voted against her leadership. The vote was triggered by Eurosceptic critics who see her Brexit deal as a betrayal of the 2016 referendum. The outcome will shape Britain's economy and determine whether London keeps its place as one of the top two global financial centres. May had warned opponents that if they toppled her, Brexit would be delayed or stopped. After two hours of voting, Graham Brady, chairman of the 1922 Committee of Conservative backbenchers, announced that 200 Conservative lawmakers had voted in support of May as leader, and 117 against, indicating a bitterly divided party over the direction of Brexit. Supporters said the result showed the party should now get behind her, but hardline Brexit supporters said she should resign. The vote comes after May cancelled a parliamentary vote on her Brexit deal, designed to maintain close future ties with the EU, after it became clear she would lose it badly.

The Mo Ibrahim Prize for African Leadership, worth $5 million, has not been awarded this year as no candidate met all the criteria required for winning the prize. The prize is given annually to a democratically elected leader who has governed well, raised living standards, and voluntarily left office. Last year's winner was Cape Verde President Pedro Verona Pires, who led the fight against Portuguese colonialism, introduced multi-party politics, and was praised for raising living standards. The prize includes $5 million spread over 10 years and a lifetime annual payment of $200,000.

In other news, two American economists, Alvin Roth and Lloyd Shapley, were awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their research into market design and its practical applications. Their work has improved the way people are matched with limited resources, such as patients with donated organs or students with their preferred high schools. The prize carries a $1.2 million award.

Roth's research focused on the residency system used to assign medical-school graduates to hospitals and determined that the system led to "stable matches." However, it couldn't accommodate doctor couples who wanted to be placed in the same region. Roth redesigned the system to take into account such requests when placing residents. The estranged wife of acclaimed concert pianist Vadym Kholodenko, Sofya Tsygankova, has been ruled mentally incompetent to stand trial for allegedly killing their two young daughters. Tsygankova, who is charged with capital murder of a person under age 10, will be committed to a state mental health facility for 120 days of treatment. She is accused of smothering daughters Nika, 5, and Michaela, 1, at their home in Texas. Kholodenko, who won the gold medal at the 14th Van Cliburn International Piano Competition in 2013, resumed playing concerts a month after his daughters were killed. Tsygankova had visited a state mental health facility a day before her daughters were found dead, and an empty prescription bottle of quetiapine, an antipsychotic drug used to treat bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, was found in the home.

Steve Weidner, a school janitor at Alan Shephard Elementary School in Bourbonnais, IL, received rock star treatment from students on June 2nd. He has been working at the school for over 15 years and is well-liked by the students. During lunchtime before school dismissal, students lined up to have Weidner sign their yearbooks. The line was so long that it wound around the playground, with some students even getting him a chair. The school confirmed that Weidner was touched and amazed by the show of affection from the students. The event was shared on Reddit, where it quickly gained thousands of upvotes and comments. However, the associated WARC files from this crawl are not currently available to the general public.

The University of Texas at Austin has released a comprehensive report aimed at training police officers to handle cases of campus sexual assault more effectively. The report, titled "Blueprint for Campus Police," was drafted by UT Austin’s Institute on Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault and will be incorporated into the training for over 600 officers across all eight academic institutions within the UT System.

The report emphasizes the need for a more specialized response to sexual assault cases due to the trauma victims often experience. It offers specific guidelines for officers, such as letting victims know they are safe and will not be judged, understanding that a victim's alcohol or drug use is an issue of increased vulnerability rather than culpability, and reinterpreting signs of deception in the context of assault.

The report also addresses common rape myths and concepts such as victim blaming. It outlines best practices for dealing with survivors of sexual assault, including adopting policies that are victim-centered, science-based, and trauma-informed. The report was based on 27 interviews with campus presidents and police officers, among others, and did not involve interviewing survivors directly to avoid reopening emotional wounds.

In summary, over 1,600 former NFL players, including notable figures like Jamal Anderson, Chris Doleman, O.J. Santiago, and Dorsey Levens, have filed a lawsuit against the NFL, claiming that the league hid the dangers of concussions from them. The lawsuit alleges that the NFL downplayed and misrepresented the risks associated with concussions, failed to take necessary steps to protect players from head injuries, and repeatedly refuted the connection between concussions and brain injury.

The NFL has denied these allegations, stating that player safety is a priority and that any claims of intentional misinformation have no merit. Similar lawsuits against the NFL are currently consolidated for trial in Philadelphia, but a trial date has not been set.

The lawsuit cites recent scientific studies linking concussions to chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a neurodegenerative disease causing Alzheimer's-like symptoms and mood swings. CTE can only be diagnosed after death, and 12 cases of it have been detected in deceased NFL players.

A Pleasant Grove mother, Alexandra Nicole Laird, has been indicted for endangering her newborn daughter who was born addicted to heroin and spent a month in an Intensive Care Unit due to withdrawals. The grand jury indictment came on April 15, and Laird had remained free on bond since her initial arrest in May 2015. Laird admitted to using heroin one to two times a week during her pregnancy. She also faces an unrelated drug possession charge and has been arrested multiple times for failure to appear in court.

In a separate development, President Barack Obama signed a law aimed at protecting drug-dependent newborns and assisting their parents. The Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act emphasizes drug treatment and overdose prevention to combat the nation's heroin and opioid epidemic. However, Obama expressed disappointment that the legislation did not provide adequate resources for addiction treatment.

Laird is currently pregnant again and has been jailed without bond due to concerns about the unborn child's health. The new law promises a non-punitive approach that includes "safe care plans" aimed at keeping newborns at home with their parents, who will receive additional help.

India's Supreme Court has ruled that adultery is no longer a crime, declaring the colonial-era law unconstitutional and discriminatory against women. The court unanimously agreed that the law was archaic and deprived women of agency, as it only held men liable for extra-marital relationships while treating women like property. The decision follows several socially progressive rulings by the court this session, including the decriminalization of homosexuality and a pending case about restricting women from entering a temple during their menstruating years. The adultery law was challenged by an Indian businessman living in Italy, who argued that it discriminated against both genders and indirectly discriminated against women. While some critics argue that the law should have been made gender-neutral instead of being struck down, many Indians support the ruling as a step towards gender equality.

A policy at a school in Nettleton, Mississippi, which has historically alternated class offices between white and black students, has sparked controversy after a mother of mixed-race children learned that her daughter was not eligible to run for the class reporter position due to her race. The policy, which has been in place for 30 years, was intended to ensure minority representation but has been criticized as outdated and discriminatory.

The NAACP called for a Justice Department investigation, and the school district announced on its website that it would no longer use race in school elections. The school acknowledged that the practice was outdated and did not reflect the growing diversity of its student body.

Brandy Springer, the mother who brought attention to the issue, moved her children to another school district after becoming frustrated with the policy. The school district did not respond to requests for comment.

The controversy highlights the complexities faced by interracial families and school officials in achieving racial equality in a state with a history of tensions between blacks and whites. Some worry that the school's efforts to ensure equal representation could leave out students from other ethnicities, such as Hispanics or Asians.

President Donald Trump announced on May 8, 2018, that he is withdrawing the United States from the Iran nuclear deal, a landmark agreement reached in 2015. The decision raises concerns about Iran potentially resuming its frozen weapons program and its impact on North Korea's denuclearization efforts. Trump plans to impose "the highest level" of sanctions that will affect not only Iran but also other countries doing business with it. The Treasury Department stated a series of primary and secondary sanctions, affecting American and foreign partners of Iran, would go back into effect after wind-down periods specified by law.

The 2015 agreement saw Iran halt its pursuit of nuclear weapons and allow international checks on its facilities in exchange for the U.S., several other countries, and the United Nations rolling back sanctions that had crippled its economy. The accord was widely seen as the biggest foreign policy accomplishment of President Barack Obama's administration. Trump has long been a critic of the agreement, calling it "the worst deal ever," maintaining that Obama gave up too much for too little.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has frozen its grant programs under the Trump administration. This freeze affects various funding streams for research, redevelopment of former industrial sites, air quality monitoring, education, and other environmental projects. The EPA staff was instructed not to discuss this order with anyone outside the agency, and an anonymous source provided information about the freeze to a congressional office out of fear of retaliation. It's unclear whether the freeze is temporary or indefinite, and its immediate impact on programs across the country is uncertain due to varying grant distribution intervals and frequencies.

The Trump administration has also imposed tight controls on external communication at the EPA, including press releases, blog posts, social media, content on the agency website, and external speaking engagements. This communication restriction is part of a broader effort by the new administration to control information flow from federal agencies. The freeze on grants and contracts extends beyond the EPA, affecting other federal agencies such as the Department of Agriculture and Health and Human Services.

The EPA's grant freeze and communication restrictions have raised concerns among former Obama administration officials who view these moves as extreme and troubling, especially considering their potential impact on state-level programs and transparency with the public. The EPA has not provided a clear answer about the implications of the freeze, and its duration remains unclear.

The article discusses a series of lawsuits against former New York Governor Eliot Spitzer, who served as Attorney General before his governorship, over an opinion piece he wrote for Slate.com defending his enforcement activity against Marsh & McLennan Cos and American International Group Inc (AIG). Two former executives of Marsh & McLennan, William Gilman and Edward McNenney, have filed lawsuits seeking a combined $90 million, claiming they were defamed in the piece. The article notes that Spitzer's column was written in response to an editorial critical of him in The Wall Street Journal, and that both men were found guilty of felony antitrust charges in 2008 but had their convictions thrown out in July 2010. The article also mentions that Spitzer resigned as New York's governor in March 2008 after a scandal involving hiring a high-priced prostitute. The lawsuits are currently ongoing.

Three California men, including a sheriff's deputy named Christopher Heath, were arrested in York County, Pennsylvania after authorities seized 247 pounds of marijuana valued at approximately $2 million during a traffic stop last week in West Manheim Township. The other two men arrested are Ryan Falsone and Tyler Long. All three have been charged with delivery, conspiracy to deliver, and possession with intent to deliver marijuana. Heath was on vacation at the time of his arrest and had his badge and service weapon with him. The bust was part of an ongoing investigation based on tips into law enforcement, and it's believed that the trio brought the drugs from California. All three men posted a $1 million bail and are out on bail. The arrest was made in collaboration with West Manheim Township police and was not a routine traffic stop. The seized drug had a street retail value of over $2 million, and authorities believe it was part of a sophisticated operation that was ongoing. No information about the men's intentions or if any of the marijuana had been distributed has been released as it is part of the ongoing investigation. Federal charges are likely to be filed since the drug was transported across state lines. The arrest was praised by law enforcement officials from several agencies, who commended their colleagues for risking their lives every day doing a dangerous job.

Joe Jackson, the patriarch and early manager of the Jackson family, died at age 89 on June 27 after a battle with cancer. He was born in 1928 and married wife Katherine in 1949, going on to have 11 children. As a manager, he launched the career of his son Michael Jackson, along with Jackie, Jermaine, Marlon, and Tito, as the Jackson 5 in the 1960s. The Jackson 5 signed with Berry Gordy's Motown Records, and their first four singles all went to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Joe was known for his iron-fisted management of his children but was honored as Best Entertainment Manager of All Time by the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2002. He was criticized at times for being a harsh taskmaster, but he defended his methods, saying they made his kids successful and kept them out of trouble. Joe Jackson died at a Las Vegas hospital.

Sally Jewell, the CEO of outdoor retailer Recreational Equipment Inc., has been confirmed as the new U.S. Interior Secretary by the Senate in a bipartisan vote of 87-11. Jewell pledged to balance conflicting demands on federal land for recreation, conservation, mining, and forestry during her confirmation hearing. She will replace outgoing Secretary Ken Salazar and oversee more than 500 million acres of national parks and other public lands, as well as 1 billion acres offshore. Jewell is a lifelong outdoors enthusiast who previously worked as a petroleum engineer and banker and served on the board of the National Parks Conservation Association. Eleven Republicans opposed her nomination, with concerns over her ties to environmental groups that have opposed oil and coal use near national parks or on government lands.

The article from CNN discusses a new study that challenges the long-held theory about the collapse of Easter Island's society. Instead of infighting and overexploitation of resources, researchers suggest that the islanders were actually part of a sophisticated and collaborative society.

The study, published in the Journal of Pacific Archaeology, uses chemical analysis of stone tools used to carve the giant statues on Easter Island. The research indicates that the people worked together and shared information, which allowed them to create nearly a thousand statues, many of which are over 70 feet tall.

The first Polynesian settlers arrived on Easter Island (also known as Rapa Nui) about 900 years ago. Over time, the population grew, forming a complex society that carved the famous moai statues. The size and number of these statues suggest a high level of sociopolitical organization.

Recent excavations revealed about 1,600 stone tools made from volcanic stone called basalt. By analyzing the chemical composition of fragments from 17 of these tools, researchers found that most came from one quarry complex. This indicates a high degree of collaboration among families and craft groups.

Alan Rickman, best known for his role as Professor Snape in the Harry Potter series, had to keep his knowledge of Snape's true allegiance a secret during filming, as J.K. Rowling hadn't yet revealed it in The Deathly Hallows. Rickman knew Snape was a secret agent working for Dumbledore, but he often hid this information from directors and journalists.

Rickman's portrayal of Snape was highly praised, with his character evolving from a brooding villain to a heartbreaking hero who would do anything for those he loved. After battling cancer, Rickman passed away at the age of 69.

A YouTube video compiles all of Snape's most important moments in the films into a 14-minute emotional rollercoaster, including his feelings for Harry's mother Lily and his eventual actions against Dumbledore. Interestingly, Tom Felton, who plays Draco Malfoy, is reportedly a kind person in real life and would not fit the Slytherin House stereotype.

The article suggests that there is a link between height and cancer risk, as taller individuals have more cells in their bodies and higher levels of a protein that encourages cell division. For every 10cm over the average height, a person's risk for cancer increases by approximately 10%. This finding is supported by new analysis of data from large cancer studies. The study found that taller people are at a much higher risk of melanoma and thyroid cancer, particularly women. However, it's important to note that the increased risk is small compared to lifestyle factors such as smoking and maintaining a healthy weight. The study also suggests that environmental effects can mask height effects for certain types of cancer, such as stomach, mouth, and cervical cancer. The link between height and cancer risk is thought to be due to the sheer number of cells, but other factors such as growth hormones and insulin-like growth factor 1 may also play a role.

In Houston, Texas, Tropical Storm Harvey has caused extensive flooding and damage, leaving many residents stranded and in need of rescue. The storm has been particularly devastating for some families, with one teenager describing her harrowing experience of being rescued from her home as the water rose around them. The National Weather Service predicts that the storm will linger for several more days, with an additional 15 to 25 inches of rain expected along the upper Texas coast and southwest Louisiana through Friday. The city of La Grange has issued a mandatory evacuation order due to flooding concerns. Emergency officials have been working around the clock to rescue stranded residents, with the Coast Guard reporting that they have rescued over 3,000 people so far. Four people have died as a result of the storm. President Trump has pledged rapid action from Congress to provide disaster relief funding to the affected areas.

The Honda Accord has been named the most stolen and recovered vehicle in the United States for the fifth year in a row, according to a report by LoJack. In 2013, $121 million worth of stolen vehicles equipped with LoJack were recovered, with the most expensive being a 2011 Porsche Panamera valued at $103,400. The high number of Accord thefts is attributed to its popularity, reliability, and interchangeable parts, making it a lucrative target for professional thieves. Honda continues to implement security measures such as the Immobilizer Theft-Deterrent System in its vehicles. Other frequently stolen vehicles include the Honda Civic, Toyota Camry, Toyota Corolla, Chevy Silverado, Acura Integra, Cadillac Escalade, Ford F350, Nissan Altima, and Chevy Tahoe.

In Wukan, a Chinese village in Guangdong province, residents have reached a compromise with local authorities following a two-week standoff over land seizures that escalated after the death of a village negotiator, Xue Jinbo, in police custody. Villagers accused the police of beating him to death, while the police claimed he died of a sudden illness.

The villagers' demands included an investigation into Xue Jinbo's death and compensation for improper land seizures by local authorities. On Wednesday, deputy provincial Communist Party secretary Zhu Mingguo met with village representatives, resulting in the release of three other detained villagers and the return of Xue Jinbo's body.

Village representative Lin Zulian expressed satisfaction with the outcome but warned that promises would need to be kept, or else protests would resume. The residents have faced thousands of land grabs-related protests in China annually, but Wukan's situation has gained significant attention due to its scale.

Meanwhile, a separate protest erupted in Haimen, also in Guangdong province, over local government plans to build a power plant. This marks recent labor walkouts and protests in southern China. The compromise reached in Wukan is considered rare as authorities often respond more forcefully to such disputes.

The missing SAT tests from Broad Run High School in Loudoun County, Virginia, were found on Monday morning after a month-long search. Approximately 236 answer sheets were discovered at the bottom of a cart in the shipping area of the school. Initially, it was believed that UPS had carried the tests out of the building, but this turned out to be a mix-up during the transfer of boxes from the guidance office to the shipping area on May 4. The affected students will not have to retake the exam as the tests will be validated and sent off to the College Board. An investigation into the loss of the tests and a review of the delivery process will be conducted by the school system.

A new study published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory and Cognition found that the belief of having had a good night's sleep can improve cognitive abilities, even if it is not true.

Researchers at Colorado College conducted an experiment with 164 students, informing them that a new technique would measure their sleep pattern from the previous night. The participants were randomly divided into two groups: those who were told they had above-average quality sleep and those who were told they had below-average quality sleep.

The students who believed they had a good night's sleep performed significantly better in a cognitive exercise called the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test, which measures listening and information processing abilities. This phenomenon is known as "placebo sleep," where the mindset about one's treatment affects cognitive states positively or negatively. The researchers concluded that this study supports the idea that mindset can influence health and cognition.

On March 10, 2014, Steve Douglass and Dean Muskett, along with other photographers, spotted three mystery aircraft while at Amarillo International Airport in Texas. Initially thinking they were B-2 bombers, upon reviewing their photos, they noticed that the planes had a different shape, resembling something boomerang-shaped rather than straight. An investigation by aviation experts concluded that the photos show something real, although larger than the Navy's X-47B drone. The mystery aircraft seems to be stealthy and may be a transport aircraft, but its exact identity remains unclear. The photographers reached out to Whiteman Air Force Base for confirmation, but did not receive a response.

The Cuban National Assembly is set to elect a new president on Wednesday, April 18, 2018, with First Vice President Miguel Mario Diaz-Canel Bermudez as the sole candidate. This political transition marks the first time in nearly six decades that someone outside the Castro family will hold the country's highest government office. Raul Castro, who is stepping down after two five-year terms, will remain head of the Communist Party and retain significant power. The new president will take over on Thursday, April 19, and is expected to focus on improving the economy, a concern for many Cubans. The election comes as part of an effort to ensure that the single-party system created by the Castro brothers outlasts them, while addressing economic stagnation, an aging population, and increasing disenchantment among younger generations.

Samuel Shaffer, a self-proclaimed cult leader and former prophet of the Knights of Crystal Blade, was convicted on Wednesday for rape of a child and child sodomy. He was sentenced to 15 years to life in prison, with a minimum of 26 years behind bars. The charges stem from his marriage to an 8-year-old girl, who is the daughter of another cult member, John Coltharp.

Coltharp, who pleaded guilty on June 13 for child sodomy and child bigamy, is scheduled for sentencing on August 8. He was married to Shaffer’s 7-year-old daughter, according to a search warrant affidavit obtained by Salt Lake Tribune.

The investigation began in December after Coltharp's ex-wife reported that he had kidnapped their four children. Two of the girls were found inside two blue plastic 50-gallon water barrels, while the other two were discovered in an abandoned single-wide mobile trailer. All four girls were in poor health and received emergency medical care at a hospital.

Shaffer was previously sentenced to 25 years to life in prison for first-degree felony rape of a child and one second-degree felony count of child abuse, which will run concurrent with his current sentence. Another cult member, John Alvin Colth

An 82-year-old man named Masafumi Nagasaki, who is known as the "naked hermit," has lived voluntarily on a deserted island called Sotobanari in Japan for nearly three decades. He became the longest surviving voluntary castaway alive and was discovered by Alvaro Cerezo, who documents island castaways. Nagasaki braved typhoons, mosquitoes, and lack of fresh water, clothes, phones, or lighters on the island. He expressed his wish to die there and had lived a strict routine, including cleaning the beach daily. However, in April 2018, authorities removed him from the island due to concerns about his health and well-being. Nagasaki is currently living in a government house near Ishigaki city.

On September 28, 2014, Mount Ontake in Japan erupted without warning, causing a massive ash fall and the death of at least 36 people. The eruption occurred during a beautiful fall day when hundreds of hikers were climbing the mountain to admire the autumn foliage. Rescue efforts were halted on Monday due to fears of toxic gases and an increase in ash. Twelve bodies have been recovered, with more found near a shrine at the summit. The search for victims continues, but the exact cause of death remains unclear. Japan is one of the world's most seismically active nations, and this was its first fatal volcanic eruption since 1991.

On October 28, 2015, a shooting occurred at the Washington Square Mall in Indianapolis, resulting in three injuries. The incident took place around 6:30 p.m., near the Target store. According to police, a male suspect had an argument with a man he knew and then shot him. Two other victims were wounded by ricochet fire.

The suspect and his intended target reportedly knew each other and had some sort of issue, but the details are not disclosed by investigators. The three victims, two men and a woman, suffered non-life-threatening injuries, though one of the male victims was initially taken to the hospital in serious condition.

Police believe that the suspect may have fled the scene to the west, and there may be a second suspect, but no descriptions have been released. Witnesses described a chaotic scene inside the mall during the shooting. Anyone with information about the incident or possible suspects is urged to contact Crime Stoppers. The mall's management issued a statement expressing concern for the victims and their families, and emphasizing their commitment to maintaining a safe shopping environment.

A suburban Philadelphia transit worker named Bob Tracey found $15,000 in cash last March and turned it in to police. After no one claimed the money, a judge ordered its return to Tracey on Monday. Upper Darby Police Superintendent Michael Chitwood was impressed by Tracey's honesty and believed the money should go to him if the owner did not come forward. However, Tracey had to petition the courts in September to get the money returned due to bureaucratic delays. The bag also contained drug paraphernalia, making it unlikely that the real owners would come forward.

In a separate news article, it was reported that Bob Tracey found $15,200 in cash in the middle of State Road in Upper Darby last March and turned it in to authorities. After more than a year, a judge agreed with Upper Darby Police Superintendent Michael Chitwood and ordered the money returned to Tracey this week. Tracey was forced to petition the courts in September due to bureaucratic delays. Under state law, Tracey had a valid claim for title of the property against all persons except the true owner. It's unclear why Tracey's legal battle dragged on for six months.

The historic summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un took place in Singapore on June 12, 2018. The two leaders signed a document pledging to work towards complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. The summit was followed by a series of meetings and a working lunch. Both Trump and Kim expressed optimism about the potential for future productive talks. However, the details of how denuclearization would be achieved were not specified in the joint statement. Critics have raised concerns that the summit may have elevated North Korea's rogue regime without securing significant concessions from Kim.

The Secret Service is embroiled in a prostitution scandal involving 11 agents who brought women back to their hotel rooms before President Obama's arrival in Colombia for an international summit. The incident occurred at the Hotel Caribe, where the agents were staying and where some White House staff and press team are also lodged.

The trouble began when one agent refused to pay a woman, presumed to be a prostitute, leading to a dispute that was reported to local police. As a result of the investigation launched by the Secret Service, at least one supervisor was among those involved. The agents were immediately recalled to Washington, and their careers are likely over due to the incident's ethical implications, potential for embarrassment to the White House, and possible vulnerability to blackmail or assassination attempts.

The scandal also involves five American service members who may have been involved in misconduct at the same hotel. The Secret Service has expressed regret for the situation, which has overshadowed President Obama's diplomatic mission to Latin America. The White House maintains that the president still has full confidence in the Secret Service.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, responsible for awarding the Oscars, has responded to criticism about its lack of diversity by inviting a record-breaking number of new members. This unprecedented move includes almost half women and 41% people of color, aiming to address concerns regarding an overwhelmingly older, male, and white membership. The list of invited professionals spans Hollywood veterans, international heavyweights, and up-and-coming directors, such as Catherine Breillat, Park Chan-wook, and Patty Jenkins. Notable acting invitees include Luis Guzmán, Idris Elba, Kate Beckinsale, and Regina King, among others. This move is a significant step towards the Academy's commitment to double the number of women and people of color in its ranks by 2020, a response to the #OscarsSoWhite movement led by April Reign.

American journalist James Foley was brutally murdered by Islamic State militants and a graphic video of his execution was uploaded to YouTube on August 19. The terrorist group had threatened to kill Foley in retaliation for US airstrikes against the Islamic State in Iraq. Foley was kidnapped nearly two years ago on Thanksgiving Day and his family, along with GlobalPost, government authorities, and private security consultants had been working to secure his release since then. The Islamic State is currently holding three American hostages in Syria, including freelance reporter Steven Sotloff, who has also been threatened with execution if the US continues its bombing campaign in Iraq. The Foley family has released an email from their son's captors that contains factual inaccuracies and offers insight into the motivations and tactics of the Islamic State. The email states that the Foley family was not given many chances to negotiate for Jim's release, but in reality, they received their first message from his captors on Nov. 26, 2013, asking for a ransom of 100 million euros (about $132 million) or the release of unspecified prisoners held by the United States.
