Lamar Austin, a military veteran and father of four, lost his job as a part-time security guard after missing work to be with his wife Lindsay at the hospital for the birth of their son Cainan, who was the first baby born in Concord on New Year's Day. However, since then, Austin has received multiple job offers, including an apprenticeship offer from the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers and the NH AFL-CIO union, as well as assistance from a staffing agency. The family has also received an outpouring of support and a fundraising page to help them financially. The story struck a chord with readers who questioned whether an employee could be fired for missing work due to the birth of a child, as New Hampshire is an "at-will" employment state, which means employers can terminate employees at any time and for any reason, with few exceptions. The family's story has also caught the attention of legislators and labor leaders who are advocating for fair labor practices and paid family leave for workers in New Hampshire.

EgyptAir Flight MS804 carrying 66 passengers and crew disappeared from radar over the Mediterranean Sea on May 19, 2016, while en route from Paris to Cairo. Initial reports suggested that debris from the plane had been found in the sea, but later it was confirmed by an EgyptAir official that no wreckage had been located yet. The search and rescue efforts are still ongoing. There were concerns about potential terrorism as the cause of the crash, with French President François Hollande and presumptive Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump both expressing their belief that it was a terrorist attack. Egyptian Civil Aviation Minister Sherif Fathi also stated that the possibility of a terror attack as the cause of the crash is "higher than that of a technical error." The plane was an Airbus A320 and had accumulated approximately 48,000 flight hours.

On Tuesday, October 30, 2018, three children were killed and another critically injured when they were struck by a pickup truck as they crossed SR 25 to board their school bus north of Rochester, Indiana. The victims were identified as 9-year-old Alivia Stahl and her twin 6-year-old brothers, Xzavier and Mason Ingle. An 11-year-old boy named Maverik Lowe was also hit and suffered multiple broken bones. He was airlifted to a hospital in critical condition for surgery.

The Tippecanoe Valley School Corp. bus had stopped with its stop-arm deployed when the accident occurred. The children were struck by a northbound pickup truck as they crossed the southbound lane. Indiana State Police Sgt. Tony Slocum stated that it was unclear if charges would be filed against the pickup driver, but noted that Indiana law requires motorists to stop when a school bus is picking up or dropping off children.

The community was deeply affected by the tragedy, with counselors being dispatched to schools and the Tippecanoe Valley School Corp. urging the community to come together to pray for the families. Gov. Eric Holcomb also expressed his condolences, stating that words could not express the depth of sorrow he and his wife felt for the families affected by the accident.

The UNESCO has published a list of 70 artworks stolen from the National Museum of Fine Arts in Havana, Cuba. The organization condemned the theft, stating that it threatens the integrity of the seized property and places them at risk of illicit trafficking. The stolen works, mostly belonging to the "Turn of the Century" period, were discovered after several pieces were put up for sale in Miami. The Cuban authorities have confirmed the robbery but have not provided specific figures on the number of stolen pieces. The theft was meticulously executed, with the canvases being cut and frames neatly repositioned to avoid detection. The Cuban Minister of Culture, Rafael Bernal, was dismissed from his post following the acknowledgement of the theft, but no reason was given. Law enforcement officials in Cuba and the United States are currently investigating the case, with a value of over $1 million for the stolen artworks.

The study conducted by Jack Levin and Arnold Arluke from Northeastern University reveals that people have more empathy for abused puppies, dogs, and children compared to adult humans. The researchers found that age plays a significant role in eliciting empathy, with adults being viewed as capable of protecting themselves while full-grown dogs are seen as larger puppies. Interestingly, the difference in empathy for children versus puppies was statistically non-significant. The study involved 240 college students and focused on dogs and humans; however, Levin believes similar findings would apply to cats and people as well since they are often considered family pets and attributed human characteristics. Women were found to be more empathetic than men towards both human and animal victims in the study. The research will be presented at the 108th Annual Meeting of the American Sociological Association this week.

North Korean authorities have arrested several hundred relatives of Jang Song-thaek, the recently deposed uncle of supreme leader Kim Jong-un, following his execution on Dec. 13 for various crimes against the state. The execution of Song-thaek set off speculation about a power struggle within North Korea's secretive government. According to South Korean intelligence officials, the clash between Kim Jong-un and his uncle was over control of North Korea's most lucrative exports, including coal, clams, and crabs. The execution of Song-thaek's two top lieutenants preceded his own execution by antiaircraft machine guns. The opaqueness of North Korea's inner circle means that many details of the struggle between Kim Jong-un and his uncle remain murky. Adam Levine, her coach on The Voice, has offered to pay for her funeral expenses and the cost of her plane flight home. Grimmie's brother Marcus shared this news on his Facebook page. Grimmie was gunned down by 27-year-old Kevin James Loibl after a meet and greet following a concert with Before You Exit at the Plaza Live.

Harrison Ford, a renowned actor known for his roles in 'Star Wars' and 'Indiana Jones', was injured when the single-engine vintage plane he was piloting crash-landed on a golf course in Venice, California on March 5, 2015. The incident occurred shortly after takeoff from Santa Monica Airport. Ford reported engine trouble and tried to return to the airport before making an emergency landing on the Penmar Golf Club. He was hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening and was expected to make a full recovery. Witnesses saw the plane clip a tree before crashing, and two doctors who were golfing at the time came to Ford's aid. The cause of the crash is still unknown. Ford is an experienced pilot and has a history of flying planes and helicopters.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has ordered 23andMe, a popular genetic-testing company, to halt sales of its Personal Genome Service (PGS). The FDA's action comes due to concerns about the test's effectiveness and potential health consequences from false positive or negative assessments. The agency stated that 23andMe has failed to provide the necessary scientific data to prove that its test works as advertised, despite multiple interactions with FDA officials. The company has 15 days to detail how it will address these concerns or face further regulatory actions such as civil fines or injunctions. This move by the FDA underscores their unease about direct-to-consumer genetic tests and highlights a contentious debate over government oversight of individual access to genetic information.

An Egyptian man named Taymour el-Sobky was sentenced to three years in prison with hard labor for making controversial comments about married women during a television show in December. El-Sobky claimed that 30% of married Egyptian women are prone to infidelity, which sparked public outrage and led to his arrest. The court deemed his comments harmful to public peace and damaging to the public interest. This sentence follows recent crackdowns on dissent under President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, and has raised concerns about free speech in Egypt. Notably, author Ahmed Naji was sentenced to two years in prison for violating "public modesty" through publishing an excerpt of his novel containing a sex scene, and other cases of harassment and threats against artists, writers, and intellectuals have been reported. Some critics argue that el-Sobky's case, along with other recent incidents, show that it is not the law but public opinion and pressure that determines guilt or innocence in Egypt.

In a press release on Friday, Rosemont authorities announced that they have closed the investigation into the death of 19-year-old Kenneka Jenkins, who was found dead in a hotel freezer after attending a party at the Crowne Plaza Chicago O'Hare Hotel. The authorities determined her death to be accidental, stating there is no evidence suggesting foul play. However, lawyers for Jenkins' mother have raised concerns about graphic police photographs taken after her body was found, which they say "raise more questions than answers."

The release of documents and videos related to the case included dozens of postmortem photographs of Jenkins, some of which were described as showing portions of her body exposed. Lawyers for Jenkins' family called these photos "graphic and disturbing" and said they were of a personal, private, and indecent nature.

Jenkins was found dead in the hotel freezer on September 10, about 21 hours after she went missing following the party. According to police reports, she was found on her side, face down, with her left arm underneath her, her right shoe off, and a small cut on her right foot. The photographs show that Jenkins was still wearing the jeans and jean jacket shown in surveillance videos of her walking through the hotel before her death, but the shirt beneath her jacket "was pulled up exposing her breasts," a police report said.

A drunk passenger attempted to enter the cockpit of an IndiGo aircraft preparing for takeoff from Mumbai to Kolkata on September 24, 2018. The man claimed he needed to charge his phone, but was offloaded due to a security violation and handed over to police for questioning. He was later released without charge.

In another incident, a passenger on a GoAir flight from New Delhi to Patna on September 22 attempted to open the plane's rear door, mistaking it for the toilet. The man was believed to be a first-time flyer and was handed over to police after the plane landed safely in Patna.

In yet another incident last week, more than 30 passengers were hospitalized with nose bleeds, headaches, and ear pain due to crew forgetting to pressurize the cabin on a Jaipur-bound flight.

USA Gymnastics has refused to voluntarily give up its status as the national governing body for gymnastics in the United States, triggering a hearing that could lead to the organization's demise. The U.S. Olympic Committee (USOC) filed a complaint 16 days ago seeking to remove USA Gymnastics' recognition due to the sexual abuse of hundreds of female athletes by former national team doctor Lawrence G. Nassar. The USOC offered USA Gymnastics the option of giving up its recognition voluntarily, but the gymnastics organization instead asked questions about the matter and the USOC hearing process.

The hearing will be chaired by a USOC board member and have representatives from the National Governing Body (NGB) and athlete advisory councils. USA Gymnastics will have the opportunity to present factual evidence and legal arguments regarding the allegations in the complaint. After the hearing, a report will be issued, and a recommendation will be made to the USOC's board of directors, who will make the final decision.

The move does not come as a complete surprise, as USA Gymnastics has continued to operate as if it plans to be around for the long-term despite being informed by the USOC on Nov. 5 that it was beginning the process to revoke its NGB status. The hearing could take several weeks or even a few months

"Creed," a new installment in the Rocky series, deviates from its trailer's promised brutal boxing melodrama, instead offering a heartwarming and formulaic sequel that pays homage to its predecessors. The film follows Adonis Johnson Creed (Michael B. Jordan), the son of Apollo Creed, as he strives to become a successful boxer like his father. Sylvester Stallone reprises his role as Rocky Balboa, who serves as Adonis' mentor in his journey towards a championship bout. The film features compelling performances from both actors and includes realistic fight scenes, with no clear villains. The story culminates in an emotional finale where Adonis and Rocky symbolically retrace the steps of the iconic Rocky run up the Philadelphia Museum of Art's steps.

Tiger Woods is planning to return to the PGA tour in the Spring after completing rehab for sexual addiction, according to RadarOnline.com. He is currently at Pine Grove Behavioral Health and Addiction Services in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, where he is undergoing a six-week program directed by Dr. Patrick Carnes, a pioneer in treating sexually compulsive behavior. Tiger's wife Elin has not visited him during his rehab, and there is speculation about the future of their marriage. Tiger has been linked to at least 14 women during his marriage, with his most recent affair being with Rachel Uchitel. He drove into a fire hydrant and tree in the early morning hours after Thanksgiving and has not been seen in public since.

The Hart family, consisting of Jennifer and Sarah Hart and their six adopted children, were traced by cell phone pings to be in the Newport area, Oregon on March 24, two days before their GMC Yukon plunged off a cliff into the Pacific Ocean, killing five people. Investigators determined that the family traveled south on US-101 from Newport until they reached Highway 1 in Legget, California. They stayed on Highway 1 until they arrived in Fort Bragg around 8 p.m. Saturday, March 24 and remained there until about 9 p.m. Sunday. Jennifer Hart was spotted at a Safeway in Fort Bragg on March 25 at 8:05 a.m., and investigators are reviewing surveillance footage from the area as a possible clue to the family's whereabouts between then and the time their SUV was found by a German tourist on Monday, March 26. The three missing children are still being searched for along the shoreline from the crash site to Fort Bragg. The couple's home in Woodland, Washington was searched on Thursday, March 29, and no suicide note was found. The family had previously lived in West Linn, Oregon since 2014, and there have been reports of child welfare concerns regarding the family going back to 2013.

The article discusses the story of two brothers, Tamerlan and Dzhokar Tsarnaev, who came to America from a war-torn part of the world seeking a new life. Tamerlan was a talented boxer who represented New England as a heavyweight in the National Golden Gloves boxing tournament and aspired to make it on an Olympic team. Dzhokar, on the other hand, graduated from Cambridge Rindge & Latin School and was awarded a scholarship. He was also an athlete, a wrestler, and was named student athlete of the month.

However, something went wrong somewhere as the brothers became the suspects behind the Boston Marathon bombings that occurred on April 15th. The manhunt for the brothers led to a massive lockdown in the Boston area, with much of it being closed or on lockdown during the investigation. The older brother, Tamerlan, was shot and killed by police early Friday, while his younger brother, Dzhokar, was taken into custody later that night.

The article also includes photographs of the aftermath of the bombings, the manhunt for the suspects, and the celebration in Boston after the capture of Dzhokar Tsarnaev. The study published in BMJ suggests that a round of golf can confer longevity benefits just as robust as a 100-mile bike ride, based on the mortality records of 9,889 Olympic athletes who competed between 1896 and 1936. The research indicates that high cardiovascular intensity exercises like cycling and rowing do not offer any added survival benefits compared to low cardiovascular intensity activities such as golf or cricket.

The study adds to a growing body of research suggesting that years-long doses of extreme exercise may be unproductive, if not counterproductive, beyond a certain point, for instance, 20 miles a week of running. The researchers argue that high-intensity exercise causes micro traumata over time, leading to an accumulation of damage and potential aging effects.

However, the study does not suggest abandoning marathons or triathlons entirely, as it is too preliminary and controversial. It also should not be used as an excuse for staying sedentary, which poses well-established risks of cardiovascular disease. The research emphasizes that extreme fitness can induce euphoria but may have long-term negative effects on health.

The article discusses the upcoming Eta Aquarid meteor shower that will be visible on May 5 and May 6, 2016. The meteor shower is caused by Earth passing through debris left behind by Halley's Comet. The radiant of the meteor shower rises along with the constellation Aquarius in the early morning hours, and should be visible from about 3 a.m. local time until dawn on both mornings. Although it is not one of the strongest meteor showers, viewers with clear skies and minimal light pollution can expect to see between 10 and 20 meteors per hour. The morning of May 5 may offer better viewing conditions, with slightly more meteors visible in the sky. NASA predicts that the exact peak of the meteor shower will occur during daylight hours on May 5.

The article also mentions that a developing La Niña could affect summer weather patterns, and encourages viewers to tune in for the Summer Forecast on May 24 at 9pm EST. For those unable to view the meteor shower due to unfavorable weather conditions or scheduling conflicts, the Slooh Community Observatory is hosting a live show that can be viewed via an embedded video at the bottom of the article. During the Democratic National Convention, President Barack Obama surprised attendees by kissing Jill Biden, Joe Biden's wife, on the lips. The incident sparked discussions about whether it was intentional or accidental. The article also discussed various scenarios that could arise from an accidental mouth kiss, such as with a crush, family friend, boss, or inappropriate person.

The article further delved into Obama's history of kissing powerful women, including Diane Sawyer, Hillary Clinton, and French First Lady Carla Bruni. The article humorously depicted these interactions, suggesting that Obama uses his lips to win over potential adversaries and reward friends.

In another section, the article discussed an incident where Obama did not kiss Carla Bruni during a meeting with the French President Nicolas Sarkozy. This lack of a customary kiss was a topic of discussion in Europe, leading to speculations about why it didn't happen. The article suggested that the situation was eventually rectified at a dinner later that night.

Finally, the article touched upon the fashion choices of Michelle Obama and Carla Bruni during the meeting, with Michelle wearing a magenta dress by Thakoon and Carla wearing a simple grey Dior coat. The article also included criticisms of Carla's outfit being too plain and prim compared to her usual style.

A former Dallas police officer, Amber Guyger, has been indicted on a murder charge for the shooting death of Botham Shem Jean, a 26-year-old unarmed black man, in his own apartment on September 6th. Guyger had initially been charged with manslaughter but was later indicted on a more serious offense of murder. The grand jury's decision comes after an investigation that involved over 300 witnesses and a "very spirited conversation" between the Dallas County District Attorney Faith Johnson and the Texas Rangers, the lead investigators in the case. Guyger had claimed she mistook Jean's apartment for her own, but at the moment of the shooting, it was determined to be an intentional act. The indictment is a step towards justice for Jean's family, who have filed a lawsuit against the City of Dallas and its police department, alleging excessive force and a pattern of using deadly force against minorities.

Coca-Cola has entered the alcoholic beverage market by launching a lemon-flavored alcopop in Japan. This is the company's first foray into selling alcohol, marking a significant shift in their 125-year history. The new product, which ranges from 3% to 8% alcohol, aims at young consumers, particularly women, and is modeled after popular Chu-Hi drinks in Japan. Coca-Cola's new drinks are not planned for release in markets outside of Japan. The launch of these alcopops comes following the popularity of alcopops like Smirnoff Ice and Bacardi Breezer in Europe and the UK during the 1990s, although these drinks were controversial due to concerns they encouraged excessive alcohol consumption among young people due to their soft drink-like taste.

The United Nations annual climate change summit in Cancun, Mexico, resulted in an historic deal on climate change that commits all major economies to greenhouse gas cuts. The agreement, brokered after four years of negotiations, includes less deforestation, transfer of technology to developing countries, and the establishment of a yearly fund potentially worth up to $100bn to help countries adapt to climate change.

The deal falls short of a global treaty but has progressed from Copenhagen by getting all countries, except Bolivia, to sign up to an official UN document. The agreement commits all countries to keeping temperature rise below 2C (3.6F) by reducing emissions. Rich countries have agreed to consider an extension of the Kyoto Protocol while poor countries will sign up to emission cuts for the first time.

The Cancun deal also sets up a "green fund" to help poor countries cope with climate change and a new scheme to halt deforestation. However, Bolivia claimed the agreement was "tantamount to genocide" because cuts are not tough enough to stop dangerous global warming. The debate continued into the early hours of the morning, but eventually, Bolivia gave in after intense pressure from other countries.

The deal will be further worked out as climate change negotiations begin in 2011, and there will be a push to produce a legally binding treaty at the annual conference

Researchers have discovered that the colorful and varied faces of Guenon monkeys, a group of more than 25 species found in Central and West Africa, have evolved as a means to avoid crossbreeding. By using human facial recognition technology, scientists found that guenons' looks have evolved to become more distinctive from their relatives living close by, providing evidence for the use of visual signals to help ensure species recognition and prevent interbreeding. This is considered the best evidence to date of visual signs acting as a barrier to breeding across species. The findings were published in the journal Nature Communications.

The latest ABC News/Washington Post poll shows that former Massachusetts Governor Mitt Romney is currently the strongest Republican candidate for the 2012 presidential election, with a close race against President Barack Obama among all Americans (47% vs. 46%) and registered voters (49% vs. 46%). However, while Romney leads other potential opponents tested in the poll, former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin faces significant challenges due to low approval ratings and doubts about her qualifications for the presidency.

The poll reveals that 64% of Americans say they definitely will not vote for Palin for president, with 63% describing her as unqualified for the job. Even within her own party, 41% of Republicans rule out voting for her, and 39% see her as unqualified.

Despite Romney's strong position, he faces potential risks from the health care plan he signed into law in Massachusetts in 2006, which is opposed by a majority of leaned Republicans (41% to 21%) and could be a significant issue in his campaign. Religion may also be a question for Romney, as he has lower support among born-again and evangelical white Protestants compared to non-evangelicals.

The head of the Senate Intelligence Committee, Sen. Dianne Feinstein, has accused the CIA of improperly searching a stand-alone computer network established for Congress as part of its investigation into allegations of CIA abuse in a Bush-era detention and interrogation program. Feinstein claims that the CIA searched the network in January, potentially violating an agreement made with the committee about monitoring the panel's use of CIA computers. The CIA Director John Brennan denies spying on the Senate Intelligence Committee and states that the matter is being investigated by the right authorities. The dispute between Congress and the agency has been referred to the Justice Department for possible criminal prosecution, and Sen. Feinstein has sought an apology and acknowledgment that the CIA's actions were wrong but has not received one yet. The Intelligence Committee is investigating CIA detention and interrogation practices that date back to when Brennan was directing that program.

The study published in the International Journal of Obesity found that adults consume nearly 92% of the food they put on their plates, with some variations depending on distractions, meal type (meal vs snack), and whether the eating occurred at home or in a lab. The urge to clean one's plate is not limited to Americans but is prevalent globally across several countries including the US, Canada, France, Taiwan, South Korea, Finland, and the Netherlands.

Children, however, eat only about 60% of what they serve themselves, possibly due to uncertainty about whether they will like a particular food. The study was conducted by Brian Wansink, director of the Cornell Food and Brand Lab, and Katherine Abowd Johnson from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

The researchers found that people who eat healthier foods (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean meat or dairy) consume more (91.2%) than those eating less healthy foods (80.6%). The study aims to fill a gap in understanding portion sizes and their connection to overweight and obesity.

The findings suggest that being mindful of appropriate portion size can help individuals make healthier food choices, as knowing that one is likely to consume almost all of what they serve themselves can encourage more thoughtful serving.

The article discusses the controversial decision by the Trump administration to ease penalties on Chinese telecommunications giant ZTE, which was banned for violating sanctions against Iran and North Korea. Critics argue that ZTE is a notorious intellectual property thief, having been sued for patent infringement over 200 times in various countries, including the U.S., China, and others. They claim that ZTE's behavior is outside the norm even among Chinese companies and that the government should not reward such behavior. The deal would require ZTE to pay a significant fine, place U.S. compliance officers at the company, and change its management team, allowing it to resume business with U.S. companies. This decision has faced immediate resistance in Congress, with Democrats and Republicans accusing Trump of bending to pressure from China and posing a risk to U.S. national security.

An Ontario Court judge has found animal activist Anita Krajnc not guilty of mischief for giving water to pigs outside a slaughterhouse in Burlington, Ontario, in June 2015. The case attracted international attention and was seen as a rallying point for animal rights activists. Justice David Harris dismissed the charge against Krajnc, who is the founder of Toronto Pig Save, stating that she did not interfere with anyone's property or obstruct the "lawful use" of the pigs. The judge also rejected comparisons made by Krajnc's lawyers to historical rights activists such as Gandhi, Nelson Mandela, and Susan B. Anthony, calling them offensive. Farm groups expressed disappointment with the decision, stating that it puts food safety at risk. Krajnc plans to celebrate the verdict with a vegan lunch and a vigil at a nearby slaughterhouse.

Isis, also known as the Islamic State, has launched a new media group called Zora Foundation that targets women supporting Islamist fighters. The organization's slogan is "preparing for the honor of jihad," and it provides advice on how to be a good supporter of jihad as a woman. Zora's material, all in Arabic, has been shared by Isis supporters across social media. The group's most recent post was a recipe shared on Twitter, which was prefaced with an introduction dedicated to women who support the fighters. Charlie Winter, a researcher at the Quilliam Foundation, said that Zora is aimed at those preparing to go out and support the group, as well as acting as a facility for women already out there. This is the first time he has come across an actual media organization giving guidance to women on their role in supporting jihad.

McDonald's has reduced the price of its Mighty Wings by 40% to $3 for five wings, or about 60 cents per wing, in an attempt to boost sales. The wings were initially launched at $1 per wing last year but did not perform well due to high prices and spiciness. McDonald's concedes that the early regional testing of Mighty Wings did not reflect consumer preferences nationally. Although the amount of spice has not been changed, there is more awareness about the wings' spicy kick. The price reduction may lead to a slight loss for McDonald's, but it aims to sell off its excess frozen wings. The success of the new pricing remains uncertain, and it could potentially discontinue the product if sales do not improve.

The article discusses the raid by U.S. special forces that resulted in the death of Osama Bin Laden, the founder of Al Qaeda. One of Bin Laden's sons, Hamza, who is often referred to as the "Crown Prince of Terror," may have escaped during the raid. This information was revealed during interrogations of Bin Laden's three wives by Pakistani investigators. It is not confirmed which son went missing, but Hamza is a strong suspect due to his prominent role in Al Qaeda and his father's apparent willingness to groom him as a successor. The article also provides details about the U.S. special forces team that was sent to find Bin Laden, including President Obama's insistence on sending a large enough force to fight off hostile Pakistani soldiers if necessary. Additionally, it is reported that three of Bin Laden's wives and several of his children were taken into custody by Pakistani intelligence after the raid.

The study reveals strong isotopic anomalies in Martian water, indicating significant water loss over time. Maps of atmospheric water and its deuterated form show a high D/H enrichment, suggesting an ancient global ocean that covered nearly half of the northern hemisphere. This ocean, which was up to a mile deep in places, held 20 million cubic kilometers of water, equivalent to more than the Arctic Ocean.

The evidence supports the idea of Mars as a warm and wet world in its youth, with flowing water, streams, river deltas, and long-standing lakes. The infrared maps show that water near the Martian ice caps is enriched with deuterium, indicating that Mars lost a vast amount of water in the past, equivalent to more than six times the current amount locked up in the polar ice caps.

The ocean covered approximately 20% of the planet's surface, suggesting potential habitability and the evolution of life on Mars. The search for life will continue with future missions, such as the European Space Agency's Exomars rover scheduled for launch in 2018.

In response to perceived Western cultural influences eroding Islamic values, Iran's morality police have been cracking down on the sale of Barbie dolls. The dolls, produced by U.S. company Mattel Inc, were first declared un-Islamic in 1996 due to their "destructive cultural and social consequences." Despite a ban, they have until recently been openly sold in Tehran shops.

To meet demand while avoiding police scrutiny, shopkeepers have been hiding Barbie dolls behind other toys. An attempt to counter demand for Barbie with officially approved dolls named Sara and Dara, wearing traditional dress, has not been successful. Iranians will soon be able to buy toy versions of the U.S. spy drone that was captured by Iran in December, as a response to tensions between the two countries. The miniature models of the RQ-170 Sentinel stealth drone will be mass produced and sold on the Iranian market for around $4.

Iran has been fighting a long battle to purge Western culture from the country since its Islamic revolution in 1979, enforcing Islamic dress codes, banning Western music, and foreign satellite television. The capture of the U.S. spy drone can be seen as another swipe at the West by Iran.

The United States is reassessing its relationship with Israel following provocative statements made by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during the recent election campaign, which appeared to reject the creation of a Palestinian state. In a phone call on Thursday, President Barack Obama expressed concern over Netanyahu's opposition to a two-state solution and emphasized the United States' commitment to this long-standing policy. Netanyahu later walked back his disavowal of a two-state solution in an interview with MSNBC, stating that he wants a sustainable, peaceful two-state solution but only under certain conditions. The White House has not yet announced any specific actions regarding a potential U.N. resolution calling for the establishment of a Palestinian state, but officials have hinted at the possibility of supporting such a resolution in response to Netanyahu's remarks. Additionally, Netanyahu walked back another controversial campaign remark about Arab voters and emphasized the importance of free and fair elections in Israel. The Israeli prime minister also downplayed strains in his personal relationship with Obama, stating that America has no greater ally than Israel and Israel has no greater ally than the United States.

A previously undiscovered sketchbook by the renowned post-Impressionist artist Vincent Van Gogh will be published in November by French publisher Seuil. The sketches, titled "Vincent Van Gogh, Le Brouillard d'Arles" (The Fog of Arles), have been described as "stunning, dazzling." Details about the origin and discovery of the sketches are scarce, with Seuil stating they will reveal more information at a press conference in Paris in mid-November. The publisher has generated excitement around the release, leaving many anticipating the contents of the sketches.

The second-born giant panda cub born on August 22 at the Smithsonian National Zoo in Washington, D.C., has unfortunately passed away. The smaller cub went into cardiac arrest and could not be revived despite efforts from the zoo's staff. The first-born cub appears to be healthy and strong, and is with its mother, Mei Xiang. This is the third time in three years that Mei Xiang has lost a cub, with the previous losses being a stillbirth in 2013 and another death after six days in 2012. However, she does have two other surviving cubs, born in 2013 and 2005. The zoo will perform a necropsy to determine the cause of the cub's death.

In a four-day siege that ended on Saturday, Islamist militants held foreign and local workers hostage at an Algerian gas plant. The Algerian authorities reported that all 32 hostage-takers were killed during the raid by troops, but at least 81 people have died in total, with many bodies found at the complex on Sunday, some of which may be captors or captives. It is unclear whether the five suspected militants arrested are among those still alive. The siege was in response to French intervention against Islamist groups in Mali, and the leader of the hostage-takers, Mokhtar Belmokhtar, has claimed responsibility for it. Western leaders have condemned the kidnappings, with UK Prime Minister David Cameron and US President Barack Obama blaming "terrorists" for the hostages' deaths. The death toll is likely to rise as bomb squads continue to search for explosives at the site.

In this article, it is reported that Pope Francis' environment encyclical was leaked to an Italian newsweekly, L'Espresso, three days before its official release. The Vatican has since indefinitely suspended the press credentials of L'Espresso's veteran Vatican correspondent, Sandro Magister, stating that the publication had been "incorrect." However, Magister claims that his editor obtained the document and decided to publish it, with Magister only writing the introduction. The encyclical, titled "Laudato Si" (Be Praised), states that global warming is mostly due to human activity and calls for a radical change in behavior to save the planet for future generations. Some speculate that the leak was aimed at taking the punch out of the official launch of the encyclical, as conservatives have been criticizing the document even before its release. There has been a history of leaked documents in the Vatican, with the last big scandal occurring in 2012 resulting in the pope's butler being put on trial for stealing his private papers and passing them off to an Italian journalist. The Vatican City State updated its criminal code to include severe penalties for anyone who leaks a Vatican document or publishes news from it, with up to two years in prison and a 5,000 euro ($5,600)

The tapes allegedly contain a private conversation between Poland's top banker and an interior minister discussing political matters, which is against Polish law as the central bank must remain independent of politics. The tapes were published earlier this week and have caused severe pressure on Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who has denied that the leaked recordings led to the replacement of Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski four months ago. The raid on Wprost's offices resulted in a siege that was broadcast live on television, with security agents attempting to seize the editor-in-chief's laptop but leaving empty-handed. Critics have pointed out several legal deficiencies and errors in the operation. The emergence of the tapes and the government's handling of the situation has put Tusk under pressure, with him threatening a snap election if the crisis in confidence continues. The timing of the conversation on the tapes is critical to understanding the comments made, as Poland's top officials had earlier expressed frustration about the United States' interest in deepening its commitment to regional security, but Russia's annexation of Crimea turned that attitude around. Colgate Total® toothpaste is a trusted brand for oral health, recommended by dentists worldwide. It contains triclosan, an antibacterial ingredient that fights harmful plaque germs causing common oral problems. There are over 90 clinical studies supporting the efficacy and safety of Colgate Total®, involving more than 20,000 people.

The toothpaste is clinically proven to reduce plaque germs leading to gingivitis (an early form of gum disease) and provide 12-hour protection against these germs. Gingivitis affects over 75% of American adults, and if unchecked, can progress to periodontitis, a more serious stage of infection that may result in tooth and bone loss.

The US FDA recognizes the benefits of triclosan in Colgate Total® toothpaste, stating it is effective in preventing gingivitis. The Cochrane Oral Health Group conducted an independent review, concluding that fluoride toothpaste containing triclosan/copolymer provides various clinical benefits, including a 22% reduction in plaque and gingivitis compared to traditional fluoride toothpaste.

However, the FDA has issued a final rule banning antibacterial soaps and body washes containing triclosan due to concerns about potential negative effects on health over long-term use.

In summary, there have been calls for investigations and hearings following a security breach at the White House where a man was able to jump the fence and enter through the North Portico doors. Rep. Peter King, a member of the House Homeland Security Committee, has demanded a full investigation and suggested that Congress may hold hearings on the issue. Meanwhile, Sen. Dianne Feinstein has urged the National Football League (NFL) to adopt a zero-tolerance policy for domestic abuse, following the arrest of San Francisco 49ers defensive lineman Ray McDonald, who remained in the team's lineup for a Sunday game. Feinstein expressed concern about the increase in violence and called for suspended action if a player is arrested or convicted, emphasizing the need for NFL teams to set an example for society.

The Sodomite Suppression Act, a ballot initiative in California proposed by lawyer Matt McLaughlin, calls for executing gays with "bullets to the head" and mandates 10 years in prison and permanent expulsion from California for anyone advocating gay rights to minors. Despite its unconstitutionality and lack of chance to collect the required signatures, it is allowed to circulate for signatures due to legal loopholes.

In response, activist Charlotte Laws plans to file the Intolerant Jackass Act, which requires anyone proposing such hateful ballot measures to attend sensitivity training and donate $5000 to pro-gay organizations. The California Bar Association is being petitioned to disbar McLaughlin for advocating murder, as he calls for the legalized killing of the LGBT community.

The Sodomite Suppression Act has sparked outrage and frustration, with many calling for swift action from the California Bar Association to disbar McLaughlin and ensure justice in the judicial system.

The Sandra Bullock and George Clooney space drama "Gravity" had a successful debut at the box office, earning $55.6 million and becoming the biggest October opening ever. The film's success was largely due to its strong performance in 3-D, which accounted for about 80% of weekend business. Meanwhile, the Justin Timberlake and Ben Affleck movie "Runner Runner" fell short of expectations with a disappointing $7.6 million start. "Gravity" has been praised by critics and audiences alike, notching a 98% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes. The film was co-financed by Warner Bros. and Brett Ratner's RatPac-Dune Entertainment for $110 million.

The general election in the UK resulted in a hung parliament, with no party having a majority. Theresa May's Conservative Party won the most seats (318) and votes, but fell short of the 326 needed for an outright majority. As a result, negotiations will begin to see if the Conservatives can find enough support from other parties, such as the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), to form a stable government. If May fails to secure the necessary support, Labour could try to do the same. A Queen's Speech must be presented by June 19th, and Parliament will meet again on June 13th, setting deadlines for a new government to be formed. The Queen does not have a say in the process. If negotiations fail, another election could potentially occur. This summary is based on an article from Reuters and the BBC.

A Cambria County woman, Theresa Plummer, aged 69, is believed to have died last week as a result of coming into contact with drug paraphernalia while cleaning up her son's bathroom following his suspected overdose. The coroner, Jeff Lees, stated that she may have absorbed a substance through her skin or had an adverse reaction after handling the drug paraphernalia. Theresa Plummer stayed at her son's bedside in intensive care last week as doctors treated him for a suspected overdose. Her son, Ronald Plummer, aged 45, died the day after his mother. The coroner has performed autopsies but is awaiting toxicology reports to confirm the exact cause of death for both individuals. This incident serves as a caution for anyone coming into contact with any type of powder substance, and authorities advise extreme caution and notification of proper authorities in such cases.

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Schiaparelli probe, part of the ExoMars program, is believed to have crashed on Mars during its descent on October 19th. NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) has identified a dark patch and white spot in the targeted landing zone that are likely the impact site and parachute. The probe's descent systems did not function properly, with its parachute jettisoned too early and retrorockets firing for only a few seconds instead of half a minute. ESA and NASA are confident that these features represent the scene of Schiaparelli's impact. Further analysis is ongoing to determine the exact cause of the malfunction and to establish when and at what speed Schiaparelli went into freefall. The investigation will provide valuable information for the 2021 ExoMars mission, which aims to search for evidence of life on Mars.

In the tiny Pacific nation of Palau, six bodies believed to be Japanese soldiers from World War II have been discovered in a recently reopened cave. The site is located on Pelileu island, one of around 200 sealed caves that were used during fierce battles between US and Japanese forces in September 1944. The team responsible for making the caves safe for investigation consists of local Palauans, two Britons, one South African, and one Australian.

The cave where the remains were found contains war relics such as hand grenades, large projectiles, small arms ammunition, and explosive remnants of war. It is understood that these may be the crew of an anti-tank gun that took several days to capture during the battle. The cave has since been resealed, and it is noted that a lot of field caves may contain human remains and should not be used as tourist attractions.

An estimated 10,000 Japanese soldiers died during the fighting in Palau, with the remains of some 2,600 troops never found. The discovery of these bodies comes ahead of an imperial visit by Japanese emperor Akihito and empress Michiko next week. The team has been operating in Palau for six years to clear remnants of WWII ordnance.

In this article, it is reported that Mary Kristene Chapa, an 18-year-old who was shot in the head along with her girlfriend Mollie Judith Olgin, 19, is making a remarkable recovery after the shooting that occurred on Saturday at Andrews Park in Portland, Texas. The Texas Rangers are investigating the double shooting, but there is currently no evidence to suggest it was a hate crime. Chapa's brother, Hilario, has shared updates on her progress, stating that she has made physical progress on her right side and is able to communicate through sign language. The family has set up an official donation page on WePay to help pay for her medical bills. Mollie Olgin's father, Mario, has expressed his confidence that justice will be served and that his daughter's killer will be brought to justice. A memorial service for Olgin will be held at 4:30 p.m. Friday, followed by a candlelight vigil at the Violet Andrews Park.

On June 26, 2018, a disgruntled Air Force veteran named John Michael Watts, aged 58 and with no current address, set himself on fire outside the Georgia State Capitol in Atlanta as a protest against the Department of Veterans Affairs. The incident caused the evacuation of nearby buildings, including a day care center, and several loud explosions were heard before a trooper extinguished the fire. Watts was rushed to Grady Memorial Hospital with burns covering 85-90% of his body. Authorities later confirmed that he indicated his dissatisfaction with the VA system during questioning. The area around the Capitol was secured, and all roads were reopened by 6:15 p.m. Multiple agencies, including the GBI and bomb squad, were involved in securing the scene and ensuring there were no explosives in Watts' vehicle.

Two young Tibetan monks set themselves on fire in western China as a protest against government religious controls, according to two exiled Tibetan sources. The incident occurred at the Kirti monastery, a site of previous protests against Chinese policies. The monks, Kelsang and Kunchak, are reported to have shouted "We need freedom of religion" before self-immolating. Both monks suffered slight burns and are in stable condition according to state news agency Xinhua, but Tibetan sources claim their bodies were removed by the Chinese military. This is the third such protest this year and could lead to renewed tension in the region.

In a separate development, China has said any successor chosen by the Dalai Lama would be "illegal", after the spiritual leader announced that he would decide on his own reincarnation. Under Tibetan tradition, monks identify a young boy who shows signs of being a reincarnation of a late leader, but China is expected to appoint its own successor to the Dalai Lama. This raises the prospect of two Dalai Lamas - one recognized by Beijing and the other chosen by exiles or with the blessing of the current Dalai Lama. The Chinese stance follows the 1995 incident where China rejected the Dalai Lama's choice for the next Panchen Lama, and picked its own reincarnation.

A mass shooting occurred at Azana Salon & Spa in Brookfield, Wisconsin, which is across the street from Brookfield Square Mall. The shooting left at least three people dead and four injured. The suspected gunman, Radcliffe F. Haughton, was reportedly estranged from Zina Haughton, a sought-after hair stylist who worked at the spa. Authorities believe the shooting was related to a domestic dispute. Haughton's two daughters were confirmed to be safe. The victims' names were not immediately released, and authorities are still searching for the suspect. The incident prompted a lockdown of nearby buildings, including the mall and a hospital. This is an ongoing investigation.

Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google's main business under Alphabet Inc., received an equity award valued at nearly $200 million in February 2014. This makes him one of the world's highest-paid executives with a total equity stake in Alphabet now worth over $650 million. The new shares vest in quarterly increments over four years, provided Pichai remains employed by Alphabet.

Pichai's award is larger than the 2011 grant given to Tim Cook when he became Apple Inc.'s CEO, but still falls short of the fortunes made by Google's co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, as well as Google's former CEO Eric Schmidt.

In addition to Pichai, Ruth Porat, Alphabet’s chief financial officer, received shares worth about $38 million, while Diane Greene, head of Google’s cloud computing business, was awarded shares worth $42.8 million. These awards come on top of previous bonuses given to these executives.

Pichai celebrated the award by watching the Super Bowl and meeting NFL legend Ronnie Lott.

On Thursday, Garry Cordell, a man involved in the Schoolcraft County triple homicide case, was sentenced to life in prison without parole. The victims were Jody Hutchinson, Carrie Nelson, and Heather Aldrich. Their families spoke at his sentencing asking for the maximum sentence. Cordell pleaded guilty to two counts of murder in the first degree and one count of felony murder last week. The bodies of the victims were discovered in a burned car in Doyle Township in April. Kenneth Brunke, another suspect in the case, pleaded guilty in October to obstruction of justice and lying to a police officer in exchange for his testimony against Cordell and Marietta Carlson, who died of natural causes while in custody. During his sentencing, Cordell said he was proud of who he is and what he did and what he stands for. The prosecuting attorney shared a video with photographs of the victims and the burned car lasting four minutes, which is how long research shows it takes to strangle someone like Cordell did three times. Kenneth Brunke will be sentenced on December 10th in Schoolcraft County Circuit Court.

The Oxford Dodo, one of the most well-preserved examples of the extinct bird and the inspiration for Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, met a violent end as researchers have discovered lead shot pellets embedded in its skull, indicating it was murdered. This specimen, housed at the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, is the only one that retains any viable DNA and includes soft tissue and skin. Using 21st-century forensic scanning technology, scientists found evidence suggesting the dodo was shot in the back of the head with a shotgun, marking a brutal end to its life. The researchers are planning to analyze the lead pellets to potentially trace their origin and determine who killed the dodo.

Actress Sean Young was released from the Hollywood LAPD police station after being arrested for allegedly slapping a security guard outside the Academy Awards' Governors Ball. The incident occurred when Young, who did not have a ticket, was asked to leave the party by security guards. Young claims she was only trying to take pictures with fellow celebrities for her Facebook page and maintains that it was the security guard who initiated any physical contact. Young has stated that footage from the night will exonerate her and has blamed the Academy's lawyer for suggesting the citizens' arrest. The Academy has released a statement stating that they did not press charges against Young.

The Census Director, Robert Groves, announced at a briefing that the United States' total population count for 2010 was 308,745,538, marking the slowest growth since the Great Depression. The South experienced the fastest growth at 14.3%, followed closely by the West at 13.8%. The Northeast had a growth of 3.2% and the Midwest had 3.9%. Nevada had the largest population growth (35.1%) while Michigan was the only state with a decline (-0.6%). Commerce Secretary Gary Locke declared the 2010 census a success, stating it saved $1.87 billion more than anticipated due to a high participation rate. This figure surpasses the initial $1.6 billion in cost savings announced in August. Locke attributed this achievement to effective management that addressed concerns about potential waste and inefficiency from government auditors. Approximately 74% of U.S. households mailed back their 10-question form, matching the rate from 2000.

Pope Francis held a vigil at Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil on Saturday, where an estimated three million Catholics gathered. This was the culmination of his first overseas trip and the largest turnout for any event during World Youth Day, a biannual gathering of young Catholics. Earlier in the day, Francis addressed Catholic bishops in Rio de Janeiro's cathedral, urging them to get out of their parishes and spread the gospel to those most in need. He also emphasized the importance of dialogue and social humility in addressing issues such as inequality and corruption. The pope's visit comes amidst ongoing protests in Brazil over political corruption, police repression, and poor infrastructure. Young people attending World Youth Day made pilgrimages to Copacabana Beach, where they spent the day playing soccer, building sandcastles, and camping out under the stars.

The leader of Al-Qaida's affiliate in Yemen, Qassim al-Rimi, released an audio recording criticizing President Donald Trump following a U.S. Navy SEAL raid on an Al-Qaida compound in Yemen last week. In the recording, al-Rimi referred to Trump as the "White House's new fool" and claimed that the raid resulted in the deaths of 25 people, including 11 women and children. However, the U.S. military maintains that only one Navy SEAL was killed in the operation. Al-Rimi also claimed that scores of U.S. soldiers were killed or wounded, but this has not been verified. It is unclear whether al-Rimi was at the compound during the raid, and both the White House and Pentagon have denied that he was a target of the operation. The objective of the raid was reportedly to gather intelligence on Al-Qaida in Yemen, but some sources suggest that capturing or killing al-Rimi may have also been a goal. The raid has been met with controversy due to reports of civilian casualties, including an 8-year-old girl.

Roseanne Barr posted a controversial tweet about Bill Cosby, joking about a physical altercation with him and making light of his mounting sexual assault allegations. The tweet was deleted after negative feedback from followers. In an interview, Barr called the scandal surrounding Cosby "the best and the worst thing" as it allows people to see the truth but also tarnishes his reputation. Three more women have come forward to accuse Cosby of sexual assault, demanding a $100 million fund for alleged victims. Bill Cosby has remained silent on the allegations but has expressed gratitude towards supporters like Whoopi Goldberg and Jill Scott.

An improvised explosive device was found in a backpack near an Elizabeth train station, which detonated unintentionally when a bomb squad robot was attempting to disarm it. The explosion occurred around 12:40 am on Monday and no one was injured. Five devices were found inside the backpack, four of which were still believed to be live after the explosion. The FBI is reviewing surveillance footage and questioning five people in connection with the incident. This explosion follows two other nearby weekend incidents in New York City and New Jersey. The FBI has asked anyone with information to call 1-800-CALL-FBI. The transit service resumed after a suspension, but train services were halted between Newark Liberty Airport and Elizabeth, as well as Amtrak trains between New York Penn Station and Newark Penn Station.

Mikhail Kalashnikov, the inventor of the AK-47 assault rifle, expressed feelings of guilt and spiritual pain before his death in December 2019, at the age of 94. In a letter written to the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Kirill, Kalashnikov questioned whether he was morally responsible for the many deaths caused by his invention. The letter, published by Izvestia, suggests that Kalashnikov felt remorse for creating a weapon that has been used in conflicts worldwide and by criminal elements. It is unclear how much of the letter was written by Kalashnikov himself, as his daughter believes a priest may have helped him compose it. The Russian Orthodox Church supported Kalashnikov's work, stating that weapons designed to protect the country are supported by the church. Kalashnikov received numerous state honors but made little money from his invention, which has become a visual hallmark of armed insurgent movements around the world.

Emma Stone and Andrew Garfield, a popular Hollywood couple, have found an innovative way to deal with persistent paparazzi: using them to promote charitable organizations. In 2012, they first held up signs promoting kids' cancer charities, which went viral. Yesterday, they repeated the gesture in New York City, promoting four charities including Gilda's Club, Worldwide Orphans, Youth Mentoring Connection, and Autism Speaks. Their quick and impactful efforts have inspired many, as they continue to use their fame to make a difference in the world.

An Arkansas inmate who escaped from prison in May 1985 after being sentenced for burglary and theft of property has been apprehended on Sunday, June 25, at a residence in Springdale. The arrest was made by the Arkansas State Police (ASP) and local law enforcement. Steven Dishman, now 60 years old, is currently being held at the Varner Unit in Grady. The ASP's Criminal Investigation Division is investigating where Dishman has been since his escape and questioning individuals who may have known him under another name. It was an anonymous tip that led to his capture. Dishman will be required to finish his original sentence, and the file regarding his escape will be forwarded for further action by the Jefferson County prosecutor. Another inmate, Joel W. Lane, was also apprehended on Sunday after escaping from a work release program in Pine Bluff. A Massachusetts resident named Josh Byrne, who was on his honeymoon in Costa Rica, was swept away by floodwaters last Friday while attempting to cross a bridge during a flash flood. Despite an extensive search-and-rescue mission led by local authorities and his family members, Byrne's body was recovered on Saturday.

Josh Byrne, who was 30 years old and from Hudson, Massachusetts, had recently married his wife Bianca in New Hampshire. The couple was honeymooning in Playa Dominicalito, Costa Rica when the incident occurred.

Byrne's father and brother traveled to Costa Rica on Friday to assist with the search efforts. The family expressed their gratitude towards the local community, Massachusetts political leaders, the Red Cross, and the U.S. Embassy and State Department for their assistance during this difficult time. They also set up a GoFundMe campaign to help cover costs related to Byrne's recovery and services.

The family remembered Josh Byrne as a kind, friendly individual with a caring demeanor, who was deeply loved by his wife Bianca. His employer, SJC Custom Drums, also expressed their condolences and shared memories of Byrne's positive impact on the company during his employment.

David Crosby, a singer-songwriter from Crosby, Stills & Nash, was involved in a car accident on Sunday in Santa Ynez, California. He hit a 46-year-old jogger named Jose Jimenez at 55 miles per hour while driving his Tesla. Emergency responders airlifted Jimenez to the hospital with multiple fractures, abrasions, and lacerations, but his injuries are not life-threatening. The accident comes as Crosby is promoting his new solo album, Croz, which he premiered via Rolling Stone last January. He has been working with Crosby, Stills & Nash for the past two decades but wanted to challenge himself by working outside the group.

The Wind River Earthquake, which struck Wyoming in 2013 with a magnitude of 4.7 Mw, is considered one of the deepest earthquakes ever recorded within a stable continental crust. Scientists have now revealed that the quake occurred not within the Earth's crust but within its mantle at a depth of approximately 75 km. This discovery raises questions about the brittleness of the mantle under the Wind River Craton and challenges current understanding of the forces needed to deform and break the mantle in such areas, leaving the true cause of the quake open to debate. The earthquake was unusual as it occurred in a region known for its tectonic quietude and lack of volcanic activity.

The U.S. government has proposed removing most of the world’s humpback whale populations from the federal endangered species list, stating that they have rebounded after 45 years of protection. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) wants to reclassify humpbacks into 14 distinct populations, with 10 of those being removed from the list. This move aims to focus protection on the whale populations that need it most.

The proposal is based on a 2010 NOAA Fisheries review, which found that humpback whales are not a single global population but instead consist of 14 distinct segments that rarely intermingle. Two of these populations would be listed as endangered (Arabian Sea and Cape Verde Islands), two as threatened (Central America and Western North Pacific), and the remaining ten would no longer be listed under the Endangered Species Act but would remain protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act.

The proposal is open to a 90-day public comment period, during which conservationists are expected to voice their concerns about the potential vulnerability of humpback whales to factors such as increased shipping, climate change, ocean acidification, entanglement in fishing gear, and boat accidents. The public is encouraged to submit comments on the proposed changes to help improve the NOAA's final determination.

The device is well-designed and thoughtfully engineered, with attention to detail that includes a satisfying kickstand hinge and a lightweight magnesium case. The screen offers vibrant colors and the device feels high quality overall.

Microsoft's goal was to create a new kind of gadget that combines the best features of both laptops and tablets, allowing for both convenience and input for work purposes. However, the Surface RT falls short in several areas, particularly with its underpowered Windows RT operating system and the Touch Cover keyboard, which is pressure-activated and spaced in a way that makes typos inevitable.

The Touch Cover also approximates the sturdiness of a laptop and cannot support itself on anything but a flat, rigid surface. The app selection for Windows RT is also limited, with no Twitter or Facebook app, a broken Kindle app, and a lackluster People app.

The owner of Eva Restaurant in Los Angeles, Mark Gold, has implemented a new policy offering a 5% discount to customers who check their phones at the door. This policy was designed to encourage patrons to engage with each other and enjoy their meals without distractions from smartphones. The initiative went viral after being featured on KPCC's AirTalk, leading to numerous media requests and international attention. Despite the increased publicity, Gold reports only a slight increase in business so far. The policy has been well-received by customers, with nearly half taking advantage of the offer without any reported complaints. The goal is to create a more intimate dining experience where patrons can connect and enjoy the food and company without the distraction of smartphones.

Due to safety concerns caused by the ongoing fighting between Israel and Hamas, Air France, Lufthansa, and several other European airlines have canceled flights to Tel Aviv and extended these cancellations through Thursday. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) imposed a 24-hour restriction on flights to Ben Gurion International Airport after a Hamas rocket landed near the airport on Tuesday. The European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) has recommended that airlines refrain from operating flights to and from Tel Aviv, citing potential risks. However, British Airways continues to fly to Israel without cancellations, stating that each airline assesses safety individually. Critics have lashed out against the FAA for extending its ban on U.S. airlines' flights to Tel Aviv, with former New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg calling it a "mistake." The Israeli government has stated that Ben Gurion Airport is safe from any rocket attack by militants in Gaza.

The New York Jets have reached a settlement of $325,000 with their cheerleading squad, known as the Flight Crew, in a class-action lawsuit filed by former cheerleader Krystal C. in 2014. Each member of the 52-person team will receive $2,500 for each season they worked during the covered period, with additional payments for photo shoots.

The suit alleged that the cheerleaders were paid only $150 per game and nothing for practice time, resulting in hourly rates well below minimum wage when accounting for required hair, makeup, and transportation expenses. The Jets denied the claims but agreed to the settlement to avoid litigation.

Similar wage suits have been filed against other NFL teams, including the Cincinnati Bengals, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Oakland Raiders, and Buffalo Bills. The Buccaneers reached a settlement of $825,000, while the Bengals and Raiders have also tentatively agreed to settlements. The Buffalo Jills, the cheerleaders for the Buffalo Bills, were recently granted class-action status in a similar suit.

State Senator Diane Savino (D-SI) applauded the settlement and called on the NFL to develop uniform rules for their teams to ensure fair pay and treatment for all cheerleaders.

Driskill was fired from Premier Health in August and did not inform the board about his termination and leave of absence. A New Zealand father, Samuel Forrest, is bringing his newborn son, Leo, who has Down syndrome, back to New Zealand from Armenia after being abandoned by Leo's mother due to societal stigma towards children with disabilities in Armenia. Despite this, he decided to keep Leo and is planning to move back to New Zealand with him for support from loved ones. Samuel has also been working with disability awareness groups to educate parents about children with special needs and to prevent similar situations in the future.

George Zimmerman, who was acquitted in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin in 2013, auctioned off the Kel-Tec PF-9 pistol he used in the incident on United Gun Group's website. The auction, initially open to the public, was later revealed to be a fake one, while a private auction for pre-qualified bidders was ongoing. The real auction received at least one verified offer of $120,000 and had 22 bidders, with a total of 42 bids made.

Zimmerman announced the successful closure of the auction, stating that funds raised would go to several worthy causes. He thanked United Gun Group for hosting the auction and expressed appreciation for the support received from members of the platform. The winning bidder's identity will be kept confidential at their request.

The Trayvon Martin Foundation declined to comment on the sale of the gun. The first listing for the gun, posted on a different website last week, prompted worldwide headlines and controversy, resulting in the auction being pulled from the site before being listed on UnitedGunGroup.com. Zimmerman touted the handgun as "a piece of American history" and wrote that it had recently been returned to him by the Department of Justice.

In response, a news organization decided to limit op-eds and letters to the editor in opposition to same-sex marriage due to their hostility and offensive nature. However, this move was met with criticism and accusations of censorship and infringement on freedom of speech.
